briefs.title: The Quran was preserved through two independent channels at once
briefs.thesis: The Quran reached us through mass oral memorisation and early written codices at the same time, each checking the other, so a corruption in one would have been caught by the other.
briefs.sum: The Quran was memorised by thousands, written under the Prophet's supervision, gathered within two years of his death and standardised within twenty. Today's text matches the first-century manuscripts. Few ancient scriptures combine a continuous oral recitation tradition with manuscripts radiocarbon-dated to within decades of the founder.

obj.q: "Oral transmission is unreliable."
obj.a: For ordinary stories, yes. But the Quran was a fixed text recited word for word, with set rhythm and rhyme, and corrected publicly in congregational prayer. A memoriser who changes a word is corrected by the people behind him. That is the opposite of a game of whispers. And the written channel ran alongside it from the start.

obj.q: "Uthman burned copies, so he must have destroyed the real Quran."
obj.a: What he destroyed were private copies with dialectal spellings, personal glosses or a different surah order. The text itself was checked against Abu Bakr's codex and against the memorisers still alive, who included the senior reciters. No Companion is reported to have accused Uthman of adding or removing a verse, although Ibn Mas'ud objected to the burning of his own codex and to the choice of Zayd. If a verse had been removed, his enemies would have said so.

obj.q: "There are variant readings (qira'at), so there are different Qurans."
obj.a: See the next argument. The readings were taught by the Prophet himself and are part of the revelation, not later copying errors.

prac.q: “Uthman burned the other Qurans, so we only have his version, not Muhammad's.”
prac.a: Uthman copied from Abu Bakr's codex, compiled within two years of the Prophet's death from written pieces confirmed by memorisers, and the senior reciters were alive to check it. Not one Companion, including his political enemies, accused him of altering a verse; Ali said he would have done the same.

briefs.evs:
The written text was not an afterthought. The Prophet ﷺ had scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mu'awiya write each revelation as it came, and the Companions recited it in their prayers every day. When many reciters were killed at the Battle of Yamama, Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the written fragments into one book. Zayd collected the Quran from written fragments and from memorisers (Bukhari 4986); later scholars such as Ibn Hajar explain that he required two witnesses for each verse.
Under Uthman (c. 650), disputes over regional pronunciations led to an official copy in the Qurayshi dialect. It was made from Abu Bakr's codex (kept with Hafsa) and sent to Kufa, Basra, Damascus and Mecca, and the private copies that differed were burned. The Companions agreed to this, including Ali, who said: "Had I been in his place I would have done the same."
The modern academic picture backs this up. Angelika Neuwirth, writing in the Cambridge Companion to the Qur'an, notes that newly found fragments support an early fixed text and that the "revisionist" theories of a late, evolving Quran have failed. Seyfeddin Kara (The Integrity of the Qur'an) concludes the codex can be dated with certainty to before Umar's death (23/644).

briefs.title: Non-Muslim scholars concede the Quran's integrity
briefs.thesis: Even scholars hostile or indifferent to Islam admit that the Quran we have is the one Muhammad ﷺ taught.
briefs.sum: From Muir to Neuwirth, scholars who have no stake in defending Islam increasingly accept that the Quran text goes back to Muhammad's generation. The manuscript discoveries of the last forty years have only made that consensus stronger.

obj.q: "These are old orientalists; modern scholars are more sceptical."
obj.a: The trend is the opposite. The revisionist school of the 1970s (Wansbrough, Crone and Cook) argued for a late Quran, but the manuscript finds since then (Sana'a, Birmingham, Tübingen) have pushed the text back to the Prophet's generation. Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, accept that most of the Quran goes back to Muhammad's lifetime, while still describing a text that developed within his community.

prac.q: “Modern scholars like Wansbrough and Crone said the Quran was compiled centuries later.”
prac.a: Their theories predate the manuscript evidence. The Birmingham folios are radiocarbon-dated to 568-645 CE, and Sana'a and Paris codices show the same text in the first century. Even critical scholars like Sinai now say the late-Quran thesis has failed.

briefs.evs:
William Muir, a missionary-minded critic of the Prophet: "There is probably in the world no other book which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."
Stanley Lane-Poole: there is no doubt of the Quran's authenticity, and it has come down unchanged.
Kenneth Cragg (Anglican bishop): there is no room for doubt that what we have is essentially what Muhammad taught.
John Burton: the Quran we have is the text "as it was arranged and approved by the Prophet".
Neal Robinson, H.A.R. Gibb, R.V.C. Bodley, C.C. Torrey, Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri make similar statements .
Source William Muir on the purity of the Quranic text

briefs.title: The qira'at are revealed readings, not copying errors
briefs.thesis: The canonical readings of the Quran go back to the Prophet ﷺ himself, differ in only a small fraction of words, and complement each other in meaning.
briefs.sum: The readings are authorised by the Prophet, transmitted by mass chains, limited to about 1% of words, and they enrich the meaning. Calling them "errors" misunderstands what they are.

obj.q: "If the text was perfectly preserved, why are there differences at all?"
obj.a: Because the differences were revealed. Preservation means the text is exactly as it was given, and it was given with these readings. The Bible's variants are the opposite case: they come from scribes changing the text after the fact, as Metzger and Ehrman document (see Corruption of the Bible).

prac.q: “Hafs and Warsh are different Qurans, so the Quran wasn't preserved.”
prac.a: They are two authorised readings. The Prophet approved different recitations (the seven ahruf), and the canonical qira'at are held by scholars to preserve authorised recitations; how exactly the ahruf relate to the qira'at is discussed among scholars. They share the same consonantal text, differing in about 1% of words, mostly vowels, with complementary meanings like 'King' and 'Master' of the Day of Judgement. Preservation means preserved as revealed, and it was revealed with these readings.

briefs.evs:
In Bukhari 2419, Umar heard Hisham ibn Hakim recite Surah al-Furqan differently from how he himself had learned it. He brought Hisham to the Prophet ﷺ, who had both recite and said of each: "It was revealed like this." He added that the Quran was revealed in seven ahruf (modes), "so recite whichever is easy for you".
Ibn Mujahid's survey found that only about 700 of the Quran's roughly 77,000 words differ between the readings, and almost all of those differences are in vowels or verb forms. They usually add meaning rather than contradict it:
Maliki/Maaliki yawm al-din (1:4): "King of" and "Master of" the Day of Judgement. Both are true of Allah.
Nunshiruha/nunshizuha (2:259): "We raise them" and "We assemble them". Both describe the bones of the man raised to life.
Ibn Taymiyya compares each reading to a separate verse (Majmu' al-Fatawa 13/391).

briefs.title: The "missing verses" reports answered
briefs.thesis: The reports critics cite (the goat, Ubayy's two extra surahs, Ibn Mas'ud's codex, the "valley of gold" and the "200 verses of al-Ahzab") are either weak, or describe abrogation that the Quran itself announces (2:106), or concern supplications rather than surahs.
briefs.sum: Each "missing verse" report is either weakly transmitted, describes abrogation the Quran itself announces, or concerns a supplication. None shows that anything meant to remain in the Quran was lost.

obj.q: "Abrogation is just a way of explaining away lost verses."
obj.a: Abrogation is announced in the Quran itself: "Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better or similar" (2:106; also 87:6-7). A verse withdrawn by the Prophet ﷺ in his lifetime was not lost; it was removed by the same authority that revealed it. Loss would mean that something meant to stay disappeared, and no authentic report says that.

prac.q: “Aisha said a goat ate the verses of stoning, so parts of the Quran are lost.”
prac.a: The goat detail comes only through Ibn Ishaq, whose solitary additions are weak. The verse's recitation was abrogated in the Prophet's lifetime, as 2:106 allows. And the Companions had memorised the Quran; Ibn Hazm said a sheep eating a page changes nothing.

briefs.evs:
The goat that ate the page (Ibn Majah 1944). The "goat" detail comes only through Muhammad ibn Ishaq, a mudallis whose solitary additions are weak (graded weak by al-Arna'ut). The verses mentioned, stoning and the suckling verse, had their recitation abrogated during the Prophet's lifetime while some rulings remained. That is why Imam Malik said the suckling text "is not acted upon".
Ibn Hazm: the Companions memorised the Quran, so "a sheep eating a paper changes nothing".
Al-Baqillani: it is absurd to think the Companions relied on one sheet under a bed.
Ubayy's "two extra surahs" (al-Khal' and al-Hafd). These are the qunut supplication, which Ubayy wrote in his personal codex as a du'a (al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra 3142). The reports about them have chain gaps of two or three generations. Ubayy himself dictated to Zayd during Uthman's compilation (Kanz al-'Ummal 4789), so he agreed with the final text.
Ibn Mas'ud's codex "of 111 surahs". No physical codex of his exists. Ibn al-Nadim saw several so-called Ibn Mas'ud codices and none of them agreed with each other. Ibn Mas'ud is reported not to have written the two Mu'awwidhatayn in his personal codex (Musnad Ahmad; see Bukhari 4977), and scholars explain this as his view that they were protective prayers or that they needed no writing. briefs.title: Hadith were written down in the first century, not invented in the third
briefs.thesis: Written hadith collections existed in the Companions' and Successors' generation, and their contents match the later canonical books almost word for word.
briefs.sum: First-century written collections exist and match the canonical books; the scholar who studied the earliest material most closely abandoned the forgery thesis; and the early critics graded narrators with measurable consistency. The hadith are a preserved source.

obj.q: "Goldziher and Schacht proved hadith were forged to support later legal positions."
obj.a:
Their method assumed a hadith was fake unless proven otherwise and looked at late legal texts. Harald Motzki studied the earlier Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq (d. 211 AH) systematically. He concluded that its reports from figures like 'Ata' and Ibn Abbas were genuinely transmitted. He wrote that rejecting hadith as a source for the first century, a view "to which I myself adhered", deprives history of an important source.
Tap to enlargeHarald Motzki, JNES 1991: the Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq as a source of authentic hadith from the 1st century AH
Source Motzki: the prophetic hadith in the Musannaf are not later fabrications
Source Motzki's conclusion after studying the Musannaf

obj.q: "The isnad system is arbitrary; critics just graded narrators as they liked."
obj.a:
Scott C. Lucas compared the grades given by three early critics (Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Ma'in and Ibn Hanbal), who worked independently. They agree on 80-87% of the narrators they all graded. Arbitrary grading would not produce that level of agreement; a consistent method does.
Source Scott C. Lucas: the 78 men graded by all three critics
Source Lucas on the agreement between Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Hanbal

prac.q: “Hadith were collected 200-250 years after Muhammad, so they're unreliable hearsay.”
prac.a: Bukhari compiled from earlier written collections. The Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih, written by a student of Abu Hurayra, survives and matches Musnad Ahmad almost word for word, and Motzki dated material in 'Abd al-Razzaq's Musannaf to the first century.

briefs.evs:
The Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih. Hammam was a student of Abu Hurayra (d. 58 AH) and wrote down 138 hadith from him in the mid-first century. The full text survives in manuscript (the Damascus MS) and is quoted whole in Musnad Ahmad. Ninety-eight of its hadith are in Bukhari or Muslim. R. Marston Speight compared the versions (Der Islam 77, 2000). He found "almost complete identity" and "practically no sign of careless or deceptive practices".
Tap to enlargeFolios of the Damascus manuscript of the Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih
Source Arabic Literature to the End of the Umayyad Period on the Sahifa of Hammam
Source Study conclusion: the Sahifa's material is uniformly prophetic hadith, preserved with its chains
Writing was permitted early. "Do not write from me anything except the Quran" (Muslim 3004) was an early precaution so that the two would not be mixed. The Prophet ﷺ later permitted writing:
"Write for Abu Shah" (Bukhari 2434).
He told 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr to write, "for only truth comes out of it" (Abu Dawud 3646).
Ali kept a written sahifa (Muslim 1370).
Letters were sent out with written rulings, such as 'Amr ibn Hazm's letter and Abu Bakr's book of zakat.

briefs.title: The argument from historical precision
briefs.thesis: An unlettered man in 7th-century Arabia stated facts about ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia that were unknown in his time, absent from the Bible and Jewish lore, and only confirmed by modern archaeology. The best explanation is a source beyond him.
briefs.sum: The Quran repeatedly corrects the Bible on ancient Near Eastern details that nobody could check until the 19th century. An unlettered man copying from the Bible would reproduce its errors, not fix them.

obj.q: "He could have heard these from Jews or Christians in Arabia."
obj.a: The test is simple: the details are not in the Jewish or Christian sources. On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus), the Bible differs from the Quran. You cannot copy a correction from the text you are correcting.

obj.q: "These are lucky guesses."
obj.a: One lucky guess is possible. A pattern across many independent details, each matching evidence found only centuries later, is not. And in each case the Quran departs from the obvious source, which is exactly where a guesser would follow it.

prac.q: “Muhammad just picked up Bible stories from travelling Christians and Jews.”
prac.a: Then he'd reproduce the Bible's details, including its errors. Instead the Quran uses 'king' for Joseph's ruler, describes baked brick in Moses' Egypt, and names the Mesopotamian astral triad: details absent from the Bible and confirmed only by modern archaeology.

briefs.evs: Egyptian sources became readable only recently. The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 and Champollion deciphered it in 1822. Before 1822, nobody could correctly read Egyptian royal titles or funerary texts, although medieval Arabic authors such as Ibn Wahshiyya attempted to decipher hieroglyphs. Cuneiform was cracked by Rawlinson and others in the 1850s. Several details below have been argued to fit evidence uncovered after those decipherments.

briefs.title: "King" in Joseph's time, "Pharaoh" in Moses' time
briefs.thesis: The Quran calls Joseph's ruler al-malik (the king) and Moses' ruler Fir'awn (Pharaoh). This fits the Egyptian use of "pharaoh" as a royal title from the New Kingdom, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler. Many Egyptologists call the biblical usage retrospective.
briefs.sum: The Bible calls every Egyptian ruler "Pharaoh"; Egyptology shows the title began in the New Kingdom. The Quran uses "king" for Joseph's era and "Pharaoh" for Moses', consistently.

obj.q: "'King' and 'Pharaoh' are synonyms, so this proves nothing."
obj.a: If they were interchangeable, we would expect the Quran to mix them, as it uses other synonyms freely. Instead it never calls Joseph's ruler Pharaoh, in a surah of over 100 verses, and it calls Moses' ruler Pharaoh 74 times. That consistency tracks the historical change exactly.

obj.q: "Maybe the Bible uses 'Pharaoh' as a modern-style label, like calling all Roman rulers 'Caesar'."
obj.a: That is precisely the anachronism. The Quran avoids it.

prac.q: “'Pharaoh' was used loosely for any Egyptian king, so the Bible isn't wrong.”
prac.a: As a title, 'Pharaoh' (per-aa, 'great house') was applied to the king only from the New Kingdom, about 1550 BCE. Joseph lived earlier. The Quran consistently uses 'king' for Joseph's ruler and 'Pharaoh' for Moses' ruler, which is exactly right.

briefs.evs:

Source British Museum Dictionary of Ancient Egypt (Shaw & Nicholson): before the New Kingdom the use of "pharaoh" is strictly anachronistic
Alan Gardiner (Egyptian Grammar, p.75) and W.V. Davies (Egyptian Hieroglyphs, p.45) give the same dating. Maurice Bucaille notes that nobody at the time of revelation could have known this distinction.

briefs.title: Pharaoh's tower of baked brick
briefs.thesis: Pharaoh orders Haman to "kindle fire upon clay" to build a tower (28:38). Baked brick was rare in Egypt, though it is attested in Middle Kingdom Nubian forts and in New Kingdom Thebes, and Petrie found Ramesside examples at Nebesheh. Many place Moses in the Ramesside era, but this is debated.
briefs.sum: "Kindle fire upon clay" describes fired brick, which Petrie found appearing in the Ramesside Delta, the time of Moses.

obj.q: "The Bible's Tower of Babel had baked bricks, so the Quran just moved the story to Egypt."
obj.a: The Babel story is set in Mesopotamia, where fired brick was normal. The Quran puts it in Egypt, where it was rare, and in an era where Egyptology finds it. A copyist relocating a Babel story would not know to choose that era.

prac.q: “Haman was Persian, from the book of Esther; the Quran mixed up the stories.”
prac.a: Haman in the Quran is Pharaoh's official in charge of building, a role, not Esther's Persian vizier. Names recur across cultures, and the detail of firing clay for a tower fits the Ramesside Delta, where Petrie found baked brick.

briefs.evs:
Tap to enlargePetrie, Tanis II (1888): "The earliest tomb opened was one built of red baked bricks", in the Ramesside Delta
Source The Quran's description: baked clay (kiln-fired brick) and a high structure "to reach the ways of the heavens"

briefs.title: Abraham and the astral triad
briefs.thesis: The Quran has Abraham reject a star, then the moon, then the sun (6:75-79). This is precisely the top triad of Mesopotamian religion: Venus (Ishtar), Moon (Sin) and Sun (Shamash).
briefs.sum: The Bible says "other gods"; Jewish legends get the list wrong. The Quran names the star, the moon and the sun, which is exactly the Mesopotamian astral triad found on kudurru stones.

prac.q: “The star-moon-sun story is just a rabbinic legend Muhammad heard.”
prac.a: The rabbinic versions list different objects and orders. The Quran names exactly the Mesopotamian top triad, Venus, the moon and the sun (Ishtar, Sin, Shamash), as shown on kudurru boundary stones, which no one in Arabia could read.

briefs.evs:
Tap to enlargeSara Pizzimenti, The Astral Family in Kassite Kudurrus Reliefs, pp.151-2: Sin, Shamash and Ishtar as the astral triad
Source Some scholars regard dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC as sustainable, though many scholars doubt he is a historical figure.
Ibn Kathir already explained the kawkab as Venus, centuries before anyone could read a kudurru inscription.

briefs.title: More Egyptian details the Bible lacks
briefs.thesis: Several smaller details in the Quran's Moses story fit Egyptian evidence better than the biblical account does.
briefs.sum: Weeping heaven and earth, a god-king with gods, rivers he owns rather than made, a small band of Israelites, a foreign "shemer": each detail fits Egypt and departs from the Bible.

obj.q: "The Quran borrowed Haman from Esther and got the era wrong."
obj.a: This assumes there can be only one person with a name or title. The Quran never links its Haman to Persia, to Esther or to Mordecai. And the Egyptian evidence gives a real setting for an official with that title.

prac.q: “These details are too small to prove anything.”
prac.a: Each is small, but each goes against the Bible and matches Egyptian evidence. A copier doesn't keep correcting his source in the direction of archaeology he can't access.

briefs.evs:
"Neither heaven nor earth wept for them" (44:29). Egyptian funerary texts promise the dead king that "the sky weeps for thee, the earth trembles" (Pyramid Text Utterance 553) and "heaven and earth weep for thee" (Songs of Isis and Nephthys). The Quran inverts the formula for the drowned Pharaoh, a motif only readable after 1822.
A deified Pharaoh who has gods (79:24 with 7:127). Critics call it a contradiction that Pharaoh says "I am your lord most high" while his chiefs speak of "your gods". New Kingdom kings like Ramesses II were worshipped as divine while themselves worshipping Amun, Ra and Ptah. The Quran describes exactly that.
The rivers beneath Pharaoh (43:51). In the Quran, Pharaoh boasts of owning the Nile's channels, which is realistic royal propaganda. In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it", a creator claim.
A small band (26:54). Pharaoh calls the Israelites "a small band". The Bible has 600,000 men leaving Egypt, a number archaeology has found no trace of. The Quran gives no number, and its "small band" is the more plausible picture.

briefs.title: Muhammad ﷺ is attested by outsiders within years of his death
briefs.thesis: Non-Muslim sources from the 630s-660s describe a prophet among the Arabs who preached the God of Abraham, forbade wine and fornication, and whose followers conquered Persia and Syria. That is the Muhammad of Islamic history, not a later invention.
briefs.sum: Within thirty years of his death, Byzantine, Syriac and Armenian Christians were describing Muhammad ﷺ as a prophet of the God of Abraham who forbade wine and fornication. Coins and inscriptions confirm it, and Islamic history is corroborated by its rivals.

obj.q: "The Islamic sources are too late; Muhammad might be a myth."
obj.a: The revisionists of the 1970s argued this, but they did not survive the evidence. Robert Hoyland (Seeing Islam as Others Saw It) collects dozens of non-Muslim witnesses within 150 years in six languages. Sinai's verdict above is now widely held.

prac.q: “Muhammad might be a later invention; the Islamic sources are late.”
prac.a: The Doctrina Jacobi (634) mentions a prophet among the Saracens; Sebeos (c. 660) describes him preaching the God of Abraham and forbidding wine and fornication; Isho'yahb III describes the Arabs. Sinai concludes a late-7th-century invention is improbable.

briefs.evs:
Doctrina Jacobi (634): "a prophet has appeared among the Saracens".
Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640): mentions "the Arabs of Muhammad" (Mhmt, which some read as a title).
The Khuzistan Chronicle (c. 660): the Arabs led by MHMD conquered Persia.
Sebeos, Armenian bishop (c. 660s): Muhammad was a merchant who preached the God of Abraham, knew the Law of Moses, and forbade carrion, wine, lying and fornication.
Source The Armenian History attributed to Sebeos (Liverpool, Translated Texts for Historians)

briefs.title: The Quran's stories are not copied from late legends
briefs.thesis: Critics say the stories of Dhul-Qarnayn, the Sleepers of the Cave and Abraham smashing the idols were borrowed from Syriac or rabbinic legends. In each case the supposed source is later than the surah or differs on the points that matter, and where an older tradition exists, the Quran confirms its true core while correcting it.
briefs.sum: The Alexander Legend postdates Surah al-Kahf and its distinctive details are absent from the Quran; the Sleepers story is told with an awareness of its variants (18:22); and some "sources" like Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer are post-Islamic.

obj.q: "The Alexander Legend could have circulated orally earlier."
obj.a: Possibly some motifs did, but then the Quran would be drawing on the same older tradition, not on the legend we have, and it still omits every fabulous element (the prophethood claim, the cave-dwellers, the named kings).

prac.q: “Surah al-Kahf copies the Syriac Alexander Legend.”
prac.a: The legend is dated after 628; al-Kahf is Meccan, before 622. The Quran never calls him Alexander, never calls him a prophet (the Prophet ﷺ said he didn't know if he was one), and leaves out every fantastic detail of the legend.

briefs.evs:
Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander Legend. The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated by most scholars to around 629-636, celebrating Heraclius' victory, while Surah al-Kahf belongs to the Meccan period. The legend makes Alexander a prophet who calls himself horned by God, has people hiding in caves from the scorching sun, names the kings of Gog and Magog, and describes a gate with iron nails. None of this is in the Quran. The Quran never names him Alexander, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "I do not know whether Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet or not" (al-Hakim; Sahih al-Jami'). 'Ali explained the name "the two-horned" as referring to blows he received on both sides of his head, not literal horns (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba). Pre-Islamic Arab poets already knew a Dhul-Qarnayn (Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari). The Bible itself praises pagan rulers as God's instruments: Cyrus is "My anointed" and "My shepherd" (Isa 44:28-45:1), and Nebuchadnezzar "My servant" (Jer 27:6).
The Sleepers of the Cave. The story of youths who fled persecution and slept for generations was told by Christians about Ephesus under Decius (c. 250), with Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) writing a homily on it. The Quran tells it with a point the Christian versions lack: people disputed their number, "three, the fourth their dog… five… seven", and "say: my Lord knows best their number" (18:22). The Quran knows the story circulates in variant forms

briefs.title: Answers to "anachronism" charges
briefs.thesis: Several details critics call anachronisms (crucifixion in Pharaoh's Egypt, a "dirham" in Joseph's story, monasticism as an innovation, Pharaoh's body preserved) are either accurate or misread.
briefs.sum: Salb covers suspension on a stake, as in Genesis 40:19; the dirham is a weight of silver; monasticism began with Antony, not Jesus; and the Quran alone says Pharaoh's body would be kept as a sign.

obj.q: "Crucifixion was invented by the Persians centuries later."
obj.a: The Roman form was, but the Quran's word is general, and the Bible's own Joseph story has an Egyptian king hanging a man on a tree.

prac.q: “The Quran has Pharaoh crucify people, but crucifixion didn't exist in Egypt.”
prac.a: Salb means fastening or suspending on a stake or tree, and Genesis 40:19 has Pharaoh hang his baker "on a tree". Impalement is attested in New Kingdom Egypt.

briefs.evs:
Crucifixion in Egypt (7:124; 20:71). The Arabic salb covers fastening or suspending a body on a stake or tree, not only the Roman cross. Genesis 40:19 has Pharaoh's baker told that Pharaoh "will hang you on a tree". Scholars of ancient execution (Samuelsson; Chapman) warn against separating crucifixion, impalement and suspension rigidly, and impalement of enemies and criminals is attested in New Kingdom Egypt.
"A few dirhams" (12:20). "Dirham" in 12:20 can be read as a weight of silver (Lisan al-Arab), and silver by weight (the deben) was used in Egyptian payments; critics note that the word dirham comes from Greek drachma. It is not a minted coin.
Monasticism "they invented" (57:27). Peter and other apostles were married (1 Cor 9:5; Mark 1:30), and the NT has no command to withdraw into celibate desert life; monasticism began with Antony of Egypt in the late 3rd century. Metzger and Ehrman note that monk-scribes even inserted "and fasting" into several verses (Mark 9:29; 1 Cor 7:5).
"We will preserve your body as a sign" (10:92). The Quran adds a detail the Bible lacks: Pharaoh's body would be kept as a sign. Royal mummies of the New Kingdom survive today. (The Pharaoh of the Exodus is not identified with certainty, so present this as consistent with the evidence rather than as proof.)

briefs.title: The splitting of the moon
briefs.thesis: The splitting of the moon (54:1-2) is reported by many Companions through independent chains, and the Quraysh's response ("continuous magic") shows they saw something they could not deny. Its absence from other records is expected for a brief night-time event.
briefs.sum: Many Companions reported the moon splitting, scholars class it as mass-transmitted, and the Quraysh called it magic (54:2) rather than deny it. Its absence elsewhere is expected for a brief night event.
briefs.caution: Use this defensively. Its strength is the mass transmission and the Quraysh's reaction, not later legends like the Kerala king.

prac.q: “If the moon split, astronomers everywhere would have recorded it.”
prac.a: It was night in Arabia and day in much of the world, brief and unannounced; ancient observation was patchy. The Quraysh, who saw it, called it magic rather than deny it, and many Companions reported it independently.

briefs.evs:
The Quran. "The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split. And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: continuous magic" (54:1-2). The surah was recited publicly in Mecca to the people who would have denied it if nothing had happened.
The reports. Bukhari and Muslim record it from several Companions; Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir (some scholars read 54:1 as eschatological). Travellers arriving in Mecca were asked and confirmed seeing it (al-Tayalisi).
Why not worldwide records? It was night in Arabia and day across much of the world, brief, unannounced, and most people were asleep; record-keeping of the sky was patchy (al-Khattabi, al-Qurtubi). A Kerala tradition that the Chera king Cheraman Perumal saw it and converted exists in Malabar sources, but it is late and should be treated with care.

briefs.title: Mecca's antiquity and the People of the Ditch
briefs.thesis: Critics say Mecca is unattested before Islam and that the Quran praises Trinitarian martyrs (the People of the Ditch, 85:4-8). Ancient sources point to a revered Arabian sanctuary, and the Najran martyrs' theology is disputed in the Christian sources themselves.
briefs.sum: Diodorus' revered Arabian temple, Ptolemy's Macoraba and Nabonidus' Hijazi towns fit an ancient Mecca. The Najran martyrs' creed is disputed in Christian sources, and the Quran praises only their faith in Allah (85:8).
briefs.caution: The pre-Islamic evidence for Mecca is suggestive rather than conclusive; Arabia is the least excavated region of the Near East. Present it as consistent evidence, not proof.

prac.q: “The Quran praises the Najran martyrs, who were Trinitarian Christians, so it endorses the Trinity.”
prac.a: The Christian sources themselves contradict each other on their creed; an Arian mission reached Himyar in the 4th century; and the Quran praises them only for believing in Allah (85:8). Ibn Abbas called them monotheists.

briefs.evs:
Mecca.
Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 3.44) describes a very holy temple among the Banizomenes of western Arabia; Gibbon read it as the Kaaba, though others dispute the location.
Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which some scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca; others (such as Patricia Crone) doubt it.
The Harran inscriptions of the Babylonian king Nabonidus (6th century BCE) name Yathrib (Medina) and Khaybar among Hijazi towns.
Anastasius of Sinai (7th century) mentions the Kaaba, and the Quran calls Mecca "Bakka" (3:96), echoing the "valley of Baca" of Psalm 84:6.
The theory that the first qibla was Petra (Dan Gibson) has been rejected by specialists, who note that the mosque orientations he relies on are imprecise.
The People of the Ditch (85:4-8). The surah praises believers burned in a trench for their faith, usually identified with the Christians of Najran killed by the Jewish king Yusuf (Dhu Nuwas) around 523. Christians argue they were Trinitarians, so the Quran praises Trinitarians. But the Christian sources disagree: the Syriac Book of the Himyarites (a damaged 12th-century manuscript) makes them Miaphysites; Chalcedonian writers claim them as Chalcedonian. Philostorgius records that the Arian missionary Theophilus the Indian converted Himyar around 354, and in the Greek Martyrdom of Arethas the persecutors ask them onl

briefs.title: What makes a prophecy count
briefs.thesis: A prophecy is evidence only if it is specific, risky, recorded before the event, and unlikely to come true by chance. Some of the prophecies below meet these four tests; others are weaker and should be used with care.
briefs.sum: Judge prophecies by specificity, risk, prior recording and improbability. The cases below pass all four tests.

prac.q: “Prophecies are vague enough to fit anything.”
prac.a: That's why the test is specificity, risk, prior recording and improbability. 'Rome will defeat Persia within three to nine years', said when Rome was collapsing, is specific, risky and recorded before the event.

briefs.evs:
At the Battle of the Trench (5 AH), Medina was under siege by a coalition of about 10,000. The Muslims were starving and the hypocrites were mocking them. The Prophet ﷺ struck a boulder and announced, in this order:
The keys of Syria (its red palaces).
The keys of Persia (the white palace of al-Mada'in).
The keys of Yemen.
Within a generation all three came under Muslim rule: Yemen in the Prophet's lifetime, then Syria (636) and Persia (637) (Musnad Ahmad). That is a prophecy made at the worst possible moment, against every expectation.

briefs.title: The Romans will be victorious (30:2-5)
briefs.thesis: The Quran predicted, at the low point of the Byzantine Empire, that Rome would defeat Persia within a few years. It did, against all expectation.
briefs.sum: In about 615, with Byzantium losing everything, the Quran said Rome would win within 3-9 years; Heraclius won at Issus in 622, inside that window, then through 625 and at Nineveh in 627. Some sceptical academics read the verses as a prediction of a Roman victory but argue they were edited after the event, and a variant reading of the verbs exists.

obj.q: "Bid' is vague."
obj.a: It is a defined term, meaning 3 to 9 in Arabic, and the Prophet himself told Abu Bakr to extend his wager to fit it. The Byzantine victory at Issus in 622 and the victories through 625 fall inside it. Nineveh (627) came later.

obj.q: "It's a lucky guess about two empires that were always at war."
obj.a: The Quran did not say "one of them will win someday". It said the side that had just been crushed would win, within a few years. Gibbon's assessment above shows how unlikely that looked at the time.

prac.q: “Anyone could guess that one empire would eventually beat the other.”
prac.a: Not 'eventually': within bid' sinin, three to nine years, at the moment Persia held Jerusalem, Egypt and was at Constantinople's gates. Gibbon wrote that no prophecy could have seemed more distant from its fulfilment. Heraclius won at Issus in 622, eight years after the fall of Jerusalem, and the war turned from there. Nineveh followed in 627.

briefs.evs:
Edward Gibbon wrote (Decline and Fall ch. 46) that "at the time when this prediction is said to have been delivered, no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment, since the first twelve years of Heraclius announced the approaching dissolution of the empire."
Tap to enlargeTommaso Tesei, "The Romans Will Win!" Q 30:2-7 (Der Islam 2018)
Tesei, a non-Muslim academic, accepts that the verse predicts a Roman victory. His way out is to argue it was edited after the event. That shows how precise the prediction is: the only escape is to deny it was made in time. But the surah is Meccan, the event was famous, and Quraysh would have mocked a failed prophecy. The early sources record a wager on it between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf (Tirmidhi 3194).

briefs.title: The fire of the Hijaz (1256 CE)
briefs.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ foretold that a fire would emerge from the land of the Hijaz that would light up the necks of camels in Busra, in Syria (Bukhari 7118, Muslim 2902). It happened in 654 AH / 1256 CE, recorded by eyewitnesses and confirmed by modern volcanology.
briefs.sum: Bukhari recorded it in the 9th century; the Harrat Rahat volcano erupted near Medina in 1256, and its glow was seen in Busra, as eyewitnesses wrote and geologists confirm.

obj.q: "Bukhari could have been edited after 1256."
obj.a: Bukhari's Sahih was transmitted in many manuscripts and through countless teachers' chains across the Muslim world centuries before 1256. Medieval scholars themselves pointed to this hadith as fulfilled in their own time, which shows it was already well known.

prac.q: “Volcanoes are common in Arabia; this was a lucky guess.”
prac.a: The hadith specified a fire from the Hijaz whose light would reach Busra in Syria, and it was recorded in Bukhari four centuries before the 1256 eruption near Medina, whose glow eyewitnesses reported seeing in Busra.

briefs.evs:
Contemporary scholars recorded it.
Abu Shama al-Maqdisi in Damascus received letters from Medina's judge describing earthquakes and a fire "like a city". People in Tayma wrote letters by its light.
Al-Qurtubi in Egypt and al-Nawawi in Syria recorded it. Al-Nawawi called the reports mutawatir (mass-transmitted).
Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Dhahabi, who wrote after the event, repeated that its light reached Busra.
Source Imam al-Nawawi: "A fire broke out during our time in al-Madinah…"
Source Ibn Taymiyya: the fire broke out in 655 AH and its light was seen in Busra
Modern geology confirms it. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and the USGS record the 1256 Harrat Rahat eruption. A study by El-Masry et al. ("Historical accounts of the AD 1256 eruption near Al-Madinah") reconstructs it from the Arabic eyewitness accounts.
Source Modern geological literature confirms the 1256 Harrat Rahat eruption
Source Abu Shama al-Maqdisi, al-Dhayl 'ala al-Rawdatayn: an eyewitness-era chronicle of the eruption

briefs.title: The Mongols and the fall of Baghdad
briefs.thesis: Authentic hadith describe a people with broad faces, small eyes and flat noses, wearing hair shoes, who would fight the Muslims and descend on a great city by the Tigris. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, a city that did not exist in the Prophet's lifetime.
briefs.sum: Small-eyed, flat-nosed invaders in hair shoes descending on a great city by the Tigris: Baghdad, which was built after the hadith's narrator died, fell to the Mongols in 1258.

obj.q: "'Turks' were known to the Arabs, so describing them is no miracle."
obj.a: The point is the whole package: their appearance, their attack on a great city by the Tigris with a bridge, and the three-way split of its people. That city was built after the narrator's death.

prac.q: “Turks or Mongols attacking Muslims is not a precise prophecy.”
prac.a: The hadith gives physical description, hair shoes, and a great city by the Tigris, and Baghdad didn't exist when it was recorded by Companions. Its sack by the Mongols in 1258 matched every element.

briefs.evs:
Ibn Taymiyya, who lived through the Mongol invasions, said that anyone who had seen Genghis Khan's and Hülegü's armies could not have described them more accurately than the Prophet ﷺ did over 600 years earlier (al-Jawab al-Sahih 2/171).
Source Ibn Taymiyya: anyone who saw these Turks could not describe them better
The common narrator of Abu Dawud's report, Sa'id ibn Jumhan, died in 136 AH, before Baghdad was built in 145 AH. The report therefore predates the city it describes.

briefs.title: Barefoot shepherds competing in tall buildings
briefs.thesis: Among the signs of the Hour, the Prophet ﷺ said "you will see barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in constructing tall buildings" (Bukhari 50, Muslim 8). Bedouin Arabia, transformed by oil wealth, is now home to the world's tallest buildings.
briefs.sum: 7th-century Bedouins were the poorest of the poor; today their descendants race to build the world's tallest towers, and Mecca's towers rise above its mountains.

prac.q: “Tall buildings exist everywhere; this is not specific.”
prac.a: The prophecy is about who builds them: barefoot, destitute Bedouin shepherds competing in height. That describes the Gulf's transformation from herders to the builders of the world's tallest towers within two generations.

briefs.evs: Al-Nawawi (d. 1277) said the prophecy was not yet fulfilled in his time: desert people would become rich and boast through buildings. That shows the hadith was understood literally long before oil.

briefs.title: Arabia will return to meadows and rivers
briefs.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ said the Hour will not come until "the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers" (Muslim 157). The word translated "returns" can imply that Arabia was once green, and palaeoclimatology has found that it was.
briefs.sum: "Return to meadows and rivers": the hadith assumes a green Arabia in the past, which palaeoclimatology has now found.

prac.q: “Saying a desert will become green is just wishful thinking.”
prac.a: The key word is 'return' (ta'ud): it presupposes Arabia was once green, which no one in the 7th century knew. Palaeoclimate research has found ancient lakes and rivers across the Arabian Peninsula.

briefs.evs:
Source Studies of ancient Arabian rivers and lakes: the deserts were once green
Source McClure's 1984 doctoral thesis: lakes in the Rub' al-Khali during humid periods

briefs.title: Idolatry returns to Dhul-Khalasa
briefs.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ said the Hour would not come until the women of the tribe of Daws sway around the idol Dhul-Khalasa (Bukhari 7116), even after Islam had destroyed it. This happened by the 19th century and the idol was demolished in the 1920s.
briefs.sum: A specific tribe returning to a specific destroyed idol in Muslim Arabia: foretold in Bukhari, recorded by Najdi historians.

prac.q: “A return to paganism is a vague prediction.”
prac.a: It names a specific tribe, Daws, and a specific destroyed idol, Dhul-Khalasa, in a land that had been Muslim for over a thousand years.

briefs.evs: Tap to enlarge'Unwan al-Majd fi Tarikh Najd by Ibn Bishr records the revival at Dhul-Khalasa

briefs.title: "The Hour will come before this boy grows old" is not a failed prophecy
briefs.thesis: Critics cite Muslim 2952 and Bukhari 6511 as a failed prophecy of the end of the world. The Prophet ﷺ was speaking about the "hour" of the people present, meaning their death.
briefs.sum: He refused to date the Final Hour all his life. In this hadith he told the questioners that their own "hour", their death, would come within that boy's lifetime.

prac.q: “Muhammad predicted the end of the world in his lifetime, like Jesus did.”
prac.a: He refused all his life to date the Final Hour (7:187), and Aisha explained that he meant the 'hour' of those present, their death. Unlike Matthew 24:34, it was fulfilled: that generation passed away within the boy's lifetime.

briefs.evs: Source Scholarly commentary: by "the Hour" he may intend the passing of that generation

briefs.title: The Trench: keys to Syria, Persia and Yemen
briefs.thesis: During the siege of Medina, when the Muslims were outnumbered and starving, the Prophet ﷺ struck a rock in the trench and announced that he had been given the keys of Syria, Persia and Yemen. Syria and Persia were conquered within about fifteen years, and Yemen accepted Islam in the Prophet's lifetime.
briefs.sum: Under siege at the Trench, the Prophet ﷺ named the keys of Syria, Persia (Mada'in's white palace) and Yemen. The hypocrites mocked it (33:12); all three were taken within about fifteen years.

prac.q: “Every leader promises his troops victory.”
prac.a: This named three specific capitals of two superpowers and Yemen, during a siege with the Muslims outnumbered three to one and the hypocrites mocking it as delusion (33:12). All three fell within about fifteen years.

briefs.evs:
The report. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib narrates that while digging the trench, the Companions met a rock. The Prophet ﷺ struck it three times, saying with the first "I have been given the keys of Syria; I see its red palaces", with the second "the keys of Persia; I see the white palace of Mada'in", and with the third "the keys of Yemen; I see the gates of San'a" (Musnad Ahmad; al-Nasa'i; gradings differ).
The circumstances. The Quran records the hypocrites' mockery at the time: "Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion" (33:12).
The fulfilment. Yemen came under Islam within the Prophet's lifetime; Syria fell after Yarmuk (636); Mada'in, the Persian capital, fell in 637, and Muslims prayed in its white palace.

briefs.title: The spread of Islam from east to west
briefs.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ said the earth was gathered for him so that he saw its east and west, and that his community's rule would reach what he saw. Within a century it stretched from Spain to Central Asia, a speed historians explain by the exhaustion of Byzantium and Persia and Arab mobility, but which still impresses them.
briefs.sum: The Prophet ﷺ foresaw his community's rule reaching east and west (Muslim 2889; 24:55); within a century it ran from Spain to the borders of China, a speed historians call hard to explain.

prac.q: “Empires rise and fall; Islam's expansion was just military success.”
prac.a: The prediction is the point: a leader of a besieged Arabian town said his community's rule would reach east and west, and within a century it ran from Spain to Central Asia, defeating both superpowers of the age at once.

briefs.evs:
The hadith. "Allah gathered the earth for me, so I saw its east and its west, and the dominion of my community will reach what was gathered for me of it" (Muslim 2889).
The Quran. "Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that He will make them successors in the land" (24:55).
The history. By 711 Muslims were in Spain and Sindh; by 751 they fought the Tang at Talas. The Cambridge History of Christianity says the speed of the Byzantine collapse "remains to be explained"; Barnaby Rogerson compared the Arabs taking on Byzantium and Persia at once to a tiny nation defeating two superpowers simultaneously.

briefs.title: The promise to Ishmael: a "great nation" that only Islam fulfilled
briefs.thesis: God promised Abraham that Ishmael would become a "great nation" (Gen 17:20; 21:13, 18). In the Bible's own terms a "great nation" is one with a covenant law and God near to it. The Ishmaelites became that only through Islam.
briefs.sum: Ishmael was promised a "great nation", which Deuteronomy defines as a people with God's law and God near. The Ishmaelites had neither until Muhammad ﷺ. Even Arab Christian apologists concede the fulfilment.

obj.q: "The covenant is with Isaac, not Ishmael (Gen 17:21)."
obj.a: Isaac's covenant does not cancel Ishmael's blessing. Both are promised separately, and Ishmael's is stated three times. The "everlasting" covenant with Isaac uses 'olam, which in Hebrew can mean a long age, not eternity. The same word describes Eli's "perpetual" priesthood, which God revoked (1 Sam 2:30), and Joseph Albo (Sefer ha-Ikkarim 3:16) concedes the point. Jesus himself said "the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation bearing its fruit" (Mt 21:43).

obj.q: "Ishmael is called a 'wild donkey of a man' (Gen 16:12), so he is cursed."
obj.a:
Pere describes a free desert dweller, not a criminal. The verse goes on to say he will "dwell over against all his brethren" (translations differ). The Samaritan Torah even reads "he will be fertile of man".
Tap to enlargeSamaritan Torah Gen 16:12: "He will be fertile of man; his hand will be with everyone"

prac.q: “Ishmael's 'great nation' just means many descendants, which the Arabs were.”
prac.a: Genesis promises Ishmael the same 'great nation' as Abraham, and Deuteronomy 4:6-8 defines a great nation as one with God near and a righteous law. The Ishmaelites had neither until Muhammad ﷺ.

briefs.evs:
Jewish commentators read "great" in a moral sense. Ibn Ezra says it means "great in [God-fearing] people", and Rabbeinu Bahya recorded that it took 2,337 years for the Ishmaelites to become a great nation, a count that lands at the rise of Islam.
Christian writers have conceded it too. The Catholic Abbé de Broglie said the progress of Islam fulfils the promise to Abraham. The Arab Christian apologist Anis Shorrosh, a fierce critic of Islam, admits the Muslim empire fulfilled "I will make him a great nation".
Source Anis Shorrosh, Islam Revealed: an Arab Christian apologist concedes the "great nation" was fulfilled in the Muslim empire
Source Ibn Ezra on Gen 17:20: "great nation" means great in its people's goodness
The land promised to Abraham's seed, "from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates" (Gen 15:18), was ruled by the Ishmaelite Muslims within twenty years of the Prophet's death.

briefs.title: Deuteronomy 18: a prophet like Moses "from among their brethren"
briefs.thesis: God promised Moses: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brethren, and I will put My words in his mouth" (Deut 18:18). Every detail fits Muhammad ﷺ better than Jesus.
briefs.sum: A lawgiving, state-founding, married, fighting prophet who spoke the exact words put in his mouth, from Israel's brethren. Deuteronomy 34:10 says no such prophet arose in Israel, and John 1:21 shows the Jews expected "the Prophet" separately from the Messiah.

obj.q: "Acts 3:22 applies Deuteronomy 18 to Jesus."
obj.a:
Peter applies Deut 18:15-18 to Jesus (Acts 3:22-26), while also speaking of his future return (3:20-21), which concedes that Jesus' ministry did not fulfil it. And John 1:21 shows that the Prophet and the Christ were different people in the minds of Jesus' contemporaries.
Source The Book of Acts presents the Deuteronomy 18 fulfilment as still future

obj.q: "'Brethren' means fellow Israelites."
obj.a: Deut 17:15 does use "brethren" for Israelites when choosing a king. But that verse belongs to the king law of 17:14-20, which many scholars date to the monarchy because it mirrors Solomon's sins (horses, wives, gold) and the Josianic "book of the law". And Deut 34:10 says outright that no prophet like Moses arose in Israel.

obj.q: "If Jesus is God, he is more than 'like Moses'."
obj.a: Exactly. The Bible says nothing is like God (Isa 40:18, 25; 46:5), so on the Christian view Jesus cannot be "like" a mere man. The prophecy must be about another human prophet.

prac.q: “Acts 3:22 applies Deuteronomy 18 to Jesus.”
prac.a: Jesus differs from Moses in nearly everything Deuteronomy stresses: no new law, no state, no marriage, and, for Christians, divine. 'From among their brethren' points outside Israel, Deuteronomy 34:10 says no such prophet arose in Israel, and John 1:21 shows the Jews still expected 'the Prophet' separate from the Messiah.

briefs.evs:
Rabbi Moshe Greenberg, a leading Bible scholar, observed: "The best analogue to Moses in the history of religions, Muhammad, exhibits the very same multiplicity of roles: oracle, political-military leader, cult founder and lawgiver."
Source Secular scholars concede Deut 34:10: no prophet like Moses ever arose in Israel
Source Matthew Poole's commentary: "face to face" means intimate, friendly revelation
The New Testament keeps "the Prophet" distinct from the Messiah. The priests ask John the Baptist: "Are you the Christ? … Are you Elijah? … Are you the Prophet?" (John 1:20-21). So the Jews of Jesus' day expected three different figures.
In the best early papyri of John 7:52 (P66, P75), the Pharisees say: "the Prophet does not arise from Galilee." So the Prophet was expected from somewhere else.

briefs.title: Isaiah 42: the Servant whom Kedar praises
briefs.thesis: Isaiah 42 describes God's chosen servant who brings justice and law to the nations, will not fail until he establishes it, and is praised by "the villages of Kedar" and "the inhabitants of Sela". Kedar is Ishmael's son and Sela is linked to Medina.
briefs.sum: A servant who brings law to the nations, is not discouraged until it is set up, and is praised by Kedar (Ishmael's son, the Arabs) and Sela (by Medina). Bukhari 2125 even quotes Isaiah 42's wording as the Prophet's description in the earlier scripture.

obj.q: "Matthew 12:18-21 applies Isaiah 42 to Jesus."
obj.a: Matthew quotes only verses 1-4 and stops before Kedar, Sela, the warrior and the destruction of idols. Jesus did not bring a law to the nations; he said he was sent "only to the lost sheep of Israel" (Mt 15:24). He did not conquer idolatry. On the Christian account, he was crushed and discouraged before justice was set on earth.

prac.q: “Matthew 12 says Isaiah 42 is about Jesus.”
prac.a: Matthew quotes only verses 1-4. The chapter's servant brings law to the nations, is not discouraged until he establishes it, fights like a warrior and is praised by Kedar and Sela, the Arabs and Medina. Bukhari 2125 records 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr quoting this description of the Prophet from the Torah.

briefs.evs:
The Companion 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who read the earlier scriptures, quoted a description of the Prophet that is "in the Torah" (Bukhari 2125); some Muslim writers compare its wording to Isaiah 42.
Source Keil-Delitzsch on Isaiah 42: "Kedar is here the collective name of the Arabic tribes generally"
Source Gesenius' lexicon on Kedar: the rabbis call the Arabs Kedarenes
Source Charles Forster: Kedar dwelt in western Arabia (the Hijaz)
Source Commentators on Isaiah 42:1: "My Spirit upon him" describes empowerment for a human servant

briefs.title: Isaiah 29:12: "Read!" "I cannot read"
briefs.thesis: Isaiah 29:12 describes a book given to one who is not learned. He is told "Read this", and he replies "I am not learned". This mirrors the first revelation in the cave of Hira, and the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus spells the word "hands" in a way that resembles "Hira" (an itacism).
briefs.sum: An unlettered man is handed a book and told "Read!"; he answers "I cannot read". That is the first revelation at Hira, and Sinaiticus' first hand writes "Hira".

obj.q: "The context of Isaiah 29 is a rebuke of Israel."
obj.a: The New Testament applies verses typologically without regard to context all the time. Matthew 2:15 applies Hosea 11:1 ("out of Egypt I called my son") to Jesus, although the next verse says that "son" sacrificed to the Baals. The Christian cannot reject typology when Muslims use it and depend on it themselves.

prac.q: “Isaiah 29 is about Jerusalem's spiritual blindness, not a future prophet.”
prac.a: The verse's image is a book given to someone unlettered who says 'I cannot read', which is exactly what happened at Hira (Bukhari 3). Context about blindness doesn't erase the parallel.

briefs.evs: Source Codex Sinaiticus, Isaiah 29:12: the original reading and the corrector's change (Milne & Skeat, Scribes and Correctors of the Codex Sinaiticus, 1938, p.49)

briefs.title: The Paraclete (John 14-16)
briefs.thesis: Jesus promised "another Paraclete" who would come after him, speak only what he hears, glorify Jesus, convict the world, and guide into all truth. These are the marks of a prophet, not of an abstract spirit, and early Muslims read the Gospel's word as "Ahmad".
briefs.sum: Another Paraclete, after Jesus leaves, who speaks only what he hears, glorifies Jesus and teaches what the disciples could not bear yet. That is a prophet like Moses, and the earliest Muslim readers of the Syriac Gospel took the word as "Muhammad".

obj.q: "John 14:26 says the Paraclete is the Holy Spirit."
obj.a: First, the word "Holy" is textually uncertain, as shown above. Second, the Bible calls prophets "spirits": "do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits… many false prophets have gone out" (1 John 4:1). A true prophet is a "spirit of truth" in that sense, and the Assumption of Moses even calls Moses a "holy spirit".

obj.q: "He proceeds from the Father, so he is divine."
obj.a: The same verb (ekporeuomai) is used for every word that "proceeds from the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4) and for evil that proceeds from the heart (Mt 15:18). It means "sent forth by God's command".

obj.q: "Jesus sends him in his name, so Jesus is divine."
obj.a: False prophets come "in my name" too (Mt 24:5). "In my name" means as my successor, and Jesus says the Father sends him in answer to Jesus' prayer (14:16).

prac.q: “John 14:26 says the Paraclete is the Holy Spirit.”
prac.a: Jesus says 'another' Paraclete, and calls himself one (1 John 2:1), so it's a person of his kind. He comes only after Jesus leaves (16:7), speaks only what he hears (16:13) and convicts the world: a prophet. Manuscripts even vary on the word 'Holy' in 14:26.

briefs.evs:
The "Holy Spirit" identification is textually unstable. In John 14:26, the Old Syriac Sinaitic palimpsest reads just "the Spirit", without "Holy". C.K. Barrett and George Johnston consider "holy" a possible harmonisation.
Scholars think the Paraclete was once an independent figure. Raymond E. Brown lists scholars (Spitta, Windisch, Bultmann, Betz) who thought the Paraclete was originally an independent figure, later identified with the Spirit.
A sceptical NT scholar concedes the point. Robert Price admits the Muslim argument is strong.
Tap to enlargeNIV Application Commentary: some manuscripts omit "holy" at John 14:26
Source Raymond E. Brown, Anchor Bible: John, on the Paraclete
Source Metzger: scribes added "Holy" to "Spirit" elsewhere in John
Early Islamic sources read the word as Muhammad's name. Ibn Ishaq (d. 150 AH) quotes John 15:23-16:1 and says Munahhemana is "Muhammad in Syriac" (the Syriac word means "comforter"). He adds that "in Syriac it is Muhammad and in Greek the Paraclete". Muqatil ibn Sulayman says the same.
The Greek word may encode "praised". Some argue the Greek encodes "the praised one". The Greek parakletos derives from parakaleo, "to call alongside". Some Muslim writers propose it was originally periklytos, "praised", but no Greek manuscript has that reading. The suggested root means "praise/glory" (as in Kleopatra and Periklytos).
