briefs.title: Supporting prophecies: the cumulative case
briefs.thesis: Alongside the strongest texts, several more passages point to the same Arabian prophet. Each alone is debatable, but together they form a pattern.
briefs.sum: Sinai, Seir, Paran; Kedar's glory fails within a year; the valley of Baca; ten thousand holy ones; a fifth kingdom that breaks the four; the "desired one" of the nations. One at a time each can be argued over, but taken together they point to Arabia and its prophet.

obj.q: "These are all forced readings."
obj.a: Some, taken alone, are open to other readings, which is why they are supporting arguments. But the pattern is hard to dismiss: Paran, Kedar, Teman, Baca, ten thousand holy ones, a law for the nations, a praised one. All of it points south, to Arabia, and every one of these texts was in the Jewish Bible centuries before Islam.

prac.q: “Paran is in Sinai, not Arabia.”
prac.a: Genesis 21:21 places Ishmael in Paran, and Ishmael's descendants are the Arabs of the Hijaz. Deuteronomy 33:2's Sinai, Seir, Paran moves from Moses to Jesus' region to Ishmael's land.

briefs.evs:
Deuteronomy 33:2. "The LORD came from Sinai, rose from Seir, shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of holy ones." That is Sinai (Moses), Seir (Jesus) and Paran (Muhammad). Paran is where Ishmael lived (Gen 21:21), and Eusebius located it south of Aila (Aqaba). The Prophet ﷺ conquered Mecca with 10,000 Companions (Bukhari 4276).
Source Rashi and the Jewish Encyclopedia on Paran
Source Ibn Ezra on Paran and the Arabian wilderness
Habakkuk 3:3. "God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran; His praise filled the earth." The nations of Cushan and Midian tremble.
Isaiah 21:13-17, the "oracle concerning Arabia": fugitives flee the drawn sword, and "within a year … all the glory of Kedar will fail". The Battle of Badr came about eighteen months after the Hijra, and the Quraysh (Kedarites) were broken. Isaiah 21:7 has a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel, which some later writers read as Jesus and Muhammad.
Psalm 84:6. Pilgrims pass "through the valley of Baca", making it a place of springs. The Quran calls Mecca "Bakka" (3:96).
Psalm 72. The desert tribes bow before him, his dominion runs "from sea to sea", "prayer shall be made for him continually; daily he shall be praised". Muslims send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ in every prayer. Solomon, who worshipped idols in old age (1 Kgs 11), hardly fits. Ibn Taymiyya refutes applying it to Jesus.
Source Ibn Ta

briefs.title: The Jews and Christians of the time recognised him
briefs.thesis: The Quran says the People of the Book "recognise him as they recognise their own sons" (2:146). The historical record shows learned Jews and Christians did exactly that.
briefs.sum: A chief rabbi who tested him and converted, a Christian scholar who recognised the angel of Moses, a Christian king who saw one lamp, and Jews who conceded he was a prophet but feared their people.

prac.q: “If the Jews recognised him, why did most reject him?”
prac.a: The Quran says many recognised him and refused out of envy (2:109). Tirmidhi 2733 records Jews who conceded his prophethood but refused because they feared their people would abandon them. Abdullah ibn Salam, a chief rabbi, tested him and converted.

briefs.evs:
'Abdullah ibn Salam, a leading rabbi of the Banu Qaynuqa', tested the Prophet ﷺ with three questions known only from rabbinic lore: the first sign of the Hour, the first food of Paradise, and why a child resembles a parent. The answers matched the rabbinic traditions, such as the banquet on the Leviathan's liver (Leviticus Rabbah), so he accepted Islam (Bukhari 3329). The Jews had called him "our best and the son of our best" before he declared his faith.
Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar, recognised the first revelation as "the Namus (angel) that came to Moses" (Bukhari 3).
The Negus of Abyssinia said Surah Maryam and the Gospel "come from the same lamp".
Jews who conceded (Tirmidhi 2733) kissed his hands and said "we bear witness you are a prophet", but would not follow him "because David prayed that his line would never lack a prophet". That blessing was conditional on obedience (Ps 132:12; 1 Kgs 9:4-7).
Heraclius, according to later Christian chronicles (such as Michael the Syrian, 12th century), ordered his governors to stop resisting the Arabs because of God's promise to Ishmael.
Source Heraclius' recognition of the biblical promise to Ishmael

briefs.title: More passages, and the expectation of an Arabian prophet
briefs.thesis: Beyond the main texts, several passages and pre-Islamic Jewish and Christian traditions expected a ruler or prophet from Arabia. They are supporting evidence, best used together.
briefs.sum: Psalm 72's king whom desert tribes serve and for whom prayer is made continually; Shiloh; Kedar's tents in Psalm 120; the Assumption of Moses' timetable; and Jewish expectation in Medina and in the Secrets of Rabbi Shimon. Use them as a supporting pattern.
briefs.caution: Each of these is debatable on its own. Present them as a pattern that adds to the stronger texts (Deuteronomy 18, Isaiah 42, the Paraclete), not as standalone proofs.

prac.q: “You can read Muhammad into anything if you try hard enough.”
prac.a: Each passage alone is arguable, which is why I lead with Deuteronomy 18 and Isaiah 42. But the pattern is real: Jews in Medina were expecting a prophet before he came, a Jewish apocalypse saw the kingdom of Ishmael as God's rescue, and several texts point to Arabia and Kedar.

briefs.evs:
Psalm 72. A king to whom "desert tribes bow down" (72:9), whose rule runs "from sea to sea" (72:8), who "delivers the needy when he calls" (72:12), and for whom "prayer shall be made continually" (72:15), which Muslims do in every prayer (the salat 'ala al-Nabi). Justin Martyr argued it was not about Solomon but about Christ.
Genesis 49:10 (Shiloh). "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples." Muslim scholars read it as the authority of prophecy and law passing from Israel to the one whom the nations obey.
Psalm 120:5. "Woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar… I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war." Kedar, Ishmael's son, is the ancestor of Quraysh; the forum reads it alongside Psalm 121's "the LORD will keep your going out and your coming in" and Quran 17:80 ("cause me to enter in truth and to exit in truth"), the Hijra and return.
The Assumption of Moses (a 1st-century CE text, surviving in a 6th-century Latin manuscript) says from Moses' death "until his advent there will be 250 times" (10:12); some read this as pointing to the 6th century CE, a speculative reading.
Expectation at the time. Ibn Ishaq records that a Jewish scholar from Syria, Ibn al-Hayyiban, settled near Medina before Islam and told its Jews that a prophet was about to appear there. The 8th-cen

briefs.sec: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
briefs.title: The Quran's literary challenge has never been met
briefs.thesis: The Quran challenged the most eloquent Arabs of its day to produce even one surah like it. They had every motive to do so and failed, and that failure is best explained by a source beyond Muhammad ﷺ.
briefs.sum: The Quran set a public challenge at the lowest possible bar to the people most able and most motivated to meet it. They chose war over a few lines of Arabic, and their best critic admitted it was unlike any known form of speech.

obj.q: "Literary quality is subjective. Shakespeare is inimitable too."
obj.a: The challenge is not "write something beautiful". It is to produce a text of the same kind, and the Quran's form is unique: it is neither poetry (shi'r, with metre) nor rhymed prose (saj'), yet it uses rhythm and rhyme throughout. The judges were not modern readers but the Arabs who knew the forms best, and they agreed it fitted none of them. Also, Shakespeare never staked his credibility on the claim that no one could match him, and his contemporaries were not trying to destroy him by matching him.

obj.q: "Maybe people did meet it and Muslims destroyed the evidence."
obj.a: The attempts that exist (Musaylima, Ibn al-Muqaffa' as alleged, al-Mutanabbi as rumoured) are preserved and recorded by Muslims themselves. A successful imitation would have been the single most useful weapon for the Quraysh, the apostates of the Ridda wars and the later Christian polemicists writing in Arabic, and none of them claims to have produced one.

obj.q: "Non-Arabs can't judge, so the argument is useless to them."
obj.a: A non-specialist can still judge the historical argument: the experts of the time, who were hostile, conceded it. That is how we accept many expert judgements we cannot check ourselves.

prac.q: “I could write a surah right now in rhymed Arabic. Does that disprove the Quran?”
prac.a: The challenge is not rhyme. It is to match the Quran's unique form and quality, judged by people who master the language. Musaylima tried and became a byword for failure. If it were easy, the Quraysh, who had the language natively and every reason to win, would have done it rather than go to war.

briefs.evs:
The challenge is narrowed step by step. First the whole Quran (17:88: "if mankind and jinn gathered to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce the like of it, even if they helped one another"), then ten surahs (11:13), then a single surah (2:23, 10:38). The shortest surah, al-Kawthar, is three lines. The bar was set as low as it could go, and it was set in public, in the market culture of Ukaz where poets competed for prizes.
The opponents' behaviour is the evidence. The Quraysh tried bribery (offering him wealth and kingship), a three-year boycott in the valley of Abu Talib, torture of the weak Muslims, and finally a plot to kill him. A short text in Arabic would have cost them nothing. They did not produce one, and those who later tried, such as Musaylima, produced lines that became a joke in Arabic literature.
The best-known account is that of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, reported in al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi (the chain is disputed). When the Quraysh asked him what to call the Quran so that pilgrims would avoid it, he rejected each label in turn: it is not poetry, for he knew all its metres; it is not the mumbling of a soothsayer; it is not the speech of a madman. He finally settled on "magic" only because it separates a man from his family, and Surah al-Muddaththir (74:18-25) records exactly this deliberation: "he thought and deliberated… then he said: this is noth

briefs.sec: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
briefs.title: The Prophet ﷺ refused to exploit the eclipse: an argument from sincerity
briefs.thesis: On the day his son Ibrahim died, the sun was eclipsed and people said it was for Ibrahim's death. The Prophet ﷺ publicly denied it, throwing away a "sign" that would have boosted his authority. Impostors do not behave like that.
briefs.sum: The eclipse on the day his son died handed him a free miracle, and he publicly refused it. Alongside the Quran's self-rebukes and his refusal of worldly offers, this makes sincerity the starting point for any honest evaluation.

obj.q: "Sincerity doesn't prove truth. Many sincere people are wrong."
obj.a: True, so this argument has a limited job: it removes the "liar" option. Combined with the others (the Quran's preservation and challenge, fulfilled prophecies, his knowledge of earlier scripture), the remaining options are "sincere and deluded" or "sincere and true". A deluded man does not produce a coherent law, a disciplined state and a book his enemies cannot match within 23 years.

obj.q: "Maybe the story was invented to make him look humble."
obj.a: The report is in Bukhari and Muslim through several Companions, and the eclipse is astronomically confirmed on the right day. Inventing a story in which he declines a miracle is an odd strategy for a community that collected miracle reports eagerly.

prac.q: “Your prophet benefited enormously from his claims: power, wives, wealth. Isn't that the profile of an impostor?”
prac.a: He refused kingship and wealth when Quraysh offered them to stop preaching, died with his armour pawned to a Jew for barley, and corrected the people when an eclipse could have served him. Power came after 13 years of persecution, not before; someone seeking it would have taken the deal in Mecca.

briefs.evs:
The event is historically anchored. Ibrahim, the Prophet's son by Mariya, died in 10 AH, and the eclipse of 27 January 632 CE is attested in the astronomical records; some Muslim sources place Ibrahim's death on that day, though the date of his death is disputed.
The point is psychological and historical. At this moment the Prophet ﷺ was grieving and the people were offering him, unprompted, a cosmic endorsement. A man inventing a religion for power would have stayed silent or accepted it. He instead gathered the people, led the eclipse prayer, and gave a sermon to correct the superstition.
This fits a wider pattern that even non-Muslim historians have noted. W. Montgomery Watt argued that his readiness to suffer persecution, the high character of those who followed him, and the greatness of what he achieved all make sincerity the default explanation, and that treating him as an impostor raises more problems than it solves. Other examples: the Quran rebukes him in his own recitation (80:1-10, the blind man; 9:43; 8:67), he lived poorly while ruling Arabia, and he refused kingship when Quraysh offered it.

briefs.sec: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
briefs.title: Prohibitions vindicated: alcohol
briefs.thesis: The Quran's total ban on intoxicants (5:90-91) anticipated what modern public health now concludes: there is no safe level of alcohol, and its social costs are enormous.
briefs.sum: The Quran banned alcohol in a wine-loving society, named its social harms precisely, and introduced the ban in a way people could accept. Modern data on cancer, violence, road deaths and fetal harm vindicate it.

obj.q: "Moderate drinking is fine; some studies even say it's good for the heart."
obj.a: Those studies have been widely challenged: they compared drinkers to "abstainers" who included ex-drinkers who quit because of illness, which made abstainers look sicker. Newer analyses correcting for this find no protective effect. And a law for a whole society must look at total harm, not the best-case individual.

obj.q: "Prohibition failed in America, so a ban is bad policy."
obj.a: US Prohibition was imposed by law on a population that did not accept it. Islam's ban is internalised as worship, and Muslim-majority societies have very low alcohol consumption as a result. The Quran's gradual method is exactly what US Prohibition lacked.

prac.q: “Jesus turned water into wine. Isn't it arrogant to say God bans what his prophet made?”
prac.a: The Quran says earlier laws were adapted to their people and Islam completes them (5:3, 7:157). Even the Bible warns that "wine is a mocker" (Prov 20:1) and forbids it to priests on duty and Nazirites. Modern evidence that there is no safe level supports the final law, not the earlier permission.

briefs.evs:
The ban came in stages, each adapted to a society that loved wine: first noting that its harm outweighs its benefit (2:219), then forbidding prayer while intoxicated (4:43), then the final prohibition (5:90-91). The Companions poured their wine into the streets of Medina when the final verse came (Bukhari 2464).
The modern data:
In 2023 the WHO stated that "no level of alcohol consumption is safe" for health, since alcohol is a group 1 carcinogen.
In the US, about 30% of traffic deaths involve an alcohol-impaired driver (NHTSA: 11,654 deaths in 2020, cited by the CDC).
Alcohol is involved in roughly 40% of violent crime in US Bureau of Justice Statistics surveys (offenders who had been drinking).
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders may affect up to 1 in 20 US schoolchildren (May et al., JAMA 2018).
Studies consistently find religiosity protects against substance abuse.
Note the Quran's diagnosis: it names social harm (enmity and hatred) before spiritual harm. That is exactly what the crime and domestic-violence numbers show.

briefs.sec: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
briefs.title: Zakat and the economics of mercy
briefs.thesis: Islam built a compulsory, rule-based welfare system into worship itself, and history reports periods in which zakat is said to have nearly eliminated poverty.
briefs.sum: Zakat makes care for the poor a pillar of worship, with fixed rates and named recipients. Combined with the ban on interest, it is a welfare system 1,200 years ahead of the modern state.

obj.q: "Modern welfare states do this better."
obj.a: Modern states arrived at taxation-for-welfare in the 19th and 20th centuries, though earlier systems (the Torah's poor tithes, Roman grain doles, the English Poor Law of 1601) existed. Islam made it a fixed religious obligation in the 7th century, tied it to worship so it does not depend on politics, and named who must receive it. The question is not whether others later copied the idea, but where a 7th-century Arabian got it.

obj.q: "The Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz report is late and idealised."
obj.a: It may be idealised in detail, but the general picture of a functioning Bayt al-Mal is well documented, and the argument rests mainly on the structure of the law, not one report.

prac.q: “Muslim countries today are among the poorest in the world. So much for zakat.”
prac.a: Most Muslim states do not apply zakat as a state system, and many run interest-based economies, so their poverty is not a test of Islamic law. Where zakat was applied systematically, sources describe poverty as nearly eliminated.

briefs.evs:
Unlike voluntary charity, zakat is a pillar of Islam, as obligatory as prayer. Abu Bakr fought those who refused to pay it after the Prophet's death, which shows it was treated as a right of the poor over the rich, not a favour. The public treasury (Bayt al-Mal) also supported non-Muslims in need: Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have granted a stipend to an old Jewish man he found begging.
T.W. Arnold's The Preaching of Islam (pp. 54, 117) records that dhimmi communities prospered under Muslim rule. The Quran also promises that charity increases rather than reduces wealth (2:261, 2:276), which fits behavioural research showing that giving increases well-being.

briefs.sec: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
briefs.title: The 360 joints and the medical hadith: use with care
briefs.thesis: Some hadith make claims about the body or medicine that are sometimes presented as scientific miracles. They are best used defensively, to show they are not absurd, rather than as primary proofs.
briefs.sum: The 360-joint, fly and camel-milk hadith are defensible but not decisive. Use them to show critics have no real case, and build your positive case on stronger ground.
briefs.caution: These arguments depend on how terms are defined and on small or preliminary studies. Don't lead with them. Use them when an opponent claims a hadith is ridiculous.

obj.q: "Then why mention them at all?"
obj.a: Because critics use them as ridicule ("Islam says dip flies in your drink"). Your goal is to neutralise the ridicule, not to win a proof.

obj.q: "The Prophet's medical advice could be wrong under your own view."
obj.a: Yes. Muslim scholarship distinguishes his role as a messenger from his ordinary human knowledge of agriculture or local medicine (Muslim 2363). Whether a given medical hadith is revelation is itself a scholarly question.

prac.q: “Your prophet told people to drink camel urine. How can anyone take that seriously?”
prac.a: It was a specific remedy for a specific group in a desert setting, following practice known to the Arabs; it is not a general command. Many scholars regard such medical advice as the Prophet's experience as a man of his environment, as he said in Muslim 2363. It tells us nothing against his prophethood, any more than the Bible's medical laws do.

briefs.evs:
360 joints (Muslim 1007). "Every human being is created with 360 joints", given as the reason each person owes a daily charity for every joint. Counts depend on what is called a joint; anatomy references give figures around 360 for synovial and other articulations, while broader counts that include all fibrous junctions reach higher (Vizniak gives about 472). The point is that 360 is a respectable count, not a guess that anatomy contradicts. Chinese and other ancient sources that mention 360 or 365 do so for calendar or cosmological reasons, and were not accessible to the Prophet ﷺ.
The fly hadith (Bukhari 3320). "If a fly falls into your drink, dip it fully, then remove it, for in one wing is a disease and in the other a cure." Classical scholars like al-Shashi read it as practical advice (irshad), not a command. Laboratory studies have reported antimicrobial activity in house-fly extracts and peptides (for example a 2023 review of Musca domestica antimicrobial peptides, PubMed 36619234), and some small studies report that dipping reduced bacterial counts. This is enough to show the hadith is not absurd; it is not enough to build a "miracle" on.
Camel milk and urine (Bukhari 233). The Prophet ﷺ prescribed these to a group of desert Arabs with a specific illness. Camel milk has documented bioactive properties. On urine, be cautious: modern health authorities warn against it bec

briefs.sec: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
briefs.title: "The fastest-growing religion" is not a proof
briefs.thesis: Islam's growth is real, but most of it is demographic, so use it as context, never as an argument for truth.
briefs.sum: Islam is the fastest-growing major religion (Pew, 2010-2020), mostly through demographics. Mention it only as context.
briefs.caution: This is not an argument for truth. Use it only to correct someone who says Islam is dying or that its people are leaving en masse.

obj.q: "Popularity doesn't make something true."
obj.a: Agreed, and you should say so first. Growth is a fact about people, not a proof about God.

prac.q: “Islam only grows because Muslims have more children.”
prac.a: Correct, and I would never use growth as a proof. The arguments for Islam are the Quran's preservation, its challenge, its prophecies and the evidence for God; growth is not one of them.

briefs.evs: Pew Research Center's report on 2010-2020 found that Muslims were the fastest-growing major religious group . Most of that growth comes from a young age profile and higher fertility, with switching playing a small role. Christianity, by contrast, lost more through switching than any other group.

briefs.title: The Quran removes human weaknesses the Bible attributes to God
briefs.thesis: Where the Bible describes God as tired, regretful or defeated, the Quran explicitly denies it, often in words that look like a direct answer to the biblical text.
briefs.sum: The Bible says God was refreshed, regretted, and was stopped by chariots; other biblical passages contradict these. The Quran sides with God's perfection every time and in several places answers the text directly.

obj.q: "These are anthropomorphisms, figures of speech. Jews and Christians don't believe God gets tired."
obj.a: Then the Quran is right to say so plainly. But notice what this concedes: the biblical text, read as written, says something false about God, and only a later interpretation rescues it. The Quran does not need rescuing on these points.

obj.q: "Muhammad was just a monotheist cleaning up stories he heard."
obj.a:
An unlettered man in Mecca would have had to know the Exodus wording about being "refreshed", the Judges verse about chariots, and an obscure rabbinic tradition about God's hand, then answer each with a precise correction. There was no Arabic Bible in his time (Metzger dates the earliest Arabic translations to the 8th or 9th century).
Tap to enlargeBruce Metzger: the earliest Arabic translations of the Bible probably date from the 8th century, after the Prophet ﷺ

prac.q: “Your Quran also says Allah "forgets" people (9:67) and "mocks" them (2:15). Isn't that anthropomorphism too?”
prac.a: Those are reciprocal expressions (mushakala): Allah "forgets" those who forgot Him means He abandons them, and the Quran itself denies literal forgetting: "My Lord neither errs nor forgets" (20:52). The Quran explains its own idiom inside the text. Exodus does not say anywhere that God never tires; it just says He rested and was refreshed.

briefs.evs:
God "rested and was refreshed". Exodus 31:17 says that on the seventh day God "rested and was refreshed" (Hebrew wayyinnafash, literally "caught his breath"). The Quran says: "We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us" (50:38). Ayat al-Kursi adds: "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him" (2:255). The wording of 50:38 contrasts with Exodus 31:17, though it also agrees with Isaiah 40:28 and Psalm 121:4.
Tap to enlargeExodus 31:17: God "rested and was refreshed". Quran 50:38 replies: "no weariness touched Us"
God "regretted" creating man. Genesis 6:6 says "the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart". Yet Numbers 23:19 says "God is not a man… that he should repent", and 1 Samuel 15 says both (v. 11 and 35 he regrets; v. 29 he does not). The Quran's God never regrets: His knowledge encompasses everything before it happens (57:22, 6:59).
God defeated by iron chariots. Judges 1:19: "the LORD was with Judah… but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain, because they had chariots of iron." The Quran: "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you" (3:160), and "Allah is never to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or the earth" (35:44).
God's hand "bound". Lamentations 2:3 says God "drew back His right hand", and later Jewish tradition (3 Enoch 48A; the midrash on La

briefs.title: The Quran restores the honour of the prophets
briefs.thesis: The Bible attributes idolatry, murder and indecency to the prophets; the Quran retells the same stories and clears them. That is consistent with one source correcting another.
briefs.sum: The Bible makes Aaron an idol-maker, Solomon an idolater and Moses a murderer; the Quran tells the same stories while preserving their prophethood, and its versions are more coherent with the rest of the narrative.

obj.q: "The Bible is honest about its heroes' flaws; the Quran sanitises them."
obj.a: The Quran does show prophets erring and repenting: Adam (7:23), Moses (28:16), David (38:24), Jonah (21:87). What it denies is the gross sins that would make them unfit to lead: idolatry by the high priest, murder by the lawgiver, idol shrines by the temple-builder. The question is not "flaws or no flaws" but which flaws are compatible with prophethood.

obj.q: "Samiri means Samaritan, and Samaritans didn't exist in Moses' time, so this is an anachronism."
obj.a: Samiri is a nisba that can refer to a person, clan or place; it need not mean "Samaritan" in the later sense. Shomer/Shemer is an old Semitic name and root ("guard"). The Quran never says he was from Samaria.

prac.q: “If the Quran is right, why does every Bible manuscript say Aaron made the calf?”
prac.a: Because the manuscripts are copies of a text that was already shaped by the time they were written; the Torah itself records its own loss and rediscovery (see the last argument in this section). And the biblical account is internally strained: Aaron is unpunished and continues as high priest while 3,000 others are killed (Exod 32:28).

briefs.evs:
Aaron and the calf. Exodus 32:2-5 says Aaron collected the gold, fashioned the calf and built an altar for it. The Quran attributes the calf to "al-Samiri" and has Aaron warn the people: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90). Moses then interrogates Samiri, not Aaron (20:95-97). Aaron was the man God appointed to speak for Moses; it makes no sense that he would build the idol and keep his office.
Solomon and idolatry. 1 Kings 11:4-10 says Solomon's wives turned his heart to Ashtoreth and Milcom and he built shrines for them. The Quran: "Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic" (2:102).
Moses and the Egyptian. Exodus 2:12: Moses "looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand", a premeditated killing. The Quran: Moses struck the man in a fight to defend an Israelite and he died; Moses immediately said, "This is from the work of Satan… My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me", and he was forgiven (28:15-16). A manslaughter followed by repentance, not a murder followed by concealment.
Isaiah walking naked. Isaiah 20:2-3 has God command Isaiah to walk "naked and barefoot" for three years, which Muslim writers contrast with the principle "Allah does not command indecency" (7:28, in a different context).

briefs.title: The Quran corrects historical and narrative details
briefs.thesis: In several stories the Quran quietly differs from the Bible on a factual detail, and in each case the Quran's version is the more plausible one.
briefs.sum: On the Exodus population, the Eden serpent, Moses' hand, Zechariah's sign and the Sinai covenant formula, the Quran's version fixes a problem in the biblical one. That is the pattern of a corrector, not a copyist.

obj.q: "Pharaoh calling them a small band is just his propaganda."
obj.a: Possibly, but the Quran nowhere gives the 600,000 figure, and its account never requires millions. If it were copying Exodus, it would have the number.

obj.q: "The Hebrew pun is a coincidence."
obj.a: The phrase "we hear and…" is the covenant formula, and the Quran uses it twice in contexts about the covenant (2:93, 4:46). Commentators also note that 4:46 mentions the Jews' play on words (ra'ina), showing the Quran is aware of bilingual wordplay.

prac.q: “Different details just mean Muhammad heard garbled oral versions.”
prac.a: Garbled versions produce random differences. These are systematic: each difference removes a problem (God being wrong in Eden, a leprous prophet, a punished priest, an impossible population). Random garbling does not repair theological and historical problems.

briefs.evs:
The size of the Exodus. Exodus 12:37 says 600,000 men on foot left Egypt, besides women and children, implying two to three million people. No archaeology supports a population that size in Sinai, and it would have outnumbered Egypt's army. The Quran has Pharaoh call them "a small band" (26:54).
The serpent told the truth in Genesis. In Genesis 2:17 God warns that "on the day you eat of it you will surely die"; the serpent says "you will not surely die… your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (3:4-5). Adam and Eve do not die that day, and God then says "the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil" (3:22). Read literally, the serpent seems right (a reading disputed by Jewish and Christian interpreters). In the Quran, Satan is the liar: he calls it "the tree of immortality and a kingdom that will not decay" (20:120), which is false.
Moses' hand. Exodus 4:6 says Moses' hand became "leprous, like snow". The Quran says it came out "white, without any harm" (20:22, 27:12, 28:32), a sign of honour rather than disease.
Zechariah's silence. Luke 1:20 says Zechariah was struck mute as a punishment for doubting the angel. In the Quran, Zechariah asks for a sign, and silence for three days is the sign granted (3:41, 19:10). Classical commentators such as al-Samarqandi call it a miracle, not a punishment.
The Israelites' words at Sinai. In Deu

briefs.title: The Quran shows knowledge of the scriptures, and cites them accurately
briefs.thesis: Where the Quran explicitly cites earlier scripture, the citation is accurate, and its themes match the earliest layers of the Jesus tradition rather than later Christian theology.
briefs.sum: The Quran quotes Psalm 37:29 accurately, uses Jewish liturgical language, and presents Jesus as the earliest sources do. It is consistent with its claim to recover the original message.

obj.q: "This proves Muhammad had Jewish and Christian informants."
obj.a: The Quran answers the informant claim itself: "the tongue of the one they allude to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic" (16:103). The supposed informants were a foreign slave or two in Mecca, and the parallels range across Hebrew wording, rabbinic tradition, Syriac usage and early Jewish-Christian themes. No single informant had all of that, and none could have given him the Quran's style.

obj.q: "Q is hypothetical."
obj.a: It is the majority scholarly hypothesis for the Synoptic problem. Even setting Q aside, James gives a picture of a Law-observant community without divine-Son theology.

prac.q: “If the Quran knows the Bible this well, why does it get the Trinity wrong, saying Christians worship Mary (5:116)?”
prac.a: 5:116 does not define the Trinity as Father, Son and Mary. It asks Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides Allah, and Marian devotion did grow to include prayers and veneration directed to her (the Collyridians even offered her cakes). The Quran rejects the worship of both, which is a fair criticism of real practice.

briefs.evs:
Psalm 37:29 in Quran 21:105. "We have written in the Psalms (al-Zabur) after the Reminder: My righteous servants shall inherit the land." Psalm 37:29: "The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell in it forever." This is the only place where the Quran explicitly quotes the Psalms by name (compare 5:45, which quotes the Torah), and the quote is exact in meaning.
"Lord of the worlds". The Quran's opening praise, rabb al-'alamin, matches the Jewish liturgical title ribbon kol ha-'olamim ("Master of all worlds").
The "Q" source. The hypothetical sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke presents Jesus as a teacher of charity, prayer and repentance who works healings, condemns the killing of the prophets (Luke 11:47-51; compare Quran 2:61, 3:21), and is accused of sorcery (Luke 11:15; compare Quran 5:110, 61:6). It has no birth narrative and no atonement theology, but it presents Jesus as the apocalyptic Son of Man, unlike the Quran.
The Epistle of James, from the Jerusalem church that stayed loyal to the Law, also reads like the Quran: say "if the Lord wills" before planning (James 4:13-15; Quran 18:23-24); trials refine faith (James 1:2-4; Quran 2:155); do not favour the rich (James 2:1-9; Quran 80:1-10); faith without works is dead (James 2:17-24; the Quran's constant "those who believe and do righteous deeds").
The Shahada pattern. Belief in God and His messenger together runs

briefs.title: The Torah's own history records loss, rewriting and scribal falsification
briefs.thesis: The Hebrew Bible itself says the book of the law was lost for generations, that scribes falsified it, and that many inspired books are gone, which is exactly what the Quran describes (2:79).
briefs.sum: The Bible records that the law was lost and rediscovered, that a prophet condemned the scribes' lying pen, that sacrifice laws were unknown to the prophets, and that many inspired books vanished. This matches the Quran's account in 2:79.

obj.q: "Jeremiah 8:8 means the scribes misinterpreted the law, not that they changed the text."
obj.a: The verse says the pen (Hebrew 'et, a stylus) of the scribes made it a lie, which points to writing. Ellicott's commentary takes it to refer to written work. Either way, a prophet accused the custodians of the law of falsifying it, which is the Quran's charge.

obj.q: "Lost books were never meant to be scripture."
obj.a: David ordered the Book of Jashar to be taught (2 Sam 1:18), and Solomon's proverbs and songs were wisdom from God by the Bible's own account. Their loss shows God did not preserve every inspired text of Israel, so "God would never let His word be lost" is not a biblical principle.

obj.q: "The documentary hypothesis is disputed."
obj.a: The details are, but that the Torah is composite and was edited over centuries is the mainstream view, and you do not need any particular version to make the point.

prac.q: “The Dead Sea Scrolls prove the Hebrew Bible was preserved.”
prac.a: They show the text was fairly stable from about the 2nd century BCE, but they also contain variant forms (some closer to the Septuagint or Samaritan text), and they come centuries after Moses. Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Scrolls reads "sons of God" where the Masoretic text has "sons of Israel", a theological change.

briefs.evs:
The book that was found. In 2 Kings 22:8 (2 Chr 34:14), the priest Hilkiah "found the book of the law" in the Temple during repairs, and King Josiah tore his clothes on hearing it because his people had not obeyed it. 2 Kings 23:22 adds that "no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges". In other words, the book of the law had been lost or neglected before Josiah's time (some scholars think it was newly composed).
The lying pen of the scribes. Jeremiah 8:8: "How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie." The Quran: "Woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say 'this is from Allah' to buy with it a small price" (2:79). Jeremiah 8:10 even adds the motive: "everyone is greedy for unjust gain".
Contradictions about sacrifice. Jeremiah 7:22: "I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices on the day I brought them out of Egypt"; Amos 5:25 asks, "Did you bring me sacrifices… forty years in the wilderness?" Yet Leviticus is full of sacrificial laws given in the wilderness. Jer 7:22 and Amos 5:25 have been read by some as denying that sacrifice was commanded in the wilderness.
Lost inspired books. The Bible cites the Book of the Wars of the LORD (Num 21:14), the Book of Jashar (Josh 10:13; 2 Sam 1:18), the chronicles of Nath

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: Those who knew Jesus called him a man and a prophet
briefs.thesis: The people closest to Jesus, including his own disciples after the resurrection, described him as a man and a prophet sent by God, not as God.
briefs.sum: From the crowds to the disciples at Emmaus to Peter at Pentecost, the first witnesses called Jesus a prophet and "a man attested by God". The Synoptics never call him God.

obj.q: "Calling him a prophet doesn't exclude him being God; he's both."
obj.a: Then the earliest sermon was the moment to say so. Peter is explaining who Jesus is to thousands of Jews, and the description he gives is "a man" through whom God worked. The two-natures doctrine is a later formulation (Chalcedon, 451) read back into texts that never state it.

obj.q: "These are the views of people who didn't yet understand."
obj.a: Acts 2 is after the resurrection and after the Spirit was given, at the moment the apostles are said to be filled with understanding. If they still described him as a man attested by God, that is the apostolic understanding.

prac.q: “The disciples worshipped him (Matt 28:17), so they knew he was God.”
prac.a: The Greek proskuneo means bowing or homage, and it is given to humans too: Israel "bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD, and the king" (1 Chr 29:20, RSV; the Greek uses proskuneo for both). Dunn shows the NT never gives Jesus latreia, the cultic worship reserved for God.

briefs.evs:
The crowds: "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee" (Matt 21:11); "a great prophet has arisen among us; God has visited His people" (Luke 7:16).
The disciples on the road to Emmaus, after the crucifixion, describe him as "a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people" (Luke 24:19).
Jesus about himself: "you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God" (John 8:40).
Peter's first sermon at Pentecost, the founding proclamation of the church: "Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him" (Acts 2:22). Notice who does the miracles: God, through him.
Others in John call him a prophet: the Samaritan woman (4:19), the crowd after the feeding (6:14, "truly the Prophet who is to come into the world"), the crowd at the feast (7:40), the blind man (9:17).
Many scholars (Dunn among them) hold that the Synoptic Gospels never explicitly call Jesus "God" and that there is no clear sign Jesus thought of himself as divine, though others dispute this. James Dunn, a believing Christian scholar, adds that the Christian worship of Jesus did not take the form of cultic worship (latreia) given to God.
Tap to enlargeJames Dunn, Did the First Christians Worship Jesus?: cultic worship (latreia) is never offered to Christ in the New Testament

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: Jesus distinguishes himself from the one true God
briefs.thesis: In his own words, Jesus places himself under God, calls the Father "the only true God", and calls God "my God".
briefs.sum: Jesus refuses to be called good in God's sense, calls the Father "the only true God", calls the Father "my God" after the resurrection, and says he can do nothing by himself. His own words place him under God.

obj.q: "In Mark 10:18 Jesus is testing the man: 'If you call me good, realise I'm God.'"
obj.a: Nothing in the passage says so, and Matthew clearly did not read it that way, because he changed it. The early fathers quoted it to show the Father's unique goodness. An interpretation that needs a hidden meaning the earliest readers missed is weak.

obj.q: "'The Father is greater' refers to Jesus' human nature only."
obj.a: That is a later distinction (the two-natures doctrine). In the text Jesus says "I", the whole person. And the same "human nature only" move can explain away any verse, which makes the doctrine unfalsifiable. If every verse that limits Jesus is "his human nature", the evidence never gets to count.

obj.q: "John 17:3 just means the Father is true God; Jesus is too."
obj.a: Then the word "only" means nothing. "You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent" lists two parties with two different descriptions.

prac.q: “Jesus said "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30).”
prac.a: The word "one" is neuter (hen), meaning one in purpose, not one person or being. Jesus prays that his disciples "may be one (hen) just as we are one" (John 17:22). And when the Jews accused him of making himself God after 10:30, he answered by quoting Psalm 82:6, where human judges are called "gods", and said he had only called himself "Son of God" (10:34-36).

briefs.evs:
"Why do you call me good?" When a man addressed him as "Good Teacher", Jesus answered: "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19). This was so uncomfortable that Matthew, copying Mark, rewrote it: "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good" (Matt 19:17). Justin (Dialogue 101) and the Clementine Homilies quote a longer form, "One is good, my Father in heaven"; Irenaeus and Hippolytus report Gnostic groups using it; Origen (CC 5.11) has "none is good but one, God the Father", as W.L. Petersen documents. The point is not that Jesus was morally bad; Barnabas is called "a good man" (Acts 11:24). It is that Jesus reserves God's absolute goodness for God alone and refuses to share it.
Tap to enlargeW.L. Petersen: early fathers quote the saying as "One is good, my Father in heaven" (Mark 10:18 / Matt 19:17)
"The only true God". In his prayer Jesus says: "This is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent" (John 17:3). The Father is "the only true God"; Jesus is the one sent. This sentence is so clear that Augustine had to rearrange it to read "that they may know You and Jesus Christ whom You have sent as the only true God" (Tractates on John 105). The same structure appears in 1 Corinthians 8:6: "for us there is one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ".
"My God and y

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: Jesus lacked the attributes of God
briefs.thesis: God is all-knowing, cannot be tempted, does not grow, and cannot die. The Gospels show Jesus did not know the Hour, grew in wisdom, was tempted, and died.
briefs.sum: Jesus did not know the Hour, grew in wisdom, was tempted, prayed for help and died. God knows all, never changes, cannot be tempted and alone is immortal. The scribes who altered Matthew 24:36 knew how serious the problem was.

obj.q: "He limited himself voluntarily (kenosis) while on earth."
obj.a: If he set aside omniscience, then during his ministry he was not omniscient, and a being who is not omniscient is not God at that time. God cannot stop being God. And Revelation 1:1 says the revelation was given to the risen Jesus by God, so even after the resurrection he receives knowledge.

obj.q: "These limits belong to his human nature; his divine nature knew."
obj.a: Then one person both knew and did not know the Hour at the same moment, which is a contradiction in a single mind. And when Jesus said "not even the Son", he did not say "not even my human nature".

prac.q: “God can do anything, so He can become a man who doesn't know things.”
prac.a: Omnipotence means power over every possible thing, not over contradictions. "An all-knowing being who doesn't know the Hour" is a contradiction, like a square circle. God can create a man and give him knowledge; He cannot be ignorant and remain God.

briefs.evs:
Ignorance of the Hour. "Concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Mark 13:32). The verse troubled the church so much that scribes deleted "nor the Son" from the parallel in Matthew 24:36 in many manuscripts, as Metzger and Ehrman document, and Luke leaves the saying out. Ambrose claimed the phrase was an Arian interpolation; Jerome noted it was missing in some Greek copies. Later the church condemned the "Agnoetae", who taught that Christ was ignorant of some things, even though earlier fathers such as Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus and Cyril had attributed ignorance to his humanity.
Tap to enlargeMetzger & Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament: scribes dropped "nor the Son" from Matthew 24:36 to protect Jesus' divinity
Some apologists say oiden ("knows") here means "declares". No Greek lexicon gives that meaning; the context is a parable about watchfulness because no one knows; and if "know" meant "declare", the angels would be forbidden to declare it, yet in Revelation 14:6-7 an angel announces "the hour of His judgement has come". Other passages show the same limit: he went to a fig tree "to see if he could find anything on it" and found nothing because "it was not the season for figs" (Mark 11:13).
Growth. "Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature" (Luke 2:52). God does not increase in wisdom.

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: The main proof texts are textually insecure
briefs.thesis: Several of the clearest "Jesus is God" verses are later scribal changes or depend on disputed punctuation, which shows that later Christians felt the original text was not clear enough.
briefs.sum: The Johannine Comma is a late forgery, "God" in 1 Timothy 3:16 was originally "who", Acts 20:28 has variants and means "the blood of His own", and Romans 9:5 depends on modern punctuation. Each change moved toward a higher Christology.

obj.q: "The Trinity doesn't depend on the Comma; scholars agree it's spurious."
obj.a: Good, then the question becomes why it was added, and why the KJV tradition defended it for centuries. It shows that the church felt the need for an explicit text that the authentic NT does not provide.

obj.q: "There are still enough verses."
obj.a: Then the case should be made from texts like John 17:3 and Mark 10:18, which are secure and say the opposite. The fact that the direction of corruption always runs toward a "higher" Jesus is evidence about how the doctrine developed.

prac.q: “Textual variants don't change any doctrine. Every major doctrine is supported by secure texts.”
prac.a: The examples show the opposite pressure: scribes changed "who" to "God", added "these three are one", and deleted "nor the Son". Even Ehrman's The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture documents changes made for theological reasons. A text being altered to support a doctrine suggests the doctrine was not secure in the original.

briefs.evs:
1 John 5:7 (the "Johannine Comma"). "There are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one" (KJV). It is absent from every Greek manuscript before the 14th-15th centuries and from all early versions except the Latin. Modern translations remove it. It is the only verse that states the Trinity in so many words, and it is a late Latin interpolation.
1 Timothy 3:16. The KJV reads "God was manifest in the flesh". The earliest manuscripts read "who was manifested". In Greek capitals the difference is a stroke: ΟΣ ("who") became ΘΣ, the abbreviation for "God". Metzger says theos arose either through misreading OS as ΘΣ or deliberately, mainly to supply a subject for the six verbs and, less probably, for greater dogmatic precision (Textual Commentary, 2nd ed., p. 574).
Acts 20:28. "The church of God, which he obtained with his own blood". Several important manuscripts read "the church of the Lord". Even with "God", the Greek dia tou haimatos tou idiou can also be read "with the blood of His own [one]", that is His own Son, just as Romans 8:32 says God "did not spare His own Son".
Rom 9:5 is read both ways: most commentators take "God over all" of Christ, while the RSV, NEB footnote and others punctuate it as a separate doxology to the Father. The RSV reads: "…the Christ. God who is over all be blessed for ever." Paul never elsewher

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: John 1:1: "the Word was God" does not mean Jesus is the one God
briefs.thesis: John 1:1 distinguishes "the God" (ho theos) from the Word, who is "god" (theos) without the article. Early Christians, including Origen, read it as making the Word divine but subordinate, which is heresy by later standards.
briefs.sum: John 1:1 distinguishes "the God" from the Word, who is "god" without the article. Origen read the Word as derived and lesser, Philo called the Logos a "second god", and the Hebrew background is God's spoken word personified, like Wisdom in Proverbs 8.

obj.q: "Colwell's rule: a definite predicate noun before the verb can drop the article and still be definite."
obj.a: Colwell's rule says definite predicates often lack the article, not that anarthrous predicates are definite. Most grammarians now read theos here as qualitative ("divine"), not "the God". Origen, a native Greek speaker, read it as lesser.

obj.q: "Jehovah's Witnesses say 'a god', and that's polytheism."
obj.a: We do not need "a god". The point is that the verse distinguishes the Word from "the God", and the Word is God's creative speech personified. Islam affirms that Jesus is "a word from Him" (3:45; 4:171) because he was created by God's command "Be".

prac.q: “John 1:14 says the Word "became flesh", so God became man.”
prac.a: It says the Word became flesh, not "the God (ho theos)". The Quran says the same in its own way: Jesus is God's word, created by "Be" (3:59; 4:171). God's word taking effect in a human being is not God turning into a human.

briefs.evs:
The Greek. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God (ton theon, with the article), and the Word was God (theos, without the article)." Origen, the greatest Christian scholar of the 3rd century, explained the difference explicitly: John uses the article for the uncreated God, and leaves it off for the Word because the Word is "not God simply" but "god" in a derived sense, though more exalted than other "gods" (Commentary on John 2.2).
The Logos background. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish contemporary of Jesus, called the Logos "the second God" (Questions on Genesis 2.62), a divine intermediary below God, not YHWH. In the Hebrew Bible, God's "word" is His speech: "God said, let there be light" (Gen 1:3); "by the word of the LORD the heavens were made" (Ps 33:6). Proverbs 8 personifies Wisdom as a "she" who was with God and helped create, yet no one thinks Wisdom is a person of the godhead. John personifies God's creative word the same way, and that word became flesh in the sense that God's word was embodied in Jesus' life and message.
Second-century readings. Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Novatian are usually read as holding a "two-stage" Logos theology: the Word was internal to God, then at a point in time God "begot" or put forth the Word for creation. Theophilus says God "begot this Word… the first-born of all creation" (To Autolycus 2.2

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58) is not a claim to be YHWH
briefs.thesis: "I am" (ego eimi) is an ordinary Greek phrase used by other people in John; the divine name in the Greek Old Testament is a different phrase; and the context is about pre-existence or destiny, not deity.
briefs.sum: The divine name in the Greek Exodus 3:14 is ho ōn, not ego eimi. A blind man uses the same words in John 9:9, and elsewhere in John they mean "I am the Messiah". 8:58 is about Jesus' place in God's plan, not a claim to be God.

obj.q: "The Jews tried to stone him, so they knew he claimed to be God."
obj.a: The Jews in John also tried to stone him in 10:31 and said it was because he "made himself God" (10:33); his reply (10:34-36) appeals to Psalm 82 and "Son of God", not "I am God". An angry crowd's reaction is not a definition of his words.

obj.q: "It's the present tense, 'I am' instead of 'I was', implying eternity."
obj.a: Greek uses the present for a state continuing from the past ("I have been"), as in John 14:9 ("so long a time I am with you"). A few translations render 8:58 "I have been"; NRSV, ESV and NIV keep "I am".

prac.q: “Isaiah uses "I am He" (ani hu, LXX ego eimi) as God's self-declaration, so John is echoing Isaiah.”
prac.a: In Isaiah the declaration is "I am He, and there is no god besides Me" (Isa 43:10-11). If Jesus were echoing that, he would be denying any other god, including the Father he prays to. And the same phrase was used by the blind man. Echo needs more than two common words.

briefs.evs:
In the Septuagint, Exodus 3:14 reads "Ego eimi ho on" ("I am the One who is"), and the name sent to Moses is ho on. Ego eimi is also used absolutely of God in LXX Isaiah 43:10, which Trinitarians cite for John 8:58.
The healed blind man says "ego eimi" ("I am the man") in John 9:9. Nobody thinks he claims to be God.
In John, ego eimi is regularly messianic: to the Samaritan woman's "I know Messiah is coming", Jesus answers "Ego eimi, the one speaking to you" (4:26); "unless you believe that ego eimi, you will die in your sins" (8:24), explained by the purpose statement "these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ" (20:31). Mark 13:6 has "many will come in my name saying ego eimi", and Matthew 24:5 interprets it: "saying, I am the Christ".
The context is about Abraham seeing Jesus' day (8:56). At most it claims pre-existence or that he existed in God's plan, as in "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world" (Rev 13:8) and Jeremiah, known before he was formed (Jer 1:5).
Jesus bearing God's name is no proof either: in Exodus 23:21 God says of His angel, "My name is in him". Jesus says the name was given to him (John 17:11-12).

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: Thomas' "My Lord and my God" and John 17:5
briefs.thesis: Thomas' exclamation comes eleven verses after Jesus calls the Father "my God", and the "glory before the world" in John 17:5 is the standard Jewish idiom of predestination.
briefs.sum: Thomas speaks three verses after Jesus says "my God and your God", and John says the point is to believe Jesus is the Messiah. The "glory before the world" uses the NT's ordinary language of predestination, the same idiom as Quran 19:30.

obj.q: "Jesus accepted Thomas' words without correcting him."
obj.a: He responds "Have you believed because you have seen me?" (20:29), praising faith, not endorsing a theology. If Thomas meant that Jesus was the God whom Jesus had just called "my God", the text would contradict itself eleven verses apart.

obj.q: "Pre-existence is different from predestination."
obj.a: Even if one insists on real pre-existence, that makes Jesus a created heavenly being before his birth, not the uncreated God. Arians believed in pre-existence too.

prac.q: “Thomas addressed Jesus directly ("he said to him"), so it can't be an exclamation to God.”
prac.a: Exclamations are often spoken to someone ("he said to him, 'Good heavens!'"). But grant that he addressed Jesus: John 10:34-35 shows that in John's own idiom human agents of God can be called "gods" (Psalm 82:6). John's stated purpose (20:31) defines the confession as Messiah and Son of God.

briefs.evs:
John 20:28. Theodore of Mopsuestia, bishop from 392 to 428, read Thomas' words as an exclamation of praise to God at the sight of the miracle, like "My God!" today. (His reading was condemned only in 553, at the Second Council of Constantinople, which shows it had been a live Christian interpretation.) Within John, Jesus had already said that seeing him is seeing the Father because the Father does the works through him (14:9-10). And the author tells us why he included it: "that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" (20:31), not "that Jesus is God".
John 17:5, "the glory I had with You before the world existed". The NT routinely describes God's plan in the past tense: grace "was given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Tim 1:9); the Lamb "slain from the foundation of the world" (Rev 13:8); believers "chosen before the foundation of the world" (Eph 1:4) and already "seated in the heavenly places" (Eph 2:6); Christ "foreknown before the foundation of the world" (1 Pet 1:20). Augustine (Tractate 105) and others read 17:5 as the predestined glory of Jesus' human nature. In 17:22 Jesus says he has given the disciples the same glory. The Quran uses the same idiom: the infant Jesus says "He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" (19:30) of what lay in the future.

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: Philippians 2:6-11: the second Adam, not God incarnate
briefs.thesis: The hymn contrasts Jesus with Adam: Adam grasped at being like God; Jesus did not, humbled himself, and was rewarded by God with exaltation and a name. Someone who is God cannot be given exaltation.
briefs.sum: Philippians 2 contrasts Jesus' obedience with Adam's grasping, then says God exalted him and gave him a name, to the glory of the Father. Being exalted and given a name is what happens to a servant, not to God.

obj.q: "'Form of God' means he had the divine nature."
obj.a: If morphe means nature, then "form of a servant" (2:7) means he had a servant's nature, so his servanthood would be his essence. Some scholars read both as status or appearance; others read morphe theou as divine nature.

obj.q: "'The name above every name' is YHWH, so Jesus is YHWH."
obj.a: The name is given to him, and the purpose clause is the glory of the Father. Angels in Scripture carry God's name ("My name is in him", Exod 23:21) without being God.

prac.q: “Paul says Jesus "emptied himself", so he had divinity to empty.”
prac.a: The same hymn says he took "the form of a servant", and in Paul's thought Jesus gave up status and privilege, as 2 Corinthians 8:9 says ("though he was rich, he became poor"). Nothing in the hymn says he emptied himself of being God, and the climax is that God exalted him, which makes no sense if he was God all along.

briefs.evs:
Some scholars (Dunn) read the hymn against Genesis 3; others reject an Adam background. Adam was made in God's image (Gen 1:27) and grasped at being "like God" (Gen 3:5). Jesus, "being in the form (morphe) of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped", but took the form of a servant and was obedient to death (Phil 2:6-8). Morphe is the outward appearance or status; Adam also bore God's image. The point is moral: the obedient second Adam versus the disobedient first.
Then: "Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name" (2:9). The exaltation is a reward. Peter says the same: God "exalted him at His right hand" (Acts 2:33; 5:31). The whole act ends "to the glory of God the Father" (2:11), not to the glory of Jesus as God. The bowing of "every knee" echoes Isaiah 45:23, where it is directed to God; here it happens through the one God has exalted, to God's glory.

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: The "divine acts" of Jesus were done by prophets too
briefs.thesis: Worship (proskuneo), forgiving sins, walking on water, knowing hearts, judging and receiving titles like "king of kings" are all given to human beings in the Bible, so none proves deity.
briefs.sum: Homage, forgiving sins, miracles, knowing hearts, judging and royal titles are all given to prophets, kings or apostles in the Bible. Jesus himself said the Father did the works through him.

obj.q: "But Jesus did these things by his own authority, while prophets did them by God's."
obj.a: Jesus says the opposite: "the Father who dwells in me does His works" (John 14:10); "I cast out demons by the Spirit of God" (Matt 12:28); before raising Lazarus he prayed "Father, I thank You that You have heard me… so that they may believe that You sent me" (John 11:41-42).

obj.q: "Stephen prayed to Jesus (Acts 7:59)."
obj.a: Stephen saw Jesus standing at God's right hand (7:56), in a vision, and asked him to receive his spirit. The Bible calls Jesus the "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). A mediator receiving a spirit on God's behalf is not God.

prac.q: “Who but God can forgive sins? The scribes said so in Mark 2:7.”
prac.a: The scribes said that, and the crowd's conclusion was that God had given such authority "to men" (Matt 9:8). Jesus then gave the same authority to the apostles (John 20:23). The scribes' objection is not the Gospel's teaching.

briefs.evs:
Homage. Proskuneo is given to King David (1 Chr 29:20, LXX) and to Joseph's brothers bowing to him (Gen 42:6).
Forgiving sins. After Jesus forgives the paralytic, the crowd "glorified God, who had given such authority to men" (Matt 9:8). Jesus gives the same power to the disciples: "if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven" (John 20:23).
Walking on water. Peter walked on water at Jesus' command (Matt 14:29); Moses parted the sea and Elisha made iron float (2 Kgs 6:6).
Raising the dead. Elijah (1 Kgs 17) and Elisha (2 Kgs 4) raised the dead; Elisha's bones raised a man (2 Kgs 13:21). The Quran says Jesus raised the dead "by Allah's permission" (5:110).
Knowing hearts. Samuel knew Saul's thoughts (1 Sam 9:19-20), Ahijah knew the disguised queen (1 Kgs 14:6), Elisha knew what the king of Aram said in his bedroom (2 Kgs 6:12).
Judging. "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son… because he is the son of man" (John 5:22, 27). The apostles will sit on twelve thrones judging Israel (Matt 19:28).
Titles. "King of kings" is used of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 2:37; Ezek 26:7). "First and last" in Revelation is spoken by the risen Jesus (1:17-18; 22:13), though Isaiah 44:6 gives the same title to YHWH.
Hebrews 1:8 "Your throne, O God". It quotes Psalm 45:6, a royal wedding psalm addressed to the human king of Israel, who is then told "God, your God, has anointed y

briefs.sec: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
briefs.title: The Gospels' own prophecy citations create problems for a divine Jesus
briefs.thesis: Several Old Testament passages the Gospels apply to Jesus, read in context, describe a sinner or a false prophet, which no Christian can accept of God.
briefs.sum: Zechariah 13:7, Psalm 41:9 and Hosea 11:1, read in context, describe a false prophet, a sinner and an idolatrous son. The Gospels' use of them shows their prophecy method ignores context.
briefs.caution: This is a rhetorical, turn-the-tables argument. Use it to show the problems with Christian proof-texting from the OT, not as a claim about Jesus, whom Muslims honour as a sinless prophet.

obj.q: "Typology applies only part of a passage."
obj.a: Then the Gospel writers chose passages about sinful figures to prove their claims. Either context matters, in which case the passages do not fit, or it doesn't, in which case they prove nothing about Jesus.

prac.q: “You are insulting Jesus.”
prac.a: No, I am showing that the Gospel writers' method of citing the Old Testament does not work. Muslims believe Jesus was sinless. It is the Christian proof-texts, read in context, that would call him a sinner.

briefs.evs:
Matthew 26:31 applies Zechariah 13:7 ("strike the shepherd") to Jesus. The verses just before (13:3-6) are about false prophets wounded "in the house of my friends".
John 13:18 applies Psalm 41:9 ("he who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me") to Judas and Jesus. The speaker of that psalm says, "heal me, for I have sinned against You" (41:4).
Matthew 2:15 applies Hosea 11:1 ("out of Egypt I called my son") to Jesus. Hosea's "son" is Israel, which in the next verse "kept sacrificing to the Baals" (11:2).

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: The Hebrew Bible teaches one God who is a single person
briefs.thesis: The Old Testament speaks of God with singular pronouns and verbs thousands of times, says He created "alone, by Myself", and was never read as triune by the people it was given to.
briefs.sum: The Shema, "by Myself" (Isa 44:24) and "no other besides Me" (Isa 45:5) teach one God who is one person. Jesus affirmed the Shema, Jews never saw a Trinity, and Christian scholars admit the doctrine is not in the Old Testament.

obj.q: "Echad can mean a compound unity, like 'one flesh' (Gen 2:24) or 'one cluster'."
obj.a: The compound idea comes from the noun ("flesh", "cluster"), not from echad. "One flesh" is one flesh, not three persons. In the Shema, echad describes God Himself, and the rest of the Bible says He made things "alone".

obj.q: "Progressive revelation: God revealed the Trinity later."
obj.a: Revelation can add, but it cannot contradict. If God told Israel for 1,500 years that He is one and alone, and then revealed that He is three persons, the earlier revelation misled everyone who received it. That is not progress but reversal.

prac.q: “Jews didn't understand the Old Testament properly; that's why they rejected Jesus.”
prac.a: Then God spoke to Israel for centuries in a way that no one in Israel, prophet or scribe, understood. Even Jesus' own disciples in Acts call him "a man attested by God". It is more reasonable that the Jews understood their own scripture on its most basic point: who God is.

briefs.evs:
The Shema. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one (echad)" (Deut 6:4). Echad is the ordinary Hebrew numeral "one": "God took one of his ribs" (Gen 2:21). The scholar S.R. Driver explains that the verse contrasts the one LORD with the many local Baals; it is about number, not a "compound unity".
Alone. "I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by Myself" (Isa 44:24). "I am the LORD and there is no other; besides Me there is no God" (Isa 45:5). "Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?" (Mal 2:10).
Jesus' own Shema. When asked which commandment is first, Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 6:4 and the scribe replied, "You are right, Teacher, He is one and there is no other besides Him", and Jesus said he was "not far from the kingdom of God" (Mark 12:29-34).
Christian concessions. The Catholic Encyclopedia says the doctrine of the Trinity is not clearly revealed in the Old Testament, though Augustine and other Fathers read hints of it there. Rabbinic Judaism has consistently rejected it.

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: By Deuteronomy 13, a Trinitarian Jesus would be a false prophet
briefs.thesis: The Torah tests every prophet: even if he works signs, if he calls Israel to a god they "have not known", he is false. A Jesus who demanded worship of himself as a divine Son would fail that test, so Christians must choose between the Trinity and the Torah.
briefs.sum: Deuteronomy 13 says even a miracle-working prophet is false if he calls to a god Israel had not known. Israel never knew a triune God, so a Trinitarian Jesus would fail the Torah's own test. The Muslim Jesus, who called to the one God, passes it.

obj.q: "It's not 'another god'; it's the same God more fully revealed."
obj.a: Israel knew God as one person, "He". A God who is three persons, one of whom is a man to be worshipped, is a different object of worship from the one Israel knew. Deuteronomy's phrase is "gods you have not known", and Israel had not known this one.

obj.q: "Jesus' miracles prove he was a true prophet."
obj.a: Deuteronomy 13 explicitly anticipates that a false prophet may perform signs. That is why the content of the message is the test.

prac.q: “Islam also brought something new: Muhammad. Doesn't he fail Deuteronomy 13?”
prac.a: No. He called to the God Israel knew: one, without partner, the God of Abraham and Moses. Deuteronomy 13 forbids new gods, not new prophets; Deuteronomy 18:18 promises a new prophet. Muhammad passes the test the Trinity fails.

briefs.evs:
The test in Deuteronomy 13 is decisive because it explicitly says signs are not enough: "If a prophet arises among you… and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign comes to pass, and he says, 'Let us go after other gods which you have not known'… you shall not listen to the words of that prophet" (13:1-3). The criterion is continuity with the God Israel already knew.
Jesus himself defines that God: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews" (John 4:22, to the Samaritan). The God "we know" is the God of the Jews, who is one person. And he identifies the Father as the God the Jews claim: "It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God'" (John 8:54).
This argument puts the Christian in a dilemma. Either the Trinity is a new revelation, in which case it introduces a God Israel did not know and fails Deuteronomy 13; or it is not new, in which case it should be visible in the Old Testament, and the rest of this section shows it is not.

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: The Angel of the LORD is God's messenger, not God
briefs.thesis: When the Angel of the LORD speaks in the first person for God, he is doing what every messenger in the ancient world did: speaking in the voice of the one who sent him.
briefs.sum: Messengers speak in their sender's voice; the Angel is sent, says "declares the LORD", and refuses offerings for himself; God appears face to face only to Moses (Num 12). Stephen calls the bush figure an angel.

obj.q: "In Exodus 3 the angel says 'I am the God of Abraham'."
obj.a: That is first-person agency, exactly as the prophet in Judges 6 says "I brought you up from Egypt". Acts 7:30-35 says it was an angel through whom God spoke.

obj.q: "The angel accepts worship and sacrifice (Judges 13)."
obj.a: In Judges 13:16 the angel tells Manoah: "If you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD". He refuses the offering for himself.

prac.q: “The Angel of the LORD disappears after Jesus is born, which shows he was the pre-incarnate Christ.”
prac.a: An "angel of the Lord" appears repeatedly in the NT after Jesus' birth: to Joseph (Matt 1:20, 2:13), the shepherds (Luke 2:9), Peter in prison (Acts 12:7). He did not disappear.

briefs.evs:
First-person agency is normal. A prophet in Judges 6:8-10 says "Thus says the LORD… I brought you up from Egypt". David's messengers speak to Abigail in David's name, and she bows to them and calls herself David's servant (1 Sam 25:40-41). Abner's messengers speak in the first person for Abner (2 Sam 3:12). In Genesis 22:15-16 the angel says "By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD", which is quoting God, not being Him.
God's appearance is limited. In Numbers 12:6-8 God says He reveals Himself to prophets only in visions and dreams, but to Moses "mouth to mouth". Yet the Angel of the LORD appears physically to Hagar, Gideon, Manoah and his wife, and others. If the Angel were God, God would be appearing face to face to many, contradicting Numbers 12.
The NT reads it as an angel. Stephen says that at the burning bush "an angel appeared to him in the flame of fire", through whom God spoke (Acts 7:30-35). Agency also explains the switch between 2 Samuel 24:1 (the LORD incited David) and 1 Chronicles 21:1 (Satan incited David): the act of an agent can be ascribed to the one who allows or sends it.
The usual "divine" features are shared. "Obey his voice… My name is in him" (Exod 23:21): God's name is placed in Jerusalem, the Temple and Israel (Jer 14:9) too. People bow to him: they also bow to David and Joseph, and Jacob tells Esau "seeing your face is like seeing the face of God"

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: Plural words ("Elohim", "Let us") do not mean plural persons
briefs.thesis: Hebrew uses plurals for majesty and excellence, and God addresses His heavenly court. If "Let us" proved three persons, the same reasoning would make many humans plural.
briefs.sum: Elohim is used for Moses and a pagan god and takes singular verbs for God; "Let us" is addressed to the heavenly court and followed by "His image"; the three visitors are angels (Gen 19:1). None of these teaches three persons.

obj.q: "God can't be addressing angels, because man is made in God's image, not angels' image."
obj.a: Verse 27 says God created man "in His image", singular, showing the image is God's alone. Including the court in the announcement of a royal decree is natural.

obj.q: "Plural of majesty didn't exist in early Hebrew."
obj.a: It doesn't need to be a grammatical rule; the Bible shows plural words used for one person (Exod 7:1, 1 Sam 28:13, Isa 54:5) and kings using "we". And even if "us" were plural persons, it gives no number three.

prac.q: “"Let us" shows more than one person in God, and nothing else in creation could be God's co-creator.”
prac.a: The next verse says "God created man in His image", singular, and Isaiah 44:24 says God made all things "alone, by Myself". If "us" meant co-creators, Isaiah would be false. A council being addressed is not a council creating.

briefs.evs:
"Elohim" with singular verbs. In Genesis 1:1, Elohim takes a singular verb (bara, "He created"). The same word is used for Moses: "I have made you elohim to Pharaoh" (Exod 7:1), for a single pagan god (Chemosh, Judges 11:24), and for the ghost of Samuel, with a plural verb (1 Sam 28:13).
Plurals of majesty and excellence. "Remember your Creators" (Eccl 12:1, a plural form in Hebrew); "your Makers is your Husbands" (Isa 54:5, plural forms for one God). Kings speak this way: King Artaxerxes writes "the letter you sent us" (Ezra 4:18).
"Let us make man" (Gen 1:26). Many Jewish and some Christian commentators read this as God addressing the heavenly court, which the Bible describes elsewhere: "the sons of God shouted for joy" at creation (Job 38:7), "the host of heaven standing beside Him" (1 Kgs 22:19). Isaiah 6:8 has the same shift: "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" The very next verse (Gen 1:27) is singular: "God created man in His image". And Isaiah 44:24 says He made everything "alone".

The three men visit Abraham (Gen 18). Two of the three are explicitly called "the two angels" when they arrive in Sodom (Gen 19:1). Augustine (City of God 16.29) read all three as angels, and Hebrews 13:2 alludes to it: "some have entertained angels unawares". Abraham bows to

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: Psalms 45 and 110 are about Israel's king
briefs.thesis: "Your throne, O God" (Ps 45:6) and "The LORD said to my lord" (Ps 110:1) are royal psalms about the human king, who has a God above him.
briefs.sum: Psalm 45 is a wedding song to the king, whose God anoints him; Psalm 110 has YHWH speaking to "my lord", a title for humans, with every detail fitting David's dynasty.

obj.q: "Jesus used Psalm 110 to show the Messiah is more than David's son (Mark 12:35-37)."
obj.a: At most that shows the Messiah is greater than David, which Muslims accept of Jesus as a great prophet. It does not show he is YHWH; YHWH is the one speaking to him.

obj.q: "The vowel points that make it 'adoni' were added later by the Masoretes."
obj.a: True, but every ancient reading tradition, including the Septuagint's to kyrio mou ("to my lord"), distinguishes the speaker YHWH from the one addressed. Two parties are present whatever the vowels.

prac.q: “Hebrews 1:8 applies Psalm 45 to Jesus and calls him God.”
prac.a: Hebrews quotes the whole passage, including "God, your God, has anointed you" (Heb 1:9). Even in Hebrews, the one addressed has a God above him, so the application proves subordination, not deity.

briefs.evs:
Psalm 45. Its own heading calls it a love song for the king's wedding. The king is praised for his beauty, his sword and his bride. Verse 6, "Your throne, O God, is forever", is followed by "God, your God, has anointed you above your companions" (v. 7). The king has a God over him. Elohim is used for human rulers (Exod 7:1; Ps 82:6), and Solomon sat on "the throne of the LORD" (1 Chr 29:23). Robert Alter translates it "your throne of God", and the NRSV Study Bible notes that the king is nowhere else called God.
Psalm 110. "YHWH said to adoni: sit at my right hand till I make your enemies your footstool." In the Masoretic text, adoni is used throughout the Hebrew Bible for human lords (Sarah calls Abraham adoni; subjects call the king adoni), while God is Adonai. The details fit a Davidic king: enemies made a footstool (David in 2 Sam 22:39-41; "the LORD put them under the soles of his feet", 1 Kgs 5:3), the right hand as a place of honour (Bathsheba at Solomon's right hand, 1 Kgs 2:19), and priestly acts by David (he wore the ephod, offered sacrifices and blessed the people, 2 Sam 6:13-18). Herbert Bateman argues Psalm 110 is a royal psalm about the Davidic king, though he concludes the NT shows Jesus is also divine Lord.
