briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: Isaiah 9:6, 48:16 and 63:9
briefs.thesis: The "Mighty God" child, the speaker "sent with His Spirit", and the "angel of His presence" are each explained by their context and by ancient readings without a Trinity.
briefs.sum: Isaiah 9:6 is a royal name and, read literally, would make the Son the Father; 48:16 has a speaker "sent with His Spirit"; 63:9 in the Septuagint says no messenger but God saved them.

obj.q: "Only God is called 'El Gibbor' in Isaiah 10:21."
obj.a: In 10:21 it describes God, but names that describe God are given to humans throughout the Bible. The question is whether the verse says the child is El Gibbor or is named with it, and Hebrew naming practice favours the second.

obj.q: "Isaiah 9:7 says his kingdom will have no end."
obj.a: God promises the same to David's line: "your throne shall be established forever" (2 Sam 7:16), which no one takes to mean David's sons are God.

prac.q: “Muslims can't explain why a mere child would be called "Mighty God".”
prac.a: Hebrew names routinely carry God's name and describe God: Elijah, "my God is YHWH". By the same logic Elijah would be God. The Septuagint, the oldest translation, didn't even render it as "Mighty God".

briefs.evs:
Isaiah 9:6. "His name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God (El Gibbor), Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." Hebrew names often contain God's name or describe God: Elijah means "my God is YHWH", Jehu "YHWH is he". Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and the JPS 1985 Tanakh, read the names as describing God: "the Mighty God is planning grace; the Eternal Father, a peaceable ruler". The Septuagint renders it "his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel". The phrase el gibbor is used in the plural of human warriors (eilei gibborim, "chiefs of the mighty", Ezek 32:21, from ayil rather than el, so only a weak parallel). Scholars such as John Hayes read the names as royal coronation titles of the kind given to Egyptian kings, applied to a Judean king (Hezekiah fits the context, 2 Kgs 18-20). And note: if the child is "Everlasting Father", the verse would make the Son the Father, which Trinitarians deny.
Isaiah 48:16. "The Lord GOD has sent me, and His Spirit." The speaker in context is the prophet, or the one God called (Cyrus, 44:28-45:1). The verb "sent" is singular, and some translators (NET, Goldingay) render "sent me with his Spirit"; NRSV and ESV read "sent me and his spirit". Sudden changes of speaker are common in the prophets.
Isaiah 63:9-10. The Hebrew says "the angel of His presence saved them… but they rebelled and grieved His holy spirit". The parallel suggests the angel

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: Daniel, Micah, Zechariah and Malachi
briefs.thesis: The "son of the gods" in Daniel 3, the "son of man" in Daniel 7, the ruler from Bethlehem in Micah 5:2 and the speakers in Zechariah are angels or human figures, not God.
briefs.sum: Daniel 3:25's figure is an angel (3:28); Daniel 7's son of man receives dominion that also goes to the saints; Micah 5:2's ruler has "origins"; Zechariah's speaker is "sent"; Malachi's messenger is Elijah. None is God.

obj.q: "Only God rides the clouds, so the son of man is divine."
obj.a: The figure comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days; he is brought, not enthroned by right. Clouds also accompany angels (Rev 10:1).

obj.q: "Jesus identified himself with the son of man."
obj.a: Muslims accept Jesus as a figure of honour exalted by God. Daniel 7 has him receive dominion from God, which supports the Muslim view.

prac.q: “Micah 5:2 says the ruler is "from everlasting", so he is eternal.”
prac.a: The Hebrew mi-yemei 'olam means "from ancient days", the same phrase used for David's time (Amos 9:11). And the word before it is "origins", which no eternal being has.

briefs.evs:
Daniel 3:25. Nebuchadnezzar sees a fourth figure "like a son of the gods" (Aramaic bar elahin), then explains in verse 28: God "sent His angel and delivered His servants".
Daniel 7:13-14. One "like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom that all peoples "serve". God gave the same to Nebuchadnezzar: "the God of heaven has given you the kingdom… all peoples… shall serve him" (Dan 2:37-38; Jer 27:6-7). And Daniel's own interpretation says the kingdom is given "to the people of the saints of the Most High" (7:27). The Aramaic verb for "serve" (pelach) is used of serving in the Temple (Ezra 7:24) and of serving humans (Targum of Gen 27:29).
Micah 5:2 can be read as "origins" or "goings forth" from of old. "Days of old" describes David's era elsewhere ("I will raise up the booth of David… as in the days of old", Amos 9:11): the ruler comes from David's ancient line.
Zechariah 2:8-11. The speaker says "you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me", the same formula that validates the prophet in Zechariah 4:9. A sent one is not the sender.
Malachi 3:1. "I send My messenger to prepare the way before Me." Malachi 4:5 names him: Elijah, whom Jesus identifies with John the Baptist (Matt 11:14). Mark 1:2-3 merges this with Isaiah 40:3 and Exodus 23:20.

briefs.sec: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
briefs.title: The Quran's method with earlier scripture is the Church's own
briefs.thesis: Christians accuse the Quran of picking and choosing from earlier scripture, but the early church judged non-canonical books the same way: true in parts, false in others, tested against a standard.
briefs.sum: Serapion, Augustine, Athanasius and Clement all judged writings as partly true and partly false by a standard. The Quran's muhaymin role uses the same method.

obj.q: "The church tested books against apostolic teaching; you test the Bible against a later book."
obj.a: Every tradition tests by its highest authority. For Christians it was the rule of faith; for Muslims it is the final revelation. The method is the same.

prac.q: “You only accept the parts of the Bible that agree with you. That's cherry-picking.”
prac.a: Serapion did the same with the Gospel of Peter, and Augustine with the apocrypha. Judging a mixed text by a reliable standard is not cherry-picking; it is the only honest way to handle a text that has both truth and additions.

briefs.evs:
Bishop Serapion of Antioch (c. 200) said of the Gospel of Peter that "most of it belongs to the true teaching of the Saviour, but some things are additions" (Eusebius, Church History 6.12).
Augustine (City of God 15.23) said the apocrypha contain "some truth" but much falsehood.
The NT itself quotes non-canonical sources: Jude 14 quotes the Book of Enoch as genuine prophecy; Acts 20:35 quotes a saying of Jesus not found in the Gospels. John says much of what Jesus did is not written (John 21:25).
Athanasius' Festal Letter 39 (367) classed books into canon, books to read for instruction, and apocrypha.
Clement of Alexandria engaged with the Gospel of the Egyptians, judging it by "the rule of the Gospel".

briefs.title: Mainstream scholars agree the New Testament does not teach the Trinity
briefs.thesis: Christian and secular scholars broadly agree that Jesus did not teach the Trinity, that no NT writer held it consciously, and that it was formulated in the 4th century.
briefs.sum: Hanson, Lamson, Matthews, Whiteley, Hurtado and the Stanford Encyclopedia agree: Jesus did not teach the Trinity and no NT writer held it. Schoeps concluded the original Jewish Christianity survived in Islam.

obj.q: "The doctrine is implicit even if the word isn't there."
obj.a: Many doctrines can be implicit, but this one contradicts explicit texts (John 17:3; 1 Cor 8:6; Mark 10:18). And scholars like Hanson do not say "implicit but not explicit"; they say no NT writer held it.

obj.q: "These are liberal scholars."
obj.a: Hanson, Matthews and Prestige were Anglican churchmen. Hurtado was an evangelical. They concede this against interest.

prac.q: “The word "Trinity" isn't in the Bible, but neither is "tawhid" in the Quran.”
prac.a: The Quran states tawhid's content directly: "Say, He is Allah, One" (112:1); "do not say three" (4:171). The NT never states the Trinity's content: three co-equal, co-eternal persons in one being. The issue is the concept, not the word.

briefs.evs:
A.T. Hanson (Anglican theologian): "No responsible New Testament scholar would claim that the doctrine of the Trinity was taught by Jesus, or preached by the earliest Christians, or consciously held by any writer in the New Testament" (The Image of the Invisible God, p. 87).
Tap to enlarge"No responsible New Testament scholar would claim that the doctrine of the Trinity was taught by Jesus"
The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ("Trinity") notes that theologians of the first three centuries were not trinitarian in the later sense.
Alvan Lamson, The Church of the First Three Centuries (p. 341): the modern doctrine of the Trinity is not found in any document of the first three centuries.
W.R. Matthews, Dean of St Paul's, said Paul would not have understood the doctrine.
D.E.H. Whiteley: for Jews, including Paul, God was one person.
Larry Hurtado holds that devotion to Jesus as a divine figure arose remarkably early among Jewish followers after Jesus' death, and that most historians doubt Jesus openly claimed to be God.
G.L. Prestige noted that the early Greek trias was often a ranked list (God, His Logos, His Spirit), while defending the continuity of the later doctrine.
H.J. Schoeps, a scholar of Jewish Christianity, concluded that Jewish Christianity "disappeared within the church but was preserved in Islam".

briefs.title: The early church fathers were not Trinitarians
briefs.thesis: Nearly every major Christian writer before Nicaea taught that the Son was subordinate to the Father, came into existence by the Father's will, or was in some sense created. By the standard of 381 they were heretics.
briefs.sum: From 1 Clement to Eusebius, the early fathers called the Father "God alone", said the Son was begotten by will, that there was a time when he was not, and that only the Father is uncreated. Tertullian even admits most believers thought his Trinity meant two or three gods.

obj.q: "They were working out the language; their faith was Trinitarian."
obj.a: Justin, Tertullian and Origen did not merely lack the words; they explicitly affirmed what Nicaea condemned: the Son begotten by will, a time when the Son was not, the Father alone uncreated. That is a different belief, not imprecise wording for the same one.

obj.q: "Gregory Thaumaturgus wrote a fully Trinitarian creed in the 3rd century."
obj.a: Scholars regard its Trinitarian articles as later: Moreschini and Norelli date the last two articles to the 4th century, Basil never cites them, and the Arabic text of the related treatise On the Trinity is classed as spurious (CPG 1787). Gregory's own teacher, Origen, contradicts it.

prac.q: “The heretics were Arius and his followers. The fathers before them were orthodox.”
prac.a: Measured by Nicene orthodoxy, Justin's "another God subject to the Maker", Tertullian's "a time when the Son was not" and Origen's "do not pray to Christ" are exactly Arian positions. Arius did not invent subordinationism; he defended the older view.

briefs.evs:
1 Clement 59:4 (c. 96), among the earliest Christian writings outside the NT: "that all nations may know that You alone are God, and that Jesus Christ is Your servant/child (pais)".
Ignatius (c. 110): Jesus is "Son of God according to the will and power of God" (Smyrnaeans 1). The later "long recension" of his letters inflates his Christology. Newman wrote that, judged only by their express statements, "Ignatius may be considered a Patripassian, Justin arianizes, and Hippolytus is a Photinian", and used this to argue the Fathers' words were incomplete, not heretical.
The Shepherd of Hermas (2nd century): the Son is exalted for his obedience, and the Holy Spirit is identified with the Son.
Justin Martyr (c. 150): the Logos is "another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things" (Dialogue 56), begotten "by an act of the Father's will" (Dialogue 61, 128), and the Father cannot appear on earth while the Son can (Dialogue 127). In 1 Apology 6 Justin names the host of good angels in a sentence scholars debate (some read it as angels being honoured, not worshipped). The Catholic Encyclopedia speaks of his "unfortunate concepts of the temporal and voluntary generation of the Word, and subordinationism".

briefs.title: The Holy Spirit's divinity was undecided until 381
briefs.thesis: As late as 380, Christian thinkers disagreed on whether the Holy Spirit was God, a creature or a divine power. Its co-equal status was decided by a council and enforced by imperial law.
briefs.sum: Around 380, Gregory of Nazianzus reported that Christian scholars called the Spirit an activity, a creature, God, or were undecided. The doctrine was settled in 381 and enforced by imperial decree.

obj.q: "The Spirit speaks and can be grieved (Eph 4:30), so it's a person."
obj.a: Wisdom also speaks and calls out in Proverbs 8, and blood "cries out" in Genesis 4:10. Personification is common. Besides, if personal language proves a person, Gabriel fits the description perfectly, as the Quran says.

obj.q: "Matthew 28:19 names the Spirit with Father and Son."
obj.a: Listing is not equality (1 Tim 5:21 lists God, Christ and the angels), and the authenticity of the triadic baptismal formula as a saying of Jesus is questioned by some scholars, although every extant manuscript contains it (see Corruption of the Bible).

prac.q: “If the Spirit's deity wasn't clear until 381, why do Christians say it's in the Bible?”
prac.a: Exactly the right question. Gregory's own testimony shows that the Bible did not settle it for the best-read Christians of his day; a council did.

briefs.evs:
Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the architects of the doctrine, says plainly: "Of the wise men among ourselves, some have conceived of Him as an Activity, some as a Creature, some as God, and some have been uncertain which to call Him" (Oration 31.5, c. 380). The Council of Constantinople (381) confessed the Spirit as "Lord and giver of life... worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son" without calling him "God" in so many words, and Theodosius' edicts enforced that faith.
Earlier, Lactantius denied that the Spirit was a distinct person (Jerome, Letter 84), and the Shepherd of Hermas identified the Spirit with the Son. Biblically, Paul compares the Spirit of God to a man's own spirit inside him: "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God" (1 Cor 2:11). A man's spirit is not a second person alongside him. In Hebrew parallelism the Spirit is God's breath and power (Ps 33:6; Job 33:4), and in the Quran al-Ruh al-Qudus is the angel Gabriel (16:102).

briefs.title: The doctrine is logically incoherent
briefs.thesis: The Trinity claims that the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, the three are distinct, and there is only one God. These claims cannot all be true together under the ordinary meaning of "is".
briefs.sum: If the Father is God and the Son is God and God is one, then the Father is the Son, which the doctrine denies. Each escape route leads to modalism, tritheism or an impersonal God. Christian thinkers admit it is beyond reason; the Quran says God is simply One.

obj.q: "Finite minds can't understand an infinite God."
obj.a: Agreed that we can't understand God fully, but we can know that contradictions are false. If finite minds cannot judge the Trinity, they also cannot judge it to be true. The Quran does not ask us to believe contradictions.

obj.q: "Three persons share one essence, like three humans share humanity."
obj.a: Three humans who share humanity are three humans. That analogy produces three gods.

obj.q: "The Trinity is like water: ice, liquid, steam."
obj.a: That is modalism (one thing in three states), which the church condemned. Most analogies end up as either modalism or tritheism.

prac.q: “God is love, and love needs another person, so God must be more than one person.”
prac.a: Then God needs something to be complete, which makes Him dependent, and the Trinity would need three persons for no reason: two would satisfy "love needs another". Allah's love is expressed in creating and showing mercy, without needing anything (Al-Ghani, the Self-Sufficient).

briefs.evs:
The classical statement of the problem is the "logical problem of the Trinity". Christian philosophers have proposed solutions, such as "relative identity" (the Father is the same God as the Son but not the same person). Critics point out that relative identity abandons the normal logic of identity, and that God has properties that should transfer under identity: if the Father begot and the Son did not, they differ in a property, so they cannot be identical to the same thing.
The incarnation adds a second problem. God is immutable: "I the LORD do not change" (Mal 3:6). If the Logos took on a human nature at a point in time, something about the Logos changed. If nothing changed, it is unclear what "became flesh" means.
Christian thinkers have often conceded the point. Luther admitted that the Trinity and two natures are beyond and contrary to reason, to be accepted on faith. The church calls the doctrine a "mystery". But a mystery is something we cannot fully understand; a contradiction is something that cannot be true. The Quran's challenge is simple: "Say, He is Allah, One" (112:1), and "had there been gods besides Allah in the heavens and earth, they would have been ruined" (21:22).

briefs.title: What the Quran actually claims
briefs.thesis: The Quran denies that Jesus was killed or crucified, says the event was made to appear so, and says Allah raised him. This answers the Jewish boast and notes that the Christians themselves were "in doubt".
briefs.sum: The Quran answers a boast that "we killed the Messiah": he was not killed or crucified, it was made to appear so, and Allah raised him. It says those who differ over the event follow conjecture.

obj.q: "God deceived everyone, which is immoral."
obj.a: God protected His messenger from his enemies, as He did Lot and Abraham. Those who plotted to kill him were the ones deceived about their success; the Quran calls it Allah's plan against their plan (3:54). Jesus' followers were not commanded to believe anything false; the later doctrine of the cross was built on assumption, as the verse says.

obj.q: "Why would God let Christianity be built on a mistake for 600 years?"
obj.a: The early Jesus movement was not uniformly built on the cross (see the next arguments), and the Quran came to settle the disagreement. Every prophet came to correct errors that had grown up after the previous one.

prac.q: “If 4:157 is true, God founded Christianity on a deception.”
prac.a: The deception was of the plotters, who thought they had won. Christianity's doctrine of atonement was built by later teachers, mainly Paul, on top of what was "made to appear". The Quran says the people who disputed it were following conjecture, and the earliest records show exactly that dispute.

briefs.evs:
The passage (4:153-158) is a list of the crimes of a group of the Children of Israel: breaking the covenant, killing prophets, slandering Mary with "a great calumny" (4:156), and saying "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of Allah". The Babylonian Talmud has a late tradition that "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu" (Sanhedrin 43a), though scholars debate its date and reliability, and slanders about Mary appear in the same literature (Shabbat 104b; Sanhedrin 67a).
Shubbiha lahum means "it was made to look like that to them". Commentators differ on how: one view is that another man was given his likeness (the substitution view), another that the scene was confused and people thought he had died. Both fit the text. The phrase "those who differ over it are in doubt" fits the Christians, who in the first centuries disagreed sharply about what happened at the cross (see below).

briefs.title: The earliest Jesus sources say nothing of the crucifixion or resurrection
briefs.thesis: The oldest reconstructable layers of the Jesus tradition (the Q sayings source, the Gospel of Thomas, the Epistle of James) have no passion narrative and no resurrection, and the passion predictions in the Gospels look like later additions.
briefs.sum: Q, Thomas and James have no passion or resurrection; Mark originally ended without any appearance; and the disciples act as if Jesus never predicted his death. The cross-centred message developed later.

obj.q: "Q is a sayings collection; you wouldn't expect a narrative."
obj.a: That is the point: the earliest followers preserved Jesus' teaching, and his teaching did not centre on a coming atoning death. If the cross were the core of the message, it would appear among the sayings.

obj.q: "Mark 16:8 implies the resurrection through the empty tomb."
obj.a: An empty tomb is exactly what the Quran's account produces: Jesus was raised. It is not evidence of a death followed by resurrection.

prac.q: “Paul's creed in 1 Corinthians 15 dates to within a few years of the crucifixion, so the belief is early.”
prac.a: Early belief is consistent with the Quran: it appeared so to them. But the creed has its own problems: it names "the Twelve" when Judas was dead, omits the women and the empty tomb, and its witnesses (like the 500) are unnamed. Paul's own "appearance" was a light and a voice (Acts 26:13-19).

briefs.evs:
Q. The sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke has no passion narrative and no resurrection, though it mentions bearing a cross (Q 14:27) and the killing of prophets.
The Gospel of Thomas, 114 sayings of Jesus, has no account of the crucifixion and no resurrection appearances.
The Epistle of James, traditionally attributed to Jesus' brother (a point many scholars dispute), never mentions the cross, the resurrection or atonement.
Mark's ending. The earliest manuscripts of Mark (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) end at 16:8: the women flee from the empty tomb "and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid". There is no appearance of the risen Jesus. Verses 9-20 were added later.
Passion predictions. Jesus predicts his death and rising on the third day again and again (Mark 8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34). Yet at his arrest the disciples flee, no one goes to the tomb expecting a resurrection, the women bring spices to anoint a corpse, and the disciples dismiss the women's report as "nonsense" (Luke 24:11). That behaviour makes sense only if the predictions were not made. Bultmann and some others regard the detailed predictions as written after the fact; many scholars accept that Jesus expected a violent death. The Oxford Bible Commentary on Mark says they "owe a lot to later Christian creativity".

briefs.title: Early followers of Jesus disputed the crucifixion
briefs.thesis: From the time of Paul onward, some Christians denied that Jesus died on the cross or said someone else was crucified, which is the "doubt" the Quran mentions.
briefs.sum: Paul, Ignatius and Polycarp argued against Christians who denied the crucifixion; Basilides, the Seth treatise and the Mandaeans said Jesus was not crucified; Allison admits some early believers thought he only seemed to die.

obj.q: "These were Gnostics who thought matter was evil; nothing like Islam."
obj.a: Basilides and the Seth treatise were Gnostic, but in Philadelphians 8 Ignatius' opponents appealed to "the archives" (the Jewish scriptures), though that dispute is about scriptural authority, not the crucifixion, which is a Jewish-Christian argument. The Quran agrees with none of the Gnostic metaphysics; it agrees only that the crucifixion was a matter of dispute and appearance.

obj.q: "These groups are late and marginal."
obj.a: Paul's opponents are mid-1st century and Ignatius' early 2nd century; the Seth treatise is 3rd century.

prac.q: “Every serious historian accepts the crucifixion.”
prac.a: Historians accept that Jesus' followers believed he was crucified, and the Quran says it was made to appear so. But "every historian" is not the same as "every early Christian": the records of Paul, Ignatius and Polycarp show Christians who denied or doubted it within living memory.

briefs.evs:
Paul's opponents. Paul calls a crucified Christ "a stumbling block to Jews" (1 Cor 1:23), though that verse does not say anyone denied the crucifixion. He says believers turn away from his message of Christ crucified (Gal 3:1), and speaks of "enemies of the cross of Christ" (Phil 3:18). His opponents preached "another Jesus" (2 Cor 11:4).
Tap to enlargeNIV Study Bible on 2 Corinthians 11: Paul's opponents preached "another Jesus"
Ignatius (d. c. 110) refers to Christ's death, "which some deny" (Magnesians 9), and to people who said he "only seemed to suffer" (Trallians 10; Smyrnaeans 2). In Philadelphians 8 he records an argument with people who said: "If I don't find it in the archives (the original documents), I don't believe it in the gospel." When Ignatius replied "it is written", they answered "that is the question". Scholars like Myllykoski argue these opponents were Jewish Christians, not Greek dualists.
Polycarp: "whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is of the devil" (Philippians 7.1), which only makes sense if some did not.
Basilides (early 2nd century), as reported by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4): Simon of Cyrene was crucified in Jesus' likeness while Jesus stood by. Hippolytus' account differs.
The Second Treatise of the Great Seth (Nag Hammadi): "It was another… Simon, who bore the cross on his shoulder… I was laughing."

briefs.title: The "independent" non-Christian witnesses are late, dependent or doctored
briefs.thesis: The non-Christian sources cited for the crucifixion (Josephus, Tacitus, Thallus, Mara bar Serapion) are either interpolated, report what Christians believed decades later, or do not mention Jesus at all.
briefs.sum: Josephus' passage was rewritten by Christians and is unknown before Eusebius; Tacitus writes 80 years later about Christian belief; Thallus and Mara say nothing about Jesus' crucifixion. They show what people believed, which the Quran grants.

obj.q: "Even sceptics like Ehrman accept the crucifixion."
obj.a:
Ehrman accepts the crucifixion on several grounds, including Paul, multiple Gospels, Josephus and Tacitus, and the embarrassment of a crucified Messiah (a crucified Messiah was embarrassing, so Christians wouldn't invent it). But the crucifixion became the centre of Paul's theology, which shows it was useful, not embarrassing. And scholars such as Rafael Rodríguez and Dale Allison have shown that these criteria are subjective. If all four Gospels proudly report it, it was not something Christians were embarrassed to tell.
Tap to enlargeJesus scholarship: the criteria of authenticity are subjective ("coherence… a rather subjective thing")

obj.q: "Multiple attestation in the Gospels proves it."
obj.a: The Gospels depend on each other (Matthew and Luke copy Mark), so they are not independent witnesses, and all reflect the community's belief, which the Quran grants.

prac.q: “Are you saying everyone in the first century was wrong?”
prac.a: I'm saying what the Quran says: it was made to appear so. Every source shows what people believed. None is an eyewitness account by a neutral party. A belief being widespread doesn't tell you whether appearances were deceptive.

briefs.evs:
Josephus (the "Testimonium Flavianum", Antiquities 18.3.3, c. 93). As it stands it calls Jesus "the Christ" and says he rose on the third day, which no believing Jew would write. No Christian writer cites it before Eusebius (c. 324), although at least eight earlier fathers quote Josephus. Origen, who knew Josephus well, says twice that Josephus did not believe Jesus was the Christ (Contra Celsum 1.47; Commentary on Matthew 10.17), which contradicts the text we have. Louis Feldman's survey of 87 discussions (1937-1980) found only 13 treating the passage as wholly interpolated; most accepted a partly authentic core. Some scholars (K.A. Olson and others) argue Eusebius composed it. Eusebius titled Praeparatio Evangelica 12.31 "that it will be necessary sometimes to use falsehood as a remedy", in a chapter citing Plato on the "noble lie", and the historian Jacob Burckhardt called him "the first thoroughly dishonest historian of antiquity".

briefs.title: The Gospel accounts of the death and resurrection contradict each other
briefs.thesis: On the day, the hour, who carried the cross, what Jesus said, who went to the tomb, what they saw, and where Jesus appeared, the Gospels disagree.
briefs.sum: The Gospels disagree on the day and hour of the crucifixion, who carried the cross, the last words, who was at the tomb, whether the women spoke, where Jesus appeared and how long he stayed. Mark 16:8 originally ended with no appearance at all.

obj.q: "Different perspectives aren't contradictions. Witnesses always vary in details."
obj.a: Some can be harmonised with effort, but not all: Jesus cannot be crucified both before and after the Passover meal, both carry and not carry the cross, and the disciples cannot both go to Galilee and stay in Jerusalem. C.K. Barrett said there is no point trying to harmonise the wine passages.

obj.q: "The core agrees: he died and rose."
obj.a: The core is what was believed. The Quran agrees that people believed it. The question is whether these accounts are reliable enough to overturn revelation, and their disagreement on basic facts shows they are not.

prac.q: “If the Gospels all agreed, you'd say they copied each other; if they differ, you call them contradictions.”
prac.a: I accept that three of them do copy each other (Matthew and Luke use Mark). The problem is that they copy and still change the facts, for example Matthew changing Mark's "the women said nothing" and John changing the day. That's editing, not independent testimony.

briefs.evs:
The day. In Mark, Jesus eats the Passover meal and is crucified the next day (Mark 14:12; 15:25). In John, he is crucified on "the day of Preparation of the Passover", before the meal (John 19:14).
The hour. Mark: "it was the third hour when they crucified him" (15:25). John: at "about the sixth hour" Jesus was still before Pilate (19:14).
The cross. Simon of Cyrene carried it (Mark 15:21, Matthew, Luke); Jesus carried it himself (John 19:17). Some scholars think John is countering the tradition that Simon was crucified in his place.
The robbers. Both mocked him (Mark 15:32); one rebuked the other and was promised paradise (Luke 23:39-43).
The wine. Jesus vowed not to drink wine until the kingdom came (Matt 26:29), but in John he drinks sour wine on the cross (19:29-30).
Last words. "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34); "Father, into Your hands I commit my spirit" (Luke 23:46); "It is finished" (John 19:30).
At the tomb. One young man (Mark), one angel (Matthew), two men (Luke), two angels (John). The women told no one (Mark 16:8) or told everything to the eleven (Luke 24:9).
Where he appeared. In Matthew the disciples are sent to Galilee (28:10, 16). In Luke they are told to stay in Jerusalem (24:49).
How long. Luke's Gospel seems to have Jesus ascend on the day of the resurrection (24:50-51), while Acts, by the same author, says forty days (Acts 1:3).

briefs.title: The Bible promised the righteous one would be rescued
briefs.thesis: Psalms and other scriptures used by Christians for Jesus promise that God would deliver His righteous servant from death, and the NT says Jesus' prayer to be saved from death was heard.
briefs.sum: Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus' prayer to be saved from death was heard. Psalms 118 and 91 and Wisdom 2, all applied to Jesus by Christians, promise God would deliver him. The ascension language matches Elijah, who was taken up alive.

obj.q: "Hebrews 5:7 means he was heard by being resurrected after death."
obj.a: The verse says God was able "to save him from death", not "out of death after dying". Resurrection after death is not being saved from death.

obj.q: "The Psalms are about David, not Jesus."
obj.a: The NT applies them to Jesus. If they are prophecies of Jesus, they promise rescue; if they are not, the NT misuses them. Either way they don't support a crucifixion.

prac.q: “Jesus said he must suffer and die.”
prac.a: Those predictions are widely regarded by scholars as written after the fact (see above), and the disciples acted as if they had never heard them. Meanwhile Hebrews says his own prayer to be saved from death was heard.

briefs.evs:
Hebrews 5:7: "…and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to Him who was able to save him from death (Greek ek thanatou, which most commentators take to mean out of death by resurrection), and he was heard because of his reverence." If he was heard, he was saved from death.
Psalm 118. The NT applies verse 22 ("the stone the builders rejected") to Jesus (Matt 21:42). The same psalm says: "I was pushed hard so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me" (v. 13); "I shall not die, but I shall live… The LORD has disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death" (vv. 17-18).
Wisdom of Solomon 2:12-20. The wicked plot against "the righteous man" who "calls himself a child of the Lord", saying: "if the righteous man is God's son, He will help him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries… let us condemn him to a shameful death". Pseudo-Hippolytus (Against the Jews 9) and Augustine (City of God 17.20) apply this passage to Christ. Wisdom 2:12-20 has the wicked expect his death, and Wisdom 3:1-5 says the righteous "seemed to have died" but are in God's hand.
Psalm 91. "He will command His angels concerning you… On their hands they will bear you up" (91:11-12), quoted of Jesus by Satan in Matthew 4:6. "Because he holds fast to Me in love, I will deliver him" (91:14).

briefs.title: The Shroud, the swoon theory and the Nazareth Inscription
briefs.thesis: The physical "evidence" Christians cite for the death and resurrection fails: the Shroud of Turin is a medieval artefact and the Nazareth Inscription is not about Jesus. And when Christians cite sceptical historians, they ignore that the same historians reject the resurrection.
briefs.sum: The Shroud dates to 1260-1390, its first record calls it a painting, and forensic studies find its bloodstains unrealistic. The Nazareth Inscription comes from Kos and never mentions Jesus.

obj.q: "The radiocarbon sample came from a medieval repair."
obj.a: This claim has been examined and rejected by the original laboratories; the sample area was chosen by textile experts, and later statistical reanalyses of the 1988 data have not changed the medieval date, though some found heterogeneity. The 1389 memo independently says it was painted.

prac.q: “The Shroud has an image science can't explain.”
prac.a: Science has explained it well enough: pigment was found, the blood patterns don't fit a body, a 2025 3D study found the image fits a low-relief sculpture better than a body, and the cloth dates to the century when it first appears in history with a bishop calling it a painting.

briefs.evs:
The Shroud of Turin. Its first documented exhibition was at Lirey in the 1350s; the 1389 memo from Bishop Pierre d'Arcis is the first record claiming it was painted. The memo was addressed to Pope Clement VII and said an earlier bishop had found it "cunningly painted" and that the artist had confessed. In 1988 three laboratories (Arizona, Oxford, Zürich) radiocarbon-dated it to AD 1260-1390. Walter McCrone found iron-oxide and vermilion pigment. Borrini and Garlaschelli (Journal of Forensic Sciences, 2018) found the bloodstain patterns inconsistent with a real body and concluded it was an "artistic or didactic representation" of the 14th century. Andrea Nicolotti has shown no Christian looked for Jesus' burial cloths before the 6th century, and many competing "shrouds" were venerated.

The Nazareth Inscription. A Roman decree against tomb robbing, sometimes linked to the empty tomb. It has no known provenance, never mentions Jesus, and a 2020 isotope study (Harper et al., Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports) traced the marble to Kos and proposed a link with the desecration of the tomb of the tyrant Nikias.

briefs.title: "Mutawaffika" (3:55) does not mean Jesus died
briefs.thesis: The verb tawaffa means "to take fully", and the Quran uses it for sleep. Some early authorities understood 3:55 as Jesus being taken up alive, while others (Wahb, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Abbas in one report) said he died briefly first. This answers both Christians and Ahmadis who claim the Quran admits his death.
briefs.sum: Tawaffa means "take fully" and is used in the Quran for sleep. Tabari, al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas understood 3:55 as Jesus taken up alive, and the "cause you to die" report has a broken chain.

obj.q: "Tawaffa usually means death."
obj.a: Often, when the context is death. Here the context is Allah rescuing Jesus from those who plotted against him (3:54) and raising him (3:55), and 4:157-158 explicitly denies his killing and says Allah raised him. Tawaffa without death is attested in the Quran itself.

prac.q: “The Quran says Jesus died (3:55), so it agrees with Christians.”
prac.a: The Quran says mutawaffika, which it uses for sleep in 6:60 and 39:42, and in 4:157-158 it denies he was killed. And it is Christians who say he died on the cross; the Quran denies that explicitly.

briefs.evs:
Sleep. "It is He who takes you (yatawaffakum) by night" (6:60); "Allah takes (yatawaffa) the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die, in their sleep" (39:42). The Prophet's ﷺ waking supplication thanks Allah "who gave us life after He caused us to die", meaning sleep (Bukhari 6324).
Tabari reports the view that tawaffa here means taking him from the earth alive; al-Rabi' said he was raised while asleep; al-Hasan al-Basri reported in a mursal narration that the Prophet ﷺ told the Jews that "Jesus did not die; he will return to you before the Day of Resurrection".
Ibn Abbas said Jesus was raised alive through an opening in the roof of the house (Ibn Abi Hatim; graded sound by Ibn Kathir). The report that Ibn Abbas glossed mutawaffika as "I will cause you to die" comes through Ali ibn Abi Talha, who did not meet him, and Ibn Abbas himself placed that death after Jesus' return, since the conjunction "and" (wa) in Arabic does not impose sequence.
5:117 ("when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them") likewise refers to his being taken up.

briefs.title: "Son of God" and "Father" are titles of closeness, not deity
briefs.thesis: In the Bible, "son of God" is used for Israel, kings, angels and righteous people. The early sermons in Acts call Jesus God's pais, "servant", which is exactly the Arabic 'Abdullah.
briefs.sum: Israel, David, Adam, angels and peacemakers are all "sons of God" in the Bible. Peter's early sermons call Jesus God's pais, his servant, which is 'Abdullah. The Father-Son language multiplies in the later Gospels.

obj.q: "Jesus is the Son, monogenes, unique."
obj.a: Monogenes means "one of a kind" and is used of Isaac (Heb 11:17), who was not Abraham's only son. Uniqueness of status is not deity: David was uniquely "begotten" as king (Ps 2:7), and Israel was uniquely God's "firstborn".

obj.q: "The Jews wanted to kill him for calling God his Father (John 5:18)."
obj.a: That is the opponents' interpretation; Jesus' reply is "the Son can do nothing of himself" (5:19). And when accused of making himself God (John 10:33), he answers that Scripture calls humans "gods" (10:34-36).

prac.q: “If "Son of God" just means "servant", why does the Quran attack it so strongly (19:88-92)?”
prac.a: Because by the Quran's time it was used literally, to mean a begotten divine being. The Quran rejects that meaning, as God rejected "Baali" in Hosea 2:16 once it carried pagan meaning. The Quran keeps the original idea under its proper name: Jesus is 'Abdullah.

briefs.evs:
Others called sons of God. Israel: "Israel is My firstborn son" (Exod 4:22). The Davidic king: "You are My son; today I have begotten you" (Ps 2:7). Adam, "the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Angels (Job 38:7). Peacemakers: "they shall be called sons of God" (Matt 5:9). "All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God" (Rom 8:14).
Jesus speaks of "my Father and your Father", which some read as sharing his relationship to God and others as distinguishing it: "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17).
The servant. In Peter's early sermons, Jesus is God's pais: "God glorified His servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13, 26; 4:27, 30). This echoes Isaiah 52:13 in the Greek: "Behold, My servant (pais) will be exalted." Joel Carmichael observed that pais tou theou, "servant of God", is exactly the Arabic 'Abdullah. The Quran's first words from the infant Jesus are "I am the servant of Allah" (19:30).
The growth of "Father". Jesus calls God "Father" about 4 times in Mark, about 15-17 in Luke, about 40-45 in Matthew and over 100 in John. The later the Gospel, the more the Father-Son language, a sign of developing theology.
Muslim scholars on the term. Ibn Taymiyya (al-Jawab al-Sahih) explained that in the earlier scriptures "father" meant the merciful Lord who nurtures, and "son" meant a beloved servant, so the words were not originally blasphemous. The Quran f

briefs.title: The original Jerusalem church was closest to Islam
briefs.thesis: The church led by James in Jerusalem, and its heirs the Ebionites (and, on some readings, the Nazarenes) held that Jesus was a human Messiah and prophet, kept the Law and rejected Paul. Some scholars regard Jewish-Christian groups as continuing the Jerusalem church, but this is disputed.
briefs.sum: Jesus' first followers, led by his brother James, kept the Law and saw him as a human Messiah. Their heirs, the Nazarenes and Ebionites, rejected Paul and Jesus' deity, and Schoeps concluded their faith survived in Islam.

obj.q: "The Ebionites were a late heretical sect."
obj.a: Irenaeus already knows them around 180, and their link to the Jerusalem church is attested by Epiphanius. They were called heretics by the Gentile church that replaced them, which is what we would expect if the Gentile church had changed the message.

obj.q: "Ebionites denied the virgin birth, which Islam affirms."
obj.a: Only some did; Origen and Eusebius (Church History 3.27) describe a group that affirmed it. Islam doesn't need to agree with every Ebionite; the point is that the original community held Jesus to be a human prophet.

prac.q: “The New Testament is the apostolic record, and it doesn't say what the Ebionites said.”
prac.a: Most of the New Testament is by Paul or from churches Paul founded. The only letter from the Jerusalem church, James, says justification is by works and never calls Jesus God. Acts 21 shows James' community "zealous for the Law" and suspicious of Paul.

briefs.evs:
They were the majority at first. Alan Segal describes Jewish Christians as a "comfortable majority" of the movement in the first generation.
James led them. Eusebius (Church History 2.1) and Hegesippus name James the Just as the first leader of the Jerusalem church. In the Gospel of Thomas (saying 12) Jesus tells the disciples: "go to James the Just".
Justin Martyr (c. 150) admits some "of our race" (Christians of Jewish origin) held Jesus to be "a man of men" who became Christ by God's election (Dialogue 48).
Epiphanius says the Nazarenes descended from the Jerusalem church that fled to Pella before 70 CE (Panarion 29). Kegan Zarley argues that a Nazarene rejection of Jesus' deity is strong evidence that the apostolic Jerusalem church held the same view.
Tap to enlargeEpiphanius, Panarion 29: the Nazoraeans and their early name "Jessaeans"
The Ebionites (from Hebrew evyonim, "the poor", cf. Gal 2:10) held Jesus to be a human being, the prophet and Messiah. Origen says there were "two kinds" of Ebionites, one of which accepted the virgin birth (Contra Celsum 5.61), just as Islam does. They kept circumcision, the Sabbath and the Law; rejected animal sacrifice; revered James; regarded Paul as an apostate; and held that false passages had entered the Hebrew Bible (H.J. Schoeps). Jerome says John's Gospel was written against them, which shows how early they were.

briefs.title: Jesus practised islam: submission to the one God
briefs.thesis: Jesus prayed by prostrating, fasted, affirmed the Shema, kept the Law and called people to obey God, exactly the practice the Quran ascribes to every prophet.
briefs.sum: Jesus prostrated, fasted, recited the Shema, upheld every letter of the Law, and submitted to God's will. His disciples in the Quran say "bear witness that we are Muslims" (3:52).

obj.q: "Jesus fulfilled the Law so Christians don't have to keep it."
obj.a: "Fulfil" in Matthew 5:17 is immediately explained by verses 18-19: not the smallest letter will pass away, and whoever relaxes the least commandment will be least in the kingdom. That is the opposite of abolition.

prac.q: “Jesus didn't pray five times a day or fast Ramadan, so he wasn't a Muslim.”
prac.a: The specific forms of law differ between prophets (5:48), but the religion is one: worship the one God and obey His messenger. Jesus prostrated, fasted, kept his Law and affirmed God's oneness, which is islam.

briefs.evs:
Prostration. "He fell on his face and prayed" (Matt 26:39), the same posture as the Muslim sujud.
Fasting. Jesus fasted forty days (Matt 4:2) and taught his disciples how to fast (Matt 6:16-18).
The Shema. "The first commandment is: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29).
The Law. "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfil… until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota… will pass from the Law" (Matt 5:17-18). "If you would enter life, keep the commandments" (Matt 19:17).
Submission. "Not my will, but Yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). "My food is to do the will of Him who sent me" (John 4:34).
Greeting. "Peace be with you" (John 20:19), the Aramaic shlama 'alaykhon, the Arabic as-salamu 'alaykum.
James' letter echoes the Sermon on the Mount repeatedly (Matt 5:3 and James 2:5; Matt 5:34-37 and James 5:12), and James calls himself "a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (James 1:1).

briefs.title: Quran 61:14: who were the "believers" who prevailed?
briefs.thesis: Christians claim 61:14 endorses Trinitarian Christianity as the "dominant" group. In context, the believers who prevailed are those who believed in Jesus as God's messenger, and their vindication came through the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
briefs.sum: 61:14's "believers" are those who believed in Jesus as the Quran describes him; the Quran calls Trinitarian belief disbelief. Their vindication came through Islam, as the surah promises in 61:9.

obj.q: "Historically, the Trinitarians are the ones who became dominant."
obj.a: The Quran does not call Trinitarians "those who believed"; it calls their belief disbelief (5:73). The verse's "believers" are defined by the Quran's own standard, and their final vindication is the spread of Islam's account of Jesus.

prac.q: “The Quran says Jesus' followers became dominant, and Trinitarian Christians are the ones who did. So the Quran endorses them.”
prac.a: That reads "believers" in a way the Quran itself rejects (5:72-73). In the Quran, believers in Jesus are those who said "we are Muslims" (3:52). Their position prevailed through the final messenger, as 61:9 promises.

briefs.evs:
The surah's context is Moses and Jesus being rejected (61:5-6), then the promise that Allah will make His religion prevail over all religions (61:9, li-yuzhirahu), which commentators apply to Islam. The same root (z-h-r) appears in 61:14 (zahirin, "dominant").
Classical commentators such as Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Muqatil explain that the believers in Jesus became dominant when Muhammad ﷺ came and confirmed their position: the truth about Jesus they held was vindicated over the views of their opponents. The Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions, a Jewish-Christian text, has a similar idea: "the truth everywhere prevailed; we who were few became far more". And Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, fled to Pella before Jerusalem's destruction in 70, so it was rescued while its enemies were punished (Church History 3.5).

briefs.title: Paul's authority rests on a private vision and was disputed by the apostles
briefs.thesis: Paul says he received his gospel from no human being, and the Jerusalem leaders (James and Peter) and their followers opposed him. Later Jewish-Christian texts (the Pseudo-Clementines, 3rd-4th century in their final form) have Peter denounce "the man who is my enemy", which many scholars read as an allusion to Paul.
briefs.sum: Paul's gospel came by private vision, he opposed Peter to his face, he said rivals preached "another Jesus", James made him prove he kept the Law, and Jewish-Christian texts call him "the enemy".

obj.q: "Galatians 2:9 says James, Peter and John gave Paul the right hand of fellowship."
obj.a: They agreed to a division of labour (Paul to the Gentiles, they to the Jews), yet the very next verses describe the Antioch clash. And Acts 21 shows James' community still suspicious years later.

obj.q: "Peter calls Paul's letters scripture (2 Pet 3:16)."
obj.a: 2 Peter is widely regarded by scholars as pseudonymous, written decades after Peter's death, and it is among the books whose canonicity was disputed longest (see Corruption of the Bible). It even concedes that Paul's letters contain things "hard to understand".

prac.q: “Paul was accepted by the church, so his authority is settled.”
prac.a: He was accepted by the Gentile church he himself founded. The Jerusalem church of Jesus' family opposed him, and their heirs called him "the enemy". Acceptance by his own converts can't validate him.

briefs.evs:
Self-certified. "…the gospel that was preached by me is not man's gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ" (Gal 1:11-12). He did not go to the apostles for three years after his conversion (Gal 1:17-18).
The vision itself is unstable. In Acts 9:7 his companions "heard the voice but saw no one"; in Acts 22:9 they "saw the light but did not hear the voice". In Acts 26 the commission comes directly from Jesus; in Acts 9 and 22 it comes later through Ananias.
Conflict with Peter and James. "When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face" because "certain men came from James" and Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles (Gal 2:11-12). Paul downplays the status of the Jerusalem leaders as "those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)" (Gal 2:6).
"Another Jesus". Paul says rival preachers came to Corinth with "another Jesus" and "a different gospel", and calls them "super-apostles" (2 Cor 11:4-5), and later "false apostles" (11:13). James Tabor argues these were envoys of James and Peter.
James' demand. When Paul reached Jerusalem, James told him thousands of believers were "all zealous for the Law" and had heard Paul taught Jews to abandon Moses; he advised Paul to join four men under a vow and pay their expenses, to show that Paul himse

briefs.title: Paul contradicted Jesus and the Torah on the Law
briefs.thesis: Jesus said not one letter of the Law would pass away; the Torah calls circumcision an everlasting covenant and the Psalmist calls the Law perfect. Paul called the Law a curse and a "ministry of death", declared circumcision worthless, and allowed food offered to idols.
briefs.sum: Jesus said not a dot of the Law would pass; the Torah calls circumcision everlasting and the Law perfect. Paul called the Law death and slavery, circumcision worthless, and permitted idol meat that the apostles and Revelation forbid.

obj.q: "Jesus fulfilled the Law, so Paul is applying that."
obj.a: Matthew 5:18-19 explains "fulfil": the commandments stay in force. Jesus never told his disciples circumcision or food laws were abolished; if he had, the Jerusalem church would not have argued about it for decades (Acts 15; Gal 2).

obj.q: "Peter's vision in Acts 10 abolished food laws."
obj.a: Peter himself interprets the vision as being about people, not food: "God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean" (Acts 10:28).

prac.q: “Islam also changed the Law of Moses, so why can't Paul?”
prac.a: The Quran says Jesus made lawful some things that had been forbidden (3:50), by God's authority, and it brought a new revelation with proof. Paul claimed no new scripture from God; he reinterpreted the existing one against its plain meaning and against the apostles who knew Jesus.

briefs.evs:
Jesus. "Not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom" (Matt 5:18-19).
Circumcision. God: "My covenant shall be in your flesh an everlasting covenant" (Gen 17:13); no uncircumcised foreigner may enter the sanctuary (Ezek 44:9). Paul: "if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you" (Gal 5:2); he calls its advocates "dogs… those who mutilate the flesh" (Phil 3:2).
The Law's value. "The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul" (Ps 19:7); "it will be righteousness for us if we are careful to do all this commandment" (Deut 6:25). Paul: the Law is a "ministry of death" (2 Cor 3:7) and a "yoke of slavery" (Gal 5:1). In Galatians 3:10 he quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 ("cursed is everyone who does not keep the Law") to prove that everyone who relies on the Law is cursed, turning a warning against neglecting the Law into a warning against keeping it.
Idol meat. The Jerusalem council told Gentile believers to "abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols" (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25). The risen Jesus condemns churches that eat it (Rev 2:14, 20), and the Didache (6.3) says to "keep strictly from food offered to idols, for it is the worship of dead gods". briefs.title: Paul's methods: "all things to all men"
briefs.thesis: Paul describes himself adapting his practice to his audience, and Acts shows him doing things he condemned in his letters. That makes his teaching hard to treat as consistent revelation.
briefs.sum: Paul says he became all things to all people, circumcised Timothy after calling circumcision worthless, performed a Temple vow to appear Law-observant, and set his judges against each other. His teaching was strategic, not fixed.
briefs.caution: Christians will reply that Romans 3:7 ("if through my lie God's truth abounds…") is a hypothetical objection Paul is answering, not a confession. That is correct, so don't use Romans 3:7 as a quote of Paul lying. The stronger evidence is 1 Corinthians 9 and his conduct in Acts.

obj.q: "Being 'all things to all people' means cultural sensitivity, not changing doctrine."
obj.a: Circumcising Timothy while teaching that circumcision cuts you off from Christ is not just culture; it is acting against his own doctrine for strategic reasons.

prac.q: “Paul was a sincere man who died for his faith.”
prac.a: Sincerity and courage don't make someone a prophet. The question is whether his message matches Jesus' and the Torah's, and his own letters show he adapted it to his audience and contradicted the apostles.

briefs.evs:
All things to all people. 1 Corinthians 9:20-22.
Timothy. Despite saying circumcision makes Christ of no advantage (Gal 5:2), Paul circumcised Timothy "because of the Jews in those places" (Acts 16:3).
The Temple vow. He paid for a Nazirite vow in the Temple to show Jewish believers he kept the Law (Acts 21:24-26), while his letters call the Law slavery.
Dividing the council. At his trial, seeing Pharisees and Sadducees present, he declared "I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial", setting them against each other (Acts 23:6-10).
Sin. The Pastoral letter 1 Timothy has him call himself the foremost of sinners (1:15), and Romans 7:14-24 is read by some as his own struggle (Rom 7:14-24), yet he condemns the Corinthians harshly. Jesus' rule: "a good tree cannot bear bad fruit" (Matt 7:18).

briefs.title: Paul and Jesus predicted the end within their generation, and it didn't come
briefs.thesis: Paul wrote as though he might be alive at Jesus' return, and the Gospels have Jesus promise it within his listeners' lifetime. It did not happen, which by the Torah's test (Deut 18:22) marks a false prophecy.
briefs.sum: Paul expected to be alive at the return, and the Gospels have Jesus promise it to "some standing here" and "this generation". 2 Peter had to answer scoffers, and C.S. Lewis called Matthew 24:34 the Bible's most embarrassing verse.

obj.q: "'This generation' means the generation that sees the signs, or the Jewish race."
obj.a: In Matthew, "this generation" always means Jesus' contemporaries (11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). And Matthew 16:28 and 26:64 use "some standing here" and "you", which leave no room for a future generation.

obj.q: "'Coming in his kingdom' was the Transfiguration or Pentecost."
obj.a: Then why did Paul expect to be alive at the coming in the clouds, and why did 2 Peter need to answer scoffers?

prac.q: “The Quran also says the Hour is near (54:1).”
prac.a: The Quran never says it will come within a generation or that the listeners will be alive to see it; it says its time is known only to Allah (7:187), and "near" is relative to the age of creation. Jesus in Matthew names his hearers and their generation.

briefs.evs:
Paul. "We who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord… will be caught up together with them in the clouds" (1 Thess 4:15-17). "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed" (1 Cor 15:51). "The appointed time has grown very short… the present form of this world is passing away", so the unmarried should stay unmarried (1 Cor 7:29-31). Scholars such as C.K. Barrett and Victor Furnish trace a declining sense of imminence through his letters.
The Gospels. "There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" (Matt 16:28). "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matt 24:34). "You will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes" (Matt 10:23). To Caiaphas: "you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds" (Matt 26:64).
Revelation. "Behold, I am coming soon (tachu)" (Rev 22:12).
The patch. 2 Peter, written late, answers "scoffers" who ask "where is the promise of his coming?" by saying that "with the Lord one day is as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:3-8). It concedes the problem existed.
C.S. Lewis called Matthew 24:34 "certainly the most embarrassing verse in the Bible", though he went on to argue that Jesus' admission of ignorance in Matthew 24:36 explains it (The World's Last Night).

briefs.title: Paul's Christ owes much to Greek religion, yet still stays below God
briefs.thesis: Paul quotes pagan poets, uses language from Greek religion, and was himself taken for a god by pagans. Even so, he consistently makes Christ subordinate to the Father, so he cannot be used for the later Trinity.
briefs.sum: Paul quotes a poem about Zeus, uses a Dionysus proverb, and was himself taken for a god. Yet even Paul says there is "one God, the Father", that the Son will be subjected to Him, and that the head of Christ is God.

obj.q: "Paul was evangelising Greeks in their own terms; that's not syncretism."
obj.a: Quoting a line about Zeus to describe the God of Abraham blurs the difference; and the Quran rejects divine sonship: "He neither begets nor is begotten" (112:3).

prac.q: “1 Corinthians 8:6 puts Jesus inside the Shema, so Paul believed Jesus was God.”
prac.a: Paul divides the Shema: "one God, the Father", and "one Lord, Jesus Christ". God is the Father alone; Jesus is the Lord "through whom". And 15:28 says the Son will be subjected to God so that "God may be all in all". That is subordination.

briefs.evs:
Pagan language.
"In Him we live and move and have our being… for we are indeed His offspring" (Acts 17:28) quotes Aratus' Phaenomena ("we are also his offspring", echoed in Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus); "in him we live and move" is traced to Epimenides, both written about Zeus.
Tap to enlargeAratus, Phaenomena: "we are his offspring", about Zeus, quoted by Paul in Acts 17:28
"It is hard for you to kick against the goads" (Acts 26:14), in Jesus' voice, is a Greek proverb found in Euripides' Bacchae (794-795), where Dionysus says it to his persecutor, and also in Aeschylus and Pindar.
At Lystra the crowd shouted "the gods have come down to us in the likeness of men" (Acts 14:11), similar in wording to "being made in the likeness of men" (Philippians 2:7), though many scholars read that hymn against Jewish backgrounds. At Malta the islanders said Paul himself was a god (Acts 28:6).
Scholars such as Thomas Wilson describe Paul's Christology as a fusion of the Jewish Messiah with the Hellenistic dying-and-rising divine saviour.
Still subordinate.
"For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things… and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things" (1 Cor 8:6).
"When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to Him who put all things under him, that God may be all in all" (1 Cor 15:28).
"The head of Christ is God" (1 Cor 11:3).

briefs.title: "Beware of false prophets… ravenous wolves" and the tribe of Benjamin
briefs.thesis: Jesus warned of "ravenous wolves" who would do miracles in his name but practise lawlessness. Genesis calls Benjamin, Paul's tribe, "a ravenous wolf", and the warning fits Paul's teaching against the Law.
briefs.sum: Jesus warned of ravenous wolves who work miracles in his name but practise lawlessness; Benjamin, Paul's tribe, is "a ravenous wolf" (Gen 49:27), and several fathers applied that verse to Paul.
briefs.caution: This is a typological argument. It is suggestive, not a proof; present it as a reading Christians themselves made of Genesis 49:27, not as a definitive identification.

obj.q: "The fathers applied Genesis 49:27 to Paul positively."
obj.a: Yes, but the text's word is "ravenous wolf", and Jesus uses the same image for false prophets. The fathers' identification is what makes the connection; the conclusion depends on whether Paul's teaching is "lawlessness", which the previous arguments address.

prac.q: “You're twisting a blessing on Benjamin into a curse on Paul.”
prac.a: I'm pointing out that the church fathers themselves identified Paul with the Benjamin wolf, and that Jesus' warning describes miracle-workers in his name who practise lawlessness. Whether Paul fits depends on his teaching about the Law, which contradicted Jesus.

briefs.evs:
Jesus: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognise them by their fruits" (Matt 7:15-16). "Many will say to me, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?' Then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness (anomia)'" (7:22-23).
Jacob's blessing: "Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil" (Gen 49:27). Paul was "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Rom 11:1; Phil 3:5). Christian fathers including Hippolytus, Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.1), Jerome (Letter 60) and Augustine applied Genesis 49:27 to Paul, as persecutor in the morning and teacher in the evening.
Ezekiel's officials are "like wolves tearing the prey" (22:27), and his priests "do violence to My law" and "make no distinction between the holy and the common, clean and unclean" (22:26), disregard the Sabbaths and announce "thus says the Lord God" when the LORD has not spoken.
Paul performed miracles and exorcisms in Jesus' name (Acts 16; 19) and taught freedom from the Law.
Jesus also said the kingdom would be taken away and given "to a nation producing its fruits" (Matt 21:43), which Muslims apply to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his community.

briefs.sec: Corruption, dating & authorship of the Bible
briefs.title: The Gospels are anonymous and not eyewitness accounts
briefs.thesis: None of the Gospels names its author; the names are first attested for all four Gospels around 180 CE; and most critical scholars hold that none is the work of an eyewitness.
briefs.sum: The Gospels name no authors; Irenaeus first named them around 180; Matthew copies Mark; Mark errs on Palestinian geography; and scholars from Tabor to the Oxford Annotated Bible agree they are not eyewitness accounts.

obj.q: "Anonymous doesn't mean unreliable; many ancient histories are anonymous."
obj.a: For history, perhaps. For scripture that claims divine authority, we need to know it came from a prophet or witness. Muslims know the Quran came through the Prophet ﷺ by mass transmission; Christians do not know who wrote the Gospels.

obj.q: "The early church unanimously attributed them."
obj.a: The attributions are unanimous only from Irenaeus on, a century after Jesus. Before that, writers quote Gospel material without names, and later disputes over John's authorship show the "unanimity" was not complete.

prac.q: “The Quran is also "anonymous": it doesn't name its human author.”
prac.a: The Quran claims to be God's speech, revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, and its transmission from him is mass-attested, with Companion codices and manuscripts within decades. The Gospels claim to be accounts by people about Jesus, so who they were matters, and we don't know.

briefs.evs:
Anonymous. No Gospel names its author in the text. The earliest Christian writers quote "the Gospel" without names (the Didache calls it "the Gospel of our Lord"). Irenaeus, around 180, is the first to name all four (Against Heresies 3.1.1). James Tabor: "All four Gospels are anonymous… names were assigned later by tradition."
Tap to enlargeJames Tabor: all four Gospels are anonymous, with names assigned later by tradition
Not eyewitnesses. The New Oxford Annotated Bible dates them roughly 40 to 70 years after the events. They are not eyewitness accounts. Richard Bauckham, who argues for eyewitness sources, acknowledges that his thesis challenges the form-critical consensus that the Gospel traditions circulated anonymously.
Tap to enlargeNew Oxford Annotated Bible: the Gospels were written 40-60 years later and are not eyewitness accounts
Tap to enlargeRichard Bauckham concedes his eyewitness thesis "runs counter to almost all recent NT scholarship"
Matthew copies Mark. Papias said Matthew compiled "the sayings" (logia) in Hebrew, but our Greek Matthew reproduces most of Mark's content (roughly 80-90%) and about half of its exact wording. An apostle who saw the events would not need to copy a non-apostle's account.
Mark's geography. Mark has Jesus go from Tyre "through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the region of the Decapolis" (Mark 7:31), a route like going from London

briefs.sec: Corruption, dating & authorship of the Bible
briefs.title: The church fathers themselves admitted the text was altered
briefs.thesis: Celsus, Origen, Dionysius of Corinth and Jerome all complained, in the first four centuries, that Christian scriptures were being altered by scribes, sometimes deliberately.
briefs.sum: Celsus, Origen, Dionysius of Corinth and Jerome all complained that texts were being altered; Jerome said there were almost as many forms of text as copies; a Vaticanus scribe wrote "Fool and knave, leave the old reading!"

obj.q: "They're talking about heretics' copies, which were caught."
obj.a: Origen speaks of "copyists" generally, and Jerome speaks of the copies in the church's own hands. If corruption was widespread enough for Jerome to see as many texts as copies, we cannot assume every change was caught, especially in the first century where we have almost no manuscripts.

obj.q: "Textual criticism lets us recover the original."
obj.a: It lets us recover the text as of the 2nd-3rd centuries, the earliest substantial manuscripts. Koester's point is that the most important changes would have happened before then.

prac.q: “You're quoting Christians who loved the Bible. They were complaining about scribes, not saying the Bible is false.”
prac.a: Exactly: they loved the Bible and still testified that copyists added and deleted "as they please". That is the Quran's charge (2:79; 4:46). Their love makes the testimony more credible, not less.

briefs.evs:
Celsus (c. 175), quoted by Origen: some believers "alter the original text of the gospel three or four or several times over, and change its character to enable them to deny difficulties" (Contra Celsum 2.27). Origen does not deny it; he says it was done by heretics.
Tap to enlargeOrigen, Contra Celsum II.27: some believers "altered the Gospel three or four times"
Origen himself: "the differences among the manuscripts have become great, either through the negligence of some copyists or through the perverse audacity of others; they either neglect to check over what they have transcribed, or in the process of checking they make additions or deletions as they please" (Commentary on Matthew 15.14).
Dionysius of Corinth (c. 170) complained that his own letters had been altered and added: "no wonder some have attempted to adulterate the Lord's writings" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23).
Jerome (383), commissioned by Pope Damasus to revise the Latin Bible: there are "almost as many forms of text as there are copies", corrupted by inaccurate translators, "the blundering alterations of confident but ignorant critics", and copyists "more asleep than awake" (Preface to the Gospels). Bruce Metzger notes that Jerome catalogues the kinds of scribal error, including conscious emendation.
Tap to enlargeMetzger, New Testament Studies, p. 199: Jerome catalogues the kinds of scribal error

briefs.sec: Corruption, dating & authorship of the Bible
briefs.title: Major passages were added later
briefs.thesis: The longer ending of Mark, the story of the adulteress, the Trinitarian baptism formula, the Johannine Comma and several smaller changes are later additions or alterations, and many of them carry central doctrines.
briefs.sum: Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 are absent from the oldest manuscripts; 1 John 5:7 is a medieval addition; Matthew 28:19's formula clashes with Acts and with Eusebius' quotations; and scribes altered Luke 23:32, John 7:8 and Matthew 24:36 for theological reasons.

obj.q: "No doctrine depends on these passages."
obj.a: The longer ending of Mark is the only resurrection appearance in Mark; the Comma was the only explicit Trinity verse; Matthew 28:19 is the only Trinitarian baptism command. That these are the passages under suspicion is exactly the point: the doctrines grew, and texts were added to match.

obj.q: "Matthew 28:19 is in every Greek manuscript."
obj.a: Our Greek manuscripts of Matthew 28 begin in the 4th century. Eusebius' pre-Nicene quotations and the practice in Acts are evidence of an earlier form. You can concede the textual question is debated while pointing out the tension with Acts and Matthew 10:5-6.

prac.q: “If the Bible was corrupted, why do Christians still have the original words in footnotes?”
prac.a: Because scholars have caught some of the later additions by comparing manuscripts. But the earliest manuscripts are themselves 2nd-4th century copies, so changes made in the first century, before our evidence starts, can't be detected the same way.

briefs.evs:
Mark 16:9-20. Absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the two oldest complete manuscripts. Eusebius and Jerome say almost all Greek copies of their time lacked it, and it is not in the Eusebian canon tables. Its style differs; it re-introduces Mary Magdalene as if she had not been mentioned (taking a detail from Luke 8:2); and it ignores Mark's own promise of a meeting in Galilee (14:28; 16:7). Scholars broadly agree it is not original to Mark and was added in the 2nd century or earlier (Irenaeus quotes it c. 180).
John 7:53-8:11 (the woman caught in adultery). Absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and the early Syriac and Coptic versions; Origen and Chrysostom skip it in their commentaries; later manuscripts place it in different spots (even in Luke). Metzger: "the evidence for the non-Johannine origin of the pericope of the adulteress is overwhelming".
Tap to enlargeNET Bible on John 7:53-8:11: the adulteress passage is not in the earliest manuscripts
Matthew 28:19 ("baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit"). In Acts, the apostles baptise only "in the name of Jesus" (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5), which is strange if Jesus had commanded the triadic formula. Eusebius quotes the verse many times before Nicaea in a short form: "Go and make disciples of all nations in my name". The medieval (14th-century) Hebrew Matthew in Sh

briefs.sec: Corruption, dating & authorship of the Bible
briefs.title: The Hebrew Bible shows deliberate theological changes
briefs.thesis: Emanuel Tov, the leading textual critic of the Hebrew Bible, accepts that scribes made theological alterations, and the Dead Sea Scrolls preserve readings that the standard Hebrew text changed.
briefs.sum: Tov accepts deliberate theological changes in the Hebrew Bible: Deuteronomy 32:8 changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel", Genesis 2:2 has competing days, a paragraph of Samuel was lost, and Jeremiah survives in two editions.

obj.q: "The Dead Sea Scrolls prove the text is accurate (Isaiah scroll)."
obj.a: The Great Isaiah Scroll is close to the Masoretic Text, but the Scrolls also show multiple text forms circulating at once (proto-Masoretic, Septuagint-like, Samaritan-like), which is the opposite of a single preserved text.

prac.q: “Small variants don't matter; the message is intact.”
prac.a: Deuteronomy 32:8 changes the theology of God's council, Genesis 2:2 changes what God did on the Sabbath, and Jeremiah exists in two editions of different length. Tov, a Jewish scholar, says most scholars accept that theological changes were made.

briefs.evs:
Theological alterations. Tov writes that "the existence of theological changes… is accepted by most scholars".
Tap to enlargeEmanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, p. 270: theological alterations by scribes
Deuteronomy 32:8. The Masoretic Text says God divided the nations "according to the number of the sons of Israel". The Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j and the Septuagint read "sons of God", which reflects the older idea of a heavenly council and was changed to avoid it.
Tap to enlargeTov, p. 269: Deuteronomy 32:8 "sons of Israel" (Masoretic) vs "sons of God" (Dead Sea Scroll, Septuagint)
Genesis 2:2. "On the seventh day God finished His work": the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint and Peshitta read "on the sixth day", avoiding the implication that God worked on the Sabbath.
A lost paragraph. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a preserves a paragraph about Nahash the Ammonite before 1 Samuel 11 that dropped out of the Masoretic Text; some modern translations (NRSV) restore it.
Two editions. The Septuagint of Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter and arranged differently; scholars recognise it as an earlier edition, with a Hebrew equivalent at Qumran (4QJer-b). Joshua also survives in a different edition.
The Masoretic Text of Samuel is "frequently corrupt", and translators often have to emend or bracket unintelligible readings.
Gospels quote the Greek. Mark 7:6-7 has Jesus quote I

briefs.sec: Corruption, dating & authorship of the Bible
briefs.title: The canon itself was disputed for centuries
briefs.thesis: Christians did not agree on which books belonged in the New Testament until the 4th century or later, and leading figures, including Reformers, rejected books that are now canonical.
briefs.sum: Eusebius listed books as disputed; Revelation was omitted by major fathers and councils; Luther demoted four books; Jude quotes Enoch; and churches still use different canons. The Bible's contents were settled by human judgement over centuries.

obj.q: "The church recognised, not decided, the canon."
obj.a: Then Luther, Zwingli, Cyril of Jerusalem and the Synod of Laodicea all failed to recognise it, and the Catholic and Protestant churches still recognise different books. Recognition that took centuries and still differs is indistinguishable from decision.

prac.q: “The Quran was also compiled after Muhammad's death.”
prac.a: It was compiled from what he dictated and what the Companions had memorised, within two years, and no Companion disputed the Quran's contents in a way that survived the standardisation; reports about Ibn Mas'ud's codex show the point was discussed and settled. The Bible's canon was disputed for 300 years and still differs between churches.

briefs.evs:
Eusebius (c. 325) lists Revelation among both "accepted" and "rejected" books and lists James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2-3 John as "disputed" (Church History 3.25).
Revelation was omitted by Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechetical Lectures 4.36), Gregory of Nazianzus, the Synod of Laodicea, Chrysostom and Theodoret. Amphilochius said "the majority say it is spurious". Dionysius of Alexandria argued from its Greek style that it was not by the author of John's Gospel. Luther called it "neither apostolic nor prophetic", and Zwingli rejected it.
Tap to enlargeCatholic Commentary on Revelation: the author's identity with the apostle John is disputed
Luther called James "an epistle of straw" and placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his Bible as of lesser rank. Calvin doubted 2 Peter.
Jude quotes the Book of Enoch as genuine prophecy (Jude 14-15, quoting 1 Enoch 1:9), and some fathers rejected Jude for that reason. Only the Ethiopian church includes Enoch in its Bible today.
Different canons today. Catholics include seven books Protestants reject; the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is commonly counted as 81 books.
The Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas are bound into Codex Sinaiticus as part of the Bible.

briefs.sec: Corruption, dating & authorship of the Bible
briefs.title: Historical errors and misquotations
briefs.thesis: The Gospels and Acts misattribute Old Testament quotations, cite prophecies that do not exist, and record events that contemporary historians do not know.
briefs.sum: Matthew cites Jeremiah for Zechariah and a non-existent "Nazarene" prophecy; Mark names the wrong priest; Matthew names the wrong Zechariah; Acts confuses two tombs; and Herod's massacre is unknown to Josephus.

obj.q: "Matthew 27:9 combines Jeremiah and Zechariah and names the major prophet."
obj.a: Matthew's quotation is about thirty pieces of silver paid and thrown to the potter, which is Zechariah's text; Jeremiah's field purchase (Jer 32:6-15) involves seventeen shekels of silver, not thirty, and the potter scene is in Jer 18-19. Scribes themselves found it a problem (some manuscripts change the name).

obj.q: "Abiathar" means "in the passage about Abiathar".
obj.a: Ahimelech is the priest in the passage; Abiathar appears only after the massacre in the next chapter. Matthew and Luke both deleted the name, which suggests they saw a problem.

prac.q: “Small errors don't affect the message.”
