prac.a: They affect the claim that the text is inspired word for word. And the Gospel writers used these quotations to prove Jesus' messiahship; if the proofs are misquoted or invented, the argument they support fails.

briefs.evs:
Matthew 27:9 attributes to Jeremiah a prophecy about thirty pieces of silver that is actually from Zechariah 11:12-13.
Tap to enlargeMetzger, Textual Commentary on Matthew 27: scribes struggled with Matthew's citations
Matthew 2:23: "he shall be called a Nazarene" is not in the Old Testament.
Tap to enlargeOxford Bible Commentary: "He will be called a Nazorean" (Matthew 2:23) is not in the Old Testament
Mark 2:26: Jesus says David ate the holy bread "in the time of Abiathar the high priest", but 1 Samuel 21:1-6 names Ahimelech. Matthew and Luke both drop the name.
Matthew 23:35: "Zechariah the son of Barachiah", murdered between the sanctuary and the altar, was actually the son of Jehoiada (2 Chr 24:20-21).
Acts 7:16: Stephen says Abraham bought a tomb at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, but Abraham bought his tomb at Hebron from Ephron (Gen 23), and it was Jacob who bought land at Shechem from Hamor (Gen 33:19).
Herod's massacre of the infants (Matt 2:16). Josephus records Herod's crimes in detail, including killing his own sons, but never mentions it. Geza Vermes notes that the star, the Magi, the massacre and the flight to Egypt are found "only in Matthew".
Eusebius' "anachronism". Christians mock the Quran for calling Abraham and Moses Muslims, yet Eusebius wrote that the righteous from Abraham back to the first man were "Christians in fact, if not in name" (Church History 1

briefs.title: Isaiah 53: the suffering servant is Israel
briefs.thesis: Isaiah repeatedly names the servant as Israel; in chapter 53 the speakers are the astonished nations; and the servant is promised offspring and long life, which does not fit a dying divine saviour.
briefs.sum: Isaiah names the servant as Israel repeatedly; chapter 53's "we" are the astonished kings of 52:15; the servant gets offspring and long life; and the Targum keeps the suffering with Israel, not the Messiah.

obj.q: "Israel is sinful, but the servant is innocent (53:9)."
obj.a: The prophets distinguish the righteous remnant from the nation as a whole, and the passage describes Israel as the nations now see it: suffering unjustly at their hands. And the servant in 42:19 is "blind" and "deaf", which hardly fits a sinless Messiah either.

obj.q: "Lamo can be singular in poetry."
obj.a: It occasionally is, but its ordinary meaning is plural, and the plural fits the many explicit identifications of the servant as Israel.

obj.q: "Jewish scholars only reinterpreted it as Israel after Christianity."
obj.a: Origen, writing around 248, reports a Jewish interlocutor who read it of the whole people (Contra Celsum 1.55)

prac.q: “Isaiah 53 describes the crucifixion so precisely it must be about Jesus.”
prac.a: Read it with 52:13-15: the servant is "exalted", kings are shocked, and he sees "offspring" and "long days". The precise details Christians see (pierced, silent, buried with the rich) are general or mistranslated. Isaiah itself names the servant as Israel at least eight times.

briefs.evs:
The servant is named. "But you, Israel, My servant, Jacob whom I have chosen" (41:8); "Jacob My servant, Israel whom I have chosen" (44:1); "you are My servant, O Israel" (44:21; 49:3). The NT applies the servant passage of Isaiah 49:6 to Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:47), so even the NT doesn't treat "servant" as a title for Jesus alone.
The speakers. 52:15 says "kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for what they had not been told they see". On this reading, chapter 53's "we" are the nations, astonished to see despised Israel exalted. The same theme appears in 49:7 ("kings shall see and arise… because of the LORD") and 60:14.
Plural. 53:8 says "for the transgression of my people, a stroke was to them (lamo)", a plural pronoun.
Offspring and long life. "He shall see his offspring (zera); he shall prolong his days" (53:10). Zera elsewhere in the Bible means physical descendants. A God-man who dies childless does not fit.
One ancient Jewish reading takes the passage as Israel; others, such as Targum Jonathan and b. Sanhedrin 98b, take it as the Messiah. Origen reports that a Jewish sage told him the passage refers "to the whole people regarded as one individual", in their dispersion and suffering (Contra Celsum 1.55). The Aramaic Targum makes the servant of 52:13 the Messiah, but transfers the suffering in chapter 53 to Israel in exile; the Messiah intercedes and rebuilds t

briefs.title: Psalm 22: "like a lion", not "they pierced"
briefs.thesis: The Hebrew of Psalm 22:16 says "like a lion [at] my hands and my feet", matching the animal imagery of the whole psalm. The Gospels quote Psalm 22 repeatedly but never verse 16.
briefs.sum: Psalm 22:16 in Hebrew says "like a lion", matching the lions, dogs and bulls of the psalm. "Pierce" is a different Hebrew word, the Gospels never quote the verse, and the psalm ends with God rescuing the sufferer.

obj.q: "The Septuagint says 'they dug/pierced'."
obj.a: The Septuagint has oryxan, "they dug", which still is not "pierced", and comes from a Hebrew text read differently. A sentence "like a lion my hands and feet" is elliptical in Hebrew, which is why translators tried other readings. The surrounding verses fix the image as animals attacking.

prac.q: “The Dead Sea Scrolls prove "pierced" is original.”
prac.a: The relevant scroll (from Nahal Hever) is damaged and debated; even its best-case reading is ka'aru, "they dug" or a variant spelling of "like a lion". It does not say "pierced", and the Gospel writers never used the verse.

briefs.evs:
The word. The Hebrew is ka'ari, "like the lion", the same word for lion used in verses 13 and 21 ("a ravening and roaring lion"; "save me from the mouth of the lion"). The psalmist is surrounded by "dogs" (v. 16a) and "bulls" (v. 12). The NIV itself notes: "most Hebrew manuscripts: like the lion".
Tap to enlargeNIV note on Psalm 22:16: "most Hebrew manuscripts: like the lion", not "pierced"
"Pierce" in Hebrew is daqar (Zech 12:10), ratsa or naqav. Even the alternative reading karu, which a Judean-desert scroll may support, would mean "dug", not "pierced", according to the standard lexicon (HALOT).
The Gospels' silence. The Gospels quote Psalm 22:1 ("My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?"), 22:7-8 (mocking) and 22:18 (dividing the garments). If verse 16 had said "they pierced my hands and feet", it would have been the strongest prophecy of all, yet no Gospel quotes it.
Other readings. The Talmud (Megillah 15b) applies Psalm 22 to Esther. The Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns apply Psalms 22 and 118 to the Teacher of Righteousness, saved from his persecutors.
The psalm ends in rescue. "He has not despised the affliction of the afflicted… he has heard when he cried to Him" (22:24). The sufferer is saved.

briefs.title: Isaiah 7:14: a sign for King Ahaz
briefs.thesis: The "young woman" of Isaiah 7:14 was already pregnant, and the sign was to come true within that child's infancy, during the war Ahaz faced in 734-732 BCE.
briefs.sum: Isaiah 7:14 is a sign to King Ahaz that the two kings attacking him would be gone before a child, already conceived, grew up. Almah means young woman, the child is named in Isaiah 8:8, and Raymond Brown agrees it doesn't predict a virgin birth.

obj.q: "The Septuagint translates almah as parthenos, 'virgin'."
obj.a: Parthenos could mean a young woman in general (it is used of Dinah after she was raped, Gen 34:3 LXX). And the Septuagint translators were reading Isaiah's own context, not predicting Jesus.

obj.q: "Prophecy can have a double fulfilment."
obj.a: Then the "sign" was already fulfilled in Ahaz's time, and the second fulfilment is a Christian reading, not something the text predicts.

prac.q: “Muslims believe in the virgin birth too, so why argue against Isaiah 7:14?”
prac.a: Muslims believe in the virgin birth because the Quran teaches it (3:47; 19:20), not because of Isaiah 7:14. The point is method: Christians claim the Old Testament predicts their doctrines, and this example shows the claim relies on ignoring context.

briefs.evs:
The crisis. Kings Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel were attacking Judah. Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear and offers a sign: "Behold, the young woman (ha-almah) is pregnant and shall bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel… before the boy knows to refuse evil and choose good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted" (7:14-16). Assyria destroyed Damascus in 732 BCE, Pekah was killed the same year, and Samaria fell about ten years later (2 Kgs 15:29-30; 16:9).
"The young woman". The Hebrew has the definite article and the adjective harah ("pregnant"), usually read as describing a specific woman who is already pregnant. Almah means a young woman of marriageable age (compare "the way of a man with an almah", Prov 30:19; the masculine elem means "young man"). When Isaiah means virgin he uses betulah, as he does five times.
The next chapter. Isaiah 8:3-4 describes the birth of a sign-child to Isaiah's wife with the same timetable, and 8:8 addresses "your land, O Immanuel". The sign belongs to Isaiah's own time.
Christian scholars agree. Raymond Brown, a Catholic priest, concluded that "the Masoretic Text of Isaiah 7:14 does not refer to a virginal conception in the distant future" (The Birth of the Messiah, pp. 146-149). Already in the 2nd century, the Jew Trypho told Justin it referred to Hezekiah (Dialogue 67).
Jesus was not named Immanuel. The angel says "you shall

briefs.title: Zechariah and Daniel: Zerubbabel, the pierced, and the seventy weeks
briefs.thesis: Zechariah's king on a donkey is the Davidic governor Zerubbabel; Zechariah 12:10 says the people mourn "to Me" for those killed in a war, and John changed it; and Daniel's seventy weeks start from Cyrus' decree, not a date picked to land on Jesus.
briefs.sum: Zechariah 9:9 is about Zerubbabel and Matthew turned its parallelism into two animals; Zechariah 12:10 mourns "to Me" for the slain, and John changed it; Daniel 9 counts from Cyrus' decree and doesn't reach Jesus.

obj.q: "Zerubbabel never became king."
obj.a: Zechariah's hopes for him were real but went unfulfilled, which is a problem for Zechariah's prediction, not evidence that it was about someone 500 years later.

obj.q: "Daniel 9 leads exactly to AD 33."
obj.a: Only by choosing the decree of Artaxerxes and using "prophetic years" of 360 days. Daniel 9:2 ties the prophecy to Jeremiah's seventy years, which ended with Cyrus.

prac.q: “The 70 weeks are the most precise prophecy in the Bible: the Messiah must come before the Temple's destruction in 70 AD.”
prac.a: Daniel calls Cyrus' era "the word to restore Jerusalem" (Isa 44:28 explicitly), and the "anointed one" can be a priest or king (Cyrus himself is called mashiach). Many evangelical scholars, like the JETS article shown, now admit Cyrus' decree is the natural starting point.

briefs.evs:
Zechariah 9:9 ("your king comes to you… riding on a donkey"). Zechariah's hopes centre on Zerubbabel, the Davidic governor who rebuilt the Temple, called "the Branch" (3:8) and God's "signet ring" (Hag 2:23), and in the received text of 6:11-12 the crown is set on Joshua the high priest. Riding a donkey or mule was part of royal coronation (Solomon in 1 Kgs 1:33). Matthew misread the Hebrew parallelism ("on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey") as two animals and has Jesus ride both (Matt 21:7), as Bart Ehrman notes.
Tap to enlargeCommentary on Haggai and Zechariah: the hopes centre on Zerubbabel, not a future divine messiah
Tap to enlargeBart Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted, p. 50: Matthew misreads Zechariah 9:9 and puts Jesus on two animals
Zechariah 12:10 ("they will look on Me, whom they have pierced"). The Hebrew says they will look "to Me concerning (et asher) the one they pierced, and mourn for him". The context is a war in which the nations attack Jerusalem (12:2-9). The Jewish Study Bible translates "they shall lament to Me about those who are slain". John 19:37 quotes it as "they will look on him whom they pierced", changing "Me" to "him".
Tap to enlargeJewish Study Bible on Zechariah 12:10: "they shall lament to me about those who are slain"
Daniel 9:24-27. The seventy "weeks" (490 years) count from "the going forth of the word to restore and build Jerusalem" (9:25)

briefs.title: Genesis 3:15, Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42
briefs.thesis: The "first gospel" of Genesis 3:15 is about humans and snakes; Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm; and the servant of Isaiah 42 does not match Jesus' ministry.
briefs.sum: Genesis 3:15 is a curse on snakes, first read as a gospel by Irenaeus; Psalm 2 is a royal coronation psalm; and Isaiah 42's servant, a warrior who brings law to the nations and shames idolaters, does not fit Jesus.

obj.q: "Matthew 12:18-21 applies Isaiah 42 to Jesus."
obj.a: Matthew quotes 42:1-4 for Jesus' quietness in withdrawing from crowds, but leaves out the rest of the chapter: the warrior, the idol-worshippers, Kedar. Selective quotation is the point at issue.

prac.q: “Psalm 2 says "kiss the Son lest he be angry", so the Son is divine.”
prac.a: The word is Aramaic bar in a Hebrew poem, which is why the Septuagint and the JPS translate it differently. Even with "son", the psalm defines him: "today I have begotten you", the coronation of a king God adopts (2 Sam 7:14).

briefs.evs:
Genesis 3:15 ("he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel"). In context, God curses the serpent to crawl on its belly (3:14) and declares enmity between snakes and human beings. Eve is "the mother of all living" (3:20), so her "seed" is humanity. Claus Westermann shows the "protoevangelium" reading begins with Irenaeus in the late 2nd century.
Tap to enlargeWestermann on Genesis 3:15: the "protoevangelium" reading begins with Irenaeus
Psalm 2. "You are My son; today I have begotten you" (2:7) is the coronation formula for the Davidic king: "I will be a father to him and he shall be a son to Me" (2 Sam 7:14, of Solomon); "he shall cry to Me, You are my Father… I will make him the firstborn" (Ps 89:26-27). God also "begot" Israel (Deut 32:18). "Kiss the son" (2:12) uses the Aramaic bar in a Hebrew psalm; the Septuagint has "embrace discipline", and the Jewish Publication Society "pay homage in good faith". Kissing was homage to the anointed king (1 Sam 10:1).
Isaiah 42. The servant "will not cry out or raise his voice in the street" (42:2), but Jesus "cried out" in the Temple (John 7:37) and overturned tables. He "will not be discouraged until he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands wait for his law (torah)" (42:4), but Jesus said he came not to abolish the Law (Matt 5:17), although he also gave "a new commandment" (John 13:34) and was distressed

briefs.title: The Jews expected a Messiah who would live, and the messianic tasks are unfulfilled
briefs.thesis: The disciples and the crowd did not expect a Messiah who would die, the prophets describe a Messiah who rebuilds Israel and brings peace, and the Bible promises that God would save His anointed, exactly as the Quran says of Jesus.
briefs.sum: Peter, the disciples, the Emmaus pair and the crowd all expected a Messiah who would not die. The Psalms promise God would save His anointed, and the prophets' messianic tasks were left unfulfilled. The Quran's Jesus, rescued and returning, fits.

obj.q: "Jesus explained the Scriptures about his suffering on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27)."
obj.a: Luke doesn't say which Scriptures, and the ones Christians usually cite are those examined above, which do not say what is claimed. Luke 24:46 ("thus it is written that the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day") quotes no actual text, and the passages Christians usually cite are answered elsewhere.

prac.q: “The Jews misunderstood their own prophecies; Jesus corrected them.”
prac.a: Then God's revelation about the Messiah's central mission was so unclear that the Messiah's closest disciples, after years with him, "understood none of it". Meanwhile the Psalms they did read say God saves His anointed, which is what the Quran says happened.

briefs.evs:
Peter: "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you" (Matt 16:22).
The disciples: "they understood none of these things; this saying was hidden from them" (Luke 18:34).
Emmaus: "we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21).
The crowd: "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever" (John 12:34).
Saving the anointed. "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heaven" (Ps 20:6). Psalm 91, which Satan applies to Jesus (Matt 4:6), though Jesus replies by quoting Deuteronomy 6:16 against that use (Matt 4:7), promises "no evil shall befall you… I will deliver him… with long life I will satisfy him" (91:10, 15-16). Angels rescued Daniel and his friends before death (Dan 3:28; 6:22).
Unfinished tasks. The prophets' Messiah reigns in justice and Israel dwells safely (Jer 23:5-6; 33:15), gathers the exiles and rebuilds under one shepherd (Ezek 34:23-28; 37:24-28), and brings peace to the ends of the earth (Mic 5:4). Instead, the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE. Christians reply that these will be fulfilled at the second coming, which concedes they were not fulfilled in Jesus' life.
The Quran's account fits. Allah restrained the Children of Israel from Jesus (5:110), raised him (4:158), and he will return, break the cross and establish justice (Bukhari 2476), a time of peace like Isaiah's wolf dwelling with the

briefs.title: Prophecies that do not exist
briefs.thesis: Several NT passages say "as it is written" or "according to the Scriptures" for statements found nowhere in the Old Testament. Either the NT authors erred, they cited loosely or interpretively, or they relied on scripture that has since been lost.
briefs.sum: "He shall be called a Nazarene", "the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day" and "rivers of living water" are quoted as Scripture but exist nowhere in the OT. Either the NT erred or scripture was lost.

obj.q: "Matthew 2:23 is a wordplay on netser (Isa 11:1)."
obj.a: Matthew says "spoken by the prophets", plural, and gives a sentence, not a pun. Christian commentators from Adam Clarke to modern apologists admit there is no tidy answer.

obj.q: "'According to the Scriptures' means the general teaching of Scripture."
obj.a: Then "it is written" doesn't mean what it says. In James 4:5 and John 7:38 the formula introduces a specific quotation.

prac.q: “These are minor; there are hundreds of real prophecies.”
prac.a: The NT writers present these as proofs. When the proof-texts are missing, misattributed or out of context, the apologetic list shrinks to texts that, as this section shows, are about Israel, Ahaz, Zerubbabel or Cyrus.

briefs.evs:
Matthew 2:23: "He shall be called a Nazarene", said to be "spoken by the prophets". No such verse exists. Geza Vermes notes that Hebrew netser ("branch") and Nazoraios are not even the same root. The Oxford Bible Commentary agrees there is no such text.
Tap to enlargeGeza Vermes, The Nativity: the Nazarene "prophecy" can be found nowhere in the Old Testament
Tap to enlargeOxford Bible Commentary: "He will be called a Nazorean" (Matthew 2:23) is not in the OT
Luke 24:46: "Thus it is written that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead." No OT text says this.
1 Corinthians 15:4: "raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures". Christians cite Hosea 6:2 ("on the third day he will raise us up"), which is about Israel's restoration and uses "us".
John 7:38: "As the Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water." No such text.
1 Corinthians 2:9: "As it is written, what no eye has seen…" Only loosely like Isaiah 64:4; Chrysostom suggested it came from lost books. Notably, the same saying appears in a hadith qudsi about Paradise ("what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined", Bukhari 3244).
James 4:5: "Do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, 'He yearns jealously over the spirit that He has made to dwell in us'?" No OT source.
Matthew 27:9: thirty pieces of silver "spoken by Jeremiah"

briefs.sec: Paganism in Christianity and in Israelite religion
briefs.title: "The gods have come down in the likeness of men" was a pagan idea
briefs.thesis: The idea of a god appearing as a man, a son of god born miraculously who works wonders and ascends, was familiar to the Greco-Roman world, and the NT itself shows pagans reading Paul's message that way.
briefs.sum: The NT itself shows pagans saying "the gods have come down in the likeness of men"; Dionysus says he took "the likeness of a man"; Apollonius and emperors were called sons of god and saviours. The incarnation fits that world, not the prophets'.

obj.q: "Christianity is Jewish; the incarnation came from Jewish categories like Wisdom and the Word."
obj.a: Jewish personified Wisdom was never worshipped or said to become a man. The only people in the NT who spontaneously recognise gods in human form are the pagans at Lystra.

obj.q: "Parallels don't prove borrowing."
obj.a: True, and you should not claim direct copying. The argument is that the idea of a god becoming man was at home in Greek religion, while Jewish scripture has only temporary appearances such as Genesis 18, so the doctrine's growth is best explained by the Gentile environment of the church.

prac.q: “Paul tore his clothes at Lystra when they called him a god, so Christianity rejects pagan ideas.”
prac.a: He rejected being called a god himself. But the belief that God had come in human form is precisely what Christianity then taught of Jesus. The Lystrans' instinct was the same, just applied to different men.

briefs.evs:
At Lystra the crowd cried "the gods have come down to us in the likeness of men", called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and a priest of Zeus brought bulls to sacrifice (Acts 14:11-13). At Malta, people said Paul was a god (Acts 28:6).
Dionysus opens Euripides' Bacchae: "I have changed my form from god to mortal" and "I have taken the likeness of a man" (lines 4, 53). Philippians 2:7: "taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men".
Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century teacher, was said, in Philostratus' Life (written c. 220-240 CE), to have had a miraculous birth announced by a divine being, to have been called a son of God, to have raised the dead and ascended (Philostratus). Bart Ehrman opens How Jesus Became God (pp. 10-15) with him, to show how normal such claims were.
Emperors were proclaimed divine: an inscription at Ephesus calls Julius Caesar "god manifest" and "saviour of human life".

briefs.sec: Paganism in Christianity and in Israelite religion
briefs.title: Divine triads were common in pagan religion
briefs.thesis: A three-fold unity of gods appears in Egyptian religion (Papyrus Leiden I 350), and the Pythagoreans gave sacred significance to the number three, and the Church fathers admitted the Trinity was a middle way between Jewish and Greek belief.
briefs.sum: An Egyptian hymn says "all gods are three… whom none equals", the Pythagoreans worshipped with triads, and Gregory of Nyssa called the Trinity a middle way between Jewish and Greek belief.

obj.q: "Pagan triads are three separate gods, not three persons in one being."
obj.a: The Leiden hymn explicitly says the three are one god with one hidden name, which is as close as the ancient world gets to the later formula. And Gregory himself says the doctrine takes the distinction of persons from the Greeks, while rejecting their polytheism.

prac.q: “Similarity isn't borrowing; you could say Islam copied pagan monotheism (Akhenaten).”
prac.a: Islam's monotheism is the continuation of Abraham, Moses and the prophets, which Jews and Christians also claim. The Trinity's three-in-one formula has no precedent in the prophets but does in Egypt and Greece, and a Cappadocian father admits it borrows from the Greeks.

briefs.evs:
Egypt. A Leiden hymn to Amun (13th century BCE): "All gods are three: Amun, Re and Ptah, whom none equals. He hides his name as Amun, he appears to the face as Re, his body is Ptah." Jan Assmann (Of God and Gods, p. 64) and Siegfried Morenz discuss it as a Trinitarian formula.
Tap to enlargeEgyptian religion: Amun, Re and Ptah as one god in three
Greece. Aristotle reports that the Pythagoreans regarded three as the number of the whole and used the triad in the worship of the gods (On the Heavens 1.1).
Gregory of Nyssa (Catechetical Oration 3) presents the doctrine as avoiding both errors: it takes the unity of nature from the Jews and the distinction of persons from the Greeks.
G.L. Prestige notes that Tertullian's trinitas meant a triad, not yet a tri-unity.

briefs.sec: Paganism in Christianity and in Israelite religion
briefs.title: Eating a god's flesh and drinking his blood
briefs.thesis: The Torah strictly forbids consuming blood, the Jerusalem apostles kept that rule for Gentiles, and the Ebionites, a later Jewish-Christian group, held a simple remembrance meal. The sacramental Eucharist, with its pagan parallels, is found in Paul, John and the Synoptic Gospels.
briefs.sum: The Torah forbids drinking blood, the apostles reaffirmed it, and disciples left Jesus over "drink my blood" in John 6. Paul is the source of the sacramental formula, Justin admits the Mithras parallel, and the Ebionites used water.

obj.q: "It's symbolic in many churches."
obj.a: Catholic and Orthodox doctrine says it becomes the real flesh and blood. Even as a symbol, drinking a person's blood is not a Jewish image; it is the reason the disciples left in John 6.

prac.q: “The Last Supper was a Passover meal, which is Jewish.”
prac.a: Passover is Jewish; "this is my blood, drink it" is not, which is why John reports disciples abandoning Jesus over it and why the Ebionites dropped wine. The Quran's version of the table (5:112-115) is a meal sent down as a sign, with no blood-drinking.

briefs.evs:
The Law. "If anyone of the house of Israel… eats any blood, I will set My face against that person… for the life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:10-11). The Jerusalem council told Gentile believers to abstain "from blood" (Acts 15:20).
John 6. When Jesus says "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53), "many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him" (6:66). John's own text shows how foreign the idea was to Jews.
Paul is the earliest source for the words of institution (1 Cor 11:23-26), which he says he "received from the Lord" (a phrase scholars read either as tradition or as direct revelation).
Mithras. Justin Martyr says "wicked devils have imitated" the Eucharist "in the mysteries of Mithras, commanding the same thing to be done: bread and a cup of water are placed with certain incantations" (1 Apology 66). He explains the similarity by demonic imitation in advance; a historian would note the existing mystery-meal pattern.
The Ebionites used unleavened bread and water in a yearly remembrance meal (Irenaeus; Epiphanius; Schoeps, Jewish Christianity, p. 62).

briefs.sec: Paganism in Christianity and in Israelite religion
briefs.title: Israelite religion itself absorbed pagan elements, and the Quran removes them
briefs.thesis: The Hebrew Bible preserves traces of a divine council of gods, a goddess paired with YHWH, and foreign gods with real power. The Quran's monotheism contains none of these, which is what a corrective revelation would look like.
briefs.sum: The Bible speaks of God "among the gods", dividing nations among "sons of God" (changed in the Masoretic Text), records an Asherah in the Temple and Chemosh's "great wrath" defeating Israel. The Quran's God has no consort, no council of gods and nothing like Him.

obj.q: "The Bible records Israel's sins, it doesn't approve of them."
obj.a: The Asherah inscriptions are outside the Bible and show popular religion. But Psalm 82, Deuteronomy 32:8 and 2 Kings 3:27 are inside the Bible and present the gods and Chemosh's wrath, though Psalm 82:6-7 pronounces judgement on the gods.

obj.q: "'Gods' in Psalm 82 are human judges."
obj.a: Jesus reads it that way (John 10:34), and Muslims can accept that reading. But Deuteronomy 32:8's "sons of God" dividing the nations, and the scribal change to remove it, show the text was being cleaned up later, which is the point.

prac.q: “Is Islam then saying the Bible was originally polytheistic?”
prac.a: No. Islam says the prophets taught pure monotheism, and the text that survives was shaped by the people who transmitted it, including their lapses into the religion around them. The Quran restores the original by removing those traces.

briefs.evs:
The divine council. "God stands in the council of El; in the midst of the gods He holds judgement" (Ps 82:1). "Who is like You among the gods, O LORD?" (Exod 15:11). Jephthah tells the Ammonites, "Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you?" (Judg 11:24).
Deuteronomy 32:8-9. In the Dead Sea Scroll and Septuagint, the Most High (Elyon) divided the nations "according to the number of the sons of God", and "the LORD's portion is His people". Scholars such as Mark Smith see here the older idea of El dividing the nations among his sons, with YHWH receiving Israel. On the prevailing scholarly reconstruction, the Masoretic Text changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel".
Tap to enlargeTov, p. 269: Deuteronomy 32:8 "sons of Israel" (Masoretic) vs "sons of God" (Dead Sea Scroll, Septuagint)
Tap to enlargeCommentary on Deuteronomy 32:8-9: scribes altered "sons of El" to avoid polytheism
Asherah. Inscriptions at Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom (8th century BCE) bless people "by YHWH and his Asherah" (whether Asherah is a goddess or a cultic symbol is debated). The Bible records an Asherah image in the Temple itself (2 Kgs 21:7; 23:4-7). Thomas Römer (The Invention of God) and Mark Smith describe this as part of ancient Israelite religion. The Quran: "He has taken neither a wife nor a son" (72:3).
Tap to enlarge"YHWH and his Asherah": ancient Israelite religion once paired Yahw

briefs.sec: Paganism in Christianity and in Israelite religion
briefs.title: Images and the cross: worship the Torah forbids
briefs.thesis: The Ten Commandments forbid making images for worship. Several early fathers agreed, but later Christianity adopted icons, and Catholic theology even assigns the cross the worship due to God.
briefs.sum: The second commandment forbids images for worship; Clement and Epiphanius opposed them; but Nicaea II mandated icons and Aquinas assigns the cross latria, the worship due to God.

obj.q: "Veneration (dulia) is different from worship (latria)."
obj.a: Aquinas himself assigns latria to the cross. And the commandment forbids bowing to images, not only "worshipping" in a technical sense.

prac.q: “Muslims bow toward the Kaaba, a building.”
prac.a: Muslims bow to Allah in the direction of the Kaaba; no one prays to it, there is no image, and Umar said of the Black Stone, "I know you are a stone that can neither harm nor benefit" (Bukhari 1597). Aquinas, by contrast, says the cross itself receives the worship due to God.

briefs.evs:
The commandment. "You shall not make for yourself a carved image… you shall not bow down to them or serve them" (Exod 20:4-5).
Early Christians. Clement of Alexandria condemns the making of idols, though he allows simple symbols such as a dove or fish on seal rings (Paedagogus 3.11). Epiphanius of Salamis (late 4th century) tore down a church curtain bearing an image of Christ or a saint as "contrary to the authority of the Scriptures" (Letter 51, preserved by Jerome).
Later practice. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) required the veneration of icons. Thomas Aquinas taught that the cross on which Christ died should be given latria, the worship due to God (Summa Theologiae III, q. 25, a. 4).
The Quran on Abraham's people: "What are these images to which you are devoted?" (21:52).

briefs.title: By their fruits: Satan does not cast out Satan
briefs.thesis: Jesus gave the "tree and fruit" test for prophets, and an argument about Satan and exorcism: Satan does not oppose himself, and a tree is known by its fruit. Muhammad ﷺ passes both: he called people away from idols and toward the one God, and his fruit was righteousness. So a Christian must either accept him or reject Jesus' own tests.
briefs.sum: Jesus said Satan doesn't cast out Satan and a tree is known by its fruit. Muhammad ﷺ ended idol worship, called Satan man's enemy and taught righteousness, and his Rome prophecy came true. By Jesus' own tests, he can't be from Satan.

obj.q: "Satan can appear as an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14), so good teachings could be a trick."
obj.a: Then the same argument applies to Jesus, and Jesus' test becomes useless. Jesus said Satan does not work against his own kingdom; a message that destroyed idol worship across Arabia and led millions to worship the God of Abraham is working against it.

obj.q: "Muhammad denied the crucifixion and deity of Christ, which is satanic."
obj.a: That assumes the conclusion. The test Jesus gave is fruit and opposition to Satan's works, not agreement with later doctrine.

prac.q: “Muhammad led wars, so his fruits were bad.”
prac.a: So did Moses, Joshua and David, whom Christians call prophets. The relevant fruit is what he taught and the society it produced: monotheism, prayer, charity, the protection of orphans and the end of infanticide. That is what Jesus' test looks at.

briefs.evs:
The Quran's constant theme is the worship of the God of Abraham alone: "Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him; and to parents do good" (4:36). It says repeatedly that Satan is man's enemy (2:168; 35:6; 36:60). The result was that within one generation Arabia moved from idol worship, infanticide and tribal blood-feuds to monotheism and law.
Non-Muslim historians have said the same about his fruits. W. Montgomery Watt: "to suppose Muhammad an impostor raises more problems than it solves". R. Bosworth Smith said he "ruled by a right Divine". Lamartine asked, measured by the greatness of aim, smallness of means and astounding results, "who could dare compare any great man in modern history with Muhammad?"
Jesus himself was accused of being in league with Beelzebub (Mark 3:22), and gave this answer; Christians who say Muhammad was inspired by Satan repeat the Pharisees' charge.
The Torah adds a second test: a prophet whose prophecies come true (Deut 18:21-22). The Quran's prophecy that Rome would defeat Persia within a few years (30:2-4) was fulfilled; Edward Gibbon wrote that at the time the prediction "is said to have been delivered", "no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment".

briefs.title: "God died": Christian doctrine against the Bible
briefs.thesis: Official Christian doctrine says the person who died on the cross was the divine Son, so "God died". The Bible says God is immortal. And Paul says a mediator implies two parties, but "God is one", and calls the mediator "the man Christ Jesus".
briefs.sum: Constantinople II says the one crucified is "one of the Holy Trinity", so God died; the Bible says God alone is immortal. Paul calls the one mediator "the man Christ Jesus", distinct from the one God.

obj.q: "Only his human nature died."
obj.a: A nature doesn't die; persons do. The council says the one crucified is "one of the Holy Trinity". If that Person did not die, then no divine Person died and the sacrifice was a human one; if he did, God died.

prac.q: “You don't understand the hypostatic union.”
prac.a: I'm quoting your own council: the one crucified is "one of the Holy Trinity". Either that Person died or he didn't. If he died, God died, against 1 Timothy 6:16. If he didn't, then only a man died, and Christianity's infinite sacrifice disappears.

briefs.evs:
The council. Constantinople II (553), canon 10: "If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ who was crucified in the flesh is true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity, let him be anathema." The Catechism of the Catholic Church (468) cites it.
The Bible. God "alone has immortality" (1 Tim 6:16); He is "immortal, invisible, the only God" (1 Tim 1:17).
The mediator. "Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one" (Gal 3:20, about the mediator of the Law). "There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). The mediator is distinguished from the one God and called a man.
Even the Catechism concedes (441) that "son of God" as a title of the Messiah-king does not in itself imply more than human.

briefs.title: Jeconiah's curse and the two genealogies
briefs.thesis: God cursed King Jeconiah's line so that none of his offspring would sit on David's throne. Matthew traces Jesus' line through Jeconiah; Luke traces a different line through Nathan, not Solomon. Either way the Christian Messiah has a problem.
briefs.sum: God barred Jeconiah's descendants from David's throne (Jer 22:30). Matthew puts Jeconiah in Jesus' line; Luke uses Nathan instead of Solomon; and both lists run through Joseph, who on Christian belief was not Jesus' father.

obj.q: "Haggai 2:23 reverses the curse by making Zerubbabel God's signet ring."
obj.a: Jeremiah 22:24 used the signet-ring image for Jeconiah's rejection. Haggai's use of it for Zerubbabel promised him authority, but he never sat on David's throne; he governed for Persia. The curse's terms (no descendant on the throne) were not lifted in the text.

prac.q: “Jesus is the legal heir through Joseph and the biological heir through Mary, so both lines are covered.”
prac.a: Luke says "Joseph, son of Heli", and the early church took both lists as Joseph's. And neither list gives Mary's ancestry in the text. So Jesus is either Jeconiah's heir (cursed) or has no stated Davidic blood line through Solomon.

briefs.evs:
Jeremiah 22:30: "Write this man down as childless… for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."
Matthew 1:11-12 includes "Jechoniah" in Jesus' line through Joseph.
Luke 3:23-31 runs from Joseph back through Nathan, a different son of David.
Whose genealogy is Luke's? Christians now often say Luke gives Mary's line. But the text says "Joseph, the son of Heli" (Luke 3:23), and early Christian writers (Julius Africanus, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 1.7; Augustine; John of Damascus) explained the two lists as both belonging to Joseph. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the "Mary's genealogy" theory became popular only from Annius of Viterbo in the 15th century.
Zerubbabel, who appears in both lists, was only a Persian governor (Hag 1:14), not a king, so the curse held for him.

briefs.title: The Bible's own confirmation fails
briefs.thesis: Christians argue that the Quran confirms the Bible, so Muslims must accept it (the "Islamic dilemma"). But the NT says "all Scripture is God-breathed" and Paul affirms "everything in the Law and the Prophets", while also misquoting them. The same dilemma hits the NT.
briefs.sum: Paul affirms everything in the Law and the Prophets but changes "received gifts" to "gave gifts" and reverses Deuteronomy 27:26. So biblical "confirmation" is general, not word-for-word, which is the Muslim view of the Quran's confirmation.

obj.q: "Paul was paraphrasing for application."
obj.a: Then the NT's "confirmation" of the OT allows interpretation and selection, which is all Muslims claim for the Quran's confirmation of earlier books (see The Quran & the earlier scriptures).

prac.q: “The Quran says the Torah and Gospel are from God, so you must accept the Bible.”
prac.a: The Quran confirms what God revealed to Moses and Jesus, and calls itself the guardian over it (5:48). Paul affirmed "everything in the Law and the Prophets" and still changed Psalm 68:18. If affirmation doesn't mean "every word in your copy", my position is the same as Paul's.

briefs.evs:
Psalm 68:18: "You ascended on high… receiving gifts among men." Ephesians 4:8: "When he ascended on high… he gave gifts to men." The change is needed for Paul's point about Christ giving gifts to the church.
Deuteronomy 27:26: "Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them." Galatians 3:10: "All who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written…" Paul turns a curse on law-breakers into a curse on law-keepers.
Variants. The OT Paul cites survives in Hebrew and Greek versions that differ (see Corruption); the NT authors usually follow the Greek.

briefs.title: The prophets say sacrifices continue in the messianic age
briefs.thesis: Hebrews says Christ's sacrifice ended the sacrificial system. But Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Zechariah say that in the messianic age, after the new covenant, Levitical priests will offer sacrifices forever, and the Messiah-prince himself offers a sin offering for himself.
briefs.sum: Jeremiah promises Levitical sacrifices forever after the new covenant; Ezekiel's Davidic prince offers a sin offering for himself; Zechariah has sacrifices in the last age. Hebrews says they ended with Christ.

obj.q: "These are symbolic or memorial sacrifices."
obj.a: Ezekiel 45:22 calls it a sin offering, and the prince offers it for himself. Calling it symbolic is a way of admitting the text does not fit.

prac.q: “Hebrews explains that the old sacrifices were shadows of Christ.”
prac.a: Hebrews says so, but Jeremiah says the Levitical priests will offer sacrifices "forever" after the new covenant, and Ezekiel's messianic prince offers one for himself. Hebrews contradicts the prophets it claims to fulfil.

briefs.evs:
Jeremiah 33:17-18: "David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of Israel, and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in My presence to offer burnt offerings… and to make sacrifices forever." Verse 21 binds the two promises together. This follows the "new covenant" promise of 31:31.
Ezekiel 45:22: in the restored Temple, "the prince shall provide for himself and all the people of the land a young bull for a sin offering". Ezekiel 37:24-25 speaks of "David My servant" as prince, which many read as the Messiah, though the prince of chapters 40-48 is not named. A sinless Messiah would not need a sin offering for himself.
Zechariah 14:21: in the final age, "all who sacrifice will come and take [the pots] and boil the meat in them".
Hebrews 10:11-18: Christ's single offering has ended sacrifice for sin.

briefs.title: "Do whatever the Pharisees tell you"
briefs.thesis: Jesus told his followers to obey the scribes and Pharisees "who sit on Moses' seat", who taught the Law, circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. Christians who follow Paul in abandoning these disobey Jesus' explicit command.
briefs.sum: Jesus said to obey whatever the Pharisees taught from Moses' seat, condemning only their hypocrisy. Paul told believers to ignore food, festival and Sabbath laws. Christians must choose.

obj.q: "This was before the cross; the Law ended afterwards."
obj.a: Jesus' instructions in Matthew are given as permanent teaching for disciples (Matt 28:20, "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you"). And the Jerusalem church continued to keep the Law after the cross (Acts 21:20).

prac.q: “Jesus condemned the Pharisees throughout Matthew 23.”
prac.a: He condemned their hypocrisy, and in the same breath said "do and observe whatever they tell you". The command is about their teaching from Moses' seat, which included the whole Law.

briefs.evs: Jesus' criticism in Matthew 23 was of hypocrisy, though he also criticised their traditions (Matt 15:1-9; 16:12). He even says they should tithe mint and dill while not neglecting justice (Matt 23:23). Compare Paul: circumcision makes Christ of no advantage (Gal 5:2), and "let no one pass judgement on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a Sabbath" (Col 2:16).

briefs.sec: Morality in the Bible & the Church
briefs.title: God forgives without blood, and no one bears another's sin
briefs.thesis: The Old Testament says God forgives the repentant without sacrifice and that a son does not bear his father's sin. The doctrines of original sin and the necessity of blood atonement contradict this.
briefs.sum: Ezekiel 18 says the son doesn't bear the father's sin and the repentant are forgiven; the Psalms, Hosea and Micah say God wants a contrite heart, not sacrifice; and Nineveh was forgiven with no blood. Original sin and blood atonement contradict the prophets.

obj.q: "Hebrews 9:22: without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness."
obj.a: Hebrews says so, but the prophets say the opposite repeatedly, and Leviticus itself allows flour as a sin offering for the poor (Lev 5:11-13). Jonah 3:10 shows a whole city forgiven without blood.

obj.q: "God's justice requires a penalty to be paid."
obj.a: Punishing an innocent person for the guilty is the opposite of justice by the Bible's own law (Deut 24:16; Ezek 18:20). A judge who lets the guilty go and executes an innocent volunteer is not just.

prac.q: “If God just forgives, He isn't just. Someone has to pay.”
prac.a: Ezekiel 18 says God forgives the repentant and "none of his transgressions shall be remembered". Forgiveness means not exacting the debt. If God must punish someone, then He never forgives; He only transfers the punishment, and to an innocent person, which Ezekiel 18:20 forbids.

briefs.evs:
Personal responsibility. "The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son" (Ezek 18:20). "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children" (Deut 24:16). The Quran: "No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (6:164).
Repentance is enough. "If a wicked person turns away from all his sins… he shall surely live; none of the transgressions he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezek 18:21-22). "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (18:23).
Not sacrifice. "You will not delight in sacrifice… the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" (Ps 51:16-17). "I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice" (Hos 6:6), which Jesus himself quotes (Matt 9:13). "With what shall I come before the LORD… with burnt offerings?… He has told you what is good: to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God" (Mic 6:6-8). "By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for" (Prov 16:6).
Nineveh. The pagan city repented with fasting and sackcloth, and "God relented of the disaster" (Jonah 3:10). No sacrifice, no blood.
Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar to "break off your sins by practising righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy t

briefs.sec: Morality in the Bible & the Church
briefs.title: War: the Bible commands killing infants; Islam forbids it
briefs.thesis: Critics call Islam violent, yet the Bible commands the destruction of whole populations, including infants, while Islamic law forbids killing women, children, the old and monks, and requires proportionality.
briefs.sum: The Bible commands killing "child and infant" (1 Sam 15:3) and keeping virgin girls (Num 31:18). Islam forbids killing women, children, the old and monks, and commands proportion, asylum and peace when offered.

obj.q: "Those were specific historical commands, not permanent law; the Quran's commands are permanent."
obj.a: Then Christians accept that God commanded killing infants in history. The Quran's permanent rules forbid it. If a permanent rule against killing children is worse than a historical command to kill them, the standard has been reversed.

obj.q: "Jesus taught love of enemies; that's what Christians follow."
obj.a: Christians also hold that the God who gave 1 Samuel 15:3 is Jesus' Father, unchanged (Mal 3:6; Heb 13:8). And Christian nations for centuries cited the Old Testament wars to justify their own.

prac.q: “The Quran has the "sword verse" (9:5), commanding Muslims to kill unbelievers wherever they find them.”
prac.a: 9:5 is about specific Arab polytheist tribes who broke treaties (9:4, 9:7-13), and the very next verse (9:6) commands granting protection to any who ask and escorting them to safety. Islamic law never permitted killing non-combatants. 1 Samuel 15:3 explicitly orders killing infants.

briefs.evs:
The Bible.
"Go and strike Amalek… do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep" (1 Sam 15:3). This sits uneasily with Deuteronomy 24:16 (children are not killed for their fathers' sins), since Amalek is punished for what its ancestors did centuries earlier (15:2).
"Kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man… but all the young girls who have not known man keep alive for yourselves" (Num 31:17-18).
"In the cities of these peoples… you shall save alive nothing that breathes" (Deut 20:16).
"Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock" (Ps 137:9, a curse, not a command); "their little ones shall be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open" (Hos 13:16).
Islam.
The Prophet ﷺ forbade killing women and children (Bukhari 3015). Abu Bakr's instructions to his army (Muwatta Malik, Book of Jihad): do not kill women, children or the elderly, do not cut down fruit trees, do not destroy buildings, leave monks in their cells.
"Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress" (2:190). "If they incline to peace, then incline to it" (8:61). "If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant it to him… then deliver him to his place of safety" (9:6). "If you punish, punish with the like of what you were made to suffer" (16:126).

briefs.sec: Morality in the Bible & the Church
briefs.title: Marriage, women and modesty in Christian tradition
briefs.thesis: The Bible's prophets practised polygyny without rebuke, Church law permitted marriage at twelve, and the fathers required women to veil their heads and even their faces. Critics who attack Islam on these points condemn their own tradition.
briefs.sum: Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon had several wives, and Luther couldn't forbid it; Paul and Clement required the veil; canon law allowed girls to marry at twelve. Critics who attack Islam on these points condemn their own tradition.

obj.q: "The New Testament moved beyond polygamy."
obj.a: No NT verse explicitly forbids it for ordinary believers; 1 Timothy 3:2 limits overseers to one wife, which implies others had more. And Luther, reading the same NT, could not forbid it.

prac.q: “Islam oppresses women with the hijab.”
prac.a: Paul commands head covering, Clement says face covered, and nuns and Orthodox women still veil. Mary is always shown veiled. The Quran's modesty rule (24:31) is the same tradition, applied to all believing women.

briefs.evs:
Polygyny. "If a man has two wives…" (Deut 21:15) regulates it. God says to David, "I gave you your master's wives into your arms" (2 Sam 12:8), and David "did what was right… except in the matter of Uriah" (1 Kgs 15:5). Tertullian says it was lawful for the patriarchs (To His Wife 1.2). Luther wrote in 1524 that he could not forbid a man to marry several wives because it does not contradict Scripture. Biblical scholar Dan McClellan: "the standard in the Bible is polygamy… nowhere identified as sinful." The Quran limits it to four with the condition of justice (4:3), and al-Shafi'i recommended limiting oneself to one.
Tap to enlargeDan McClellan: "the standard in the Bible is polygamy… nowhere identified as sinful"
Tap to enlargeClassical fiqh: al-Shafi'i preferred limiting oneself to one wife (4:3)
The veil. Paul: "every wife who prays with her head uncovered dishonours her head… if a wife will not cover her head, let her cut her hair short" (1 Cor 11:5-6). Clement of Alexandria: a woman should go out "with her head veiled and her face covered" (Paedagogus 3.11). The Apostolic Tradition (18.5) requires women to cover their heads with an opaque cloth. Tertullian wrote a whole treatise On the Veiling of Virgins.
Age of marriage. The Protevangelium of James (2nd century) says Mary was entrusted to an elderly Joseph at twelve. Medieval canon law set the minimum age of marriage at t

briefs.sec: Morality in the Bible & the Church
briefs.title: The Church's own moral record
briefs.thesis: Indulgences sold for money, heretics executed by Church teaching, unbaptised infants consigned to hell, the Crusades and the Inquisition: the Church's moral record does not entitle critics to treat Christianity as morally superior.
briefs.sum: Popes sold indulgences, Augustine damned unbaptised infants, Aquinas taught heretics should be killed, and the Crusades massacred Jews and sacked Constantinople. The Church is in no position to judge Islam by its followers' conduct.

obj.q: "These are people's sins, not Christianity's teaching."
obj.a: Indulgence sales were papal policy, and infant damnation and the death of heretics were taught by Augustine and Aquinas, though Aquinas' view was also condemned in effect by Exsurge Domine (1520)

prac.q: “Islam spread by the sword.”
prac.a: Islam spread by conquest in some regions and by trade and preaching in others (Indonesia, West Africa); the Quran says "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256), and Christian communities survived under Muslim rule for 1,400 years. Christianity was imposed by imperial edicts in 380 and by the Inquisition.

briefs.evs:
Indulgences. Pope Leo X authorised indulgences to fund St Peter's Basilica; the preacher Johann Tetzel was associated with the slogan "as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs". Luther's 95 Theses (1517) attacked this. The Catholic Encyclopedia admits the abuses, which continued until the Council of Trent.
Tap to enlargeCatholic Encyclopedia, "Indulgences": the Church admits the abuses
Infants in hell. Augustine taught that unbaptised infants are damned and that promising them heaven is heresy (On the Soul and its Origin 1.9-11).
Heretics. Thomas Aquinas taught that heretics, after a second warning, may be handed to the secular power "to be exterminated from the world by death" (Summa II-II, q. 11, a. 3). Emperor Theodosius' edict of 380 made Nicene Christianity compulsory.
The Crusades included the massacres of Rhineland Jews (1096), the slaughter in Jerusalem (1099), and the sack of Christian Constantinople (1204).
Prostitution. Augustine wrote, "remove prostitutes from society and you will disturb everything with lust" (On Order 2.4.12), and some medieval bishops (e.g. the Bishop of Winchester) drew income from brothels.

briefs.sec: Morality in the Bible & the Church
briefs.title: "Allah does not love the disbelievers" and the biblical God's hatred
briefs.thesis: Christians contrast "God is love" with Quranic verses saying Allah does not love the wrongdoers. The Bible says God hates evildoers, hated Esau, and makes His love conditional on obedience.
briefs.sum: The Bible says God hates evildoers (Ps 5:5; 11:5), hated Esau (Mal 1:3; Rom 9:13), and loves those who keep His commandments (John 14:21). The Quran's "Allah does not love the wrongdoers" says the same.

obj.q: "'Hate' in Malachi means 'love less'."
obj.a: Then the Quran's "does not love" can be read the same way, as the withholding of special favour, not malice. The standard has to be applied equally.

prac.q: “The Christian God loved the world so much he died for it; the Muslim God loves only the obedient.”
prac.a: The Bible's God "hates all evildoers" (Ps 5:5) and loves those who keep His commandments (John 14:21). The Quran says Allah's mercy encompasses everything (7:156) and He forgives all sins of those who repent (39:53).

briefs.evs:
"You hate all evildoers" (Ps 5:5); "His soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence" (Ps 11:5).
"Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" (Mal 1:2-3), repeated by Paul (Rom 9:13).
"Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of My house; I will love them no more" (Hos 9:15).
"Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father" (John 14:21). "Because you listen to these rules and keep them… He will love you" (Deut 7:12-13).
The Quran also says Allah loves the doers of good, the repentant, the just and the patient (2:195, 2:222, 5:42, 3:146), and His mercy encompasses everything (7:156).

briefs.sec: Morality in the Bible & the Church
briefs.title: Use with care: the "embarrassing passages" list
briefs.thesis: When a critic mocks a hadith as disgusting or bizarre, there is almost always a biblical passage at least as striking. Use these only as a mirror, never as mockery of the earlier prophets.
briefs.sum: Saul's evil spirit from the LORD, Ezekiel's dung-baked bread, Elisha's bones and bears, and "statutes that were not good" show that critics who mock hadith would have to mock their own Bible.
briefs.caution: This is purely a tu quoque tool. Muslims believe in the prophets named here and must not mock them; the point is that the critic's standard condemns his own book.

prac.q: “Your hadith say the Prophet was bewitched. How can a prophet be affected by magic?”
prac.a: The magic affected his body temporarily, not his revelation, and the Quran's last two surahs were the cure. The Bible says an evil spirit "from the LORD" tormented Saul, a prophet; if that doesn't disqualify the Bible, the hadith doesn't disqualify the Prophet ﷺ.

briefs.evs:
"The Prophet ﷺ was bewitched / Gabriel squeezed him." Saul, whom the Bible counts among the prophets (1 Sam 10:11), was tormented by "an evil spirit from the LORD" (1 Sam 16:14); Josephus says it choked and suffocated him (Antiquities 6.8.2).
"Camel urine is disgusting." God tells Ezekiel to bake bread on human dung, then allows cow dung instead (Ezek 4:12-15).
"Hadith about relics and blessings." Elisha's bones raised a dead man (2 Kgs 13:21); power went out of Jesus' garment (Luke 8:46).
Violent stories. Elisha's curse brings bears that maul 42 boys for mocking his baldness (2 Kgs 2:23-24); Jephthah sacrifices his daughter (Judg 11); a Levite throws his concubine to a mob (Judg 19:25); David pays for Michal with 200 Philistine foreskins (1 Sam 18:25-27).
"Statutes that were not good." God says He gave Israel "statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not live", making them offer their firstborn (Ezek 20:25-26).
Cosmology. The earth on pillars (1 Sam 2:8; Job 9:6) and a tree visible "to the end of the whole earth" (Dan 4:11).

briefs.sec: Christian miracle claims and later traditions
briefs.title: What a miracle can and cannot prove
briefs.thesis: A miracle is evidence for a prophet only when it accompanies a claim to prophethood and a message. Apparitions and wonders without a claimant or message prove nothing, every religion reports them, and the Bible itself warns that deceptive signs occur.
briefs.sum: Miracles authenticate a prophet's message; Fatima, Zeitoun and bleeding hosts have no prophet, other religions report equivalent wonders, and the Bible warns of deceptive signs. They prove nothing.

obj.q: "Muslims also report miracles of saints."
obj.a: Islam does not base its truth on them. The Quran rests its case on the Quran itself, the Prophet's ﷺ fulfilled prophecies and his character, which are public and checkable. Karamat of saints are not proof of Islam.

prac.q: “Millions saw the sun dance at Fatima. How do you explain that?”
prac.a: The accounts conflict, people at other locations saw nothing, and staring at the sun produces visual effects. But even granting something happened, it came with no prophet and no new revelation. The Bible itself says deceptive signs will appear (Matt 24:24; 2 Cor 11:14).

briefs.evs:
The criterion. In the Quran and the Bible, signs come with prophets as proof of their message (Exod 4:1-9; Quran 7:106-108). An unexplained light or image with no message is not a credential for anyone.
Apparitions. Witness accounts of the Fatima "miracle of the sun" (1917) contradict each other; Kevin McClure's study documents the inconsistencies. The Zeitoun lights (1968) carried no message.
Other religions. In 1995 statues of Ganesha across India were reported to "drink milk"; scientists explained it by capillary action. If such events prove a religion, they prove Hinduism too.
Eucharistic miracles. Catholic sites report consecrated hosts bleeding "type AB blood". Kelly Kearse, a Catholic immunologist, has written that bacteria can share surface antigens with blood types, so AB typing does not show a human source.
Relics. In the Middle Ages several churches claimed to hold Jesus' foreskin (the "Holy Prepuce"); Marc Shell documents the competition. A relic economy is not evidence of truth.
The Bible's warning. "False christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect" (Matt 24:24).

briefs.sec: Christian miracle claims and later traditions
briefs.title: Christmas and the papacy have no New Testament basis
briefs.thesis: Two of the most visible features of Christianity, the feast of Christmas and the authority of the Pope, are absent from the NT and the earliest church.
briefs.sum: The NT never mentions Christmas, and 25 December appears in the 4th century. Clement of Rome writes for a church, not a pope, and Ignatius' letter to Rome mentions no bishop.

obj.q: "Matthew 16:18 makes Peter the rock and founds the papacy."
obj.a: It mentions Peter, not Rome or successors. Eastern Orthodox and Protestant churches read it differently, and the earliest sources show no universal Roman jurisdiction.

prac.q: “Muslims celebrate the Prophet's birthday too.”
prac.a: Many Muslim scholars reject the Mawlid as an innovation precisely because it has no basis in the Quran or Sunnah. Islam distinguishes revelation from later custom; the point is that Christianity has no such check.

briefs.evs:
Christmas. The NT never mentions a feast of Jesus' birth or its date. The sermons in Acts focus on the resurrection; Paul never mentions a birth festival. The 25 December date is first attested in the 4th century.
The papacy. 1 Clement (c. 96), written from Rome to Corinth, speaks for "the church of God in Rome", not for a single bishop with universal jurisdiction. Ignatius of Antioch writes to six churches emphasising their bishop, but his letter to Rome mentions no bishop at all and describes the Roman church as the one that "presides in the region of the Romans".

briefs.sec: Historical problems in the Old Testament
briefs.title: Solomon's Temple: a huge workforce for a small building
briefs.thesis: 1 Kings lists 183,300 men (including a rotating levy of 30,000) for Solomon's building work, with seven years spent on a temple roughly 27 metres long and 9 metres wide, about the floor area of a large house. The numbers are not credible as history.
briefs.sum: 183,300 workers for seven years and over 3,000 tonnes of gold for a building of about 27 by 9 metres, in a region whose population archaeologists put in the thousands or low tens of thousands. The figures are not history.

obj.q: "The workers built Solomon's palace and other projects too."
obj.a: The text ties the Temple work to the levy (1 Kgs 5:5, 13-18), but 1 Kgs 9:15 says the levy also built the palace, the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. And even spread across all his building, 183,000 workers exceeds the population archaeology allows for the region.

obj.q: "Archaeologists like Eilat Mazar found Solomonic structures."
obj.a: Mazar's identifications are disputed, and even if accepted they show a modest administrative centre, not an empire able to field nearly 200,000 labourers and thousands of tonnes of gold.

prac.q: “You're relying on Finkelstein, a minimalist.”
prac.a: Finkelstein is a mainstream Israeli archaeologist, not a minimalist. But set his population estimate aside: 3,000 tonnes of gold for a temple in a hill kingdom is impossible on any reckoning, and Kings and Chronicles don't even agree on the number of officers.

briefs.evs:
The workforce. "King Solomon drafted forced labour out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men… Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country, besides 3,300 chief officers" (1 Kgs 5:13-16). That is 183,300 men. 2 Chronicles 2:18 gives 3,600 officers instead of 3,300.
The time. "He was seven years in building it" (1 Kgs 6:38). His own palace took thirteen (7:1).
The building. "The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high" (1 Kgs 6:2): about 27 by 9 metres, roughly 240 square metres of floor, plus a porch and side rooms.
The population. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman (The Bible Unearthed, 2001) estimate the population of the Judean highlands in the 10th century BCE at around 5,000 people in some twenty small villages, and Jerusalem as no more than a modest town. Even the higher estimates of other archaeologists cannot supply 183,000 labourers.
The gold. David is said to have set aside 100,000 talents of gold and a million talents of silver for the Temple (1 Chr 22:14). A talent was roughly 30-34 kg, so that is over 3,000 tonnes of gold, comparable to the whole world's annual gold mining today, for a small hill kingdom.

briefs.sec: Historical problems in the Old Testament
briefs.title: The Exodus and the wilderness leave no trace
briefs.thesis: The Bible describes over two million Israelites leaving Egypt and living forty years in Sinai. Egyptian records never mention it and excavations at the key wilderness sites have found nothing from that period. The Quran, by contrast, never gives the inflated numbers.
briefs.sum: Exodus gives 603,550 men, two to three million people, for forty years in Sinai; Egyptian records are silent and Kadesh-barnea has nothing from that age. The Quran's "small band" (26:54) avoids the problem.

obj.q: "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence."
obj.a: It is, when evidence is expected and searched for. Two million people for forty years would leave far more than nomads do, and Sinai has been surveyed intensively. Muslims accept that an Exodus happened; the problem is the biblical scale and details.

obj.q: "Elef means 'clan' or 'unit', not 'thousand'."
obj.a: Some scholars propose this to shrink the numbers, but then Numbers 1:46's exact total of 603,550 and the arithmetic of Numbers 3:43-51 (the redemption money for 273 firstborn) make no sense. The proposal admits the plain text is unhistorical.

prac.q: “Muslims also believe in the Exodus, so you can't use archaeology against it.”
prac.a: Correct, I believe Moses led the Israelites out. The point is the Bible's version, with over two million people and exact census totals, which the evidence contradicts. The Quran's "small band" fits the evidence; the Bible's numbers don't.

briefs.evs:
The numbers. 600,000 men on foot besides women and children (Exod 12:37); the census in Numbers 1:46 gives exactly 603,550 fighting men. With families that is two to three million people, more than the estimated population of Egypt at the time.
No Egyptian record. Egyptian sources mention Semitic workers and the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) mentions "Israel" as a people in Canaan, but no Egyptian text mentions a mass departure, plagues or the loss of an army.
The wilderness. Excavations at Kadesh-barnea (Tell el-Qudeirat) by Rudolph Cohen found no Late Bronze or Iron I settlement; the earliest fortress there dates to the 10th century BCE. Finkelstein and Silberman write that repeated surveys of Sinai have found no evidence of the wanderings.
Contrast with the Quran. The Quran's Pharaoh calls the Israelites "a small band" (26:54) and gives no census. See The Quran correcting earlier scripture.

briefs.sec: Historical problems in the Old Testament
briefs.title: The conquest of Canaan: Jericho and Ai
briefs.thesis: Joshua describes the dramatic destruction of Jericho and Ai. Excavation shows Jericho had no walled city in the relevant period, and Ai had been a ruin for a thousand years.
briefs.sum: Kenyon dated Jericho's destruction to about 1550 BCE with no 13th-century city; Ai was a ruin from about 2400 BCE until a small village around 1200. The conquest as written does not fit the evidence.

obj.q: "Bryant Wood redated Jericho's destruction to about 1400 BCE."
obj.a: Wood's redating was rejected by most archaeologists, and radiocarbon dating of the destruction layer (Bruins and van der Plicht, 1995) supported the 16th-century date.

obj.q: "Ai is at a different site (Khirbet el-Maqatir)."
obj.a: That is a minority proposal; most archaeologists accept et-Tell, though Maqatir is also east of Bethel and the identification is debated. Moving the site to rescue the story concedes the problem at the obvious location.

prac.q: “Archaeology keeps confirming the Bible.”
prac.a: It confirms that places like Jericho existed. It doesn't confirm Joshua's account: Jericho's walls fell around 1550 BCE and Ai, "the ruin", lay abandoned for over a thousand years before the Iron I village, and was already a ruin before Joshua's time. Radiocarbon dating backs Kenyon.

briefs.evs:
Jericho. Joshua 6 describes the walls falling and the city burned. Kathleen Kenyon's excavations (1952-58) dated the destruction of the walled city to about 1550 BCE, long before any likely date for Joshua, with only slight occupation in the 14th century and none in the 13th. John Garstang's earlier date for the walls was corrected by Kenyon.
Ai. Joshua 7-8 describes Ai as a city with a king and 12,000 inhabitants killed. The name Ai (ha-'Ay) means "the ruin". At et-Tell, the standard identification, excavations found a large Early Bronze city destroyed around 2400 BCE and an unwalled hamlet only around 1200 BCE. Callaway, a Southern Baptist archaeologist, concluded that the biblical account cannot be reconciled with the site.
Joshua vs Judges. Joshua says "Joshua took the whole land… and the land had rest from war" (Josh 11:23), while Judges 1 lists the many cities the tribes failed to conquer. See Contradictions in Old Testament stories.
The scholarly consensus. William Dever, Finkelstein and most archaeologists now see Israel emerging gradually from within Canaan rather than through a sudden conquest.

briefs.sec: Historical problems in the Old Testament
briefs.title: Camels, Philistines and Chaldeans in the time of Abraham
briefs.thesis: The patriarchal stories mention domesticated camels, Philistines and "Ur of the Chaldeans", all of which belong to centuries after the time the stories describe. They show the stories were written much later.
briefs.sum: Domesticated camels (10th century BCE), Philistines (12th century BCE), Chaldeans (9th century BCE), the city of Dan, and "before any king reigned over Israel" all place Genesis' writing long after Abraham and Moses.

obj.q: "Camels could have been used occasionally earlier."
obj.a: Some wild or rare camels may have been known, but Genesis describes them as ordinary property and transport, like flocks and donkeys. The anachronism is in treating them as common.

obj.q: "'Philistines' is just an updated name for the earlier people there."
obj.a: Then the text was updated by later editors, which is the point: the stories as we have them were reworked centuries later.

prac.q: “These are tiny details; they don't affect the message.”
prac.a: They show when the text was written: by people living after camels were common, after the Philistines arrived, and after Israel had kings. A text written that late can't be Moses' own record, which is what the claim of a preserved Torah requires.

briefs.evs:
Camels. Abraham receives camels from Pharaoh (Gen 12:16); Abraham's servant takes ten camels to find Rebekah (Gen 24:10). Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef (Tel Aviv journal, 2013), studying camel bones in the copper mines of the Aravah, dated the introduction of domesticated camels in the region to the last third of the 10th century BCE.
Philistines. Abraham and Isaac deal with "Abimelech king of the Philistines" in Gerar (Gen 21:32-34; 26:1). The Philistines settled in Canaan around 1175 BCE as part of the Sea Peoples' movement. Claus Westermann (Genesis 12-36) notes the anachronism.
Ur of the Chaldeans. Abraham comes from "Ur of the Chaldeans" (Gen 11:31). The Chaldeans appear in Assyrian records only from the 9th century BCE.
"Dan". Abraham pursues his enemies "as far as Dan" (Gen 14:14), but the city received that name only after the tribe of Dan conquered it in Judges 18:29.
"Before any king reigned over Israel". Genesis 36:31 lists the kings of Edom "before any king reigned over the Israelites", which most critical scholars read as written after Israel had kings (traditional readers take it as anticipating the monarchy, Gen 17:6; Deut 17:14-20).

briefs.sec: Historical problems in the Old Testament
briefs.title: Daniel and Esther get the Persian and Babylonian world wrong
briefs.thesis: Daniel calls Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar and king of Babylon, and invents a "Darius the Mede" who took Babylon. Esther has Mordecai exiled in 597 BCE yet serving Xerxes over a century later. These are the errors of writers far removed from the events.
briefs.sum: Belshazzar was Nabonidus' son and never king, against Daniel 5; "Darius the Mede" is unknown to history; Mordecai would be over 110 under Xerxes. These books were written well after the events.

obj.q: "'Father' can mean ancestor or predecessor."
obj.a: It can, but Daniel 5 builds a family drama around it (the queen mother's speech, 5:10-12), and Belshazzar was not Nebuchadnezzar's descendant at all. "King" for a regent is also a stretch, yet the text has him offer the "third" rank in the kingdom because he knew he was second, which suggests the author knew he was not the true king but not why.

obj.q: "Darius the Mede is another name for Cyrus or Gubaru."
obj.a: These identifications are guesses made to save the text, and none is proven. Gubaru is attested in the Nabonidus Chronicle as a governor, but nothing calls him king or 'Darius'. Daniel 6:28 distinguishes "Darius" from "Cyrus the Persian".

prac.q: “The discovery of Belshazzar's name vindicated Daniel against sceptics.”
prac.a: It showed Belshazzar existed, and that he was Nabonidus' son, not Nebuchadnezzar's, and never king. The same inscriptions are hard to square with Daniel's wording on both points.

briefs.evs:
Belshazzar. Daniel 5 calls Belshazzar "king" and repeatedly says Nebuchadnezzar was "his father" (5:2, 11, 13, 18). The Nabonidus Chronicle and cylinder inscriptions show Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus, who was not Nebuchadnezzar's son (a family link through marriage is disputed), and that Belshazzar acted as regent but was never king.
Darius the Mede. "Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old" (Dan 5:31). No such king is known. Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BCE, and the Darius of history (Darius I) came later. Scholars generally see a confusion of Persian kings.
The date of Daniel. Most scholars date Daniel to the 160s BCE because its "predictions" are accurate up to the persecution of Antiochus IV and then go wrong about his death (Dan 11:40-45).
Esther. Esth 2:5-6 can be read to say Mordecai himself was carried away with Jeconiah in 597 BCE (though the Hebrew may refer to his ancestor Kish). Esther is set under Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, 486-465 BCE), which on that reading would make Mordecai well over 110 when he became prime minister. Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther, and Herodotus (3.84) says Persian kings were to marry only into the seven noble families, which does not fit a Jewish commoner becoming queen.

briefs.sec: Historical problems in the Old Testament
briefs.title: Impossible numbers in Kings and Chronicles
briefs.thesis: Chronicles and Kings give army sizes and death tolls in the hundreds of thousands, sometimes a million, for small kingdoms. They contradict each other and are impossible for the population of the time.
briefs.sum: 500,000 killed in one battle, a million-man army, census totals that differ between books, and 40,000 vs 4,000 stalls. Even Assyria's largest recorded armies were a fraction of these numbers.

obj.q: "These are copying errors in numbers."
obj.a: Then the Bible's numbers were corrupted in transmission, which is the Quran's point. And the 2 Chronicles figures are consistent with each other (400,000, 800,000, 500,000), suggesting deliberate exaggeration rather than one slip.

prac.q: “Numbers in ancient texts are often symbolic; you're reading them too literally.”
prac.a: Then you concede the history isn't literal. But these aren't round symbolic figures in poetry; they're census totals and battle reports, and Samuel and Chronicles give different census totals (800,000 vs 1,100,000).

briefs.evs:
Abijah vs Jeroboam. Abijah of Judah fights with 400,000 men against Jeroboam's 800,000, and "there fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men" (2 Chr 13:3, 17), in one battle.
Zerah the Cushite attacks Judah "with an army of a million men" (2 Chr 14:9).
The census. 2 Samuel 24:9 counts 800,000 men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah; 1 Chronicles 21:5 says 1,100,000 and 470,000.
Solomon's horses. 40,000 stalls (1 Kgs 4:26) or 4,000 (2 Chr 9:25).
For scale. The largest armies of the great empires of the day, such as Assyria, are recorded at tens of thousands in their own inscriptions. Shalmaneser III boasts of mustering 120,000 troops for a campaign in 845 BCE, one of the largest numbers in the ancient Near East, and historians treat even that as inflated.

briefs.title: Joseph sold by Ishmaelites or Midianites? (Genesis 37)
briefs.thesis: Genesis 37 combines two accounts: in one, Judah has the brothers sell Joseph to Ishmaelites; in the other, Reuben plans to rescue him and Midianites take him from the pit without the brothers knowing. The two are woven together and contradict each other.
briefs.sum: Judah proposes selling to Ishmaelites; Midianites pull him out; Reuben finds the pit empty and is shocked; Midianites sell him to Potiphar, who buys him from Ishmaelites. Two stories merged. The Quran tells one coherent account (12:10-20).

obj.q: "'Midianites' and 'Ishmaelites' are the same group; Judges 8:24 calls Midianites Ishmaelites."
obj.a: In Genesis they descend from different sons of Abraham, but Judges 8:24 shows the names could overlap, so the argument rests on 37:28-36 reading as two groups. Ishmael is Abraham's son by Hagar (Gen 16) and Midian his son by Keturah (Gen 25:2). And in 37:28 the Midianites sell him to the Ishmaelites, which makes no sense if they are the same people.

obj.q: "'They' in 37:28 means the brothers drew him up and sold him."
obj.a: The nearest antecedent is the Midianites, and if the brothers sold him, Reuben's shock at the empty pit (37:29-30) makes no sense.

prac.q: “Different names for traders don't change the story; Joseph went to Egypt either way.”
prac.a: The problem isn't the destination; it's who did what. In one strand the brothers sell him; in the other he is taken without their knowledge and Reuben is shocked to find the pit empty. Both can't be true, and 37:36 and 39:1 even disagree about who sold him to Potiphar.

briefs.evs:
The text in order.
