The brothers throw Joseph into an empty pit, on Reuben's advice: Reuben intended "to rescue him out of their hand to restore him to his father" (37:21-22).
They sit down to eat and see "a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead" (37:25).
Judah proposes: "Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites" (37:27). The brothers agree.
"Then Midianite traders passed by. And they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver" (37:28).
"When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes and said: the boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?" (37:29-30). Reuben apparently knows nothing of a sale; the text says he 'returned to the pit', so he was away at the time.
"Meanwhile the Midianites [Hebrew: Medanites] had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar" (37:36).
"Potiphar… bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there" (39:1).
Yet later Joseph tells his brothers "you sold me here" (45:4-5).
The two stories. Read separately, one version runs: Judah, Ishmaelites, sale by the brothers, Ishmaelites sell to Potiphar (37:25-27, 28b; 39:1). The other: Reuben, the pit, Midianites take him unseen, Reuben's shock, Midianites sell to Potiphar (37:22-24, 28a, 29-30, 36). Richard Friedman (Who Wrote the Bible?) and most source critics assign these to the J and E sources. Even tradi

briefs.title: Two creation stories in a different order (Genesis 1 and 2)
briefs.thesis: Genesis 1 creates plants, then animals, then man and woman together. Genesis 2 creates man first, then plants, then animals, then woman. The order of creation is reversed.
briefs.sum: Genesis 1: plants, animals, then man and woman together. Genesis 2: man before plants, then animals, then woman. Different divine names and styles mark two sources.

obj.q: "Genesis 2:19 means 'had formed' the animals earlier (pluperfect)."
obj.a: Some translations (NIV) render it that way, but the Hebrew is the normal narrative form, and the context ("it is not good for the man to be alone… so the LORD God formed…") presents the animals as made in response to the man's loneliness.

obj.q: "Genesis 2 is about the garden, not the whole creation."
obj.a: It begins "when no bush of the field was yet in the land" (2:5), describing the world before plants, and has man formed before them.

prac.q: “Genesis 2 is a close-up of day six, not a second account.”
prac.a: Then man would be created after the plants, but Genesis 2:5-7 says he was formed when no plant had yet sprung up. And the animals are made after him to find him a helper (2:18-19), while Genesis 1 makes them before him.

briefs.evs:
Genesis 1. Vegetation on day 3 (1:11-13), birds and fish on day 5 (1:20-23), land animals on day 6 (1:24-25), then "God created man… male and female He created them" (1:27).
Genesis 2. "When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant had yet sprung up… the LORD God formed the man" (2:5-7). Then "the LORD God planted a garden" (2:8-9). Then "it is not good that the man should be alone… so out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird" and brought them to the man (2:18-19). Finally the woman is made from his rib (2:21-22).
Style. Genesis 1 uses Elohim (God) and a repetitive day structure; Genesis 2 uses YHWH Elohim (the LORD God) and a story form. Scholars assign Genesis 1:1-2:3 to the Priestly source and 2:4b onward to the Yahwist.

briefs.title: The Flood: how many animals, how long?
briefs.thesis: The Flood story gives two different instructions about the animals and two different timescales, again showing two sources combined.
briefs.sum: Two of every kind (6:19) or seven pairs of the clean (7:2); forty days (7:17) or 150 (7:24); a raven and a dove. The Quran says simply "a pair of every kind" (11:40).

obj.q: "Seven pairs of clean animals is just an extra detail, for sacrifice later."
obj.a: The first command is "two of every sort" with no exception; and the clean/unclean distinction is given in the Law at Sinai, centuries later in the story.

obj.q: "Forty days of rain, then 150 days of high water."
obj.a: That's a possible harmonisation of the timing, but the two counts come from different strands, and the animal instructions still conflict.

prac.q: “Seven pairs is just more specific; it doesn't contradict "two of every kind".”
prac.a: 6:19 says two of every living thing; 7:2 says seven pairs of clean ones. And 7:9 then says they went in "two and two". The text isn't refining one command; it's holding two.

briefs.evs:
Animals. "Of every living thing… you shall bring two of every sort into the ark" (6:19). "Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals… and a pair of the animals that are not clean, and seven pairs of the birds" (7:2-3). Then "two and two… went into the ark with Noah" (7:9).
Duration. "Rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights" (7:12); "the flood continued forty days on the earth" (7:17). But "the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days" (7:24) and receded "at the end of 150 days" (8:3).
Birds. Noah sends out a raven (8:7) and then a dove three times (8:8-12), which many scholars read as two versions of the same scene.
Scholarship. The Flood story is a textbook example of interwoven Yahwist (seven pairs, forty days) and Priestly (one pair, 150 days) sources.
The Quran's version is short and consistent: "Load into it of every kind a pair" (11:40; 23:27).

briefs.title: Who killed Goliath? How did Saul die? When did David meet Saul?
briefs.thesis: The books of Samuel give two killers of Goliath, two first meetings of David and Saul, and several conflicting accounts of Saul's death; Chronicles then rewrites some of them.
briefs.sum: David or Elhanan killed Goliath; Saul knew David as his beloved armour-bearer yet didn't know whose son he was; Saul died by his own sword, by an Amalekite, by the Philistines or by the LORD. The Septuagint lacks the second David-Saul story.

obj.q: "The Amalekite lied to win David's favour."
obj.a: Possible for that one, and many Christians argue it. But the Goliath and first-meeting problems remain, and Chronicles' claim that Saul did not inquire of the LORD directly contradicts 1 Samuel 28:6.

obj.q: "There were two Goliaths."
obj.a: 2 Samuel 21:19 describes the same man, from the same city, with the same weaver's-beam spear. Chronicles' change to "brother of Goliath" is itself the evidence that later writers saw the problem.

prac.q: “Chronicles clarifies that Elhanan killed Goliath's brother.”
prac.a: Chronicles was written centuries after Samuel and changes "the Bethlehemite" into a name, "Lahmi". That is a later scribe smoothing over a contradiction, which is exactly the editing the Quran describes. Even the KJV prints "the brother of" in italics because it isn't in the Hebrew.

briefs.evs:
Goliath. David kills "Goliath of Gath" (1 Sam 17:4, 50). But "Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam" (2 Sam 21:19), the same description as 1 Samuel 17:7. Chronicles later says Elhanan killed "Lahmi the brother of Goliath" (1 Chr 20:5), which scholars see as a harmonisation (Lahmi looks like a corruption of Beit-ha-Lahmi, "the Bethlehemite"). The KJV adds "the brother of" in 2 Samuel 21:19 in italics, admitting it is not in the Hebrew.
David and Saul. In 1 Samuel 16:18-23 David is brought to Saul as a musician; "Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armour-bearer", and Saul sends word to Jesse. In 17:55-58, after Goliath, Saul asks "whose son is this youth?" and Abner says he doesn't know. Notably, the oldest Greek text (Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus) lacks 17:12-31 and 17:55-18:5, suggesting to many scholars that the second version may be a later addition to the Hebrew (others think the Greek omitted it to harmonise).
Saul's death.
Saul "took his own sword and fell upon it" (1 Sam 31:4).
An Amalekite says: "I stood beside him and killed him" (2 Sam 1:10).
"The Philistines had struck down Saul on Gilboa" (2 Sam 21:12), a passing remark that is compatible with 1 Sam 31 on a loose reading.
"He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death" (1 Chr 10:13-14),

briefs.title: More contradictions in names, ages and events
briefs.thesis: Kings, Chronicles and the Pentateuch disagree on names, ages and whether enemies were wiped out. Some of the ages are impossible.
briefs.sum: Ahaziah 22 or 42; Jehoiachin 18 or 8; the LORD or Satan incites David; three names for Moses' father-in-law; Midianites and Amalekites wiped out then back in force; Joshua took all the land, or didn't. Compare the Quran's challenge in 4:82.

obj.q: "These are copyist errors in numbers, not errors in the originals."
obj.a: Then the text we have was corrupted in transmission, which is the Muslim position; and many of these (Midianites, Amalekites, Saul's death, the conquest) are narrative contradictions, not numbers.

obj.q: "'Face to face' is idiomatic for intimacy."
obj.a: Then Exodus 33:11 and 33:20 use the same "face" language in opposite senses within ten verses, and Exodus 24:10 says they "saw the God of Israel" with a description of His feet.

prac.q: “Every apparent contradiction has been answered by scholars like Gleason Archer.”
prac.a: Archer's harmonisations often require assumptions the text doesn't make, like two Goliaths or a Jehoiachin who was co-regent at 8. Chronicles itself had to rewrite Samuel; the KJV prints its fix in italics. When the Bible's own later books and translators patch the earlier ones, the contradictions are real.

briefs.evs:
Ahaziah's age. 22 when he began to reign (2 Kgs 8:26) or 42 (2 Chr 22:2 in Hebrew). At 42 he would be two years older than his father Jehoram, who died at 40 (2 Chr 21:20).
Jehoiachin. 18 when he began to reign (2 Kgs 24:8) or 8 (2 Chr 36:9) in the Masoretic reading (some manuscripts have 18). Chronicles, like Kings (2 Kgs 24:9), says he "did what was evil in the sight of the LORD".
Who incited the census? "The anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and He incited David" (2 Sam 24:1), versus "Satan stood against Israel and incited David" (1 Chr 21:1).
Moses' father-in-law is called Reuel (Exod 2:18) and Jethro (Exod 3:1); Judg 4:11 calls Hobab his father-in-law, though Num 10:29 makes Hobab Reuel's son.
Esau's wives are Judith, Basemath daughter of Elon, and Mahalath daughter of Ishmael (Gen 26:34; 28:9), or Adah daughter of Elon, Oholibamah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael (Gen 36:2-3).
Ishmael's age. Ishmael is 14 when Isaac is born (Gen 16:16; 21:5), so about 16 or 17 when Hagar is sent away; yet Hagar carries "the child" and casts him under a bush, and the angel tells her to "lift up the boy and hold him by the hand" (Gen 21:14-18), as with an infant.
Destroyed enemies return. Moses' army kills every male Midianite (Num 31:7); a few generations later Midianites "as numerous as locusts" oppress Israel for seven years (Judg 6:1-5). Saul "utterly destroyed all the peop

briefs.title: What the contradictions show
briefs.thesis: The doublets and contradictions point to a text compiled from earlier sources and edited over centuries. That is exactly what the Quran says happened to the earlier scriptures, and it is the opposite of what the Quran claims for itself.
briefs.sum: The doublets show the Old Testament was compiled from sources and edited over centuries, as scholars from Wellhausen to Friedman and Baden explain and as the Quran says (2:79). The Quran's own versions don't contain these contradictions (4:82).

obj.q: "The documentary hypothesis is outdated."
obj.a: The specific four-source model has been revised, but the conclusion that the Pentateuch is composite and edited is accepted across critical scholarship, Jewish and Christian. Alternatives (supplementary or fragmentary models) agree it was compiled over time.

prac.q: “If the Bible contains contradictions, so does the Quran; critics have lists of them too.”
prac.a: Those lists are answered verse by verse (see Objections to the Quran), and none is a doublet like Genesis 37, where one chapter tells two incompatible versions of the same event. The Quran challenges readers to find contradictions (4:82); the Bible's own later books had to rewrite its earlier ones.

briefs.evs:
The documentary hypothesis, developed by Julius Wellhausen and refined by later scholars (Richard Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible?; Joel Baden, The Composition of the Pentateuch), explains the doublets by sources with different names for God, styles and concerns.
Chronicles (around the 4th century BCE) reworks Samuel-Kings, omitting David's sin with Bathsheba and changing details such as Goliath's killer and the census instigator.
Jeremiah 8:8 already complains of "the lying pen of the scribes" (see The Quran correcting earlier scripture).
The Quran's stories of Joseph, Noah, Moses and Saul (Talut) do not contain Genesis-style contradictory accounts within a single narrative (the Quran does retell stories with differing emphasis); where they differ from the Bible they remove the problem (a "small band", one sale of Joseph).

briefs.title: The Quran answers rabbinic teachings precisely
briefs.thesis: The Quran quotes or answers specific rabbinic sayings: the Mishnah on saving a soul, the claim that all Israel has a share in the next world, the claim that Jews will be in Hell only briefly, the authority of the rabbis, and God's "chained hand".
briefs.sum: The Quran cites the Mishnah's "whoever saves a soul" in its older universal form, answers "all Israel has a share", the limited-Hell belief, the rabbis' authority and the "bound hand" laments. It knows rabbinic tradition and corrects it.

obj.q: "This shows Muhammad copied from Jews."
obj.a: Copying would reproduce the texts; the Quran corrects them (a universal soul, no guaranteed share in the next world, no limited Hell, no human legislators over God). And the rabbinic material was in Hebrew and Aramaic, in academies in Babylonia and Palestine, not in Mecca.

prac.q: “5:32 copies the Talmud, so the Quran isn't revelation.”
prac.a: The Quran says "We decreed this for the Children of Israel". It is telling you the ruling is in their tradition; that's a citation, not plagiarism. And it gives the universal version found in the oldest Mishnah manuscripts, not the later "of Israel".

briefs.evs:
Saving one soul (5:32). "We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had killed all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind." The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 4:5) has a similar saying, that whoever destroys one soul is treated as if he destroyed a whole world, in the context of the creation of Adam. The printed versions read "whoever destroys a single soul of Israel", but the oldest manuscripts (such as the Kaufmann manuscript) lack "of Israel", and scholars regard it as a later addition. The Quran cites the universal form, says it was "decreed for the Children of Israel", which is exactly where it is found.
Tap to enlargeQuran 3:77 "no share in the Hereafter", answering the Talmud's "all Israel has a share in the world to come"
"All Israel has a share in the world to come" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). The Quran answers: "those who sell Allah's covenant… will have no share in the Hereafter" (3:77), and "say: if the home of the Hereafter is for you alone… then wish for death" (2:94).
"The Fire will touch us only for a few days" (2:80; 3:24). The Talmud (Eruvin 19a) says Abraham sits at the gate of Gehinnom and rescues circumcised Israelites, and the Mishnah (Eduyot 2:10) limits the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom to twelve months. José Costa has studied the parallels.
"They took their rabbis as lords besides Allah" (9:31).

briefs.title: Jewish thought allows a later prophet to change the Law
briefs.thesis: Jews argue the Torah is eternal and cannot be replaced. But the Torah's "forever" is conditional, the prophets foretold a new covenant and a new Torah, and Jewish thinkers such as Joseph Albo admitted a later prophet could change commandments.
briefs.sum: Eli's "forever" priesthood was revoked, Jeremiah promises a new covenant, the midrash reads Isaiah 51:4 as "a new Torah", and Joseph Albo allowed a later prophet to change commandments. Abrogation is not foreign to Jewish thought.

obj.q: "Maimonides' ninth principle says the Torah will never be changed."
obj.a: Maimonides' principles are a medieval creed, and Albo, a major Jewish philosopher, disagreed with parts of them. The question is what the Bible says, and the Bible has conditional eternities, a new covenant and a new Torah.

prac.q: “God's Law is eternal; a God who changes His law is fickle.”
prac.a: The Torah itself changed things: Jacob married two sisters, which Leviticus 18:18 later forbids; Abraham's descendants ate what Moses later forbade. Adapting law to a people's circumstances is wisdom, not fickleness, and Jeremiah 31:31 announces a new covenant.

briefs.evs:
Conditional "forever". God promised Eli's house the priesthood "forever", then said: "far be it from Me… those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" (1 Sam 2:30). The Torah is a covenant (Exod 24:7) with conditions (Deut 28). 'Olam can mean "for a long time": a slave who stays serves his master "forever" (le'olam, Exod 21:6), meaning for life.
New covenant. "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… not like the covenant that I made with their fathers" (Jer 31:31-32).
A new Torah. "A Torah shall go forth from Me" (Isa 51:4). The midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 13:3, Rabbi Avin) reads it as "a new Torah will go forth from Me", which Jewish tradition usually takes as new teaching of the same Torah. Another midrash says that in the future all the festivals will be abolished except Purim (and Yom Kippur).
Joseph Albo (Sefer ha-Ikkarim, book 3, 15th century) held that it is possible in principle for a divine law to be replaced, since a law may be given to suit the people at a particular time, but that the Torah of Moses will not in fact be replaced.
Ezekiel contradicts the Torah on details of sacrifice so seriously that the Talmud says his book was nearly withdrawn until Hananiah ben Hezekiah reconciled it (Shabbat 13b; Menachot 45a).

briefs.title: Rabbis recognised Muslims as true monotheists, and prophets outside Israel
briefs.thesis: Maimonides ruled that Muslims are not idolaters and affirm God's unity correctly, and Jewish tradition recognises prophets from outside Israel, such as Job and Balaam.
briefs.sum: Maimonides ruled that Muslims affirm God's unity without defect; Jewish tradition accepts non-Israelite prophets like Job and Balaam; and the Samaritan Torah's Deuteronomy 34:10 looks forward to a coming prophet like Moses.

obj.q: "Maimonides also called Muhammad a madman."
obj.a: He did, in the Epistle to Yemen. But his legal ruling that Muslim worship is true monotheism stands, and it is that ruling, not his polemic, that bears on whether Islam's God is the God of Israel.

prac.q: “God's covenant is only with Israel; there can't be an Arab prophet.”
prac.a: The Torah promises Ishmael a great nation, Job and Balaam were non-Israelite recipients of revelation, and Maimonides ruled that Muslims worship the one God with a unity "in which there is no defect".

briefs.evs:
Maimonides (12th century), in a responsum to Obadiah the proselyte: "The Ishmaelites are not idolaters at all… they affirm the unity of God with a proper unity, in which there is no defect." He contrasted this with Christianity, which he regarded as idolatrous.
Non-Israelite prophets. Some rabbis (Bava Batra 15a-b) held Job to be a gentile prophet; others disagreed; Balaam prophesied (Num 22-24); the rabbis say there were prophets among the nations. The Torah promises Ishmael a great nation (Gen 17:20; 21:13, 18).
"A prophet like you from among their brothers" (Deut 18:18). Gen 16:12 and 25:18 speak of Ishmael dwelling 'over against all his brothers', and Muslim readers take 'their brothers' in Deut 18:18 as including Ishmael's line (Jews read it as Israelites, cf. Deut 17:15).
Tap to enlargeSamaritan Pentateuch, Deuteronomy 34:10: "never again will there arise a prophet like Moses"

briefs.title: The Torah's own text: authorship, variants and edits
briefs.thesis: The Torah was not transmitted as a single fixed text from Moses: the book of the law was found under Josiah, the Samaritan and Masoretic versions differ on theological points, and the Samaritan text removes anthropomorphisms.
briefs.sum: The book of the law was found under Josiah; the Samaritan and Masoretic Torahs differ theologically; Deuteronomy 34 was written after Moses. The Torah was shaped by its transmitters, as the Quran says.

obj.q: "The Masoretic Text is the faithful one; the Samaritans changed theirs."
obj.a: Both show changes; the Dead Sea Scrolls preserve a different reading at Deut 32:8 ("sons of God"), which most scholars regard as older than the MT's "sons of Israel". The point is not which is better but that the Torah was not preserved as one untouched text.

prac.q: “The Torah has been copied letter by letter for 3,000 years.”
prac.a: Our oldest full Masoretic manuscripts are from around 1000 CE; the Dead Sea Scrolls show several text forms circulating in the same period; and the Samaritan version differs from it in thousands of places. Letter-by-letter copying came late, after the text was already shaped.

briefs.evs:
Found, not transmitted. The book of the law was "found" in the Temple under Josiah after generations of neglect (2 Kgs 22:8; see The Quran correcting earlier scripture).
Samaritan vs Masoretic. The Samaritan Pentateuch removes or softens anthropomorphic expressions (for example in Exod 15:8 and Deut 32:6), and inserts a command to build the altar on Mount Gerizim into the Ten Commandments. Each community shaped the text toward its own theology (Anderson and Giles).
Deuteronomy 34, describing Moses' death and saying "no prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses", was obviously written after him.
Mark Smith and others trace how the God of Israel absorbed the titles of El and features of Baal, and early Egyptian texts mention "YHW" in the land of the Shasu nomads of Edom/Midian.

briefs.title: Fitrah: belief in a Creator is natural, not taught
briefs.thesis: Children across cultures spontaneously believe nature is designed and that a powerful mind made it; atheism has to be learned and is never fully secure even in committed atheists. This is what the Quran and hadith call the fitrah.
briefs.sum: Children everywhere naturally see the world as designed by a powerful mind; the Oxford project found it across 20 countries; atheist scientists revert to design thinking under pressure. That is the fitrah of 30:30, and it shifts the burden of proof onto atheism.

obj.q: "A natural belief can be false, like seeing faces in clouds."
obj.a: True, so fitrah does not prove God by itself. But in philosophy a natural, universal belief is rational to hold unless defeated (like belief in other minds or the external world). It puts the burden of proof on the atheist, who must show the intuition is false.

obj.q: "Evolution explains religious belief as a by-product."
obj.a: Explaining how a belief arises does not show it is false; evolution also explains why we believe in mathematics. And if our belief-forming faculties were shaped only for survival, not truth, that undermines the atheist's own reasoning too.

prac.q: “Children also believe in Santa Claus.”
prac.a: Children are taught Santa, and they drop him without difficulty. Belief in a creator arises without teaching, across cultures, and atheists still show it under pressure. Santa has no such hold on anyone.

briefs.evs:
The Quran and hadith. "So set your face to the religion, inclining to truth: the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created people" (30:30). "Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian or a Magian" (Bukhari 1385). The covenant of all souls: "Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes" (7:172).
Justin Barrett (Born Believers, 2012): children naturally believe in a powerful, all-knowing creator and in life after death. The Oxford "Cognition, Religion and Theology" project (57 researchers, 20 countries, over 40 studies) found that people naturally believe in a god and an afterlife across cultures.

Tap to enlargeThe Oxford "Cognition, Religion and Theology" project, compared with the hadith of fitrah
Olivera Petrovich's developmental studies at Oxford found young children readily attribute the origin of natural things to a creator rather than to humans; atheism is not the default.
Deborah Kelemen calls children "intuitive theists" because they see natural objects as made for a purpose. In "The divided mind of a disbeliever" (2015), Järnefelt, Canfield and Kelemen found that even non-religious adults, when forced to answer quickly, endorsed the view that nature was purposefully created.
Under stress. A small Finnish study (Lindeman et al., Helsinki, 2

briefs.title: Dependent things need an independent cause
briefs.thesis: Everything we observe depends on something else for its existence. A chain of dependent things cannot explain itself, even if infinitely long, so there must be an independent, necessary being: Allah.
briefs.sum: Every dependent thing needs a cause, and a chain of dependent things, even infinite, never explains itself, like soldiers each waiting for permission. So there is an independent being. "Who made God?" misunderstands the argument: the independent being has no cause by definition.

obj.q: "Then who created God?"
obj.a: The argument is about dependent things. A being that depends on nothing doesn't need a creator; asking who made it is asking for the cause of something defined as uncaused. If God had a creator, that creator would be the independent one, and the question stops there.

obj.q: "Maybe the universe itself is the necessary being."
obj.a: The universe is made of parts that change and depend on each other, and it began to exist. What changes and begins is dependent. The necessary being must be unchanging and without beginning, which the universe is not.

obj.q: "Quantum events happen without causes."
obj.a: Quantum events happen within a quantum field governed by laws; they are not things popping out of absolutely nothing. "Nothing" in physics is not nothing.

prac.q: “The universe could just be a brute fact with no explanation.”
prac.a: Then you give up explanation exactly where you most need it. Scientists never accept "brute fact" for anything else in the universe; it is special pleading to accept it for the whole. The Quran asks: were they created by nothing?

briefs.evs:
The Quran's version. "Were they created by nothing, or were they themselves the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth?" (52:35-36). There are three options for something that begins to exist: it came from nothing, it made itself, or something else made it. The first two are absurd, so the third must be true.
The soldier analogy (from Ibn Taymiyya's reasoning on regress). A soldier is ordered to fire only once he receives permission from the soldier behind him, who must wait for permission from the one behind him, and so on forever. If the chain never ends in someone who can give permission without waiting, the shot is never fired. The shot was fired, so the chain ends in someone independent. Likewise, things exist, so the chain of dependence ends in a being that does not depend.
Avoid a weak version. Some argue "an infinite past is impossible because one infinite chain would have one more year than another". Mathematicians reply (via Cantor) that infinite sets can be matched one-to-one, so this argument fails. The stronger point is not about the length of time but about dependence: a series of things that each need a cause cannot supply what none of them has.
Modern cosmology dates the expansion of the observable universe from a hot, dense state to about 13.8 billion years ago; whether that was an absolute beginning is debated, though most models still point to

briefs.title: The universe is fine-tuned for life
briefs.thesis: The laws and constants of physics fall within extremely narrow ranges that permit life. Design explains this better than chance.
briefs.sum: The cosmological constant, the nuclear forces and Rees' "six numbers" fall in tiny life-permitting ranges. Necessity and chance don't explain this; the multiverse is unobserved and needs tuning itself. Design is the best explanation.

obj.q: "The multiverse: with infinitely many universes, one like ours is inevitable."
obj.a: There is no observational evidence for a multiverse, and some philosophers argue that a mechanism that produces universes would itself need fine-tuning. Positing infinitely many unobservable universes to avoid one Creator is less simple, not more.

obj.q: "If the universe weren't fine-tuned, we wouldn't be here to notice (the anthropic principle)."
obj.a: That explains why we observe fine-tuning, not why it exists. A man facing a firing squad of fifty marksmen who all miss shouldn't conclude "of course, otherwise I wouldn't be here to wonder"; he should conclude it was arranged.

prac.q: “The universe is mostly empty and hostile to life, so it isn't designed for us.”
prac.a: Its size and age are part of the fine-tuning: the elements of life are made in stars over billions of years. The question is why the laws allow life at all, and that needs the narrow ranges physicists describe.

briefs.evs:
The cosmological constant, which governs the expansion of space, is about 10^120 times smaller than naive quantum-field-theory estimates of vacuum energy, and anthropic arguments (Weinberg 1987) show it could not be more than a few hundred times its observed value without preventing galaxy formation. A slightly larger positive value would have blown matter apart before galaxies formed; a large negative value would have caused recollapse.
Martin Rees, the Astronomer Royal, identified six numbers (Just Six Numbers, 1999) that must be finely set for a universe with life.
The strength of the strong nuclear force: Rees notes the fusion efficiency 0.007 cannot be much lower than 0.006 (no atoms beyond hydrogen) or higher than 0.008 (no hydrogen left).
The Quran: "We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play" (21:16); "You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency; look again: do you see any flaw?" (67:3).

briefs.title: Consciousness points beyond matter
briefs.thesis: Matter in motion does not explain subjective experience, the unity of the self or free decision. These are what the Quran calls the ruh, the soul.
briefs.sum: Physical descriptions don't explain subjective experience; Penfield could trigger movement and memory but never a decision; nothing in the brain binds experience into one self. The Quran's ruh fits the evidence.

obj.q: "Science will explain consciousness eventually."
obj.a: That is a promissory note, not an argument. The problem is not missing data but a category gap: no amount of information about neurons tells you what it is like to be the person.

obj.q: "Brain damage changes the mind, so the mind is the brain."
obj.a: A damaged instrument changes the music, but the musician is not the instrument. Dependence of expression on the brain does not show identity.

prac.q: “The soul is just a "god of the gaps".”
prac.a: The argument doesn't rely on a gap in data but on a difference in kind: physics describes quantities, structures and causes, while experience is qualitative and first-person. That is a principled limit, not a temporary gap.

briefs.evs:
The hard problem. Philosopher David Chalmers distinguished explaining brain functions (the "easy problems") from explaining why there is subjective experience at all. No physical theory explains the second.
Wilder Penfield, the neurosurgeon who mapped the cortex by electrical stimulation, found he could make patients move limbs, recall memories or see lights, but never make them decide or will anything. Patients would say "I didn't do that. You did". Penfield concluded that the mind is not simply a product of the brain (The Mystery of the Mind, 1975). Nobel laureate John Eccles reached a similar view.
The binding problem. The brain processes colour, shape, sound and motion in different regions, yet we have one unified experience. No region has been found that unifies it.
Psychophysical harmony. Our experiences match the physical world in an orderly way: pain goes with damage, pleasure with benefit, and our perceptions track reality. On a purely physical view there is no reason the felt quality of experience should line up with what it represents; on theism, God made mind and world to fit.

briefs.title: Objective morality needs God
briefs.thesis: If there is no God, there is no objective moral standard, only preferences and conventions. Most people, including atheists, believe some things are really wrong. So that belief points to God.
briefs.sum: Without God there is no ground for objective morality, as Nietzsche admitted, and Hume's is-ought gap shows facts alone can't create obligation. Since some things really are wrong, God exists.

obj.q: "Atheists can be moral."
obj.a: Of course; the argument is not about whether atheists behave well but about what makes moral claims true. An atheist can know murder is wrong; he can't explain why it is objectively wrong.

obj.q: "Euthyphro: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it's good?"
obj.a: Neither: God's commands flow from His nature, which is good and wise (al-Hakim). Good is not an arbitrary decree nor a standard above God; it is grounded in who He is.

obj.q: "Morality evolved because it helped survival."
obj.a: Then it is useful, not true. If evolution had made us value cruelty, cruelty would be "moral" in the same sense. That is exactly the relativism the atheist wanted to avoid.

prac.q: “Morality is just about reducing harm; you don't need God for that.”
prac.a: Why is harm bad objectively? If the answer is "because we don't like it", that's preference, not morality. And whose harm counts: animals, embryos, future people? Utilitarians like Singer reach conclusions most people find horrifying from that same principle.

briefs.evs:
Nietzsche, an atheist philosopher who saw the consequences of atheism clearly, warned that if you abandon Christian belief you cannot keep Christian morality: "when one gives up the Christian faith, one pulls the right to Christian morality out from under one's feet" (Twilight of the Idols).
Hume's is-ought gap. From facts about what is (evolution, pleasure, harm) you cannot derive what ought to be. Secular moral systems choose a starting value (harm, wellbeing) without being able to justify why we are obliged to pursue it.
Where secular ethics leads. Peter Singer, a leading utilitarian, has defended infanticide of severely disabled newborns and argued in his 2001 essay 'Heavy Petting' that sex with animals is not always abusive and not necessarily seriously wrong, conclusions most people find monstrous but which follow from his premises. In a debate with Mohammed Hijab, the Norwegian philosopher Lars Gule struggled to say incest between consenting adults is objectively wrong.
The Quran grounds morality in God's wisdom and in the fitrah: "and [by] the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness" (91:7-8).

briefs.title: The problem of evil and suffering
briefs.thesis: Suffering does not disprove an All-Wise, All-Merciful God. The logical problem has been abandoned even by atheist philosophers, and the evidential problem assumes we can see what an infinitely wise God sees.
briefs.sum: Mackie himself conceded the logical problem fails. Suffering serves testing, growth, expiation and human freedom; we can't expect to see every reason of an All-Wise God; and only theism offers final justice to victims.

obj.q: "What about animal suffering or children with cancer, where no one grows?"
obj.a: We often cannot see the reason, and Islam does not claim we always can. Robin Collins' analogy: you can't conclude there is no snake in a garden just because you can't see one, if snakes are the kind of thing you'd expect not to see. If God exists, we would expect many of His reasons to be beyond us. Children of believers who die are in Paradise (see the Prophet's dream of Abraham surrounded by children, Bukhari 7047); scholars differ on the children of non-Muslims, and every creature will be compensated (Muslim 2582).

obj.q: "An all-powerful God could achieve the goods without the suffering."
obj.a: Not if the goods (patience, courage, forgiveness, sacrifice) logically require hardship. Even omnipotence cannot make courage without danger.

prac.q: “If God were good, He'd stop the suffering of innocent children.”
prac.a: You are assuming this life is the whole story. Islam says it is a short test followed by eternal justice and mercy; children who die go to Paradise. Atheism has the bigger problem: on atheism, that child's suffering means nothing and is never put right.

briefs.evs:
The logical version is widely regarded as defeated. Alvin Plantinga's free-will defence showed there is no contradiction between God and evil. J.L. Mackie, who made the logical argument famous, conceded that "the problem of evil does not, after all, show that the central doctrines of theism are logically inconsistent with one another" (The Miracle of Theism, p. 154).
Wisdom. A surgeon cuts, a parent refuses a child sweets; a child cannot see the reason. "Perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you… Allah knows and you do not know" (2:216). The story of Moses and al-Khidr (18:65-82) makes this point: each apparent harm had a hidden good.
Testing and growth. "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives and fruits; but give good tidings to the patient" (2:155). Patience, courage and compassion cannot exist without hardship.
Expiation. "No fatigue, illness, worry, grief or harm befalls a Muslim, even a thorn prick, except that Allah expiates some of his sins by it" (Bukhari 5641). "When Allah loves a people He tests them" (Tirmidhi 2396); the prophets were tested most.
Human responsibility. "Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned, so that He may let them taste some of what they did, that perhaps they will return" (30:41).
Justice deferred, not denied. This world is temporary; every wrong will

briefs.title: Free will and divine decree (qadar)
briefs.thesis: God's knowledge and decree do not remove human choice. Knowing an act is not causing it, and God creates the act while the human being chooses it.
briefs.sum: Knowledge isn't causation; God creates the act and the person chooses it (kasb); the Quran affirms human will (18:29) and God's will (81:29) together; and the Prophet ﷺ said "act, for each is eased toward what he was created for".

obj.q: "If God already wrote my fate, why should I act?"
obj.a: The Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ this, and he said: "Act, for everyone is eased toward what he was created for" (Bukhari 4949). The decree includes the means; you don't know your decree, so you act.

prac.q: “If God knew I'd go to Hell, how is it fair to punish me?”
prac.a: God's knowledge doesn't make you choose; it records what you freely choose. A recording of a crime doesn't cause the crime. You are judged by what you did with real choices.

briefs.evs:
Both affirmed. "Whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). "And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds" (81:29).
Ibn al-Qayyim: two independent, complete agents for one act is impossible; but a dependent agent acting through power given by the Creator is not. The person truly chooses; God creates and permits.
Coercion vs causation. The objection confuses being the ultimate cause of everything with forcing someone against his will. We experience our choices as our own, and God judges us by them.

briefs.title: Darwinism as an atheist worldview
briefs.thesis: Evolution, even if true in full, does not remove the need for a Creator, and "Darwinism" as an atheist philosophy goes far beyond the science. Mainstream biologists themselves now debate the adequacy of the standard theory, and the origin of life remains unexplained.
briefs.sum: Evolution can't explain the universe, its laws or the origin of life. Biologists at the Royal Society debated the standard theory's "explanatory deficits", the origin-of-life prize is unclaimed, and the field's history includes Piltdown and Nebraska Man.

obj.q: "Evolution is a fact; you're anti-science."
obj.a: The argument doesn't depend on rejecting all evolution. It shows that evolution, true or not, can't explain the universe, its fine-tuning or the origin of life, and that turning it into an atheist worldview is philosophy.

obj.q: "Frauds were exposed by science, which shows it works."
obj.a: Agreed, and that is why we shouldn't treat current models as final truth. Science corrects itself; worldviews built on its present state should be modest.

prac.q: “Evolution shows design is unnecessary: natural selection explains complexity.”
prac.a: Natural selection needs self-replicating life to start with, which it can't explain, and works within laws that are fine-tuned. Even the Royal Society meeting discussed unexplained origins of novelty. A process doesn't make a designer unnecessary; a car factory's robots don't disprove engineers.

briefs.evs:
A worldview. Richard Dawkins: Darwin "made it possible to be an intellectually fulfilled atheist". Julian Huxley promoted "evolutionary humanism" as a substitute religion; Michael Ruse wrote Darwinism as Religion (2016). Lynn Margulis predicted neo-Darwinism would be judged "a minor twentieth-century religious sect".
Debate within biology. At the Royal Society's 2016 meeting on "New trends in evolutionary biology", Gerd Müller spoke of the 'explanatory deficits' of the Modern Synthesis, especially the origin of complexity and novelty, and argued for extending it
Tap to enlargeRoyal Society 2016 meeting: calls to revise or replace standard neo-Darwinian theory
Origin of life. The Miller-Urey experiment (1953) produced some amino acids and tar, not life. No accepted pathway from chemistry to the first self-replicating cell exists; chemist James Tour has criticised overstated claims. A US$10 million prize offered by businessman Perry Marshall (Evolution 2.0 Prize) for explaining the natural origin of the genetic code remains unclaimed, though it is a private, non-scientific prize
Frauds and errors. Piltdown Man (a human skull with an orangutan jaw) was accepted for 40 years until exposed in 1953; "Nebraska Man" (1922) was built from a peccary's tooth and was retracted within five years; anthropologist Reiner Protsch was found in 2005 to have falsified dates of fossils. Textbook ph

briefs.title: Religion, and Islam in particular, makes for healthier lives
briefs.thesis: Large studies associate religious belief and practice, and Islam especially, with lower suicide, less substance abuse and higher life satisfaction. This doesn't prove Islam true, but it answers the claim that religion is harmful and fits the Quran's promise of a "good life" (16:97).
briefs.sum: Suicide is lowest among Muslims and highest among the non-religious; Muslims report the least extramarital sex and high life satisfaction; religiosity reduces substance abuse. This answers "religion is harmful", not "religion is true".
briefs.caution: Wellbeing data show benefit, not truth. Use this to answer "religion poisons everything", not as a proof of God.

prac.q: “Religious people are just happier because of community, not God.”
prac.a: Possibly in part, but then the atheist must explain why religion produces such communities and meaning reliably. The Quran says the good life comes from faith and righteous action together (16:97), which is what the data show.

briefs.evs:
Suicide. WHO-related research (Bertolote and Fleischmann, 2002) compared countries by predominant religion (not individuals) and found the lowest recorded suicide rates in Muslim-majority countries, though suicide is under-reported there.
Tap to enlargeWHO data (Bertolote & Fleischmann): suicide rates by religion; lowest among Muslims
Family and sexual behaviour. A study in the American Sociological Review (77:5, 2012) found Muslims the least likely to report extramarital sex, and Hindus and Muslims less likely than Christians and Jews to report premarital sex.
Tap to enlargeAmerican Sociological Review 77(5): Muslims least likely to report extramarital sex
Life satisfaction. A German study (Erdinger-Schons, 2019) found Muslims scored highest on beliefs in oneness, and that oneness beliefs predicted higher life satisfaction
Tap to enlargeStudy on oneness beliefs and life satisfaction: Muslim respondents scored highest
Substance use. Religiosity is consistently linked with less drug and alcohol abuse, and the Islamic ban is associated with much lower alcohol consumption in Muslim societies (see Miracles & the wisdom of the law).
Body image. Research by Viren Swami and colleagues associated wearing the hijab with more positive body image.

briefs.title: The Quran and Muslim scholars held the earth to be round
briefs.thesis: Classical Muslim scholars reported a consensus that the earth and heavens are spherical, and the Quran's language of night "wrapping" day and bodies "swimming" in orbits fits a round world.
briefs.sum: Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Hazm, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim reported consensus that the earth is round. "Wrapping" night around day (39:5) uses the root of "ball", and "spread out" describes how a huge sphere looks from its surface.

obj.q: "Some Muslims today believe in a flat earth, and al-Suyuti did."
obj.a: Even al-Suyuti acknowledged the reports of consensus; a few individuals' views don't define the text. The mainstream classical position, stated by scholars from every school, is a spherical earth.

prac.q: “The Quran says the earth is "spread out like a carpet" (71:19), so it's flat.”
prac.a: A carpet describes how the ground is laid out for us to walk on, not the planet's shape; Abu Hayyan explains a vast sphere appears flat to those on it. The scholars who knew these verses best agreed the earth is round.

briefs.evs:
The consensus. Ibn Taymiyya says the scholars agree the earth is spherical, citing the Hanbali scholar Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Munadi (d. 336 AH) and Ibn Hazm, and adds that only an ignorant person denies it (Majmu' al-Fatawa 5/150; 6/586-587). Ibn al-Jawzi notes the sun rises in the east before the west, which requires a sphere. Ibn Kathir (al-Bidaya 1/31) and Ibn al-Qayyim (the heavens surround the earth like an egg) agree. Al-Ghazali, al-Razi and Ibn Khaldun took sphericity for granted.
Tap to enlargeIbn Taymiyya, Majmu' al-Fatawa vol. 5: scholars agree the earth is spherical
Tap to enlargeIbn al-Qayyim, al-Sawa'iq al-Mursala: classical discussion of the spherical heavens and earth
"He wraps the night over the day" (39:5). The verb yukawwir means to wind or wrap, as a turban is wound around the head; Ibn Hazm took it to imply a round earth.
"Each swims in an orbit (falak)" (21:33; 36:40). Ibn Abbas compared the falak to the whorl of a spindle (Tabari), something round and turning.
"Spread out" (13:3; 79:30). Abu Hayyan explains that a huge sphere appears flat to someone standing on it (al-Bahr al-Muhit 5/355). That is why the earth is described as spread out: from where we stand, it is.

briefs.title: "The sun setting in a muddy spring" (18:86)
briefs.thesis: The verse says Dhul-Qarnayn "found it" setting in a dark spring, describing what he saw, as we say "the sun sets in the sea". The hadith wording that seems to make it literal comes through a weak link.
briefs.sum: "He found it setting" reports Dhul-Qarnayn's view, as commentators said; "sunset" is still normal language; and the hadith wording "in a hot spring" is a weak, singular addition.

obj.q: "Why would God report a mistaken perception?"
obj.a: Reporting what someone saw is not endorsing a false belief; the Quran is telling a story from his viewpoint, and the same Quran says the sun "runs to a resting place" and swims in its own orbit (36:38-40).

prac.q: “If the Quran was from God it would say "the sun appeared to set".”
prac.a: That's exactly what wajadaha does: "he found it setting". The commentators understood it as appearance a thousand years ago. Your own Bible says the sun "hastens to its place".

briefs.evs:
"He found it". The verb wajada reports perception from Dhul-Qarnayn's viewpoint. The commentators said this explicitly: Ibn Kathir says he saw it as if setting in the sea, as anyone at the shore sees; al-Shinqiti, the Jalalayn and al-Sa'di say the same.
Ordinary language. Astronomers and NASA still speak of "sunset" and "sunrise". No one accuses them of geocentrism.
The hadith. A report of Abu Dharr has the Prophet ﷺ say the sun "sets in a hot spring". That wording comes only through Sufyan ibn Husayn, whose narrations from al-Zuhri are weak and who is confused here; five stronger narrators (al-A'mash, Yunus ibn 'Ubayd, Musa ibn al-Musayyab, Harun ibn Sa'd and 'Abd al-A'la) narrate from Ibrahim al-Taymi without the addition. Al-Bazzar noted the wording is singular.
The Bible: "The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises" (Eccl 1:5); it "comes out like a bridegroom… its rising is from the end of the heavens and its circuit to the end of them" (Ps 19:5-6).

briefs.title: "Between the backbone and the ribs" (86:6-7)
briefs.thesis: The verse does not say semen is made between the backbone and ribs. Its subject can be the human being who emerges, and the surah's theme is creation and resurrection.
briefs.sum: 86:7's verb can refer to man emerging (Ibn 'Atiyya, Qurtubi), yakhruj is used for life coming forth, and the surah is about resurrection: "He is able to bring him back" (86:8).

obj.q: "Most classical commentators said it refers to the fluid."
obj.a: Many did, and they read sulb and tara'ib as the man's back and the woman's chest, interpreting with the knowledge of their time. The Quran's wording allows the other reading, which classical scholars also recorded, and the critic needs to show the text must mean his reading.

prac.q: “Semen comes from the testes, not between the backbone and ribs.”
prac.a: The verse doesn't say semen is produced there; it says "it/he emerges from between", and classical scholars recorded that the subject is man, emerging between the mother's back and front. Embryologically, the testes also originate in the abdomen near the kidneys before descending.

briefs.evs:
The grammar. Verse 5: "Let man consider from what he was created." Verse 6: "He was created from a fluid, gushing." Verse 7: "It/he emerges (yakhruj) from between the backbone and the ribs." The pronoun in yakhruj can refer to the fluid or to man. Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz 5/465), al-Mahdawi, Makki and al-Qurtubi record the view that it refers to man.
Usage. The Quran uses yakhruj for life emerging: "He brings the living out of the dead" (30:19); "then you will be brought out (takhrujun)" from the earth at resurrection (30:25).
The theme. M.A.S. Abdel Haleem shows the surah is about resurrection: the very next verse says "Indeed, He is able to bring him back" (86:8). The argument is: the God who brought you out once can bring you out again.
The Quran's embryology is described in stages: nutfa (drop), 'alaqa (clinging thing), mudgha (chewed lump), bones, flesh clothing the bones, then "another creation" (23:12-14).

briefs.title: The Quran did not copy Greek embryology
briefs.thesis: Greek medical works were not yet translated into Arabic in the Prophet's time, though Greek-trained physicians such as al-Harith ibn Kalada were known in Arabia. Greek medicine was full of errors the Quran does not contain. A copier cannot filter out every error without knowing the truth.
briefs.sum: Greek medicine reached Arabic in the 8th-9th centuries, and it taught that the fetus forms from menstrual blood and seed comes from every body part. The Quran has none of these errors, which a copyist couldn't avoid.

obj.q: "Galen also had stages, so the Quran copied the idea of stages."
obj.a: Stages are observable in miscarriages; describing them is not copying. What would show copying is reproducing Galen's specific theory, and the Quran doesn't.

prac.q: “Christian doctors in Arabia like al-Harith ibn Kalada knew Greek medicine and taught Muhammad.”
prac.a: There's no evidence al-Harith taught the Prophet anything, and the reports about his training are late and thin. More importantly, if Greek medicine had been the source, its errors would show up. They don't.

briefs.evs:
No access. The Prophet ﷺ was unlettered (29:48), and the great translation movement in Baghdad came over a century after him.
Greek errors. Galen and Aristotle taught that the fetus forms from menstrual blood shaped by semen. Hippocrates taught pangenesis, that seed is drawn from every part of the body. The four humours, the "rete mirabile" network in the human brain, and the screaming mandrake legend (Pliny and medieval herbals) were all part of Greek medicine.
The Quran says the human being is created from a mixed drop (nutfa amshaj, 76:2) and describes stages, with none of these errors.
Women's contribution. Arabs commonly believed the mother was only a vessel. The hadith describes the woman's fluid as contributing to the child and to resemblance (Muslim 311; Bukhari 3329), correcting that belief.

briefs.title: Six days or eight? (41:9-12)
briefs.thesis: The "four days" of 41:10 include the two days of 41:9, so the total is six, consistent with the rest of the Quran.
briefs.sum: The "four days" in 41:10 includes the first two, so the total is six; thumma can order speech rather than time (6:154; 7:11).

obj.q: "That's an ad hoc fix."
obj.a: It is the classical reading, given long before modern critics raised the objection, and Arabic usage supports running totals. A sentence must be read in its language's idiom.

prac.q: “2 + 4 + 2 = 8, which contradicts six days.”
prac.a: Only if "four days" is additional. Arabic often states cumulative totals; the commentators centuries ago read it as four days in all for the earth. And thumma in 6:154 shows "then" can order the speech, not the events.

briefs.evs:
The Arabic "in four days" (fi arba'ati ayyam) is a running total, as when one says "I reached the city in ten days and Mecca in fifteen", where the fifteen includes the ten. Al-Zamakhshari and other commentators read it this way.
Thumma ("then") in 41:11 does not always mean sequence in time; it can mean "moreover" or ordering in speech. In 6:151-154, after listing commands to Muhammad's ﷺ community, the Quran says "then We gave Moses the Book", although Moses came earlier. In 7:11: "We created you, then We shaped you, then We told the angels to bow to Adam."

briefs.title: The seven earths (65:12)
briefs.thesis: "Seven earths like them" has several classical readings: seven layers of the earth or seven earth-like worlds with creatures, as Ibn Abbas suggested. Neither is a scientific error, and many of the colourful details critics cite are weak Israelite narrations.
briefs.sum: 65:12 says only "seven earths like them". Early readings are layers or seven worlds with creatures (Ibn Abbas, Qatada). The fish and mountain Qaf stories are weak Isra'iliyyat.

obj.q: "Geology doesn't have exactly seven layers."
obj.a: The "layers" reading is one view, and geologists divide the earth differently depending on criteria. The "seven worlds" reading, held by many early authorities, makes no claim about geological layers.

prac.q: “Muslims believe the earth rests on a giant fish, which is absurd.”
prac.a: Ibn Kathir graded those stories weak; they come from Isra'iliyyat, not the Quran. The Quran says only "seven earths like them", and Ibn Abbas read it as other worlds with creatures, which modern astronomy has made quite plausible.

briefs.evs:
The verse. "Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them; the command descends among them" (65:12).
Hadith. "Whoever wrongfully takes a hand-span of land will have it hung around his neck from seven earths" (Bukhari 2452; Muslim 1610).
Ibn Abbas is reported to have said that in each earth there is a prophet like yours, and that "if I told you its explanation you would reject it". Qatada said there are creatures and commands in every earth. Al-Bayhaqi said the chain is sound but the text is unsupported (shadh), and Ibn Kathir thought it may be from Isra'iliyyat
Weak details. Ibn Kathir graded weak the stories of the earth on a fish or a bull and of the mountain Qaf; they are not Quran or authentic hadith.
Modern context. Astronomers have now found thousands of planets, some Earth-sized in habitable zones (such as TRAPPIST-1e). The idea of other "earths" is no longer strange.

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: Agnosticism is a claim, and it carries a burden
briefs.thesis: "We can't know whether God exists" is not the absence of a position. It is a claim about knowledge that needs evidence, and the agnostic usually offers none.
briefs.sum: "No one can know" is a claim needing proof, and it undermines itself. Suspending judgement is only rational if the evidence is balanced, and the agnostic must show that. Given the stakes, not investigating is not caution.

obj.q: "I just lack belief; I'm not claiming anything."
obj.a: Then you are not an agnostic about the evidence but someone who hasn't evaluated it. The right response is to look at it, which this library sets out.

obj.q: "Both sides have good arguments, so I suspend judgement."
obj.a: That requires showing they are evenly balanced. Ask which arguments for God the agnostic finds weak and why. Usually the conversation shows the "balance" was assumed.

prac.q: “I'm agnostic: you can't prove God, and I can't disprove Him, so it's 50/50.”
prac.a: Not knowing which side is right doesn't make the odds 50/50; it means you haven't weighed the evidence. Let's weigh it: do you think things that depend on other things can explain themselves? If not, something independent exists. Then we can ask what it must be like.

briefs.evs:
Two kinds of agnosticism. "I don't know" (personal agnosticism) is an honest report, and the cure is to examine the arguments. "No one can know" (strong agnosticism) is a sweeping claim about all possible evidence, and it is self-undermining if pushed: how does the agnostic know that no one can know?
The stakes. A person who says "maybe there is a God who will judge me" and then stops investigating is not being cautious; he is being careless about the most important question he could ask. The Quran addresses this directly: "Do they not reflect within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth and for an appointed term" (30:8).
The fitrah. Belief in a Creator is the natural default (see Arguments for God); the agnostic is the one departing from it.
Doubt that is not reasoned. The Quran describes people who "follow nothing but assumption, and assumption avails nothing against the truth" (53:28), and calls on them to "bring your proof if you are truthful" (2:111).

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: Why the first cause must be one
briefs.thesis: There cannot be two independent, necessary beings. If there were two, something would have to distinguish them, and whatever distinguishes them would make them composite or dependent. So the necessary being is one.
briefs.sum: Two necessary beings would need something to distinguish them, making them composite and dependent; and two all-powerful wills could block each other (21:22; 23:91). So the necessary being is one.

obj.q: "Two gods could just agree."
obj.a: If they agree because each could not act otherwise, neither is free and all-powerful; if they agree by choice, each could have willed differently and one of them would then be overpowered. Either way, a being that could be blocked is not the ultimate cause.

obj.q: "Doesn't this argument work against the Trinity too?"
obj.a: Yes, which is one reason Christianity must insist the three are one being. The Quran's argument shows that ultimate reality is one, and the problems with saying that one being is three persons are covered in How the Trinity developed.

prac.q: “Maybe there are many first causes, a committee of gods.”
prac.a: Then each would need something that makes it different from the others, so each would be composite and dependent on its parts, and none would be the ultimate, independent cause. And as 21:22 says, rival ultimate wills would mean a world that could be pulled apart, but we see one consistent order.

briefs.evs:
The Quran's version. "Had there been in the heavens and earth gods besides Allah, they would both have been ruined" (21:22). "Allah has not taken any son, nor has there been with Him any god; then each god would have taken what it created, and some of them would have overpowered others" (23:91). This is the burhan al-tamanu' (argument from mutual hindrance) developed by the theologians: two all-powerful wills either agree necessarily (so neither is independent) or can conflict (so one or both is limited).
The philosophical version argues that what is purely necessary, with no distinction between what it is and that it is, cannot be multiplied: there is nothing by which two such beings could differ.
Observation supports it. The universe runs on one consistent set of laws; there is no sign of rival designers.

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: Eternal, self-sufficient and not physical
briefs.thesis: Whatever exists necessarily cannot begin or end, cannot depend on anything, and cannot be made of parts. So it is eternal, self-sufficient (al-Samad, al-Ghani) and not material, since matter is composite, changing and dependent.
briefs.sum: A necessary being can't begin or end, depends on nothing, and can't be made of parts; the universe, matter and energy fail all three. So the first cause is eternal, self-sufficient and beyond the physical (57:3; 112:2; 42:11).

obj.q: "Maybe the first cause is a physical quantum vacuum."
obj.a: A quantum vacuum has properties, obeys laws and fluctuates; it is something with parts and conditions, so it needs an explanation too. It is not "nothing" and it is not independent.

prac.q: “Why can't the universe itself be eternal and necessary?”
prac.a: Because it has a beginning by the best cosmology, is made of parts that depend on each other, and is constantly changing. A necessary being can't begin, can't depend on parts, and can't be different from what it must be.

briefs.evs:
The Quran. "He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden" (57:3); "Allah, al-Samad" (112:2), the one on whom all depend while He depends on none; "O people, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), the Praiseworthy" (35:15).
Why the universe can't be it. The universe began (standard cosmology), is made of parts, and changes. Each of these marks it as dependent.
Why "energy" or "the laws of physics" can't be it. Energy is a measurable quantity of something physical; laws describe how physical things behave; neither explains why physical things exist.
"Nothing is like Him" (42:11). Being uncaused and non-physical, God is not one more thing among things.

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: Living, knowing, willing and powerful
briefs.thesis: The first cause chose to create this particular universe out of many possibilities, so it has will; to choose, it must know; to bring the universe into being, it must have power; and what knows, wills and acts is living. An "unconscious force" cannot explain the specific universe we have.
briefs.sum: The universe is one specific option among many and had a beginning; a blind cause would produce an eternal, uniform effect. Choosing requires will and knowledge, acting requires power, and these require life (2:255; 36:82; 67:14).

obj.q: "Maybe the universe is the only possible universe, so no choice was needed."
obj.a: Nothing in physics requires these constants or this universe; physicists treat the constants as free parameters, which is why fine-tuning is discussed at all. Claiming this is the only possible universe is an assertion with no support.

obj.q: "An unconscious process like evolution produces order without a mind."
obj.a: Evolution operates inside a universe already governed by laws and already containing self-replicating life; it can't explain why there is a universe with laws suited to life at all.

prac.q: “Fine, there's a first cause, but it could be an unconscious force.”
prac.a: An unconscious force acting by necessity would produce its effect always and the same way, so it couldn't explain a universe that began at a point and has these particular laws among many possible ones. Choosing one possibility over others is what a will does, and a will needs knowledge. That's a living, personal Creator.

briefs.evs:
The argument from particularisation (dalil al-takhsis) of the Muslim theologians, developed by al-Ghazali and others: the world has a specific size, shape, time of beginning and order. Nothing in the world's nature requires those specifics, so a chooser specified them.
Ibn Rushd's two arguments (al-Kashf 'an Manahij al-Adilla): the argument from providence (dalil al-'inaya), that the world is suited to life and human needs, which points to a knowing purpose; and the argument from invention (dalil al-ikhtira'), that living things and their properties are brought into being, pointing to a maker.
Knowledge. "Would He not know, the One who created, while He is the Subtle, the Acquainted?" (67:14). The fine-tuning of the universe for life (see Arguments for God) is a mark of knowledge.
The beginning. A cause that acted by necessity, without will, would have its effect as long as it existed, so an eternal impersonal cause would produce an eternal universe. A universe that began points to a cause that chose when to act. William Lane Craig puts this as the argument that the first cause must be personal.
Life. Knowledge, will and power are attributes only of a living being: "Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all" (2:255).

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: Perfect, wise and merciful
briefs.thesis: The source of all existence and all perfections must itself have those perfections without limit and without the defects that come with them in creatures. This gives the attributes of perfection: wisdom, mercy, justice, and freedom from every deficiency.
briefs.sum: Creatures' perfections come from the Creator, who has them more fully and without defect (Ibn Taymiyya's qiyas al-awla). Hence His wisdom (32:7), mercy (Bukhari 5999) and freedom from every deficiency (42:11).

obj.q: "If God is merciful, why is there suffering?"
obj.a: See The problem of evil and suffering: the argument there shows suffering is consistent with wisdom and mercy, especially given an afterlife of justice.

obj.q: "Projecting human qualities onto God is anthropomorphism."
obj.a: The principle explicitly removes the limitations that come with creaturely qualities. "Knowing" for God doesn't mean learning; "merciful" doesn't mean emotional need. The Quran affirms the attributes while denying likeness (42:11).

prac.q: “You've proved a powerful creator, but not a good one.”
prac.a: Every good in the world, including our own sense of justice and mercy, comes from the Creator, and a cause can't give what it lacks. A being who is self-sufficient has no need that could drive it to cruelty, and a wise being acts for good ends. That's why the Quran calls Him al-Rahman and al-Hakim.

briefs.evs:
Ibn Taymiyya's principle (qiyas al-awla, the argument a fortiori). Every perfection found in a creature, without any defect attached to it, belongs to the Creator more fittingly; every defect from which creatures are free, the Creator is more fittingly free of. The creature's knower implies the Creator knows; the creature's merciful parent implies the Creator is more merciful.
The hadith of mercy. Seeing a mother clutching her baby, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child" (Bukhari 5999).
Wisdom in creation. "He who perfected everything He created" (32:7); the fine-tuning, the order of nature and the suitability of the world for life all display wisdom.
No defects. He neither sleeps nor tires (2:255; 50:38), does not forget (20:52), does not wrong anyone (4:40), and there is nothing like Him (42:11).

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: A wise and merciful God would guide us: from God to prophethood
briefs.thesis: Some agnostics and deists accept a Creator but deny He communicates. But a wise Creator who made beings capable of moral choice, with a purpose, would guide them, and human reason alone cannot reach the details of that guidance. This makes revelation expected and the next question is which revelation is true.
briefs.sum: A wise, merciful Creator who made moral beings for a purpose would guide them (23:115; 17:15). Reason knows God; revelation gives the details. Deism accepts the premises and refuses the conclusion.

obj.q: "If God wanted to communicate, He'd write it in the sky."
obj.a: Then belief would be compelled and the test of free choice would disappear. God gave clear but not overwhelming signs: a preserved book, fulfilled prophecies, a messenger of evident character. These are enough for the sincere (see Proofs for Islam).

obj.q: "There are many claimed revelations; how do I choose?"
obj.a: By the same reasoning used here: which one is consistent with the attributes proved (one, perfect, merciful, just), and which has the strongest evidence of divine origin.

prac.q: “I believe in a creator, but not in religion; God doesn't need to talk to us.”
prac.a: A wise and merciful Creator who made you able to choose good and evil and longing for meaning would hardly leave you without guidance. A deist God is less wise than the God your own reasoning points to. So the question isn't whether God speaks but where.

briefs.evs:
Purpose. "Did you think We created you without purpose and that you would not be returned to Us?" (23:115). "I did not create jinn and humankind except to worship Me" (51:56).
Guidance sent. "We never punish until We have sent a messenger" (17:15). "And for every nation there is a guide" (13:7).
Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim argue that reason and fitrah know God and the broad shape of good and evil, but the details of worship and the unseen need revelation; and that sending prophets is required by God's wisdom and mercy.
Deism's weakness. A deist God who creates moral beings with a longing for Him and then remains silent is less wise and less merciful than the God the arguments establish, so deism is unstable: it accepts the premises and refuses the conclusion.

briefs.sec: Refuting agnosticism: from a Creator to His attributes
briefs.title: Answering the agnostic's favourite objections
briefs.thesis: The common reasons for agnosticism (divine hiddenness, religious diversity, "we can't know anything beyond science") either undermine themselves or are answered by the attributes already proved.
briefs.sum: Hiddenness: God is knowable but doesn't compel belief (67:2). Religious diversity doesn't mean no answer. Scientism refutes itself. "We can't know anything about God" is itself a claim of knowledge about God.

prac.q: “God is hidden; if He wanted me to believe, I'd believe.”
prac.a: He made Himself known through creation, your own nature and a preserved revelation, but He doesn't force belief, because life is a test of what we do with the evidence (67:2). Have you examined the evidence seriously, or are you waiting to be compelled?

briefs.evs:
"If God existed, He would make Himself obvious" (the hiddenness argument, J.L. Schellenberg). God has made Himself knowable through creation, the fitrah and revelation; what He has not done is force belief. A test of sincerity needs some freedom to turn away (67:2). And the people the argument imagines as "non-resistant non-believers" usually haven't investigated seriously.
"So many religions disagree, so none can be known." Disagreement doesn't mean no answer is right: people disagree about history and science too. And the major theistic religions largely agree on a Creator; the disagreement is about details that can be tested (preservation of scripture, coherence of the doctrine of God, prophecy).
"Only science gives knowledge" (scientism). That statement is not itself a scientific finding, so by its own standard it can't be known. Science also depends on things it cannot prove scientifically: the reliability of reason, the uniformity of nature, the reality of the external world (see Philosophy for debaters).
"We can't know anything about what's beyond the universe." We know some things by reasoning alone: that contradictions are impossible, that dependent things need a cause. These apply beyond the universe as much as within it. "We can't know anything about God" is itself a claim to know something about Him.
"I'll believe when I see a miracle." The Quran records people who

briefs.title: "Confirming" means affirming what God revealed, not endorsing the texts in circulation
briefs.thesis: The Quran confirms the revelation God gave to Moses and Jesus. It never confirms the later compilations as they stood in the 7th century, and Christians accept the same kind of selective confirmation when Jesus confirms the Torah.
briefs.sum: The Quran confirms what God revealed, not every book in circulation; it calls itself muhaymin, the arbiter over earlier scripture (Sinai); and Jesus' own "confirmation" of the Torah involved changes. The dilemma's first premise is false.

obj.q: "The Quran says 'confirming what is with you' (2:41), meaning the texts they had."
obj.a: It confirms what is with them in the sense of the prophecies and teachings they possessed. The same Quran says, in the same surah, that they "conceal the truth while you know it" (2:42), "distort it after understanding it" (2:75) and "write the book with their hands" (2:79). The Quran cannot be confirming a text it describes as altered in the same passage.

obj.q: "Then the Quran should have said clearly which parts are true."
obj.a: It does: it is the criterion (furqan, 25:1) and guardian (5:48). What agrees with it is confirmed; what contradicts it is rejected. That's exactly how the early commentators read it.

prac.q: “The Quran says it confirms the Torah and Gospel, and those contradict the Quran, so Islam refutes itself.”
prac.a: The Quran confirms what God revealed to Moses and Jesus. The Gospels aren't the Injil revealed to Jesus; they're accounts written about him. Jesus "confirmed" the Torah while overriding its oath law, and you don't say he refuted himself. Same standard.

briefs.evs:
The idiom. Musaddiqan lima bayna yadayhi means "confirming what came before it" (Lane's Lexicon: bayna yadayhi, "before it" in time). It describes the Quran's relationship to earlier revelation, not to particular manuscripts.
Jesus' "confirmation". Jesus confirmed the Torah (Matt 5:17) and told people to obey the teachers on Moses' seat (Matt 23:2-3), yet he set aside the Torah's rules on oaths (Matt 5:33-37 against Num 30:2) and "eye for an eye" (Matt 5:38-39 against Exod 21:24). Christians don't say Jesus contradicted himself. Confirmation is not a blanket endorsement of every line.
Fulfilment. "Believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you" (2:41). A key sense of confirmation is fulfilment: the Quran and the Prophet ﷺ are what the earlier scriptures foretold (7:157; 61:6), the same way Christians say Jesus "confirmed" the Old Testament by fulfilling it. It also confirms the shared creed: one God, prophets, angels, judgement.
Naming the corrupted book. The Quran can call the book in their hands "the Torah" because that is what they claim it is, as Joseph speaks of 'many separate lords' when addressing his fellow prisoners (12:39), and because it used to be that, as "give the orphans their property" (4:2) is said of orphans who have grown up.
Nicolai Sinai, an Oxford scholar, explains that the Quran's term muhaymin (5:48) makes a stronger claim than "confirming

briefs.title: The Quran describes the earlier scriptures as altered, and every early Muslim authority agreed
briefs.thesis: The Quran names at least five kinds of corruption, and from the Companions onward Muslim scholars understood that the books in Jewish and Christian hands had been changed.
briefs.sum: The Quran names concealment, tongue-twisting, writing by hand, changing words and moving words. Ibn Abbas (Bukhari 7363) says they altered what Allah wrote. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Taymiyya, al-Jahiz and al-Qadi Isma'il agree. The "meaning only" quote is not a hadith.

obj.q: "Those verses are about a few Jews in Medina twisting meaning orally."
obj.a: Some are. But 2:79 is about writing and attributing to God, and 6:91 about hiding parts of scripture. And Ibn Abbas explicitly says the People of the Book "changed and altered what Allah wrote".

obj.q: "The Prophet put the Torah on a cushion and said 'I believe in you' (Abu Dawud 4449)."
obj.a: That wording is missing from the versions in Bukhari (3635; 6841) and Muslim (1699), and its chain includes Hisham ibn Sa'd, whom Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Hajar weakened (al-Albani nonetheless graded it hasan). Even if accepted, the story is about the Jews of Medina hiding the verse on stoning with a hand while reading the Torah (Bukhari 3635): it shows concealment, and the Prophet ﷺ honouring what God revealed while exposing what they hid.

prac.q: “Early Muslims only believed in tahrif of meaning; textual corruption is a later idea invented by Ibn Hazm.”
prac.a: Ibn Abbas, a Companion, says in Bukhari 7363 that they "changed and altered what Allah wrote and wrote the book with their own hands". That is textual. The "meaning only" quote is a chapter-heading comment, not a hadith.

briefs.evs:
Six patterns of tahrif in the Quran.
Concealment: "you conceal the truth while you know it" (2:42; 3:71; 3:187).
Twisting with the tongue: "a party of them twist their tongues with the Book so you think it is from the Book, but it is not" (3:78).
Writing by hand: "woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say, this is from Allah" (2:79).
Exchanging words: "the wrongdoers changed the word to other than what was said to them" (2:59).
Moving words from their places: "they distort words from their places" (4:46; 5:13).
And making scripture into pages, "showing some and hiding much" (6:91).
The Companions. Ibn Abbas: "How can you ask the People of the Book about anything when your Book… is the most recent? Allah has told you that the People of the Book changed and altered what Allah wrote, and wrote the book with their own hands and said 'this is from Allah'" (Bukhari 7363; 2685).
