The scholars. Ibn Kathir on 3:78: the books in their hands have certainly been changed, added to and subtracted from. Ibn Taymiyya held a middle view: some wording and much meaning were altered. Al-Jahiz noted that two of the four Evangelists were not disciples and that the Gospels' contradictions show they were not protected from error. Al-Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq explained the difference: Allah entrusted the Torah to its people to preserve (5:44, "bima ustuhfizu", "what they were entrusted

briefs.title: "None can change the words of Allah" is about His decree, not the Bible's text
briefs.thesis: Verses like 6:115 and 10:64 say no one can change Allah's kalimat, meaning His decrees and promises. The Quran guarantees preservation only for itself (15:9), while the Torah was entrusted to humans (5:44).
briefs.sum: "None can change the words of Allah" refers to His decrees and promises (6:34; 10:64). Allah guards the Quran Himself (15:9), but entrusted the Torah to the rabbis (5:44).

obj.q: "If God could preserve the Quran, why not the Torah?"
obj.a: He could have; He chose to entrust the Torah to the rabbis (5:44) and to preserve the final revelation Himself (15:9). Each earlier revelation was for a people and a time; the last is for all people until the end. A test given to a community to guard its book is not a failure of God.

prac.q: “If the words of God can't be changed, how can the Bible be corrupted?”
prac.a: Read 6:34: the "words" there are God's promise of help to His messengers. The Quran says people did change written scripture (2:79). The only book God promised to guard Himself is the Quran (15:9); the Torah was entrusted to the rabbis (5:44).

briefs.evs:
6:34: "Messengers before you were denied, and they were patient… until Our help came to them. None can alter the words of Allah." The "words" are His promise of help.
10:64: "For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and the Hereafter. No change is there in the words of Allah." The promise of glad tidings.
18:27: "Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can change His words." This concerns the Quran, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ.
Tabari and Qatada explain kalimat as His decrees and promises.
15:9 promises the preservation of "the Reminder" (the Quran) by Allah Himself. 5:44 says the rabbis judged by "what they were entrusted to preserve of Allah's Book", making them the guardians, and humans can fail.
The word "dhikr". 16:43 tells people to "ask the people of the Reminder (ahl al-dhikr) if you do not know". There dhikr refers to the earlier revelation and its people, who can be asked about shared basics (that earlier prophets were men). In 15:9, the commentators agree, dhikr is the Quran. The meaning depends on context.

briefs.title: 10:94: "Ask those who read the Book before you"
briefs.thesis: 10:94 is a conditional, rhetorical statement directed through the Prophet ﷺ to doubters, about the stories of Noah and Moses just told; the people to ask are the believing People of the Book who recognised the Prophet. It does not endorse their scriptures as preserved.
briefs.sum: 10:94 comes right after the stories of Noah and Moses, is conditional and rhetorical, and points to believing scholars like Abdullah ibn Salam. The Prophet ﷺ told Muslims neither to believe nor deny the People of the Book.

obj.q: "'Those who read the Book' means all Jews and Christians, so their books are reliable."
obj.a: Reliable enough to confirm the story of Noah's flood or the Exodus, which are still there. The verse doesn't say their books are free of change, and the same Quran says they were changed.

prac.q: “10:94 tells Muhammad to check his revelation against the Bible, so the Bible must be the standard.”
prac.a: The verse ends "the truth has come to you from your Lord, so never be among the doubters". The Quran is the standard (5:48). The People of the Book can confirm shared stories, and the believers among them (like Abdullah ibn Salam) confirmed that the Prophet was the one their books foretold.

briefs.evs:
Context. The preceding verses tell how Noah was rejected and saved, and how Moses and Aaron confronted Pharaoh, who drowned. These are in Genesis 6-9 and Exodus 2-14, and anyone who read the Torah could confirm them.
Rhetorical. "If you are in doubt" does not mean the Prophet doubted. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "He neither doubted nor asked" (Tabari). The grammarians Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad, and al-Qurtubi, explain that the address is to the doubting listener through the Prophet.
Who to ask. Ibn Abbas and Tabari: those of the People of the Book who knew Muhammad ﷺ from their books and believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam (46:10; 13:43; 28:52-53). Ibn Kathir links it to their recognising him "as they recognise their own sons" (2:146).
The Prophet's own instruction. "Do not believe the People of the Book and do not deny them; say: we believe in Allah and what was revealed" (Bukhari 4485). That makes no sense if 10:94 told him to treat their books as authoritative.
Ibn Taymiyya (al-Jawab al-Sahih) lists what the earlier books still testify to: the monotheism of the prophets, that messengers were human, how nations treated their prophets, the core of religion, and the signs of Muhammad ﷺ.

briefs.title: "Let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed in it" (5:47)
briefs.thesis: 5:47 tells Christians to judge by what Allah revealed in the Gospel, not by every text in their books, and the next verse makes the Quran the guardian. Islamic law itself overrides their books, which shows the Quran never treated them as fully binding.
briefs.sum: 5:47 says judge by "what Allah revealed in it"; 5:48 makes the Quran the guardian; 9:29 binds the People of the Book to the Prophet's prohibitions; and Moses himself would have had to follow Muhammad ﷺ. The Quran never treats their books as fully binding.

obj.q: "5:47 shows the Gospel existed in the Prophet's time."
obj.a: Some form of the Christian Gospel existed (possibly the Diatessaron among Arabic-speaking Christians; see next argument). The verse tells its people to act on what God revealed in it, chief of which is the prophecy of the coming messenger (7:157; 61:6).

prac.q: “The Quran tells Christians to judge by the Gospel, so it must be reliable.”
prac.a: It says judge by "what Allah revealed in it", and the next verse makes the Quran the guardian over it. And the Quran overrides it: 9:29 binds them to what Allah and His Messenger forbade. A book that is overridden is not treated as fully authoritative.

briefs.evs:
The wording. "Let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed in it" (5:47). It is not "judge by it". The commentator Muqatil explains this as the true commands within it, such as the command to pardon a killer.
The next verse (5:48) makes the Quran muhaymin over the earlier books and tells the Prophet to judge between them by what Allah revealed to him.
5:66 and 5:68 ("if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord") include "what was revealed to them from their Lord", which the commentators take to include the Quran.
9:29 criticises the People of the Book who "do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden". If the Torah and Gospel were sufficient, the Prophet's prohibitions would not bind them.
6:146 says the Jewish dietary restrictions were imposed "for their transgression", and the Prophet ﷺ said that if Moses were alive he would have to follow him (Ahmad and al-Darimi, from Jabir; the chain is disputed and some graders accept it as hasan through supporting reports).

briefs.title: The Quran's Torah and Injil are revelations, not the Bible's books, and there was no Arabic Bible
briefs.thesis: In the Quran, the Torah is what was given to Moses and the Injil is what was given to Jesus. Neither is the Pentateuch or the four Gospels. And there was no Arabic Bible in the Prophet's time from which he could have learned or copied.
briefs.sum: The Quran's Injil is what God gave Jesus, not the four Gospels. There was no Arabic Bible before the 8th-9th centuries, no Christian community in the Hijaz, and the Arab Christians' Gospel was probably the Diatessaron.

obj.q: "The Quran calls the Christian scripture 'Injil', so it means the Gospels."
obj.a: The Quran uses the name its audience used, while defining the Injil as what God gave Jesus. Christians call the Gospels "the Gospel" too, but no Christian says Jesus wrote them.

prac.q: “Muhammad heard Bible stories from Christians and Jews he met on trade journeys.”
prac.a: The Quran's knowledge goes into Hebrew wordplay, rabbinic debates and Syriac Christian traditions, while correcting them (see The Quran correcting earlier scripture). Brief trade contacts and a few foreign slaves (16:103) can't explain that. And the Quraysh, who knew his life closely, couldn't name a teacher.

briefs.evs:
The Injil was given to Jesus. "He will teach him the Book and wisdom, the Torah and the Injil" (3:48); "We gave him the Injil, in which was guidance and light" (5:46). The four Gospels are "according to" Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, written decades after Jesus.
The Torah. The Quran speaks of the Tablets given to Moses containing "instruction concerning all things" (7:145). It never says Moses wrote five books including his own death (Deut 34).
No Arabic Bible. Bruce Metzger: the earliest Arabic Bible translations probably date from the 8th century. Among the earliest Arabic Gospel manuscripts are Vatican Arabic 13 (undated, 9th century) and Sinai Arabic 72 (dated 897). Sidney Griffith (The Bible in Arabic) agrees, and notes that the Gospel the Quran confirms is not the Gospel as Christians had it.
Tap to enlargeBruce Metzger, The Bible in Translation, p. 46: the earliest Arabic Bible translations probably date from the 8th century
Tap to enlargeVatican Arabic 13, among the earliest Arabic Gospel manuscripts (9th century)
No Christian community in the Hijaz. Stephen Shoemaker (Creating the Qur'an) notes that the Hijaz shows little or no evidence of an organised Christian community (citing Beaucamp, Robin, Trimingham). Arthur Vööbus called the idea that Muhammad used an Arabic New Testament unsubstantiated.
The Diatessaron. The "Gospel" known to Arabic-speaking Christians, like

briefs.title: The Quran did not copy the apocrypha
briefs.thesis: The Quran shares some stories with non-canonical texts (Jesus' clay birds, "what no eye has seen", Moses in Midian), but the parallels are with older, shared traditions, the Quran's versions differ in theologically significant ways, and the supposed sources are often later than the Quran.
briefs.sum: The clay-bird story in the Quran lacks the Infancy Gospel's distinctive content and adds "by Allah's permission"; "what no eye has seen" is an older saying Paul himself quotes; and the "Jacob" details in Moses' Midian story come from later tafsir, not the Quran.

obj.q: "Even if not copied directly, Muhammad heard these stories orally."
obj.a: Then the source was oral tradition circulating among Christians, which may preserve true events about Jesus that the canonical Gospels did not record (John 21:25). The Quran presents its account as revelation that corrects the theology around such stories.

prac.q: “The Quran copies a 2nd-century fairy tale about clay birds.”
prac.a: The Quran's account shares only the miracle itself, and puts it "by Allah's permission", while dropping the Infancy Gospel's child Jesus who kills people. Irenaeus already knew stories from this tradition in 180, so it may preserve an early memory. A shared event isn't a copy.

briefs.evs:
The clay birds (3:49; 5:110) and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas. In the Infancy Gospel, a five-year-old Jesus makes twelve sparrows on the Sabbath, quarrels about the Sabbath, and elsewhere kills a teacher and a child with curses and is worshipped. In the Quran, Jesus as a prophet makes "the form of a bird", and it becomes a bird "by Allah's permission" (bi-idhni-llah), repeated pointedly. The Quran takes nothing of the Infancy Gospel's distinctive content and adds what it lacks: dependence on God. The Infancy Gospel's oldest fragment is a 4th/5th-century papyrus, and complete manuscripts of the story are medieval. Scholars like Fred Lapham think some stories go back to early oral tradition, and Irenaeus (c. 180) knew one. John 21:25 itself says much of what Jesus did was never written. Even the critic Sean Anthony concedes the Quran did not copy the Infancy Gospel.
"What no eye has seen" (hadith qudsi, Bukhari 3244; 1 Cor 2:9). Paul introduces it with "as it is written", so he is quoting an older source. The same saying appears, attributed to Jesus, in the Gospel of Thomas (17), in 1 Clement (34:8), the Gospel of Judas and other texts. Origen thought Paul was citing an apocryphon (Clivaz and Schulthess). A shared earlier prophetic saying is not copying from Paul.
Moses in Midian (28:22-28) "confused with Jacob". The "Jacob" details critics cite (a rock on the well, seven years'

briefs.title: "The Jews say Ezra is the son of God" (9:30)
briefs.thesis: 9:30 reports what a group of Jews said, not the official creed of all Judaism. Jewish texts of the period exalted Ezra to a near-heavenly status, the Jews of Medina never denied the verse, and the Quran's style uses a general term for a particular group.
briefs.sum: 9:30 reports a saying "with their mouths". 4 Ezra has Ezra taken to live with God's "Son", 3 Enoch calls the exalted scribe "the lesser YHWH", the Medinan Jews never objected, and Arabic uses general terms for part of a group (3:173).

obj.q: "No Jewish text calls Ezra 'son of God' in those words."
obj.a: The Quran reports what people said in 7th-century Arabia, not a quotation from a surviving text. 4 Ezra shows Ezra's elevation to heaven with God's "Son", 3 Enoch shows a scribe exalted as "lesser YHWH", and the Medinan Jews did not deny the claim.

prac.q: “No Jew has ever believed Ezra is the son of God. That proves the Quran is wrong.”
prac.a: The Quran reports a saying of some Jews of its time; the Medinan Jews heard the verse and didn't deny it; and 4 Ezra and 3 Enoch show exactly this kind of exaltation of the Scribe. Absence of a surviving text isn't proof of absence, especially for Arabian Judaism, whose literature is lost.

briefs.evs:
"With their mouths." The verse continues: "that is their saying with their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before" (9:30). It describes speech, not scripture.
Ezra exalted. In 4 Ezra (late 1st century CE), Ezra restores the lost scriptures by divine inspiration and is told: "you shall be taken up from among men, and henceforth you shall live with My Son (the Messiah in 4 Ezra's usage)" (4 Ezra 14:9). Ezra 7:6 already describes him as a scribe on whom "the hand of the LORD his God" rested and who was granted all he asked. Jewish tradition fused the figure of the inspired Scribe (Ezra/Enoch) with angelic status; in 3 Enoch, Enoch becomes Metatron, called "the lesser YHWH" (3 Enoch 12:5). Angels were called "sons of God" in Jewish texts (Gen 6:2; Job 1:6).
Scholars. Gordon Newby (A History of the Jews of Arabia) argues Ezra could be counted among the bene elohim in Arabian Jewish circles; Reuven Firestone finds it plausible that a Jewish group elevated Ezra to near-divine status.
Medina's Jews didn't object. Ibn Abbas reports that Jewish leaders of Medina (Sallam ibn Mishkam and others) told the Prophet ﷺ they could not follow him because he did not hold Uzayr to be the son of Allah. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr says the saying came from Finhas ibn 'Azura. Ibn al-'Arabi notes that the Jews of Medina never objected to the verse, which they would have if it were basele

briefs.title: Mary and the Trinity (5:116; 5:73)
briefs.thesis: The Quran does not define the official Trinity as Father, Son and Mary. It condemns every form of "God is one of three", and it accurately condemns the deification of Mary that was real among Christians of its time.
briefs.sum: 5:73 rejects any "third of three"; 5:116 condemns the worship of Jesus and Mary, which was real (Collyridians, Mariamites, Mary as Constantinople's protector in 626). The Quran never says the Trinity is Father, Son and Mary.

obj.q: "Taking Mary as a 'god' isn't Catholic doctrine; Catholics only venerate her."
obj.a: The Quran describes practice, and practice included prayers, offerings and attributions of power that belong to God. When she is called on for salvation and protection, critics argue that this practice amounts to treating her as divine, though Catholic doctrine distinguishes veneration from worship .

prac.q: “The Quran thinks the Trinity is Father, Son and Mary, which shows its author didn't know Christianity.”
prac.a: The Quran never says that. It rejects "third of three" (any Trinity) in 5:73, and in 5:116 separately condemns worshipping Jesus and Mary, which Christians of the 620s did in practice: Constantinople credited Mary with defeating the Avars.

briefs.evs:
What the verses say. 5:73: "They have disbelieved who say Allah is the third of three." 5:116: "Did you say to people, take me and my mother as gods besides Allah?" Neither says that the official Trinity consists of Father, Son and Mary. "Third of three" matches the Christian formula that the Son is "one of the Trinity" (unus ex Trinitate), promoted under Justinian. 5:72's "Allah is the Messiah" echoes the Syriac theologian Henana, criticised by Babai the Great for saying "Christ is God and God is Christ".
Mary worshipped. Epiphanius describes the Collyridians, women who offered cakes to Mary as to a goddess (Panarion 79). The Christian historian Eutychius (Sa'id ibn Batriq, 9th-10th century) mentions "Mariamites" who held Jesus and his mother to be two gods besides God.
Mary as divine protector. In the 620s, as the Quran was being revealed, Constantinople credited Mary with saving the city from the Avar siege of 626, when Patriarch Sergius carried her icon on the walls (Heraclius had sailed with a Marian icon in 610). She was hailed as the city's invincible protector (the Akathistos tradition, traditionally linked to 626). The Quran answers: "who could do anything against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother?" (5:17); "they both used to eat food" (5:75).
Later Marian devotion. Alphonsus Liguori's The Glories of Mary quotes Bernardine of Siena

briefs.title: "O sister of Aaron" (19:28)
briefs.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ himself explained that the Israelites named people after earlier prophets and righteous figures; "sister" means kinswoman or descendant; and Luke places Mary's relative Elizabeth among "the daughters of Aaron".
briefs.sum: The Prophet ﷺ explained that Israelites named people after earlier prophets (Muslim 2135); "sister" means kinswoman; Luke makes Mary a relative of a "daughter of Aaron"; and the Quran knows many prophets came between Moses and Jesus.

obj.q: "Mary's father is called 'Imran, Moses' father's name, so the Quran confuses the two Marys."
obj.a: Mary's father 'Imran (3:35) is a different person, and Christians themselves didn't know her father's name from the Gospels (later tradition says Joachim). Repeated family names, especially in priestly lines, were normal.

prac.q: “The Quran confuses Mary the mother of Jesus with Miriam the sister of Moses.”
prac.a: The Prophet ﷺ himself answered this: Israelites named people after earlier prophets (Muslim 2135). Luke puts Mary among the relatives of the "daughters of Aaron". And the Quran says plainly that many messengers came between Moses and Jesus.

briefs.evs:
The Prophet's answer. Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba was asked by the Christians of Najran how the Quran could call Mary "sister of Aaron" when Moses lived long before Jesus. The Prophet ﷺ said: "They used to name people after the prophets and righteous people before them" (Muslim 2135).
"Sister" as kin. The Prophet ﷺ told his wife Safiyya, of Jewish descent, to answer taunts by saying "my father is Aaron, my uncle is Moses" (Tirmidhi 3894). The Quran calls Hud "brother" of 'Ad (7:65) and Salih "brother" of Thamud (7:73), meaning kinsman.
Luke. Elizabeth "was of the daughters of Aaron" (Luke 1:5), and the angel calls Mary her "relative" (Luke 1:36). By the same Semitic usage, Mary could be called "sister of Aaron". Commentators like Ellicott and Poole draw this inference from Luke.
No confusion in the Quran. The Quran never puts Moses or Aaron in the same scene as Jesus, and says many messengers came between them (2:87; 5:46). Gregory of Nyssa saw Miriam, "the sister of Aaron" (Exod 15:20), as a type of Mary; modern scholars like Michael Marx read 19:28 as deliberate typology, not confusion.
The Bible repeats names. There are several Zechariahs and several Marys in the Bible; repeated names don't imply confusion.

briefs.title: The names Yahya and 'Isa
briefs.thesis: The Quran's "Yahya" is not a misspelling of Yuhanna; it says God gave John a name no one had borne before, which parallels, only in part, Luke's note that none of his relatives bore the name. "'Isa" is the Arabised form of the Syriac name of Jesus, attested before Islam.
briefs.sum: Yahya is a unique name God gave John (19:7), matching Luke's family objection (Luke 1:61); Jeffery admits it has no earlier trace. 'Isa reflects Syriac Isho' and is attested in a pre-Islamic inscription.

obj.q: "There were many people named John before John the Baptist."
obj.a: The Quran's name is Yahya, not Yuhanna (the Arabic for John). It claims God gave a new name, and that name is indeed unattested before.

prac.q: “The Quran gets Jesus' name wrong. It should be Yasu'.”
prac.a: "Jesus" itself is a Greek-Latin form of Yeshua. Every language adapts names. 'Isa reflects the Syriac Isho', and al-Jallad has found it in a pre-Islamic Arabian inscription.

briefs.evs:
19:7. "O Zechariah, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not made (naj'al) for anyone before him a namesake." Arthur Jeffery admits the name Yahya has no trace in earlier literature, which is what the verse claims: a unique name from God. Luke 1:59-61 records that the family objected: "none of your relatives is called by this name." Some commentators also read samiyy as "equal", as in 19:65 ("do you know any equal (samiyy) to Him?").
'Isa. Syriac Christians called Jesus Isho'. Ahmad al-Jallad cites a pre-Islamic Safaitic (North Arabian) inscription, and Sidney Griffith calls the Syriac origin "the most reasonable explanation". Names change form between languages, like "Jesus" from Greek Iesous from Hebrew Yeshua.

briefs.title: The story of the cow (2:67-74)
briefs.thesis: Critics say the Quran confused the red heifer (Numbers 19) with the heifer of an unsolved murder (Deuteronomy 21). In fact it deliberately combines and reverses them to make a point about Israel's hardness of heart, and its sequence follows the Torah's own order.
briefs.sum: The Quran combines Numbers 19's flawless, unyoked cow with Deuteronomy 21's murder ritual, reverses them (a concealed crime exposed), and follows Numbers' order from the heifer to water from the rock, ending with Ezekiel's "heart of stone".

obj.q: "Mixing two laws is still a mistake."
obj.a: The Quran isn't restating Torah law; it's narrating an episode in which Israel's stalling and concealment are exposed, and it draws on two Torah passages to do it, just as the NT writers merge OT texts (Mark 1:2-3 merges three).

prac.q: “The Quran mixes up the red heifer and the unsolved murder heifer.”
prac.a: It uses both on purpose and reverses their points: the murder is concealed, not unknown, and the guilty community is exposed instead of cleared. It then follows Numbers' own sequence from the heifer to water from the rock (2:74). That is skilful allusion, not confusion.

briefs.evs:
Numbers 19 describes a red heifer, without blemish, "on which a yoke has never come". The Quran's cow is a specific colour, flawless, "not trained to plough the earth or water the fields" (2:69-71).
Deuteronomy 21:1-9 prescribes a heifer when a murdered man is found and the killer is unknown; the elders declare "our hands did not shed this blood". In the Quran, the community knows more than it admits: "you disputed over it, but Allah was to bring out what you were concealing" (2:72), and the cow's part restores the dead man to name his killer (2:73).
The sequence. Numbers 19 (red heifer) is followed by Numbers 20 (water from the rock). The Quran follows the cow with: "then your hearts became hardened like stones, or even harder; for there are stones from which rivers gush forth" (2:74), echoing both the rock and Ezekiel's "heart of stone" (Ezek 36:26).
Rabbinic links. Rabbinic tradition connects the red heifer with atonement for the golden calf, which the Quran mentions just before (2:51-54).
No ashes. The Quran omits the ashes used for purification, because in its story the cow serves a single miraculous purpose.

briefs.title: Inheritance: the shares and the fractions (4:11-12)
briefs.thesis: The inheritance verses are not mathematically flawed: Islamic law has always handled cases where shares exceed or fall short of the estate ('awl and radd). And the woman's "half share" applies only in some cases, tied to financial duties that fall on men.
briefs.sum: 'Awl scales shares when they exceed the estate and radd distributes any remainder. A son's double share matches his duty to pay mahr and maintain the family, and in many cases women get equal or larger shares.

obj.q: "If God wrote the shares, why would they ever add up to more than one?"
obj.a: The verses give each heir's entitlement in the normal case; how claims combine depends on which heirs survive, which varies endlessly. A rule for proportional reduction is part of the system, applied from the earliest generation.

obj.q: "Giving a son double is still unequal."
obj.a: It is unequal in amount but matched by unequal duty. A brother who inherits twice as much must spend it on his family; his sister keeps hers. Equality of outcome under unequal obligations would be unjust.

prac.q: “The Quran's inheritance shares add up to more than 100%, so it can't be from God.”
prac.a: Fixed shares have to be combined for whichever heirs survive, and Islamic law has a proportional rule ('awl) from Umar's time, exactly as modern law scales claims. The verses also set different shares by duty: a son must pay dowry and maintenance, a daughter keeps hers.

briefs.evs:
'Awl. When fixed shares add up to more than the estate (for example a wife 1/8, two daughters 2/3, both parents 1/6 each), all shares are reduced proportionally. The Caliph Umar introduced this, and the Sunni schools later adopted it (Ibn Abbas dissented). Any modern law that guarantees several fixed claims must scale them when assets fall short, as in bankruptcy.
Radd. When shares add up to less, most schools (Hanafi, Hanbali, later Shafi'i) return the remainder to the share-holders other than spouses; Malikis and early Shafi'is send it to the public treasury.
Why some men get double. Shares are set by (1) closeness of kinship, (2) generation (the younger generation, who have life ahead, often inherit more than the older), and (3) financial duty. Only in the third category does a son receive twice a daughter's share, because he must pay the dowry (mahr) and maintain his wife, children and often his parents and sisters, while a woman's wealth is entirely her own and she has no duty to spend it on the family.
Women often equal or more. Uterine brothers and sisters inherit equally (4:12). A father and mother each get a sixth when there are children (4:11). In some cases a daughter receives more than a male relative, such as the deceased's brother.

briefs.title: The "severed aorta" (69:44-46)
briefs.thesis: 69:44-46 says that if the Prophet ﷺ had fabricated revelation, Allah would have seized him and cut his aorta: a threat of swift death. The Prophet's later words about his aorta in pain were an idiom for severe pain, and he lived about four years after the poisoning.
briefs.sum: 69:46 threatens immediate execution for fabrication. The Prophet ﷺ felt pain "as if" his aorta were cut (Bukhari 4428) four years after Khaybar, having completed his mission. That fulfils nothing.

obj.q: "He used the same word, watin, so he admitted the verse came true."
obj.a: He described a feeling ("as if"), not an event. And the verse's punishment is immediate seizure while fabricating, not a slow death years later after his mission was complete.

prac.q: “Muhammad himself said his aorta was being cut, fulfilling the Quran's curse on false prophets.”
prac.a: He said "I feel as if my aorta is being cut", describing pain four years after the poison, at the end of a mission that had succeeded. The verse threatens being seized and executed at once if he fabricated. Neither happened.

briefs.evs:
The verse. "Had he fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut his aorta (al-watin), and none of you could have shielded him" (69:44-47). It describes an immediate seizure and execution.
The hadith. In his final illness, the Prophet ﷺ told Aisha: "I still feel the pain of the food I ate at Khaybar, and now I feel as if my aorta is being cut" (Bukhari 4428). Khaybar was in 7 AH; he died in 11 AH, about four years later, after the conquest of Mecca and the Farewell Pilgrimage.
An idiom. "As if my aorta is being cut" is an Arabic expression for intense pain, like "my heart is breaking".
The poisoning made him a martyr, as Ibn Mas'ud and others said, and he was not "seized by the right hand" in the act of fabricating.

briefs.title: The war verses do not cancel the peace verses
briefs.thesis: The claim that 9:5 abrogated all peace verses has no basis in the Quran or Sunnah, according to major commentators. Most classical jurists (Hanafi, Maliki, Hanbali) held that the cause of fighting is being a combatant or belonging to a hostile polity, not disbelief itself; Shafi'is disagreed.
briefs.sum: Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zarkashi reject the abrogation of 8:61; 9:5 is about treaty-breaking tribes who attacked first (9:13); 9:6 and 60:8 command asylum and kindness; and the majority of jurists made aggression the cause of fighting.

obj.q: "Some classical scholars did say 9:5 abrogated over a hundred verses."
obj.a: Some did, using "abrogation" broadly (naskh for specification or context). Leading commentators rejected the claim of outright cancellation, and the law of war developed by the jurists kept treaties, asylum and non-combatant immunity.

prac.q: “9:5 says kill the polytheists wherever you find them. That's the final word.”
prac.a: Read 9:4-13: it excludes those who kept their treaties (9:4), commands asylum for any who ask (9:6), and explains the fight is against those who broke oaths and attacked first (9:13). 60:8 commands kindness and justice to non-combatants.

briefs.evs:
8:61 "If they incline to peace, then incline to it." Tabari rejects the view that it was abrogated by 9:5, saying there is no evidence for it in the Book or the Sunnah. Ibn Kathir and al-Zarkashi (al-Burhan 1/48) say the same.
Medinan peace verses. 2:190 ("do not transgress"), 8:61, 9:4 (honour treaties with those who kept them), 9:6 (grant asylum to any polytheist who asks), and 60:8 ("Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who did not fight you") are all Medinan.
9:5 in context. It concerns Arab polytheist tribes who broke their treaties (9:1-13: "will you not fight people who broke their oaths… and began against you first?", 9:13).
The cause of fighting. Muhammad Sa'id Ramadan al-Buti (al-Jihad fi al-Islam, p. 94) shows that the majority of schools hold the cause of fighting is aggression (hiraba), not disbelief. Sufyan al-Thawri: fighting the polytheists is not obligatory unless they begin it.
Rules of war: no killing women, children, the elderly or monks (Bukhari 3015; Abu Bakr's instructions). See Morality in the Bible & the Church.

briefs.title: Quick answers to smaller objections
briefs.thesis: Many objections disappear with a careful reading of the Arabic and the context.
briefs.sum: 6:101 denies begetting, 39:4 discusses adoption; makr is requiting plotters; salat from Allah is blessing; "all things" means all needed for guidance; Jesus is a sign of the Hour, not its knower.

prac.q: “Your Quran says Allah is a plotter and deceiver.”
prac.a: Makr from Allah means turning the plotters' schemes back on them (3:54 is about the plot against Jesus). The Bible says God sent a lying spirit to Ahab and sends "strong delusion" (2 Thess 2:11), far stronger wording.

briefs.evs:
"Allah has no consort, so how could He have a son" (6:101) vs "had Allah wanted to take a son, He could have chosen" (39:4). 6:101 denies begetting, which would require a partner. 39:4 concerns taking (ittakhadha, adopting), which is possible but which Allah did not do. No contradiction.
"Allah is the best of plotters" (3:54). Makr used of Allah means turning the plotters' schemes against them (Lane's Lexicon); the context is the plot against Jesus. The Bible goes further: God sends "a lying spirit" to entice Ahab (1 Kgs 22:20-23), and "God sends them a strong delusion so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thess 2:11).
"Allah prays on the Prophet" (33:56). Salat from Allah means blessing and mercy (al-Khalil, al-Jawhari, Lane, Hans Wehr): "He sends salat on you… to bring you out of darkness into light" (33:43). Hebrew uses one verb, barak, both for God blessing Abraham (Gen 12:2) and people blessing God. Arabic Gospel manuscripts render "pray for those who persecute you" (Matt 5:44) as sallu 'ala.
"An explanation of all things" (16:89). It means all things needed for guidance, as the context shows (16:64). The Torah is likewise called "an explanation of all things" (6:154; 7:145), and Jesus says the Spirit will guide "into all truth" (John 16:13), not into physics.
"First of the Muslims" (said of Muhammad, Moses and others) means first of their time or community (Tabari).

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: The experience of revelation was not epilepsy or possession
briefs.thesis: The physical signs that accompanied revelation (sweating, heaviness, the sound like a bell) do not match epilepsy, and they parallel what the Bible says happened to prophets like Daniel. The Prophet's ﷺ faculties were intact to the end, and Satan does not preach against Satan.
briefs.sum: Revelation came with sweat, heaviness and a sound "like a bell", followed by exact recitation. Watt rejects epilepsy since the Prophet's ﷺ faculties stayed sharp. Daniel, Jacob and Zechariah were overwhelmed by angels too.

obj.q: "Even if not epilepsy, it could be a psychological condition."
obj.a: A condition that produced, over 23 years, a text that its hostile audience couldn't match, a coherent law and a successful community, while its subject remained lucid and was trusted by everyone as al-Amin, is not like any known disorder.

prac.q: “Muhammad had seizures, foamed at the mouth and thought he was possessed.”
prac.a: The sources say he sweated, felt heaviness and heard a sound "like a bell", and then recited exact verses. Watt rejects epilepsy because it degrades the mind, while his remained sharp. Daniel fell on his face breathless before an angel; no one calls him epileptic.

briefs.evs:
What happened. Aisha: "I saw him receiving revelation on a very cold day, and when it ended his forehead was dripping with sweat" (Bukhari 2). His face reddened and he breathed heavily (Bukhari 4985). The Quran calls it "a weighty word" (73:5). He said it sometimes came "like the ringing of a bell" (Bukhari 2), a simile for its intensity, and sometimes the angel came in the form of a man, which was easier.
Not epilepsy. W. Montgomery Watt (Muhammad at Mecca, p. 57) rejects the epilepsy theory: epilepsy causes degeneration, while Muhammad kept full mental vigour to the end; such physical accompaniments neither prove nor disprove revelation.
Ibn Khaldun explains the strain as the prophetic soul being lifted momentarily from human to angelic perception.
Biblical parallels. Daniel, seeing the angel: "no strength was left in me… I fell into a deep sleep on my face… I have no strength, and no breath is left in me" (Dan 10:8-17). Jacob was wrestled and his hip dislocated (Gen 32:24-25); Zechariah was terrified and struck mute (Luke 1:12, 20).
The first revelation. Gabriel pressed him at Hira (Bukhari 3), as angels overwhelmed Daniel. Later reports say Gabriel reassured him: "O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of Allah" (al-Bidaya 3/21), and further comfort followed (Surah al-Duha; Bukhari 1125).
Satan's work? Abu Lahab's wife taunted that his "devil" had left him. Jesus too was accused

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: Allah is not Hubal or a moon god
briefs.thesis: Hubal was a specific imported idol whom the Prophet ﷺ opposed by name; the moon-god theory has no evidence; and Allah is the name Arab Christians and Jews used for the God of Abraham.
briefs.sum: Hubal was an imported red-agate idol the Prophet ﷺ opposed by name at Uhud (Bukhari 3039). The moon-god theory has no evidence, the crescent is an Ottoman symbol, and Arab Christians call God Allah.

obj.q: "The pagan Meccans worshipped 'Allah' too, so Islam continued paganism."
obj.a: The Meccans knew Allah as the supreme Creator (29:61) but worshipped idols as intercessors; Islam's message was to worship Him alone. That is restoration of Abraham's monotheism, not paganism.

prac.q: “Allah was the moon god of pre-Islamic Arabia.”
prac.a: There's no inscription or text saying so; it's a modern invention. At Uhud the pagans cried "Exalted be Hubal" and the Prophet answered "Allah is higher". Arab Christians call God "Allah" in their Bibles today.

briefs.evs:
Hubal. Ibn al-Kalbi's Book of Idols describes Hubal as a statue of red agate with a broken hand replaced in gold, brought to Mecca by 'Amr ibn Luhayy. At Uhud the contrast was explicit (Bukhari 3039). Orientalists such as Margoliouth and F.E. Peters treat Hubal and Allah as distinct. "Hubal" is not "Baal" either: the Arabic ba'l has an 'ayn that Hubal lacks.
No moon god. The idea comes from 20th-century writers relying on a misreading of South Arabian religion; the nature of the Sabaean god Almaqah is debated and the claim that he was a moon god is not secure. The crescent became a general emblem of Islam only in late Ottoman and modern times. A statue from Hazor sometimes cited is not identified as a moon god.
Arab Christians and Jews used "Allah". Arabic Bibles use Allah for God, and the word is the Arabic cognate of Elah/Eloah. An early inscription quoting Surah al-Ikhlas ("Say: He is Allah, One… He neither begets nor is begotten") is dated 29 AH.
Turnabout. God says in Hosea 2:16 that Israel will "no longer call Me 'Baali'", which shows YHWH had been called by the title used for Baal.

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: The Kaaba and Hajj restore Abraham's worship
briefs.thesis: The Kaaba was built by Abraham and Ishmael for the one God; pagans corrupted the rites (naked circumambulation, idols); Islam restored them. The Bible itself describes pilgrimage-feasts and circling God's altar.
briefs.sum: Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba; the pagans added idols and naked rites, which Islam removed. The Hebrew hag (Exod 5:1) is cognate with hajj, and Psalm 26:6 describes circling the altar. Umar said the Black Stone neither harms nor benefits.

obj.q: "Kissing a stone is idolatry."
obj.a: Idolatry is worshipping something besides God. Umar's statement shows the opposite intention. Aquinas assigned the cross the worship due to God (latria); Islam never assigns the stone any worship.

prac.q: “The Kaaba, the Black Stone and circumambulation all come from pre-Islamic paganism.”
prac.a: The rites are older than paganism: Abraham and Ishmael built the House (2:127), and pagans later corrupted it with idols, which the Prophet ﷺ destroyed. Exodus 5:1 uses hag, the cognate of hajj, and Psalm 26:6 describes circling God's altar.

briefs.evs:
Abraham and Ishmael. "When Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of the House" (2:127). Hagar, Ishmael and Zamzam (Bukhari 3364).
Pagan corruption removed. The Quraysh performed the circuit naked and filled the Kaaba with 360 idols; the Prophet ﷺ destroyed the idols and banned naked circumambulation.
The Hebrew hag. In Exodus 5:1 Moses asks Pharaoh: "Let My people go, that they may hold a feast (yahoggu) to Me in the wilderness." The root h-g-g means to keep a pilgrim-feast and, according to the Brown-Driver-Briggs lexicon, is related to Arabic hajj; many translations say "make a pilgrimage".
Circling. "I will go around (asobbah) Your altar, O LORD" (Ps 26:6). Israel circled Jericho seven times at God's command (Josh 6).
Zamzam in Jewish commentary? Ibn Ezra says the well of Hagar (Gen 21:19) was known in his time by a name like "Zemum"; John Gill took this to be Zamzam. Ptolemy lists a place 'Macoraba', which some have identified with Mecca (the identification is disputed).
Stones. Umar said to the Black Stone: "I know you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits; had I not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not kiss you" (Bukhari 1597). Jacob anointed a stone pillar as "God's house" (Gen 28:18-22).

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: The "Satanic verses" story is not authentic
briefs.thesis: The story that the Prophet ﷺ praised the pagan goddesses (the gharaniq incident) comes only through broken chains, and it was rejected by the major scholars of hadith and tafsir.
briefs.sum: Every chain of the gharaniq story is broken; Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, Qadi 'Iyad, Ibn Hazm and al-Albani rejected it; and Surah al-Najm itself condemns the goddesses as "nothing but names" (53:23).

obj.q: "Early historians like Tabari and Ibn Sa'd record it, so it must be true."
obj.a: Tabari recorded many reports with their chains, explicitly warning that the responsibility lies with the narrators. A report's appearance in a collection is not a verdict on its authenticity.

prac.q: “Your own historians record that Muhammad praised the pagan goddesses.”
prac.a: They record a story whose every chain is broken, and the leading hadith scholars rejected it. The same surah calls the goddesses "nothing but names". It fails the standard Muslims use for every report.

briefs.evs:
The chains. All versions are mursal or come through weak narrators; none reaches a Companion who witnessed the event. Al-Albani's treatise Nasb al-Majaniq li-Nasf Qissat al-Gharaniq goes through every chain and shows each one fails.
The scholars. Ibn Kathir says all its chains are mursal and he has not seen it with a connected sound chain. It was rejected by al-Baghawi, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qadi 'Iyad, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Hazm. Al-Razi reports that Ibn Khuzayma called it a fabrication of heretics (zanadiqa).
The Quran's own context. The surah in question (al-Najm) condemns the goddesses outright: "they are nothing but names you have named" (53:23). The Prophet ﷺ is protected from adding to revelation (69:44-47).
Even if one took the story seriously, 22:52 says Satan's insertions are cancelled by Allah, which means the Quran was corrected and preserved, not corrupted.

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: Zaynab and Zayd
briefs.thesis: The Prophet's ﷺ marriage to Zaynab after her divorce from Zayd was commanded to end the pre-Islamic custom of treating adopted sons as blood sons. The Prophet had urged Zayd to keep his wife, and Zaynab was his own cousin whom he could have married years earlier.
briefs.sum: Zaynab was the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, whom he married to Zayd; he urged Zayd to keep her (33:37); the later marriage abolished the adoption taboo (33:4-5, 37). Compare David and Bathsheba.

prac.q: “Muhammad desired his adopted son's wife and got a revelation to marry her.”
prac.a: She was his cousin, whom he himself married to Zayd; he told Zayd to keep her (33:37); and the marriage abolished a custom the Quran had already ended (33:4-5). If he had wanted her, he could have married her before she married Zayd.

briefs.evs:
Background. Zayd ibn Haritha chose to stay with the Prophet ﷺ rather than return to his own father, and was adopted under pre-Islamic custom. The Prophet ﷺ married him to Zaynab bint Jahsh, a noble woman of Quraysh and the Prophet's own cousin, whom he had known all her life.
He urged the marriage to continue. "You said to the one whom Allah had favoured and you had favoured: keep your wife and fear Allah" (33:37). Zayd divorced her by his own choice.
The purpose. "So that there may be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons" (33:37). The Quran had already declared adopted sons are not sons by blood: "call them by their fathers' names" (33:4-5).
Double standard. David took Bathsheba and arranged her husband's death (2 Sam 11), and the NT still calls him a prophet (Acts 2:30).

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: Islam is not racist
briefs.thesis: Reports used to show racism ("Satan as a black man", the Zutt) are misread; Arabic colour terms describe complexion among Arabs; and the Prophet ﷺ explicitly condemned racial superiority.
briefs.sum: The "Satan" reports refer to an Arab hypocrite; aswad described Arab complexions; Moses was compared to the Zutt; and the Prophet ﷺ declared no superiority of white over black except by piety (49:13; the Farewell Sermon).

prac.q: “Your hadith say Satan is a black man.”
prac.a: The "Satan" in that report was Nabtal, an Arab hypocrite, and aswad described complexion among Arabs. The Prophet ﷺ compared Moses to the dark-skinned Zutt and said there is no superiority of white over black. It's Athanasius who describes the devil as a black boy.

briefs.evs:
Nabtal ibn al-Harith, whom the Prophet ﷺ described as having a devil's look, was an Arab hypocrite of Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf (Tabari on 9:61). It was a comment on his hypocrisy, like Jesus' "Get behind me, Satan" to Peter.
Dhu al-Thudayya was a Kharijite figure, identified in some sources as Hurqus ibn Zuhayr (the identification is disputed). He was an Arab.
Colour words. Arabs called each other aswad (dark) and abyad (fair) by complexion; the Prophet ﷺ himself is described as abyad. (Akande, Illuminating the Darkness.)
The Zutt. The Prophet ﷺ described Moses as "tall, as if he were one of the men of the Zutt" (Bukhari 3438), a dark-skinned people from Sind. Comparing a prophet to them is the opposite of contempt.
Teaching. The Farewell Sermon: "No Arab has superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor white over black, nor black over white, except by piety" (Ahmad). Of Bilal and Salman: "If you angered them, you angered your Lord" (Muslim 2504). "The most noble of you in Allah's sight is the most righteous" (49:13).
Church fathers. Athanasius' Life of Antony describes the devil appearing as a black boy, and Palladius describes a demon as an Ethiopian girl.

briefs.sec: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
briefs.title: Other objections about the Prophet ﷺ
briefs.thesis: Several further charges collapse when the sources are read in full.
briefs.sum: The idol-meat report has a version where both refused it, before revelation; the expulsion order concerned the Hijaz; the "jinn rode him" report is weak and means crowding; and Nawawi holds all children, including polytheists', are in Paradise.

prac.q: “Muhammad expelled all Jews and Christians from Arabia.”
prac.a: The order concerned the Hijaz after Khaybar's hostility, Jews stayed under treaty during his life, and he died with his armour pawned to a Jewish merchant (Bukhari 2916). Islam commands kindness to peaceful non-Muslims (60:8).

briefs.evs:
"He worshipped idols before Islam." The report about meat offered to Zayd ibn 'Amr (Bukhari 3826; 5499) comes in another version in which both refused it, and in any case it was before revelation. The Bible says Solomon built shrines to idols during his prophethood (1 Kgs 11:4-9).
"Expel the Jews and Christians from Arabia" (Muslim 1767). It concerns the Hijaz and its holy sites, after the hostilities at Khaybar. Jews remained under treaty (Muslim 1551) until Umar relocated them, and the Prophet ﷺ died with his armour pawned to a Jew for barley (Bukhari 2916). 60:8 commands kindness to peaceful non-Muslims.
"The jinn rode him" (Musnad Ahmad 3788). The chain is weak: 'Amr al-Bikali is not known to have heard from Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Mas'ud himself said, "I was not with the Prophet on the Night of the Jinn" (Muslim 450). Yarkabun in Arabic idiom means crowding closely, as in 72:19, where the jinn "almost became a mass around him" (libadan) to hear the Quran.
"Babies in Hell" (Musnad Ahmad: the girl buried alive and the one who buried her are in the Fire). Ibn 'Abd al-Barr explains it as an answer about a specific case. Al-Nawawi reports consensus that Muslim children are in Paradise, and says the verified view is that the children of polytheists are too, citing the Prophet's dream of Abraham surrounded by children "including the children of the polytheists" (Bukhari 7047) and 17:

briefs.title: Hadith criticism is rigorous, even about the Sahih collections
briefs.thesis: Muslim scholars criticised and rejected weak reports, including a narration in Sahih Muslim, by examining both chains and content. That honesty is why a critic cannot treat every report as "what Islam teaches".
briefs.sum: Bukhari traced Muslim 2789 to Ka'b al-Ahbar, not the Prophet; Ibn Taymiyya agreed. Hadith critics examined chains, memory decline and content, even in the Sahihs, so critics can't treat every report as Islam.

obj.q: "Muslims just call any hadith they don't like weak."
obj.a: The gradings are centuries old, made by scholars who had no stake in modern debates, using fixed criteria that apply equally to reports Muslims like.

prac.q: “Your own Sahih Muslim says creation took seven days, contradicting the Quran.”
prac.a: Bukhari himself identified that narration as Ka'b al-Ahbar's saying, not the Prophet's, and Ibn Taymiyya agreed. Muslim scholars caught the error inside their own most respected books, which shows the system works.

briefs.evs:
Muslim 2789 ("Allah created the soil on Saturday…", seven days of creation). Bukhari, in al-Tarikh al-Kabir, identified it as a saying of Ka'b al-Ahbar (a convert from Judaism), not the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Taymiyya (Majmu' 17/235) and 'Ali al-Qari agreed. It contradicts the Quran's six days. Scholars flagged a defect in a narration inside Sahih Muslim, the second most respected collection.
The methods. Narrators were judged on memory and honesty; chains were checked for breaks; a narrator's memory decline (ikhtilat) dates were recorded so that late hearing could be rejected; and content (matn) was checked against the Quran and established Sunnah.
Western scholarship. Harald Motzki's study of the Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq argued that much of the material can be traced to the late first or early second Islamic century (see Preservation of the Hadith).

briefs.title: Abu Hurayra's large number of hadith
briefs.thesis: Abu Hurayra narrated many hadith because he devoted himself to the Prophet's ﷺ company and teaching, the Prophet prayed for his memory, and other young Companions also narrated thousands.
briefs.sum: Abu Hurayra stayed constantly with the Prophet ﷺ, had his memory blessed, and taught for decades. Ibn Umar (2,600) and Ibn Abbas (1,700) also narrated thousands, and 5,300 counts chains, not distinct reports.

prac.q: “Abu Hurayra was with the Prophet for only three years but narrated more than anyone, so he must have invented hadith.”
prac.a: He spent those years at the Prophet's side full-time (Bukhari 118), the Prophet prayed for his memory (Bukhari 119), and he taught for decades after. Ibn Abbas was a child and still narrated 1,700. The 5,300 counts chains, not distinct reports.

briefs.evs:
Devotion. Abu Hurayra said: "My brothers among the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their property, while I stayed with the Messenger of Allah to fill my stomach" (Bukhari 118). He was one of the People of the Suffa who lived at the mosque.
The prayer for memory. He spread his cloak, the Prophet ﷺ spoke, and he never forgot afterward (Bukhari 119).
Others. Ibn Umar has about 2,600 narrations and Ibn Abbas, who was only nine to fourteen when the Prophet died, about 1,700. Jonathan Brown (Hadith, pp. 18-19) notes that junior Companions who lived long and taught widely narrated the most.
Counting. The 5,300 figure counts every chain separately; the number of distinct reports is far smaller.

briefs.title: The "assassinations" attributed to the Prophet ﷺ
briefs.thesis: The killings critics cite are either fabricated (Asma bint Marwan), weakly transmitted and contradicting known law (Umm Qirfa), or were punishments for murder and acts of war (Abu 'Afak, Miqyas, al-Huwayrith), not for mere words or poetry.
briefs.sum: Asma bint Marwan's story is fabricated (al-Albani); Umm Qirfa's is weak and contradicts the ban on killing women; Abu 'Afak, Miqyas and al-Huwayrith were combatants or murderers. The Prophet ﷺ never took personal revenge.

prac.q: “Muhammad had poets killed for mocking him.”
prac.a: The Asma bint Marwan story is fabricated by a known liar; Abu 'Afak was inciting war; Miqyas was a murderer. Aisha said he never took revenge for himself, and he pardoned all of Mecca.

briefs.evs:
Asma bint Marwan. The story comes through Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Lakhmi, whom Bukhari, Ibn Ma'in and al-Daraqutni called a liar; al-Albani graded it fabricated (mawdu').
Umm Qirfa. Her brutal killing is reported through an interrupted chain with weak narrators (Ibn Humayd, Salama). Al-Dhahabi calls it munkar. It contradicts the Prophet's explicit bans on mutilation and on killing women.
Abu 'Afak. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Kathir and al-Zurqani describe him as inciting war against the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims; the reports are weak and describe him as composing verses against the Prophet; defenders read this as incitement to war
Miqyas ibn Subaba killed the Ansari who had paid him blood money for his brother, then apostatised and fled. His execution was retaliation (qisas) for murder.
Al-Huwayrith attacked the Prophet's daughters as they fled Mecca and fought the Muslims.
The principle. Aisha: "The Messenger of Allah never took revenge for himself" (Bukhari 3560). At the conquest of Mecca he pardoned almost everyone who had persecuted him for 20 years.

briefs.title: "The Prophet ﷺ attempted suicide"
briefs.thesis: The passage in Bukhari 6982 about the Prophet ﷺ going to throw himself from a mountain is an unconnected addition by al-Zuhri ("it reached us that…"), not part of Aisha's connected narration.
briefs.sum: The mountain passage in Bukhari 6982 is al-Zuhri's unconnected "it reached us" (balaghat), not part of Aisha's connected narration in Bukhari 3.

prac.q: “Sahih Bukhari says Muhammad tried to kill himself, so he doubted his prophethood.”
prac.a: The passage is al-Zuhri's "it reached us", without a chain, attached to Aisha's narration. Aisha's own connected report in Bukhari 3 doesn't contain it. Unchained hearsay isn't a hadith.

briefs.evs:
In Bukhari 6982, after Aisha's account of the first revelation and the pause in revelation, the text continues "and the Prophet ﷺ was so grieved, as it reached us, that he went several times to throw himself from the mountain tops…". Ibn Hajar notes this is among al-Zuhri's balaghat, unconnected reports.
Bukhari includes it inside a longer narration but does not present it as a sound hadith in its own right; the authentic version of the first revelation (Bukhari 3; 4953) does not contain it.
Even in the report, Gabriel appears each time and reassures him, and he does not harm himself.

briefs.title: Other hadith objections answered
briefs.thesis: Most remaining objections come from weak reports, reports not from the Prophet ﷺ, or misreadings.
briefs.sum: Buda'ah has an unknown narrator and states a purity rule; the Black Stone report is weak; Ibn Abbas condemned 'Ali's burning with the Prophet's ban; the "ransom" hadith is about places in Hell; the monkey story is a Successor's observation; and "forgive them" was said at Uhud or by Noah, not on a cross.

prac.q: “Islam says water polluted by menstrual cloths and dog flesh is pure (the well of Buda'ah).”
prac.a: The narrator is unknown, the Companions didn't throw filth in (rain washed it from the ground, per al-Khattabi), and the rule is that water becomes impure when its smell, colour or taste changes. Islam forbids even urinating in standing water.

briefs.evs:
The well of Buda'ah (Abu Dawud 67). The hadith is graded sahih or hasan (Ahmad, Tirmidhi, al-Albani) and states a purity rule, so the answer is to explain it. The principle in the hadith is that water stays pure unless its smell, colour or taste changes. Al-Khattabi explains that the Companions never threw filth in; rain washed refuse into the well from the surrounding ground. Islam forbids urinating in standing water.
"The Black Stone expiates sins" (Tirmidhi). The Black Stone report (Tirmidhi 959) is graded hasan by Tirmidhi and sahih by al-Albani, so the answer is to explain it as expiation through obedience, not worship of the stone.
'Ali burning heretics. Reports differ (some say he burned their house or their corpses after execution). Ibn Abbas condemned it, quoting the Prophet's ﷺ ban: "Do not punish with Allah's punishment [fire]" (Bukhari 3017). At most it was 'Ali's error, corrected by a Companion with the Prophet's ruling.
"Allah will give each Muslim a Jew or Christian as ransom from Hell" (Muslim 2767). Every person has a place in Paradise and a place in Hell; the believer's place in Hell goes to the disbeliever who earned it. Al-Nawawi explains it as ransom (fida'), not transferring sins.
"If you did not sin, Allah would replace you with people who sin and seek forgiveness" (Muslim 2749). It is about Allah's love of repentance, not encouraging sin. Compare Luke 15

briefs.title: Women's intellect, testimony and status
briefs.thesis: The hadith about women's "deficiency in intellect and religion" refers to reduced legal burdens, was said lightly in praise of women's persuasive power, and Islamic law weighs testimony by reliability, not sex. Women were among Islam's leading scholars.
briefs.sum: The "deficiency" hadith refers to two legal concessions and was said in light praise; naqs means reduction (13:41); the two-witness rule is for contracts, with a stated practical reason; and Aisha and over a hundred women narrators shaped Islamic scholarship.

obj.q: "Two women for one man still says women are less reliable."
obj.a: The verse gives a practical reason (one may remind the other), applies only to financial contracts, and the scholars made reliability, not sex, the criterion. In matters where women had expertise, their testimony alone was accepted.

prac.q: “Islam says women are deficient in intelligence.”
prac.a: The Prophet ﷺ explained exactly what he meant: two legal concessions, the commercial testimony rule and exemption from prayer during menses. He said it while praising women's power to sway a resolute man. Aisha was the person the Companions consulted on their hardest questions.

briefs.evs:
The text. The Prophet ﷺ told a group of women: "I have not seen anyone deficient in intellect and religion more able to take away the reason of a resolute man than one of you." When a woman asked what the deficiency was, he explained: the testimony of two women in place of one man (2:282), and not praying or fasting during menstruation. Both are legal concessions. The tone is gentle teasing, and one of the women who questioned him is described as "highly intelligent" (jazla, Muslim 79).
Tap to enlargeSahih al-Bukhari 1462: the hadith on women's "deficiency" in its full context
"Naqs" means reduction. The Quran uses the same root for "reducing the land from its borders" (13:41); it means a smaller share, not a defect.
The two-woman rule is limited to commercial contracts, and the verse gives the reason: "so that if one errs, the other can remind her" (2:282), reflecting women's limited involvement in trade at the time. Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim held that the purpose is reliability, so a more credible woman's testimony can outweigh a man's, and in many matters a woman's testimony alone is accepted.
Women scholars. The Companions brought their hardest questions to Aisha (Tirmidhi 3883). Al-Dhahabi lists over a hundred women hadith narrators, and he said no woman was ever accused of lying in hadith.
Christian comparison. Paul: "women should keep silent in the churches… if they

briefs.title: 4:34 and domestic violence
briefs.thesis: 4:34 allows, as a last resort after admonition and separation, a light, non-injurious strike (ghayr mubarrih) that may not injure, break skin or leave a mark. The Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman, condemned men who did, and the jurists allowed a wife to divorce and claim redress if harmed. The hadith "a man will not be asked why he beat his wife" is weak.
briefs.sum: 4:34's strike is a last resort, limited to a symbolic tap with a siwak (Ibn Abbas), never to cause harm. The Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman, condemned those who did, and let a struck wife leave; the "don't ask why he beat her" hadith is weak.

obj.q: "Any striking is abuse."
obj.a: The verse addressed a society where husbands beat wives freely; it restricted that to a last-resort symbolic gesture that the Prophet ﷺ himself never used and scholars discouraged. Abuse, causing pain or injury, is forbidden and punishable in Islamic law.

obj.q: "The Prophet ﷺ struck Aisha" (Muslim 974, lahadani).
obj.a: Lahada means a push or nudge on the chest (Lisan al-'Arab; al-Nawawi), a gesture he used with Ubayy ibn Ka'b and others to dispel doubt or anxiety. It was a push on the chest, not a blow with the hand, though Aisha says it hurt her. She also reported that he never struck a woman (Muslim 2328).

obj.q: "Tabari said a husband can tie his wife up."
obj.a: Tabari offered that reading of hajr (separation), and later scholars rejected it: al-Zamakhshari called it "the interpretation of the ignorant", and al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya rejected it too.

prac.q: “The Quran tells men to beat their wives.”
prac.a: The Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman (Muslim 2328), called men who did "not the best of you" (Abu Dawud 2146), and let a struck wife divorce (Abu Dawud 2228). The jurists limited it to a symbolic touch with a tooth-stick, leaving no mark, as a last resort, with judges punishing abusers.

briefs.evs:
The Prophet's practice. "The Messenger of Allah never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant" (Muslim 2328).
His condemnation. When many women came complaining that their husbands beat them, he said: "These are not the best of you" (Abu Dawud 2146). In the Farewell Sermon: "Treat women well; they are your partners."
A wife's redress. When Thabit ibn Qays struck his wife Habiba bint Sahl, the Prophet ﷺ allowed her to leave the marriage (Abu Dawud 2228).
The limit. Ibn Abbas explained the strike as with a siwak (a small tooth-stick) or similar; al-Hasan al-Basri said "not leaving a mark". Al-Shafi'i: leaving it is better (al-Umm). Al-Buhuti: at most a rolled handkerchief, never a whip or stick.
The jurists' protections. If a husband harms her, she can seek divorce and retribution (al-Dardir, al-Sharh al-Kabir); the judge punishes the abusive husband (al-Kasani, Bada'i'); Ibn 'Abidin: he may not bruise or break skin; Ibn Qudama provides arbitration (4:35).
The weak hadith. "A man will not be asked why he beat his wife" (Abu Dawud 2147; Ibn Majah 1986) comes through the unknown narrator 'Abd al-Rahman al-Musli; al-Albani and al-Dhahabi grade it weak.
Christian comparison. Basil of Caesarea advised a wife to endure her husband's abuse rather than separate.

briefs.title: Polygyny: limited, conditioned and discouraged
briefs.thesis: Islam took unlimited polygamy and limited it to four, conditioned on justice, and the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools recommended keeping to one. A wife may stipulate in her contract that her husband take no second wife.
briefs.sum: The Quran limited unlimited polygamy to four, conditioned on justice (4:3); major scholars recommended one; and a wife can stipulate no second wife. The Bible sets no limit.

prac.q: “Polygamy is degrading to women.”
prac.a: Islam inherited unlimited polygamy and capped it at four with a condition of justice; scholars recommended one; a wife can contractually forbid a second wife. The Bible has no cap at all, and Luther couldn't forbid it.

briefs.evs:
The limit. A man who became Muslim with eight wives was told to keep four (Abu Dawud 2241).
The condition. "Marry those that please you, two, three or four; but if you fear you will not be just, then one" (4:3). "A man who has two wives and favours one will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side leaning" (Abu Dawud 2133).
Recommended one. Al-Shafi'i, Ibn Qudama, al-Buhuti, al-Nawawi and al-Mawardi recommend keeping to one wife.
Tap to enlargeClassical fiqh: al-Shafi'i preferred limiting oneself to one wife (4:3)
The wife's right. Imam Ahmad's school allows a wife to stipulate in the marriage contract that her husband will take no other wife, and the stipulation is binding.
The Prophet's marriages were mostly to widows and for social or political reasons: his marriage to Juwayriya led the Companions to free a hundred families of her tribe.
The Bible has no limit: Solomon had 700 wives (1 Kgs 11:3), and God "gave" David Saul's wives (2 Sam 12:8). See Morality in the Bible & the Church.

briefs.title: Slavery: regulated toward abolition
briefs.thesis: Islam inherited a world in which slavery was universal. It closed most routes into slavery, opened many routes out, made freeing slaves an act of worship and expiation, punished abuse by freeing the slave, and forbade forcing slave women into prostitution (24:33), with some jurists objecting to compelled intercourse.
briefs.sum: Islam banned enslaving free people, encouraged freeing captives, required freedom contracts (24:33), made freeing slaves the expiation for many sins, freed a struck slave (Muslim 1657), and forbade forcing a slave woman. The Bible lets a master beat a slave "because he is his money".

obj.q: "Why not abolish it outright?"
obj.a: No society abolished slavery at scale until the late 18th and 19th centuries. Islam did what was possible in the 7th century: close the main sources, open many exits, and tie freeing slaves to worship. The direction was toward freedom.

prac.q: “Islam allowed sex slavery.”
prac.a: Al-Shafi'i ruled no one may be forced into intercourse; Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim said forcing a slave woman frees her; striking a slave required freeing him (Muslim 1657). Compare Exodus 21:21: a master who beats his slave goes unpunished if the slave survives "because he is his money".

briefs.evs:
Routes in closed. Selling a free person is a major sin (Bukhari 2227). Captives may be freed as a favour or for ransom (47:4); at Badr the ransom for some literate captives was teaching Muslims to read. At the conquest of Mecca he said: "Go, you are free." Ibn Qudama: the elderly, sick, blind and monks may not be killed.
Routes out. Slaves who ask for a contract of freedom must be granted one (24:33). Zakat funds freeing slaves (9:60). Freeing a slave is the expiation for manslaughter (4:92), breaking oaths (5:89), and other sins, and the "steep path" to righteousness (90:13).
Protection. "Whoever slaps or beats his slave, his expiation is to free him" (Muslim 1657). When Abu Mas'ud struck his slave, the Prophet ﷺ said "Allah has more power over you than you have over him", and he freed him (Muslim 1659). "Feed them from what you eat and clothe them from what you wear" (Bukhari 30). Among the Prophet's last words: "the prayer, and those your right hands possess."
No forced intercourse. Al-Shafi'i: "no one can be compelled to it" (al-Umm). Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim held that forcing a slave woman into intercourse is a form of mutilation that frees her; al-Halimi said if she dislikes his touch he must not touch her without her permission and must sell her if she wishes. Jonathan Brown's Slavery and Islam discusses these rulings.
The Bible permits buying slaves from the natio

briefs.title: Non-Muslims under Islamic rule
briefs.thesis: Jews and Christians under Islam were protected, kept their courts and churches, and often welcomed Muslim rule over Byzantine persecution. Historians such as Mark Cohen find that Jews generally fared better under Islam than under medieval Christendom, though it was far from an interfaith utopia.
briefs.sum: A 7th-century patriarch said the Arabs honoured his priests; 'Amr restored the Coptic Pope; Abu 'Ubayda returned the jizya to Hims; Umar refused to pray in the Holy Sepulchre; and Mark Cohen finds Jews far safer under Islam than under Christendom.

prac.q: “Non-Muslims under Islam were second-class citizens paying a humiliating tax.”
prac.a: Jizya replaced military service and zakat; Christians who served in the army were exempt, and Abu 'Ubayda returned it when he couldn't protect them. Isho'yahb III, a patriarch, said the Arabs honoured his priests. Jews fled to Muslim lands from Christian Spain.

briefs.evs:
Christian testimony. Isho'yahb III, patriarch of the Church of the East in the 7th century: the Arabs "do not persecute the Christian religion; on the contrary they favour it, honour our priests and the saints of the Lord and confer benefits on churches and monasteries."
Tap to enlargeIsho'yahb III (Church of the East, 7th c.): the Arabs "are not enemies to Christianity… they honour our priests"
Relief from Byzantium. Michael the Syrian, writing in the 12th century, recorded that God sent the sons of Ishmael to free Christians from the Romans; Christoph Baumer describes Syriac Christians seeing Arab rule as relief from Byzantine persecution.
Tap to enlargeChristoph Baumer, The Church of the East: Syriac Christians saw Arab rule as relief from Byzantium
Egypt. 'Amr ibn al-'As restored the Coptic Pope Benjamin, who had been hiding from the Byzantines for 13 years, and returned the churches (History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria; Coptic Synaxarium).
Tap to enlargeCoptic Synaxarium: 'Amr returned Pope Benjamin after 13 years in hiding and restored the churches
Hims. When Abu 'Ubayda had to withdraw from Hims before the Byzantine army, he returned the jizya to its Christians because he could no longer protect them; they prayed for the Muslims' return (al-Baladhuri; T.W. Arnold, The Preaching of Islam).
Jerusalem. Umar entered Jerusalem peacefully in 637 and declined to pray in the

briefs.title: Banu Qurayza
briefs.thesis: The Banu Qurayza broke their treaty and sided with the besieging army during the Battle of the Trench. Their fate was decided by an arbiter they chose themselves, in a way that matches Deuteronomy 20:12-14, though no early source says Sa'd cited it, and the men were executed, including adolescents judged to have reached puberty, and one woman is reported killed.
briefs.sum: Qurayza betrayed their pact during the Trench siege, chose their ally Sa'd ibn Mu'adh as judge, and his ruling followed Deuteronomy 20:12-14, sparing women and children. Some historians question the reported numbers.

prac.q: “Muhammad massacred hundreds of Jews.”
prac.a: Qurayza betrayed a defensive pact during a siege that could have wiped out Medina. They chose their own ally as judge, and he applied their own Torah's law of war (Deut 20:12-14), sparing women and children. Treason in war was capital in every legal system of the time.

briefs.evs:
The treaty and the betrayal. The Constitution of Medina bound the Jewish tribes to defend the city. During the siege of the Trench (5 AH), when 10,000 Confederates surrounded Medina, Qurayza opened negotiations with the enemy, threatening the Muslims from behind.
Their own arbiter. After the siege, Qurayza agreed to the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh of the Aws, their old ally.
Their own law. Sa'd's ruling, that the fighting men be killed and the rest taken captive, matches Deuteronomy 20:12-14 for a city that makes war: "you shall put all its males to the sword, but the women and the little ones… you shall take as plunder." Freedman and McClymond (The Rivers of Paradise) note the parallel. The ruling is milder than Deuteronomy 20:16 ("save alive nothing that breathes").
Numbers. Reported figures vary widely; historians such as W.N. Arafat and Barakat Ahmad have questioned the large numbers in later sources.

briefs.title: Hijab and modesty
briefs.thesis: The hijab is a command to cover the head and body in public, shared with Jewish and Christian tradition, and its stated purpose is dignity and protection from harassment.
briefs.sum: Khimar is a head covering, extended over the chest (24:31); 33:59 says it's for recognition and protection. Rebekah, Paul, Clement, Jerome and Aquinas all endorsed veiling.

prac.q: “The Quran never commands a headscarf; it only says cover your chest.”
prac.a: The word used is khimar, which by definition is a head covering; the verse tells women to extend it over their chests. The command presupposes the head is covered.

briefs.evs:
The words. Khimar is "that with which a woman covers her head" (Lisan al-'Arab, root kh-m-r). "Let them draw their head-coverings over their chests" (24:31). "Tell your wives, daughters and the believing women to draw their outer garments over themselves; that is more suitable so they will be recognised and not harassed" (33:59).
Earlier traditions. Rebekah covered herself with her veil on meeting Isaac (Gen 24:65); Paul required head covering (1 Cor 11:5-6); Clement of Alexandria said women should go out "with face covered"; Jerome advised covering all but the eyes; Aquinas held a married woman should not uncover her hair. Ancient Greek women of status were also depicted veiled.
Studies. Research has associated wearing the hijab with less self-objectification and better body image (Swami et al.).

briefs.title: The Prophet ﷺ did not use revelation for personal gain
briefs.thesis: Critics say revelations conveniently served the Prophet ﷺ. His lifestyle shows the opposite: he lived in poverty while ruling Arabia, forbade charity to his own family, and the Quran rebuked him.
briefs.sum: He slept on a reed mat, died with his armour pawned, barred his family from zakat, prayed until his feet swelled, and recited rebukes of himself. "Convenient revelations" doesn't fit the record.

prac.q: “Whenever Muhammad wanted something, a verse came down to allow it.”
prac.a: He lived on a reed mat, died in debt to a Jewish merchant, barred his own family from zakat, and recited verses rebuking himself (80:1-2; 9:43). A man inventing revelation for gain would not choose that life.

briefs.evs:
Poverty. Umar wept seeing the marks of the reed mat on the Prophet's side while kings slept on silk (Ibn Majah 4153). He said he would not want gold the size of Mount Uhud to remain with him more than three days (Bukhari 6444). He died with his armour pawned for barley (Bukhari 2916).
Worship. He prayed at night until his feet swelled, saying "Should I not be a grateful servant?" (Bukhari 4836).
His family barred from charity. Zakat may not be given to the Prophet's family (Muslim 1072).
Self-rebuke. "He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him" (80:1-2); "Allah pardon you, why did you give them leave?" (9:43); "it is not for a prophet to take captives…" (8:67).
Refused worldly offers. The Quraysh offered him kingship, wealth and the most beautiful women to stop preaching; he refused.

briefs.sec: Aisha's age, 65:4 and the end of Surah at-Tawbah
briefs.title: The authentic reports put Aisha's age at marriage at nine
briefs.thesis: The age of six at the contract and nine at consummation is narrated through several independent chains and was agreed upon by classical scholars. The "she was 19" arguments rely on weak or misread reports.
briefs.sum: Six at contract and nine at consummation come through several chains (Bukhari 5133; Muslim 1422 without Hisham), with classical consensus. The "19" arguments use a chainless report about Asma and misread Uhud.

obj.q: "Why not accept the 19 theory? It solves the problem."
obj.a: Because it is false history, and an apologetic built on weak evidence collapses as soon as an informed opponent checks it. The strong answer is the context argument below.

prac.q: “Many Muslims say Aisha was really 19, so even Muslims are embarrassed.”
prac.a: Some do, but the evidence for six and nine comes through several independent chains, and classical scholars reported no disagreement. The real question is whether the marriage was wrong in its context, and the evidence says it was not.

briefs.evs:
Multiple chains. Bukhari 5133, 5134 and 5158 (through Hisham ibn 'Urwa); Muslim 1422 through al-A'mash from Ibrahim from al-Aswad, with no Hisham in the chain; and through Yahya ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hatib (Abu Dawud 4937).
Hisham's reliability. Al-Dhahabi calls him "a proof, an imam" and rejects the claim that his memory became confused (Mizan 4/301). Ibn al-Salah and al-Nawawi note that the narrations in Bukhari and Muslim come from his sound period.
Agreement. Ibn Hazm said it was "without any difference"; Ibn Kathir "there is no disagreement among people"; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr "I know of no one who differed". Ahmad Shakir called claims to the contrary fabricated.
The counter-arguments fail. The report that Asma was ten years older comes only from Ibn Abi al-Zinad, born after Aisha's death, without a chain, and he is weak per Ibn Ma'in, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i. At Uhud, Aisha carried water as a helper, not as a combatant, so the age limit for fighters doesn't apply. The report about Fatima's age mixes two inconsistent dates. Aisha's memory of Surah al-Qamar's revelation ("I was a playful young girl, jariya") fits a girl of about four or five, and children like Ibn Abbas narrated events from age three. The idea that Arabs counted age from puberty has no basis and would make Asma 110.

briefs.sec: Aisha's age, 65:4 and the end of Surah at-Tawbah
briefs.title: The marriage judged by its own time, and by its outcome
briefs.thesis: Marriage soon after puberty was normal across the ancient and medieval world, including Christian, Jewish, Persian and Roman law. The marriage was consummated after Aisha reached physical maturity, with her consent and her family's, it was never criticised by the Prophet's enemies, and she became one of the greatest scholars of Islam.
briefs.sum: Marriage around puberty was universal (Persian, Roman, canon law; Mary at twelve). Aisha's marriage was consummated after maturity, she was previously engaged, she chose the Prophet when offered a way out, no enemy objected, and she thrived as a scholar.

obj.q: "Morality is timeless; it was wrong then too."
obj.a: Islam agrees that harm is always wrong, which is why the law forbids harmful marriages. But age norms for marriage are not timeless; they track physical maturity and social structure. If marriage at 12-14 is timelessly evil, then most of humanity's ancestors, including Mary according to Christian tradition, were in evil marriages.

obj.q: "Should Muslims follow this today?"
