obj.a: Islamic law requires maturity, the absence of harm and, for a mature woman, her consent, and allows states to set minimum ages to prevent harm. Following the Prophet ﷺ does not mean reproducing the social age norms of 7th-century Arabia.

prac.q: “Muhammad married a child; no context excuses that.”
prac.a: Every society of the time, including Christian canon law, Roman law and Persian law, accepted marriage around puberty; the Christian tradition says Mary was twelve. Aisha's marriage was consummated after maturity, she chose to stay when given the choice (Bukhari 4785), no enemy of the Prophet objected, and she became the greatest scholar of her generation.

briefs.evs:
Universal norm.
Sasanian Persian law expected girls to marry from nine and consummate by twelve (Encyclopaedia Iranica, "Children").
Roman law set the minimum age for girls at twelve; medieval canon law did the same, with betrothal from seven.
Geza Vermes thought Mary was likely about twelve when betrothed to Joseph; the Protevangelium of James says she was given to an elderly Joseph at twelve. Augustine's fiancée was about ten (Confessions 6.13).
In the 19th century, the age of consent in many US states was ten or even seven, and a few US states had no statutory minimum marriage age as recently as 2026.
Historians such as Neil Postman (The Disappearance of Childhood) show that "childhood" as an extended protected stage is a modern idea; Gluckman and Hanson (Mismatch) note that physical puberty and social maturity coincided historically.
Maturity.
Puberty varies widely: the average range is about 9-14, and medical references give menarche from 9 to 17. Hot climates are associated with earlier onset. Al-Shafi'i said he saw girls in Yemen reach puberty at nine, and a grandmother aged 21 (al-Bayhaqi).
Aisha said, "When a girl reaches nine, she is a woman" (Tirmidhi). She described her illness before the marriage and her hair growing back (Bukhari 3894). Jonathan Brown (Misquoting Muhammad) explains that consummation took place only after physical maturity; contract and consummatio

briefs.sec: Aisha's age, 65:4 and the end of Surah at-Tawbah
briefs.title: 65:4: "those who have not menstruated"
briefs.thesis: 65:4 sets the waiting period after divorce for women who do not menstruate. Classical tafsir includes young girls in this category, and the verse does not itself authorise intercourse, which is governed by separate rules on capacity and harm.
briefs.sum: 65:4 sets a three-month waiting period for women who do not menstruate, whether past it, not yet started, or medically absent. Puberty precedes menarche, and consummation requires maturity and no harm.

prac.q: “65:4 gives the waiting period for divorced girls who haven't had their period, so it allows sex with children.”
prac.a: Puberty begins years before first menstruation, and some women never menstruate. The verse gives all women without periods a waiting period. Whether consummation is allowed depends on maturity and harm, which Islamic law requires separately.

briefs.evs:
The verse. "Those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months, and [also for] those who have not menstruated" (65:4).
Biology. Puberty begins around ages 8-13 with physical changes, while menarche usually comes later, around 12-13, and can be delayed into the late teens. Some women have primary amenorrhoea (never menstruating) due to medical conditions, or very irregular cycles.
The law elsewhere. Consummation requires the ability to bear it without harm; the jurists ruled that a girl who cannot bear it may not be given to her husband. The waiting period also applies after the death of a husband even without consummation, so it does not imply intercourse.

briefs.sec: Aisha's age, 65:4 and the end of Surah at-Tawbah
briefs.title: The end of Surah at-Tawbah (9:128-129)
briefs.thesis: Zayd ibn Thabit found the last two verses of Surah at-Tawbah written only with Abu Khuzayma, but they were memorised by many Companions; written proof was an extra check. The verses appear in first-century manuscripts.
briefs.sum: Zayd found the written copy of 9:128-129 only with Abu Khuzayma (Bukhari 4986), but the verses were memorised widely, and a first-century manuscript (BnF Arabe 328) contains them. Rashad Khalifa's removal claim is baseless.

prac.q: “Your Quran depends on one man, Abu Khuzayma, for two verses.”
prac.a: He had the only written copy found during collection, but Zayd, Ubayy and Umar knew the verses by heart, and Zayd required both writing and memory. The verses appear in first-century manuscripts.

briefs.evs:
Bukhari 4986. Zayd says: "I found the end of Surah at-Tawbah with Abu Khuzayma al-Ansari; I did not find it with anyone else." He means the written copy; Zayd's method required both a written record made in the Prophet's presence and confirmation by memorisers.
Memorised by many. Zayd himself knew the verses; Ibn Abi Dawud reports Umar testifying that he heard them from the Prophet ﷺ, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b reported them. Abu Khuzayma's single written copy was a check on what was already known by heart.
Manuscript evidence. Codex Parisino-Petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328), a first-century Hijazi manuscript, contains the folio running from 9:129 into 10:1. No manuscript ends Surah at-Tawbah at 9:127.
Tap to enlargeCorpus Coranicum: BnF Arabe manuscript with the end of Surah at-Tawbah (9:128-129)
Rashad Khalifa claimed the verses should be removed to make his "code 19" work. That reverses scholarship: a theory must fit the text, not the other way round.

briefs.title: The Quran itself requires the Sunnah (against Quranists)
briefs.thesis: The Quran refers to revelation outside its text, commands obedience to the Messenger separately, calls him its explainer, and cannot be practised without the Sunnah. Rejecting hadith therefore contradicts the Quran.
briefs.sum: The Quran refers to revelation it never records (3:124; 2:143; 2:187), distinguishes the Book and the Wisdom, and makes the Prophet its explainer (16:44). Prayer and zakat can't be performed without the Sunnah.

obj.q: "'We have neglected nothing in the Book' (6:38)."
obj.a: Many commentators take the 'Book' to be the Preserved Tablet (others say the Quran), and 6:38 speaks of animals and birds. Even if it meant the Quran, the Quran includes the command to follow the Messenger, so it "neglects" nothing by referring us to him.

prac.q: “The Quran is complete and fully detailed (6:114). Why do we need hadith?”
prac.a: The Quran itself tells you to obey the Messenger and calls him its explainer (16:44; 59:7). It refers to a qibla and a promise of angels that it never stated, which proves there was revelation outside its text. Without hadith you can't even pray.

briefs.evs:
Revelation not in the Quran. "Is it not sufficient that your Lord reinforces you with three thousand angels?" (3:124), a promise recorded in no earlier verse. "We did not make the qibla you used to face except to know who follows the Messenger" (2:143), but no verse ever commanded the earlier qibla. "Allah knows you used to deceive yourselves" about intercourse at night in Ramadan (2:187), a prohibition never stated in the Quran.
The Book and the Wisdom. "He teaches them the Book and the Wisdom" (2:129; 62:2); the two are distinct.
The explainer. "We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to people what was sent down to them" (16:44). "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; whatever he forbids you, refrain" (59:7). "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah" (4:80).
Practice. How to pray, the zakat rates and thresholds, the rites of Hajj, and even the seven modes of recitation are known only from the Sunnah.
Same transmitters. The Quran and the hadith were carried by the same Companions and their students; rejecting their reliability for one undermines the other.
The clarity dilemma. Quranists say the Quran is clear on its own. Yet the overwhelming majority of Muslims across 1,400 years understood it to require the Sunnah. If a "clear" book was misunderstood by almost everyone, it was not clear in the Quranist sense.

briefs.title: Rashad Khalifa and "code 19"
briefs.thesis: Khalifa claimed to be a messenger on the basis of a numerical pattern ("code 19") in the Quran, and removed two verses that did not fit. A pattern in an already-miraculous text is not a new miracle, and a theory that requires deleting verses is falsified by the text.
briefs.sum: A numerical pattern in the Quran wouldn't prove Khalifa's messengership, and his code required deleting 9:128-129, which are in first-century manuscripts.

prac.q: “Code 19 is a mathematical miracle that proves Rashad was a messenger.”
prac.a: Any long text contains patterns if you choose what to count, and Khalifa deleted two verses that broke his count. A pattern in the Quran would be the Quran's miracle, not his.

briefs.evs:
The Quran was already a miracle; finding patterns in it adds nothing to Khalifa's personal claim.
To make his counts work, Khalifa declared 9:128-129 not part of the Quran, though they are in first-century manuscripts (see Aisha's age & Surah at-Tawbah).
The Quran says Muhammad ﷺ is "the seal of the prophets" (33:40), and Khalifa's reinterpretation of that to allow a later "messenger" contradicts the consensus of the entire community.

briefs.title: No prophet after Muhammad ﷺ (against Ahmadis)
briefs.thesis: The Quran calls Muhammad ﷺ the seal of the prophets and declares the religion perfected. Mirza Ghulam Ahmad's claims rely on a forged gospel and on misreading the Quran about Jesus' death.
briefs.sum: 33:40 seals prophethood, 5:3 perfects the religion, and the Prophet ﷺ said "no prophet after me". Ghulam Ahmad endorsed the forged Gospel of Barnabas and misread 3:55.

obj.q: "'Seal' means the best, like a seal of approval, not the last."
obj.a: The Prophet ﷺ explained it himself: "there is no prophet after me" and the last brick of the building. The Companions and every generation after understood it as last.

prac.q: “Khatam means "seal of approval", so later prophets can come with Muhammad's seal.”
prac.a: The Prophet ﷺ explained it: "There is no prophet after me" (Bukhari 3455) and he is the last brick of the building (Bukhari 3535). And 5:3 says the religion is already perfected.

briefs.evs:
The seal. "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets" (33:40). "There will be no prophet after me" (Bukhari 3455; Muslim 1842). The Prophet ﷺ compared himself to the last brick completing a building (Bukhari 3535).
Religion perfected. "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you" (5:3). No further prophet is needed.
The Gospel of Barnabas. Mirza Ghulam Ahmad called it authentic and early (Jesus in India), but it is a medieval forgery, with errors such as referring to the Jubilee every hundred years (a 14th-century papal practice) and to wine casks of a European type.
Jesus' death. Ahmadis argue that mutawaffika (3:55) means Jesus died. The Quran uses tawaffa for sleep (6:60; 39:42), and the report from Ibn Abbas glossing it as "I will cause you to die" comes through Ali ibn Abi Talha, who did not meet Ibn Abbas; Ibn Abbas himself held Jesus will die after returning (see The crucifixion & resurrection).

briefs.title: The Companions are praised by the Quran (against Shia polemics)
briefs.thesis: The Quran declares Allah pleased with the first emigrants and helpers and with those who pledged allegiance under the tree. Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman were among them, so condemning them contradicts the Quran.
briefs.sum: 9:100 declares Allah pleased with the first Muhajirun and Ansar, 48:18 with those who pledged under the tree, and 9:40 names Abu Bakr as the companion in the cave. Condemning them contradicts the Quran.

prac.q: “The Companions apostatised after the Prophet's death by denying Ali.”
prac.a: The Quran says Allah is pleased with the first Muhajirun and Ansar and promised them Paradise (9:100). Allah knew what they would do later; He wouldn't declare permanent pleasure with people He knew would apostatise. And Ali himself pledged to Abu Bakr and named his sons Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman.

briefs.evs:
9:100: "The first forerunners among the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and those who followed them in goodness: Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens."
48:18: "Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree."
9:40: "the second of two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, do not grieve, Allah is with us." This is Abu Bakr.
Historians. Even non-Muslim historians such as Michael Cook and Fred Donner treat Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman as among the earliest and closest Companions.
Early Shia anthropomorphism. The Twelver heresiographer al-Nawbakhti reports that early Imami theologians such as Hisham ibn al-Hakam described God as "a body unlike bodies"; a Shia source says all the scholars of Qum except Ibn Babawayh were anthropomorphists. Useful when Shia accuse Sunnis of anthropomorphism.

briefs.title: Creed points for debates with Christians
briefs.thesis: Surah al-Ikhlas answers the Nicene Creed point by point; the Trinity and the incarnation use opposite logic; and objections to Allah's attributes in hadith apply equally to the Bible.
briefs.sum: Al-Ikhlas answers Nicaea: one, self-sufficient, unbegotten, without equal. Ibn Taymiyya shows the Trinity (one will, three persons) and incarnation (two wills, one person) use opposite principles. "Wonder" and "Time" objections apply to the Bible too.

prac.q: “Allah "wonders" and "is Time" in your hadith; your God has human traits.”
prac.a: Wonder from Allah implies no ignorance, and the Bible says YHWH "wondered" (Isa 59:16). "I am Time" means Allah controls what the Arabs blamed on time. Meanwhile your creed says God was born and died.

briefs.evs:
Al-Ikhlas as a counter-creed. "Say: He is Allah, One (ahad)" universalises the Shema (Deut 6:4) for all humanity. "Allah, al-Samad": the self-sufficient on whom all depend, the uncaused cause. "He neither begets nor is begotten" answers the Nicene "begotten, not made". "And there is none comparable to Him" answers homoousios, "of one substance with the Father". In Nicene theology the Son is eternally begotten and the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father, so they are not self-sufficient (samad), and by al-Ikhlas' logic not God.
Ibn Taymiyya's dilemma (al-Jawab al-Sahih): Christians say Christ has two natures and two wills but is one person; yet God has one nature and one will but is three persons. By the first rule (persons follow wills), God is one person; by the second, Christ is two persons (the Nestorian position Christians condemn). The two doctrines use opposite principles.
Analogies fail. The sun, its rays and its heat; a man, his speech and his spirit: in each, only the first is a substance, and the others are attributes or effects, which is modalism or subordination, not three co-equal persons.
"Allah wonders" (37:12, in one reading, "I wondered"). Wonder from Allah implies no ignorance (Lane's Lexicon). The Bible says Jesus "marvelled" (Matt 8:10; Mark 6:6) and that YHWH "wondered that there was no one to intercede" (Isa 59:16).
"I am Time (al-dahr)" (Bukhari 4826

briefs.title: The laws of logic: what everyone is bound by
briefs.thesis: Three laws of logic bind every person in every debate: identity, non-contradiction and excluded middle. Almost every meaningful assertion presupposes them, and anyone who denies them in ordinary reasoning still relies on them to make the denial. They are the first thing you can hold anyone to.
briefs.sum: Identity, non-contradiction and excluded middle bind everyone; denying them uses them. Mystery is acceptable; contradiction is not. These are the first rules you can hold any opponent to.

obj.q: "Quantum mechanics shows things can be in two states at once, so non-contradiction fails."
obj.a: Superposition is a mathematical description of a state that is not either of the classical values; it is not a particle being "here and not here in the same sense at the same time". Physicists use logic to state quantum mechanics.

obj.q: "Paraconsistent logics allow contradictions."
obj.a: Paraconsistent logics are formal systems built to avoid 'explosion' when inconsistent information is present; even dialetheists restrict true contradictions to special cases like the Liar paradox, not ordinary claims like God's existence.

prac.q: “The Trinity is beyond human logic; you can't judge God with logic.”
prac.a: If logic doesn't apply, you can't say the Trinity is true rather than false either, because "true and not false" is logic. God is beyond our full understanding, but He doesn't make contradictions true. A mystery is something we don't fully grasp; a contradiction is something that can't be.

briefs.evs:
Identity. A is A: a thing is what it is. "God" in your premise must mean the same in your conclusion (or you commit equivocation).
Non-contradiction. Not both A and not-A, in the same sense at the same time. Aristotle called it the firmest of all principles (Metaphysics IV). This is the law you use against the Trinity's formula when the 'is' is read as strict identity (Trinitarians reply that 'is' differs in sense): "the Father is God, the Son is God, the Father is not the Son, there is one God" (see How the Trinity developed), and against "Jesus knew and did not know the Hour".
Excluded middle. Either A or not-A. "Jesus is God" is either true or false; there is no third option once terms are fixed.
Self-refutation. Someone who says "logic is just a Western construct" is making a claim he wants you to accept as true and not false, which uses logic. Point that out calmly.
"Mystery" vs "contradiction". A mystery is something not fully understood; a contradiction is something that cannot be true. You can accept mysteries (how Allah's attributes are, kayfiyya); no one should accept contradictions.

briefs.title: How arguments work: validity, soundness and the three kinds of inference
briefs.thesis: Every argument can be checked in two places: are the premises true, and does the conclusion follow? Learn the difference between deduction, induction and abduction, and you will know exactly where to attack, and where your own arguments are exposed.
briefs.sum: Valid means the conclusion follows; sound means valid with true premises. Know modus ponens, modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism and reductio, and the invalid forms. Deduction gives certainty, induction probability, abduction the best explanation. Always ask: which premise do you reject?

prac.q: “Your argument is just your opinion.”
prac.a: It's a valid argument: if the premises are true, the conclusion follows. So which premise do you reject, and why? If you can't name one, you're rejecting the conclusion without a reason.

briefs.evs:
Deductive arguments. If the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion must be true. Valid means the conclusion follows; sound means valid with true premises. Common valid forms:
Modus ponens: if P then Q; P; so Q.
Modus tollens: if P then Q; not Q; so not P. (Example: "If Jesus were omniscient he would know the Hour; he did not know it; so he was not omniscient.")
Disjunctive syllogism: P or Q; not P; so Q. (Example: 52:35 — created from nothing, self-created, or created by another.)
Reductio ad absurdum: assume the opponent's claim, derive a contradiction or absurdity, so reject the claim.
Invalid forms to watch for. Affirming the consequent: if P then Q; Q; so P. Denying the antecedent: if P then Q; not P; so not Q.
Inductive arguments reason from many cases to a general conclusion. They make conclusions probable, not certain. (Example: the Oxford Cognition, Religion and Theology Project's studies in 20 countries on natural predispositions to belief.)
Abductive arguments (inference to the best explanation) choose the hypothesis that best explains the evidence, judged by explanatory power, scope, simplicity, fit with background knowledge and lack of ad hoc additions. Most historical arguments (the Quran's preservation, the resurrection debate) are abductive.
How to attack. Grant the form and attack a premise, or grant the premises and show the conclusion doesn't

briefs.title: Burden of proof and what you can hold someone to
briefs.thesis: Whoever makes a claim has the burden to support it, including negative claims like "there is no God" or "the Quran was copied". Learn to identify each side's claims, demand support, and refuse to carry burdens that aren't yours.
briefs.sum: Whoever claims must prove, including negative claims. Use internal critiques where you can, hold opponents to their own standards consistently, define terms first, and challenge vague slogans like "extraordinary evidence".

prac.q: “I don't have to prove anything; I just don't believe your claims.”
prac.a: Then you have no case against them, only against the premises, so tell me which premise is false. But the moment you say "there's no evidence for God" or "the Quran was copied", you're making a claim, and it's your turn to support it.

briefs.evs:
The rule. "Whoever asserts must prove." This applies to positive claims ("God exists") and to negative ones ("God doesn't exist", "the Bible was not corrupted", "Muhammad copied from the Bible"). Islamic jurisprudence has an analogous litigation rule: "the burden of proof is on the claimant" (al-bayyina 'ala al-mudda'i, al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra).
The "lack of belief" move. Some atheists define atheism as "lack of belief" to avoid any burden. Fine, then they have made no claim and have nothing to say against your arguments except to show which premise fails. If they say "there is no good evidence for God", that is a claim, and they must support it.
Internal critique vs external critique. In an internal critique you show that a position fails by its own standards (the Bible contradicts itself; Christian doctrine contradicts Christian scripture). You don't need the opponent to accept Islam for this to work. In an external critique you judge it by your standards. Internal critiques are usually stronger because the opponent can't reject the standard.
Consistency. You can always hold an opponent to his own standards. If he demands early manuscripts for the Quran, apply the same demand to the Gospels. If he accepts Paul's vision as revelation, ask why Muhammad's ﷺ revelation fails the same test. This is legitimate; it only becomes the tu quoque fallacy if you use it to dodge the

briefs.title: The fallacies you will meet most often
briefs.thesis: Fallacies are patterns of bad reasoning. Learn to name the common ones briefly and without arrogance, and avoid committing them yourself.
briefs.sum: Know ad hominem, straw man, red herring, tu quoque, genetic fallacy, begging the question, false dilemma, special pleading, moving goalposts, equivocation, composition, argument from ignorance and the Gish gallop. Name them briefly, answer the substance, and don't commit them yourself.

prac.q: “That's an ad hominem! (when you note a scholar's bias)”
prac.a: Pointing out a source's bias goes to how much weight their testimony gets, not whether their argument is valid. When I criticise an argument, I'll address its premises; when I assess a witness, credibility is relevant.

briefs.evs:
Fallacies of relevance
Ad hominem: attacking the person, not the argument ("you're just a Muslim apologist"). Answer: "Even if that's true, which premise is false?"
Straw man: attacking a weaker version of the view. Answer by restating your view accurately. Avoid it yourself: represent the Trinity as Christians define it before you criticise it.
Red herring: changing the subject (asked about Gospel authorship, the opponent talks about Islamic violence).
Tu quoque ("you too"): dismissing a criticism because the critic is guilty of something similar. Use consistency arguments only to expose double standards, not to avoid answering.
Appeal to emotion or popularity: "billions of Christians can't be wrong."
Genetic fallacy: judging a claim by its origin rather than its merit ("you only believe because you were raised Muslim"). Note the inverse: showing a doctrine developed historically is not a genetic fallacy if the question is whether it was originally taught.
Fallacies of presumption
Begging the question (circular reasoning): assuming what you're trying to prove ("the Bible is true because the Bible says so").
False dilemma: presenting two options when there are more ("Jesus was a liar, lunatic, or Lord" omits "legend" and "misreported").
Complex question: "Have you stopped defending violence?"
Special pleading: exempting your case from a rule you apply to others (demanding manus

briefs.title: Epistemology: what knowledge is and how we get it
briefs.thesis: Debates about God turn on what counts as knowledge. Know the main sources of knowledge, the self-refuting positions (radical scepticism, scientism, verificationism), and the Islamic view that reason, the senses, reliable testimony and the fitrah are all legitimate sources.
briefs.sum: Sources of knowledge: senses, reason, memory, testimony, introspection, fitrah and revelation. Scepticism, verificationism and scientism refute themselves. Mass-transmitted testimony (tawatur) gives certainty, which is how the Quran is known.

prac.q: “You can only believe what's proven by evidence.”
prac.a: Can you prove that principle with evidence? You believe other people have minds, that the past happened and that your reasoning is reliable, without proving them. Those are rational basic beliefs, and so is the natural recognition of a Creator, which the evidence then confirms.

briefs.evs:
Knowledge. The classical definition is justified true belief; Edmund Gettier (1963) showed cases where that isn't enough, and philosophers still debate what must be added. For debate, what matters is justification: what makes a belief rational.
Sources of knowledge. Sense perception; reason (logic, mathematics, necessary truths); memory; testimony (most of what we know about history, science and geography comes from trusting others); introspection; and, in Islamic thought, the fitrah and revelation.
Foundationalism. Some beliefs are basic: they are rational without being inferred from others (that other minds exist, that the past was real, that I am conscious). Alvin Plantinga argued belief in God can be "properly basic". This fits the Islamic fitrah.
Testimony and mass transmission. Islam developed a sophisticated theory of testimony: reports transmitted by so many independent people that collusion is impossible (mutawatir) give certain knowledge on the majority view of the usul scholars. This is how the Quran's text is known, and it is the same principle by which we know cities we have never visited exist.
Dogmatic scepticism ("we can't know anything") refutes itself, since it claims to know that knowledge is impossible; Pyrrhonian scepticism avoids this by suspending judgment, so press it on why we should doubt reliable faculties.
Verificationism (logical positivism: only em

briefs.title: Metaphysics: the concepts behind the arguments for God
briefs.thesis: Arguments for God use a small set of metaphysical concepts. Learn them precisely: necessary and contingent, essence and existence, causation and the principle of sufficient reason, actual and potential infinity, and the theologians' categories.
briefs.sum: Necessary, contingent, impossible (wajib, mumkin, mustahil); essence vs existence; sustaining vs temporal causes; the principle of sufficient reason; actual vs potential infinity; possible worlds; substance and accident. These are the tools of the God arguments.

prac.q: “Everything has a cause, so God needs a cause.”
prac.a: The principle is that every contingent thing, everything that could have failed to exist, has a cause. A necessary being, which can't fail to exist, doesn't need one. That's not special pleading; it's the distinction the argument is built on.

briefs.evs:
Necessary, contingent, impossible. The rational categories: wajib (must exist), ja'iz/mumkin (can exist or not, so needs a cause), mustahil (cannot exist, like a square circle); Avicenna's wajib al-wujud/mumkin al-wujud sharpened the first two. Avicenna built his proof of God on this division.
Essence and existence. On Avicenna's view, for any created thing what it is doesn't include that it is (a distinction Ibn Rushd and Ibn Taymiyya reject): knowing what a horse is doesn't tell you whether one exists. Something must give it existence. In God, existence is not added to essence.
Causation. Distinguish causes in time (a match lighting a fire) from causes here and now that sustain existence (the fire depends on oxygen now). The strongest cosmological arguments (Aquinas and Ibn Taymiyya's argument from essential dependence) concern sustaining causes, which can't regress infinitely (Ibn Taymiyya allowed an endless past series of events, so the kalam beginning-argument is not his).
The principle of sufficient reason (Leibniz): there is an explanation for why anything exists rather than not. Opponents who deny it must explain why they still expect explanations in science.
Actual vs potential infinity. A potential infinite is a series that can always be extended (counting). An actual infinite is a completed infinite collection. Kalam arguments say an actually infinite series of past

briefs.title: Philosophy of religion: the map of the debate about God
briefs.thesis: Know the families of arguments for God and the main objections, with a one-line answer to each, so that nothing in a debate surprises you.
briefs.sum: Arguments for God: cosmological (kalam, contingency, Thomist, Ibn Taymiyya), design, moral, mind and reason, fitrah, ontological. Objections: who made God, evil, hiddenness, Euthyphro, omnipotence paradox, many gods; each has a short answer.

prac.q: “You're just an atheist about the other gods; I go one god further.”
prac.a: The arguments don't pick a god from a list. They show there must be one necessary, perfect, uncaused being. Zeus was born, had parents and limits, so he fails the description; the God of Abraham fits it. I reject the other gods for the same reason you should accept this one.

briefs.evs:
Arguments for God
Cosmological. (1) The kalam argument: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; so it has a cause (al-Ghazali, William Lane Craig). (2) The contingency argument: contingent things need a necessary cause (Avicenna, Leibniz). (3) The Thomist argument from sustaining causes (Aquinas, Feser). (4) Ibn Taymiyya's argument from the dependence of created things, rooted in 52:35.
Teleological. Design from fine-tuning (Robin Collins), from the intelligibility of the universe, from biological complexity (contested; use carefully).
Moral. Objective moral values need a transcendent ground.
Consciousness and reason. The argument from mind (Swinburne) and the evolutionary argument against naturalism (Plantinga): if our faculties evolved only for survival, we can't trust them to produce true beliefs, including naturalism.
Fitrah / religious experience. Natural, widespread belief (Barrett) and the rationality of basic beliefs.
Ontological (Anselm, Plantinga's modal version): a maximally great being is possible, and if possible then actual (Plantinga says this makes theism rational, not that it compels belief). Use with care; many philosophers, including Muslim ones, find it unpersuasive.
Objections and short answers
Who made God? Only contingent things need a cause.
Problem of evil. The logical version is widely regarded as defeated by Plantinga's free will def

briefs.title: Ethics: what grounds right and wrong
briefs.thesis: Debates about morality turn on metaethics: whether moral facts are objective, and what grounds them. Know the main positions and their weaknesses.
briefs.sum: Know realism vs anti-realism, the is-ought gap, consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, divine command and natural law. Islam grounds morality in Allah's wise nature, known generally through fitrah and in detail through revelation. Relativism condemns all moral reformers.

prac.q: “Morality is just about well-being; we don't need God.”
prac.a: Why is well-being objectively good, and whose well-being counts? Animals', embryos', future people's? Your starting point is a value you've assumed. Theism explains why it's actually true that cruelty is wrong; naturalism only explains why we feel that it is.

briefs.evs:
Moral realism vs anti-realism. Realists hold some moral claims are objectively true; anti-realists hold they are expressions of feeling (emotivism), conventions, or simply false (error theory, J.L. Mackie).
The is-ought gap (Hume): you can't derive an "ought" from facts alone. Secular realists need some starting value; ask them to justify it.
The main normative theories. Consequentialism (the right act produces the best outcome; can lead to conclusions such as Peter Singer's on infanticide, given his preference utilitarianism); deontology (duties and rights, Kant; struggles to ground the duties); virtue ethics (Aristotle; needs an account of human nature and purpose, which theism supplies); divine command theory and natural law.
The Islamic position. On the view of Maturidis and Ibn Taymiyya, good and evil are grounded in Allah's wise and perfect nature and expressed in His commands; the fitrah gives humans a general moral sense (91:7-8), and revelation gives the details. Muslim theologians debated whether reason alone can know good and evil (the Mu'tazila said yes, the Ash'aris said good, evil and obligation are known and fixed by revelation, the Maturidis sided with reason on knowing good and evil, and Ibn Taymiyya held that reason knows good and evil but obligation and reward come through revelation).
Moral relativism ("morality is relative to culture") refutes itself when p

briefs.title: Philosophy of science: what science can and can't do
briefs.thesis: Science is a powerful method for studying the natural world, but it rests on philosophical assumptions it cannot prove, and it cannot answer questions about why there is a natural world at all. Know the limits, so you can resist "science disproves God".
briefs.sum: Science assumes an external world, reliable reason, uniformity and intelligibility; it can't prove them. Know Hume's problem of induction, Popper's falsifiability, Kuhn's theory change, and the difference between methodological and metaphysical naturalism. Argue from what science shows, not from gaps.

prac.q: “Science has explained everything that used to be attributed to God.”
prac.a: Science explains how natural things behave by natural laws. It can't explain why there are laws, why anything exists at all, or why the universe is intelligible, because science assumes all of those. My arguments are from what science shows, not from gaps in it.

briefs.evs:
Assumptions of science. The reality of an external world; the reliability of our senses and reason; the uniformity of nature (that the laws will hold tomorrow); that nature is intelligible. None of these can be proved by science, and theism explains them (an intelligent Creator made an ordered world and minds to understand it).
The problem of induction (Hume): no number of observations proves the next will be the same. Science proceeds anyway, on trust in nature's uniformity.
Falsifiability (Karl Popper): a scientific theory must risk being proved wrong. This is a criterion for science, not for truth; mathematics and history are not falsifiable in the same way but give knowledge.
Underdetermination (Duhem and Quine) and theory change (Thomas Kuhn): theories are revised and sometimes replaced. Scientific claims are provisional. That's why Islamic arguments should not depend on a current scientific model, and why critics can't treat today's theory as final.
Methodological vs metaphysical naturalism. Science limits itself to natural causes as a method (methodological naturalism). That is not a finding that only natural causes exist (metaphysical naturalism). Confusing the two is the most common error in "science vs God" debates.
The God of the gaps. Don't argue "science can't explain X, so God". Argue from what science does show (a beginning, fine-tuned laws, order) and from what

briefs.title: Philosophy of mind and the self
briefs.thesis: Questions about consciousness, the soul and free will are central to debates with materialists. Know the main positions and why materialism struggles.
briefs.sum: Physicalism (identity, functionalism, eliminativism) vs dualism (substance, property). Use Mary's room, the hard problem, intentionality and the unity of consciousness against materialism. Know libertarian, compatibilist and determinist views of free will.

prac.q: “Consciousness is just neurons firing.”
prac.a: Neurons firing is what happens in the brain when you see red; it doesn't explain why there is something it is like to see red. Jackson's Mary argument (1982; Jackson later gave it up, but many still defend it) says she learns something new when she sees red. That suggests experience isn't just a physical fact.

briefs.evs:
Physicalism: the mind is the brain or what the brain does. Versions: identity theory, functionalism (mind is what the brain computes), eliminativism (folk-psychological states like belief and desire do not really exist, Paul and Patricia Churchland; illusionism about consciousness, Keith Frankish and Daniel Dennett).
Dualism: the mind or soul is not wholly physical. Substance dualism (Descartes; the Islamic ruh), property dualism (mental properties aren't physical, Chalmers).
Key arguments against physicalism. The knowledge argument (Frank Jackson's "Mary's room": a scientist who knows every physical fact about colour still learns something when she first sees red); the hard problem (Chalmers); intentionality (thoughts are about things; physical states aren't intrinsically about anything); the unity of consciousness.
Free will. Libertarian free will (our choices are not fully determined); compatibilism (free will is compatible with determinism, Hume, Dennett); hard determinism (no free will). Islam affirms real human choice under God's decree (see Free will and qadar). Note: if materialism is true, many philosophers concede libertarian free will is hard to defend, and with it moral responsibility.
Personal identity. What makes you the same person over time? Physical continuity (but your cells are replaced), psychological continuity (but memory fails). The soul gives a simple an

briefs.title: Debate conduct: charity, Socratic questions and staying in control
briefs.thesis: Winning a debate is not the same as winning a person. Apply the principle of charity, ask questions more than you assert, concede what is true, and keep the discussion on the strongest ground.
briefs.sum: Steelman your opponent, ask Socratic questions, concede true points, lead with your strongest arguments, control the frame, and argue "in the way that is best" (16:125).

prac.q: “You just ask questions; why won't you make your own case?”
prac.a: Questions are how we find out whether a view holds up. But here's my case, numbered so you can tell me which premise you reject: one, two, three. Now, back to my question about your standard of evidence.

briefs.evs:
Steelmanning and charity. State your opponent's view in a form he would accept before criticising it. It earns trust, prevents straw men, and makes your critique land.
The Socratic method. Ask questions that expose assumptions: "How do you know that?" "What would count as evidence?" "Does that standard apply to your own view?" A person who reaches the problem himself is more convinced than one who is told.
Concede what is true. If the opponent makes a good point (a weak hadith, a debated Quranic variant), concede it and show why it doesn't affect your conclusion. Credibility is your main asset.
Lead with your strongest material. One strong argument well defended beats ten weak ones; weak arguments let the opponent win the exchange and discredit the rest (see the Use with care flags throughout this library).
Control the frame. Begin by agreeing on the question and the standard of evidence. Keep returning to it when the debate drifts.
Adab. The Quran: "Argue with them in the way that is best" (16:125); "Do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner" (29:46). Good manners are not weakness; they are part of dawah.

briefs.title: Islam and philosophy: what Muslim scholars accepted and rejected
briefs.thesis: The Islamic tradition engaged deeply with Greek philosophy. Some scholars adopted its logic and metaphysics; others criticised it. Knowing this history lets you use philosophy confidently while knowing where its claims conflict with revelation.
briefs.sum: The falasifa (al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, Ibn Rushd), al-Ghazali's Tahafut (three doctrines condemned), the mutakallimun, and Ibn Taymiyya's critique of Greek logic and defence of reason-revelation harmony. Use philosophy as a tool, not a rival authority.

prac.q: “Islam is anti-intellectual; al-Ghazali killed philosophy.”
prac.a: Al-Ghazali mastered philosophy and used logic; he criticised specific doctrines, and Ibn Rushd answered him, and the debate continued for centuries. Philosophy flourished after him in Persia and the Ottoman lands. The Quran commands reflection over and over (3:190-191).

briefs.evs:
The falasifa. Al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and Ibn Rushd (Averroes) developed Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy in Arabic. Avicenna's necessary-contingent distinction became a standard tool even among his critics.
Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) mastered their philosophy, accepted logic as a neutral tool (Mi'yar al-'Ilm, al-Qistas al-Mustaqim), and in Tahafut al-Falasifa (The Incoherence of the Philosophers) refuted twenty of their doctrines, condemning three as unbelief: the eternity of the world, God's not knowing particulars, and denial of bodily resurrection.
Ibn Rushd replied in Tahafut al-Tahafut (The Incoherence of the Incoherence), defending philosophy, and argued in Fasl al-Maqal that the Quran commands rational reflection.
The theologians (mutakallimun). The Mu'tazila and Ash'aris built rational theology (kalam), including the arguments from the createdness of the world.
Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328), in al-Radd 'ala al-Mantiqiyyin (Refutation of the Logicians) and Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa al-Naql (Averting the Conflict between Reason and Revelation), criticised Aristotelian logic's claims (for example, that real definitions are the only path to concepts, see Hallaq, Ibn Taymiyya Against the Greek Logicians) and argued that sound reason never contradicts authentic revelation. He grounded the arguments for God in the fitrah and in the Quran's own reasoning, which he hel

briefs.title: The Quran: preservation, text and its challenge
briefs.sum: Read al-A'zami first, then Qadhi for the sciences, Nasser and van Putten for the readings and manuscripts, and Sadeghi on Sana'a. Know Small and Brubaker's arguments.
briefs.evs:
Start here: M.M. al-A'zami, The History of the Qur'anic Text from Revelation to Compilation (2003). This compares the Quran's transmission with the Bible's.
Yasir Qadhi, An Introduction to the Sciences of the Qur'aan (1999). The best English primer on 'ulum al-Qur'an: revelation, compilation, the qira'at and abrogation.
Ahmad von Denffer, 'Ulum al-Qur'an (1983). A shorter alternative.
Muhammad Abdullah Draz, The Qur'an: An Eternal Challenge (al-Naba' al-'Azim). The classic modern case for the Quran's inimitability.
Shady Nasser, The Transmission of the Variant Readings of the Qur'an (2013), which argues the readings were not strictly mutawatir, and The Second Canonization of the Qur'an (2020). Essential for the qira'at debate.
Marijn van Putten, Quranic Arabic: From its Hijazi Origins to its Classical Reading Traditions (2022). Also his articles on the shared spelling "fingerprints" of the Uthmanic codices.
Behnam Sadeghi & Mohsen Goudarzi (they argue the lower text is a pre-'Uthmanic codex; read it critically), "Ṣan'ā' 1 and the Origins of the Qur'ān," Der Islam 87 (2012). The key article on the Sana'a palimpsest.
Nicolai Sinai, The Qur'an: A Historical-Critical Introduction (2017). An academic, non-Muslim account that rejects late-date theories.
Other side: Daniel Brubaker, Corrections in Early Qur'an Manuscripts: Twenty Examples (2019); Keith Small, Textual Criticism and Qur

briefs.title: Hadith, the life of the Prophet ﷺ and the history of early Islam
briefs.sum: Brown first, then al-A'zami and Motzki against the sceptics, a sira (Mubarakpuri or Lings), and Hoyland for the outside sources. Know Schacht and Hagarism.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Jonathan A.C. Brown, Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World (2nd ed. 2017).
M.M. al-A'zami, Studies in Early Hadith Literature (1968) and On Schacht's Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence (1985). These answer the Western sceptics.
Harald Motzki, The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence (2002). Dates material to the first Islamic century.
Gregor Schoeler, The Biography of Muhammad: Nature and Authenticity (2011).
Safi-ur-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (al-Raheeq al-Makhtum). A standard sira.
Martin Lings, Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources (1983). A readable narrative.
Ibn Ishaq / Ibn Hisham, The Life of Muhammad, translated by A. Guillaume (1955). The primary source critics quote; read it in context.
Robert Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It (1997). Non-Muslim 7th-century sources on the Prophet ﷺ and the conquests.
al-Bayhaqi, Dala'il al-Nubuwwa, and al-Qadi 'Iyad, al-Shifa. Classical collections of the proofs of prophethood.
Other side: Joseph Schacht, The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence (1950); Patricia Crone & Michael Cook, Hagarism (1977), which its own authors later stepped back from.

briefs.title: Muhammad ﷺ in earlier scripture and the Quran–Bible relationship
briefs.sum: Kairanawi and Ibn Taymiyya are the classical foundation; Ameri compares the texts; Reynolds and Zellentin show the academic picture of the Quran's dialogue with the Bible.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Rahmatullah Kairanawi, Izhar al-Haqq (1864; English abridgement The Truth Revealed). The classic 19th-century response to the missionaries (note its sources are dated): textual corruption, contradictions and prophecies.
Ibn Taymiyya, al-Jawab al-Sahih li-man Baddala Din al-Masih. The most comprehensive classical answer to Christianity. A partial English version is A Muslim Theologian's Response to Christianity, translated by Thomas Michel (1984).
Abdul-Ahad Dawud (formerly Rev. David Benjamin Keldani), Muhammad in the Bible. Use with care and check every claim.
Sami Ameri, Hunting for the Word of God (2013). Compares the textual criticism of the New Testament and the Quran.
Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur'an and the Bible: Text and Commentary (2018). An academic Catholic author; useful for parallels, but his interpretations are contestable.
Holger Zellentin, The Qur'an's Legal Culture (2013). Shows the Quran engaging Jewish-Christian law.

briefs.title: Christianity: Jesus, the Trinity, Paul and the New Testament text
briefs.sum: Ehrman and Metzger for the text, Dunn and Hanson for how Christology and the Trinity developed, Fredriksen and Tabor for Paul, Vermes and Allison for the historical Jesus. Know Hurtado, Bauckham, Licona and Wright, the strongest Christian scholars.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Bart Ehrman, Misquoting Jesus (2005). Then How Jesus Became God (2014), Jesus, Interrupted (2009), Forged (2011), Lost Christianities (2003) and The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture (2nd ed. 2011).
Bruce Metzger & Bart Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament (4th ed. 2005); Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament (2nd ed. 1994). Use it to check any variant.
James D.G. Dunn, Christology in the Making (1980) and Did the First Christians Worship Jesus? (2010).
R.P.C. Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God: The Arian Controversy 318–381 (1988). The standard history of how the Trinity was fixed.
Anthony Buzzard & Charles Hunting, The Doctrine of the Trinity: Christianity's Self-Inflicted Wound (1998); Dale Tuggy, What is the Trinity? Thinking About the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (2017, self-published). Unitarian Christian critiques.

briefs.title: The Old Testament: history, archaeology and authorship
briefs.sum: Finkelstein & Silberman and Dever for archaeology, Friedman and Baden for the sources behind the contradictions, Tov for the text, Collins for Daniel. Know Kitchen and Archer, whose answers you will hear.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Israel Finkelstein & Neil Asher Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001). Archaeology versus the biblical narrative, from the patriarchs to Josiah. Their David and Solomon (2006) covers the united monarchy and Solomon's Temple.
William G. Dever, What Did the Biblical Writers Know and When Did They Know It? (2001) and Who Were the Early Israelites and Where Did They Come From? (2003). A more moderate archaeologist who still rejects the Exodus and conquest as written.
Richard Elliott Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible? (1987) and The Bible with Sources Revealed (2003). These show the J, E, P and D sources. Use them for the doubled stories (Genesis 37, the Flood, creation).
Joel S. Baden, The Composition of the Pentateuch (2012). The neo-documentary case.
Marc Zvi Brettler, How to Read the Bible (2005). A Jewish scholar on reading the Hebrew Bible critically.
Mark S. Smith, The Early History of God (2nd ed. 2002). The development of Israelite monotheism.
Lester Grabbe, Ancient Israel: What Do We Know and How Do We Know It? (2nd ed. 2017).
John J. Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia commentary, 1993). The scholarly dating of Daniel and its historical problems.
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (3rd ed. 2012). The Masoretic text, the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Other side: Kenneth Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003); James Hoffmeier, Israel i

briefs.title: Judaism
briefs.sum: Singer for Jewish arguments against Christian readings, Ibn Hazm and al-Maghribi for the classical Muslim case.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Tovia Singer, Let's Get Biblical (2 vols., 2014). A rabbi's refutation of Christian proof-texts. Very useful against Christian prophecy claims; Muslims should note where it also targets Islam.
Ibn Hazm, al-Fisal fi al-Milal wa al-Ahwa' wa al-Nihal. A classical Muslim critique of the Torah's text.
Samau'al al-Maghribi, Ifham al-Yahud (Silencing the Jews). By a 12th-century Jewish convert to Islam.
Zellentin, The Qur'an's Legal Culture, and Reynolds, The Qur'an and the Bible, listed above.

briefs.title: Atheism, arguments for God and science
briefs.sum: Tzortzis first, then Feser for rigour, Swinburne and the Blackwell Companion for depth, Barnes & Lewis for fine-tuning, Nagel and Plantinga against materialism. Know Mackie and Oppy, the serious atheist cases.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Hamza Andreas Tzortzis, The Divine Reality: God, Islam and the Mirage of Atheism (rev. ed. 2019). A widely read Muslim book against atheism.
Edward Feser, Five Proofs of the Existence of God (2017). Rigorous arguments, each followed by deriving the divine attributes and answering objections. His The Last Superstition (2008) is a polemical companion.
Richard Swinburne, The Existence of God (2nd ed. 2004). The probabilistic case.
William Lane Craig & J.P. Moreland (eds.), The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology (2009). Academic chapters on every argument.
Luke Barnes & Geraint Lewis, A Fortunate Universe: Life in a Finely Tuned Cosmos (2016). Fine-tuning by two cosmologists (they do not draw a theistic conclusion).
Justin Barrett, Born Believers: The Science of Children's Religious Belief (2012). Cognitive science of children's religious belief, which Muslim authors relate to the fitrah.
Thomas Nagel, Mind and Cosmos (2012). An atheist on why materialism fails to explain mind.
Alvin Plantinga, Where the Conflict Really Lies: Science, Religion, and Naturalism (2011). Includes the evolutionary argument against naturalism.
Antony Flew, There Is a God (2007, written with Roy Abraham Varghese). Flew, a famous atheist philosopher, became a deist; critics dispute how much of the book is his own work.
Sherman Jackson, Islam and the Problem of Black Suffering (2009); Jon H

briefs.title: Agnosticism and the divine attributes
briefs.sum: Feser, al-Ghazali's Iqtisad and Ibn Rushd's Kashf show how to move from a Creator to His attributes; Ibn Taymiyya grounds it in the fitrah. Know Schellenberg's hiddenness argument.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Feser, Five Proofs of the Existence of God (above). Its chapters derive the divine attributes (unity, simplicity, eternity, omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness) from each proof
al-Ghazali, al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad, translated by Aladdin Yaqub as Al-Ghazali's Moderation in Belief (2013). A systematic proof of God's existence and attributes.
Ibn Rushd, al-Kashf 'an Manahij al-Adilla, translated by Ibrahim Najjar as Faith and Reason in Islam (2001). The arguments from providence ('inaya) and invention (ikhtira').
Ibn Taymiyya, Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa al-Naql. Reason, fitrah and the attributes; the argument "whatever perfection is in creation, the Creator is more entitled to".
Avicenna, The Metaphysics of The Healing, translated by Michael Marmura (2005). The necessary being and why it must be one.
Brian Davies, An Introduction to the Philosophy of Religion (4th ed. 2020).
Other side: J.L. Schellenberg, Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (1993); Robin Le Poidevin, Agnosticism: A Very Short Introduction (2010).

briefs.title: Philosophy: logic, fallacies and the main fields
briefs.sum: Begin with Blackburn or Warburton, then Kreeft's logic and Damer's fallacies. Pick one book per field. For the Islamic tradition, read Adamson, then al-Ghazali's Incoherence and Hallaq's Ibn Taymiyya.
briefs.evs:
Introductions
Start here: Simon Blackburn, Think (1999), or Nigel Warburton, Philosophy: The Basics (5th ed. 2012).
Thomas Nagel, What Does It All Mean? (1987). Very short.
Logic and argument
Peter Kreeft, Socratic Logic (3rd ed. 2008). Classical (Aristotelian) logic for beginners, written for debate.
Anthony Weston, A Rulebook for Arguments (5th ed. 2017). Short and practical.
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic (many editions) or Irving Copi, Introduction to Logic. Standard textbooks.
T. Edward Damer, Attacking Faulty Reasoning (7th ed. 2012). The fallacies with examples and how to answer them.
Mortimer Adler, How to Read a Book (1972). For reading opponents' books analytically.
The fields
Epistemology: Robert Audi, Epistemology: A Contemporary Introduction; Alvin Plantinga, Warranted Christian Belief (2000) on properly basic belief.
Metaphysics: Edward Feser, Scholastic Metaphysics (2014); Michael Loux, Metaphysics: A Contemporary Introduction.
Philosophy of religion: Michael Peterson et al., Reason and Religious Belief (5th ed. 2012).
Ethics: James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy; Russ Shafer-Landau, Moral Realism: A Defence (2003).
Philosophy of science: Samir Okasha, Philosophy of Science: A Very Short Introduction (2nd ed. 2016); A.F. Chalmers, What Is This Thing Called Science? (4th ed. 2013).
Philosophy of mind: Edward Feser, Philosophy of Mind: A

briefs.title: Answering objections: morality, slavery, Aisha and the sects
briefs.sum: Brown's Misquoting Muhammad and Slavery and Islam, the classical tafsirs for context, and Ibn Taymiyya for sectarian debates.
briefs.evs:
Start here: Jonathan A.C. Brown, Misquoting Muhammad (2014). How the tradition interprets hard texts.
Jonathan A.C. Brown, Slavery and Islam (2019).
Tafsir Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Sa'di. Always check a verse's classical explanation before answering an objection.
Ibn Taymiyya, Minhaj al-Sunna al-Nabawiyya. The classical Sunni answer to Shi'i arguments.
Ibn al-Qayyim, Hidayat al-Hayara. Answers Jewish and Christian objections to Islam.

briefs.title: Online tools
briefs.sum: Corpus Coranicum and dorar.net to check manuscripts and gradings, the online Bible manuscript sites for variants, and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy for any philosophical term.
briefs.evs:
Quran: Corpus Coranicum (manuscripts, variant readings and late-antique parallel texts for the Quran), quran.com, quran.ksu.edu.sa, altafsir.com.
Hadith: sunnah.com, dorar.net (gradings), isnad.io.
Classical library: shamela.ws.
Bible: Codex Sinaiticus online, the NT Virtual Manuscript Room, CSNTM (Center for the Study of NT Manuscripts), the Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library, and biblehub.com interlinear.
Philosophy: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu) and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (iep.utm.edu). These are free and scholarly, and the first place to check any philosophical term.

briefs.title: Equal in worth, different in role
briefs.thesis: The Quran addresses men and women as equals in worth, reward and accountability, and gives them different but complementary roles in some areas. Equality of worth is not the same claim as sameness of every role.
briefs.sum: Men and women are equal in worth, reward and accountability (33:35, 16:97, 49:13) and have complementary roles with matching duties. “Different” is not “unequal” unless you assume identical roles are the only fair design.

obj.q: “‘Equal but different’ is what every sexist said.”
obj.a: The test is whether the difference is arbitrary and one-sided. Here each difference comes with a matching duty: the man carries the financial obligation (maintenance, the dowry) while the woman’s property stays entirely her own (4:32). The critic also uses a role-based standard of his own when he accepts separate sports categories or maternity leave, so “different treatment” cannot be the thing that is wrong in itself.

obj.q: “2:228 says men have a degree over women.”
obj.a:
The same verse opens: “And due to the wives is similar to what is expected of them, in a reasonable manner” (wa lahunna mithlu alladhi ‘alayhinna bil-ma‘ruf), then adds “and men have a degree over them.”
Commentators differ: some link the degree to maintenance and leadership, and Ibn Abbas read it as the husband's forbearance and generosity, none as superior worth. Ibn Abbas, quoted above, read the verse as a mutual duty to treat each other well.

prac.q: “If men and women are really equal, why does Islam not make everything identical?”
prac.a: Because equal worth does not require identical roles, and no society treats them as the same: every legal system separates some categories by sex or by family role. What matters is whether the rule is fair and whether duties match rights. In Islam the woman’s worth, property, reward and accountability are equal to the man’s (33:35, 4:32), and the extra financial burden falls on him. If you think roles must be identical to be fair, that is a premise you have to defend, not a fact we both accept.

briefs.evs:
Parallel address. 33:35 lists ten qualities (Muslim, believing, obedient, truthful, patient, humble, charitable, fasting, chaste, remembering God) for men and women in matching pairs, and ends with one shared reward: “Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.”
The same reward. “Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do” (16:97). And “I will not allow the work of any worker among you, male or female, to be lost; you are of one another” (3:195).
No ranking by sex. “We created you from a male and a female… the most honoured of you with God is the most God-conscious” (49:13). The only ranking is taqwa.
Eve is not blamed alone. The Quran never makes the woman the cause of the Fall. Adam is named as the one who disobeyed (20:121), and the two say together “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves” (7:23). Compare 1 Timothy 2:14 (“Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived”) and Sirach 25:24 (“From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die”).
The Prophet ﷺ. “Women are the twin halves of men” (Abu Dawud 236, Tirmidhi 113; graded sahih by al-Albani). On 2:228 Ibn Abbas said: “I like to adorn myself for my wife as I like her to adorn herself for me” (Tabari).

briefs.title: What feminism got right, and where Islam differs
briefs.thesis: Islam agrees with the core early feminist demands (property, education, consent, protection from abuse) and established most of them in the seventh century. It parts company with parts of later feminism on identical roles, sexual autonomy and the status of the family. A debater should concede the agreement before stating the differences.
briefs.sum: Islam gave women property, education and consent early, and Muslims should condemn societies that deny them; it differs from parts of later feminism on identical roles, sexual autonomy and the family.

obj.q: “Muslim feminists like Amina Wadud show Islam can be feminist.”
obj.a: Some Muslim women scholars have raised real issues about patriarchal readings, and challenging culture presented as religion is legitimate. But when a reading sets aside explicit rulings (Wadud led a mixed-gender Friday prayer in New York in 2005), the great majority of scholars reject it. Distinguish between correcting a cultural reading and discarding a text.

obj.q: “Women in Muslim countries are oppressed.”
obj.a: Some are, and often in ways the sources forbid: denying inheritance, schooling or consent. Others are not, and several Muslim-majority countries have elected women as heads of government (Benazir Bhutto in Pakistan in 1988, Tansu Çiller in Turkey, Khaleda Zia and Sheikh Hasina in Bangladesh, Megawati Sukarnoputri as president of Indonesia (2001)). The question is whether the rule is in the sources, not whether every society follows it.

prac.q: “You cannot call yourself pro-woman unless you accept feminism.”
prac.a: Feminism is several different positions, so tell me which one. If you mean property, education, consent and protection from violence, Islam established those in the seventh century (4:7, 4:32, Bukhari 101) when most legal systems did not, and I criticise Muslim societies that deny them. If you mean that sex roles are only a social construct or that sexual freedom is liberation, I disagree and I will say why. Rejecting a package is not the same as rejecting women’s dignity.

briefs.evs:
Property. “For men is a share of what the parents and relatives leave, and for women is a share” (4:7). “For women is a share of what they have earned” (4:32). The dowry belongs to the bride: “Give women their dowries as a gift” (4:4). In England, a married woman’s property passed to her husband until the Married Women’s Property Acts of 1870 and 1882.
Education. Women came to the Prophet ﷺ and said men had taken all his time, so he set aside a day for them and taught them (Bukhari 101). Aisha became one of the great teachers of the first generation.
The vote, for context. Women got the vote in the United States in 1920, in Britain on equal terms in 1928, in France in 1944 and in Swiss federal elections in 1971.
Where Muslim societies fail. Denying daughters their inheritance, their education or a say in marriage contradicts the sources. When the Taliban banned girls’ secondary schooling (2021) and women’s university education (2022), Al-Azhar and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation criticised the decisions as contrary to Islam.
Where Islam differs: sameness. In the story of Mary's birth the Quran quotes her mother saying “the male is not like the female” (3:36), and the Quran elsewhere treats sex as real and meaningful (53:45; see the section on sexuality and gender).
Where Islam differs: motherhood. A man asked who most deserved his good company and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Y

briefs.title: Women in public life: scholars, traders, advisers and rulers
briefs.thesis: Islamic history shows women as traders, scholars, teachers, advisers, fighters and, rarely, rulers. The main objection, Bukhari 4425, is read by most jurists as restricting the supreme leadership of the community, and other public roles remain open.
briefs.sum: Women were merchants, scholars, advisers, defenders and rulers in Muslim history. The one restriction, from Bukhari 4425, is read by most as limiting the supreme leadership of the community.

obj.q: “So a woman cannot be head of state in Islam.”
obj.a: Most classical jurists held that the supreme leadership of the community is for a man, and a few contemporary scholars argue the hadith concerns a specific absolute monarchy. State the majority view and say the disagreement exists. In the modern state, where the head of government is not the caliph, many Muslim scholars and countries accept women in the highest offices.

obj.q: “Women are told to stay at home (33:33).”
obj.a: 33:33 is addressed to the Prophet’s ﷺ wives, who held a special status (33:32), and the same wives travelled, taught and advised. Women in general prayed in the mosque, traded and taught in the Prophet’s time. The ruling concerns decorum, not exclusion.

prac.q: “Islam locks women in the home.”
prac.a: Look at the record: Khadija was a merchant who employed the Prophet ﷺ, Umm Salama’s advice resolved the crisis at Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari 2731), Aisha taught and corrected Companions, thousands of women were hadith scholars, and queens ruled in Yemen, Egypt and Delhi. There is a majority opinion that the top office of the whole community is for men, based on Bukhari 4425, and I would state that openly. Everything else, from scholarship to commerce, was open.

briefs.evs:
Khadija. A successful merchant who hired Muhammad ﷺ to trade for her before their marriage (Ibn Ishaq), and the first person to believe in him.
Umm Salama at Hudaybiyyah. When the Companions hesitated to obey the order to slaughter and shave after the treaty, the Prophet ﷺ followed Umm Salama’s advice, and they obeyed (Bukhari 2731-2732).
Aisha. She narrated over two thousand hadith and corrected senior Companions, which al-Zarkashi collected in al-Ijaba li-irad ma istadrakat-hu ‘A’isha ‘ala al-sahaba.
Women scholars. Mohammad Akram Nadwi’s al-Muhaddithat documents thousands of women hadith scholars across the centuries. Karima al-Marwaziyya (d. 1070) was one of the most sought-after transmitters of Sahih al-Bukhari.
Defenders. Nusayba bint Ka‘b defended the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa‘d).
Rulers. Arwa al-Sulayhi ruled Yemen (d. 1138), Shajar al-Durr was sultana of Egypt in 1250, Razia Sultan ruled Delhi in 1236-40, and several sultanas ruled Aceh in the seventeenth century.
The hadith. “A people who entrust their affairs to a woman will not prosper” (Bukhari 4425) was said when the Prophet ﷺ learned the Persians had crowned the daughter of Khosrow. The majority hold it restricts the supreme leadership (al-imama al-kubra) to men. Abu Hanifa allowed women as judges in matters where their testimony is accepted, and al-Tabari is reported to have allowed it in all matters.

briefs.title: Marriage: consent, the dowry and a wife’s way out
briefs.thesis: In Islamic law a marriage needs the bride’s consent, the dowry is her own property, and she can leave through khul‘ or judicial dissolution. Forced marriage violates the law, and the Prophet ﷺ annulled one.
briefs.sum: A valid Islamic marriage requires the bride’s consent (Bukhari 5136), the Prophet ﷺ annulled a forced one (5138), the dowry is hers, and she can leave through khul‘ (5273) or the court.

obj.q: “The wali requirement means a woman cannot choose her own husband.”
obj.a: The majority require a guardian for the marriage as protection and public witness, and that guardian cannot force her against her consent (Bukhari 5136, 5138). The Hanafi school holds that an adult woman may contract her own marriage. The shared principle is that her consent is required.

obj.q: “Men can divorce by talaq but women cannot.”
obj.a: The procedures differ: the husband pronounces talaq, and the wife can obtain khul‘ or a judicial dissolution, and can be given the power to divorce herself (tafwid) in the contract. Defend the substance, that she has routes out, and say that in practice courts and customs vary, which is often where abuses occur.

prac.q: “Muslim women are married off against their will.”
prac.a: That is forced marriage and Islamic law does not accept it. The Prophet ﷺ said a woman must be asked and her permission sought (Bukhari 5136), and when Khansa’s father married her against her will, he annulled it (Bukhari 5138). She also owns her dowry (4:4) and can leave through khul‘ (Bukhari 5273). Where forced marriages happen, they come from custom and they violate the sources.

briefs.evs:
Consent. “A previously married woman is not to be married until she is consulted, and a virgin is not to be married until her permission is sought.” They asked how a virgin gives permission and he said: “By her silence” (Bukhari 5136).
A forced marriage annulled. Khansa bint Khidham’s father married her against her will, and the Prophet ﷺ annulled the marriage (Bukhari 5138). In another report a girl said her father had married her to his nephew; the Prophet ﷺ gave her the choice, and she replied that she accepted but wanted women to know that fathers have no power to force them (Ibn Majah 1874).
The dowry. “Give women their dowries as a gift” (4:4). It is the wife’s property and she may spend it as she wishes.
Conditions. “The conditions most deserving to be fulfilled are those by which you make intimacy lawful” (Bukhari 2721), which the Hanbali school applies to conditions such as no second wife or no relocation.
Khul‘. Thabit ibn Qays's wife (named Habiba bint Sahl in some reports, Jamila in others) told the Prophet ﷺ she did not fault her husband’s character or religion but could not live with him; he asked her to return the garden she had received from him and told Thabit to accept it and divorce her (Bukhari 5273). See also 2:229.
Barira. A freed slave woman chose to leave her husband Mughith. The Prophet ﷺ interceded for him, she asked whether he was commanding her, he s

briefs.title: Honour killing, forced marriage and FGM: customs, not Islamic law
briefs.thesis: Honour killing and forced marriage are forbidden by Islamic law. FGM is not in the Quran, its hadith basis is weak and major Muslim institutions now prohibit it, though some classical jurists recommended or required it. State the record honestly, because the strongest reply concedes what is true.
briefs.sum: Honour killing and forced marriage are forbidden by Islamic law. FGM has no Quranic basis, a weak hadith, mixed classical opinion and is now prohibited by major authorities; state the history honestly.

obj.q: “Muslims do it, so it is Islamic.”
obj.a: Prevalence shows custom, not doctrine. Honour killings and FGM also occur among non-Muslims, and many Muslim societies do not practise them. The test is what the sources and the scholars say, and on honour killing the sources are clear, while on FGM the better-supported modern position forbids it.

obj.q: “Some classical scholars made FGM obligatory.”
obj.a: That is true, and a Muslim should say so. Those opinions were based on a weak report and on the medical knowledge of their time. The jurists’ own principle that harm must be removed is why contemporary bodies, among them Al-Azhar’s scholars and Egypt’s Dar al-Ifta, prohibit it.

prac.q: “Honour killings and genital cutting show what Islam does to women.”
prac.a: On honour killing, Islamic law calls killing outside a court murder (5:32, 17:33) and demands four eyewitnesses before an accusation of zina (24:4, 24:13), so nothing in the law permits it, and it occurs in other religions too. On FGM, it is not in the Quran, the hadith cited is weak by its own collector’s verdict, some classical jurists did recommend it, and today Egypt’s Grand Mufti and Al-Azhar’s scholars forbid it. I condemn both, and I am telling you what the sources say and where scholars differed.

briefs.evs:
Killing. “Whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely” (5:32); “Do not kill the soul that Allah has made sacred except by right” (17:33). A father or brother has no right to execute anyone.
The standard of proof. Zina requires four eyewitnesses to the act itself (24:13), and a false accusation without them is punished with eighty lashes (24:4). In li‘an a husband who accuses his wife without witnesses must swear oaths, not kill (24:6-9).
Not Islamic alone. Honour-based killings are reported among Hindus, Sikhs and Christians too, for example in parts of India, and Italy’s penal code gave reduced sentences for “crimes of honour” until 1981, so they cannot be traced to Islam alone.
Forced marriage. Invalid, as in the previous argument (Bukhari 5136, 5138).
FGM: the sources. The Quran does not mention it. The report usually cited (Abu Dawud 5271) advises “do not cut severely”, and Abu Dawud himself said that it is weak. The classical schools differ: some Shafi‘i texts call it obligatory, while the Hanafis, Malikis and Hanbalis describe it as a recommended or “honourable” custom for women.
FGM: the practice. UNICEF notes that FGM is found among Muslims, Christians and followers of traditional religions in the places where it occurs.
Modern rulings. In 2007, after a girl’s death, Egypt’s Grand Mufti Ali Goma

briefs.sec: Sexuality, gender identity and LGBT questions
briefs.title: What Islam says, and what it does not
briefs.thesis: Islam prohibits same-sex sexual acts, as Judaism and Christianity historically did, and judges them as acts, not as an identity. The same limit on sexual conduct binds every person, including heterosexuals outside marriage.
briefs.sum: Islam forbids same-sex acts as it forbids all sex outside marriage, judges acts and not persons, forbids spying, vigilantism and harassment, and demands very high proof for any legal penalty.

obj.q: “So you think gay people are evil.”
obj.a: No. Islam does not call a person evil for feeling an attraction; it asks every believer to refrain from certain acts, the unmarried heterosexual included. People are judged on their conduct and their effort, and God alone knows the heart. Mocking, shaming or harming anyone is itself forbidden.

obj.q: “Your position leads to violence against gay people.”
obj.a: Violence by individuals is forbidden in Islamic law, and no jurist allows a private person to punish. Where violence occurs it is a crime, as when any group is attacked. A moral belief that a practice is wrong is not an incitement to attack people, and neither is believing that adultery is wrong.

obj.q: “A Muslim minority in the West should therefore want such acts banned.”
obj.a: Muslims living in a non-Muslim country are bound by their agreements with their society and have no duty to impose their ethics by force. They can hold a belief and argue for it by persuasion while obeying the law of the land.

prac.q: “Do you really believe that being gay is a sin?”
prac.a: I believe Islam forbids same-sex sexual acts, as it forbids all sex outside marriage, and as Judaism and Christianity historically did. It does not say that a person is sinful for an attraction. The rule is about conduct and it applies to everyone. Nobody has the right to harass or harm anyone over it, and Islamic law forbids spying on people’s private lives.

briefs.evs:
The Quran. “Indeed you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a transgressing people” (7:81). See also 26:165-166, 27:54-55 and 29:28-29.
The consensus. The four Sunni schools and the Shia jurists agree the act is forbidden. They differ on penalties: some treat it as a fixed punishment, Abu Hanifa as a discretionary matter (ta‘zir). The report that prescribes death (Abu Dawud 4462) is disputed in grading, so do not build your case on it; the prohibition rests on the Quran and the consensus.
Same standard as zina. The same sexual ethic forbids sex outside marriage between a man and a woman, and zina carries a more clearly stated penalty in the Quran (24:2). The rule is about the act and not about the person’s orientation.
No spying, high proof. “Do not spy on one another” (49:12). A hadd offence needs a confession or four eyewitnesses to the act itself (24:4, 24:13 for zina), and the Prophet ﷺ urged concealing others’ sins (Bukhari 2442). In practice, private conduct was almost never prosecuted.
Vigilantism is forbidden. Only a court may impose a fixed penalty, and a private person who attacks another commits a grave wrong (5:32).

briefs.sec: Sexuality, gender identity and LGBT questions
briefs.title: “Born this way” does not settle the moral question
briefs.thesis: Even if sexual orientation is partly innate, it does not follow that acting on it is permissible. People accept that inclinations they did not choose still may need restraint, and Islam treats such inclinations as a test, not as a verdict.
briefs.sum: Innate does not mean permitted: the is-ought gap applies, the science shows influences and no single cause, and Islam treats inclinations as a test that every believer faces and that God does not make unbearable.

obj.q: “If God made them this way, why would He forbid it?”
obj.a: The same question applies to anyone with a strong desire they are asked to restrain, whether it is for sex outside marriage, for revenge or for another person’s property. The Islamic answer is that life is a test, that restraint is rewarded, and that God does not impose what a person cannot bear (2:286).

obj.q: “That is cruel. It asks people to be alone.”
obj.a: Islam asks all unmarried people to refrain until marriage, and for some of them that lasts a lifetime. It values celibacy, forbids shaming those who struggle, and places a heavy duty on the community to support them. The difficulty of a rule is a reason for compassion in applying it, not proof that it is false.

prac.q: “People do not choose their orientation, so condemning acting on it is bigotry.”
prac.a: Whether it is chosen is one question and whether it is right to act on it is another. Plenty of things people did not choose, like a quick temper or a desire for many partners, are still things we ask them to restrain. The research shows influences and not a single cause, and it cannot tell us what is permitted. Islam’s answer is that God tests us with desires and does not burden anyone beyond capacity, and that applies to every Muslim, whatever their desire.

briefs.evs:
The is-ought gap. David Hume’s point that moral conclusions do not follow from facts alone is accepted across moral philosophy. Natural does not equal good, and the reverse also fails.
The science is not what the slogan claims. A large 2019 genome-wide study of nearly half a million people (Ganna et al., Science) found no single “gay gene”, with common genetic variants together accounting for roughly 8 to 25 percent of the variation in same-sex behaviour. A review by Bailey and colleagues (Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2016) concluded that orientation has multiple biological and non-social influences, with little support for social or learned causes; either way, the moral question is not settled by causes.
