Islam’s framework. “He who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed” (67:2). “Hell is surrounded by desires and Paradise is surrounded by hardships” (Muslim 2822). “Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity” (2:286).
The unmarried. Islam asks every unmarried person to restrain sexual desire. The Prophet ﷺ told young men who could not marry to fast (Bukhari 5066), and the Quran praises Yahya (John) as hasur, one who restrained himself (3:39).
Complementarity. The Quran presents the male-female pairing as part of creation: “And of everything We created two mates” (51:49), and marriage as a source of tranquillity (30:21).

briefs.sec: Sexuality, gender identity and LGBT questions
briefs.title: The revisionist reading of Lot’s people
briefs.thesis: Some claim the story of Lot is about rape or inhospitality and not about same-sex relations. The Quran’s own wording rules that out, and every major classical commentary reads it the same way.
briefs.sum: The Quran names the act (7:81, 26:165-166), the other crimes in 29:29 are additional and not a replacement, and every major commentary reads the story the same way.

obj.q: “The Quran never mentions lesbians or consensual same-sex love.”
obj.a: The Quran’s statements on this are addressed to the act in general terms, and the jurists derived the prohibition from them and from the Prophetic rulings on sexual conduct. The absence of a modern category in a seventh-century text is not an absence of a ruling on the act.

obj.q: “Kugle is a scholar and you are not.”
obj.a: He is entitled to his views, but the Quranic text he is reinterpreting can be read by anyone who reads Arabic, and the phrase “instead of women” cannot be explained as a reference to rape. A scholar’s argument must be judged on whether it fits the evidence, and this one does not.

prac.q: “Lot’s people were destroyed for rape and inhospitality, not for being gay.”
prac.a: Read what God says to them: “You approach men with desire instead of women” (7:81) and “Do you approach males and leave what your Lord created for you of your wives?” (26:165-166). That names the act itself. 29:29 lists other crimes as well, but it does not erase the first. If the sin were only rape, God’s rebuke would have no reason to compare men with wives. Tabari, Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir all read it this way, and so did Jews and Christians reading the same story.

briefs.evs:
The wording. “Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord has created for you of your wives? Rather, you are a people transgressing” (26:165-166). “You approach men with desire instead of women” (7:81). The Quran calls it fahisha, “an immorality no one in the worlds preceded you in” (7:80).
The revisionist point. 29:29 adds that they “cut the road” and commit “evil in your gatherings”, and revisionists argue that the real crime was highway robbery and assault. But the verse begins with the act (“Do you approach men…?”) and lists other crimes in addition to it, so the act is not erased.
Lot’s offer. “These are my daughters; they are purer for you” (11:78; compare 15:71). The commentators (Tabari, Ibn Kathir) read this as an appeal to lawful marriage, which makes sense only if the issue is the kind of relation sought, not rape of anyone.
Across scripture. The same story and the same prohibition appear in Genesis 19, Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 and Jude 7. Muslims, Jews and Christians read these as condemning the act for most of their history.
The revisionists. The best-known contemporary argument is Scott Siraj al-Haqq Kugle’s Homosexuality in Islam (2010). Kugle argues from philological and hadith analysis that the Lot narrative concerns rape, inhospitality and violence, and mainstream scholars in every school reject that reading because it sets aside the expli

briefs.sec: Sexuality, gender identity and LGBT questions
briefs.title: Sex, gender and the categories Islamic law uses
briefs.thesis: Islamic law treats male and female as real and meaningful categories, recognises the rare intersex condition (khuntha) with detailed rulings, and forbids imitation of the other sex. A person’s felt identity is not treated as changing their legal sex, though scholars differ on some medical questions.
briefs.sum: Islamic law recognises male, female and the rare intersex exception, forbids imitation of the other sex (Bukhari 5885), and does not treat self-defined identity as changing legal sex; rulings on surgery differ.

obj.q: “Intersex people prove sex is not binary.”
obj.a: Intersex conditions are rare variations in development, and classical Islamic law, like modern medicine, treats them as exceptions needing their own rulings. A rare exception does not turn a binary into a spectrum, just as the existence of people born with six fingers does not mean humans have a variable number of fingers.

obj.q: “Different Muslim scholars disagree about transition, so Islam has no position.”
obj.a: They disagree on the medical question of surgery, but they do not disagree that God created male and female and that men and women should not imitate each other’s sex. Distinguish a disagreement on details from the absence of any position.

prac.q: “Gender is an identity, not biology. Who are you to say what anyone is?”
prac.a: Islamic law works with male and female as real categories, and has always had a special rule for the rare intersex person, which only makes sense if the two categories are real. Muslims believe that is how God created humanity (53:45). That does not mean anyone may mock or mistreat another person. Muslim scholars differ on questions of surgery, and I would tell you that honestly, but none of them says identity alone changes someone’s legal sex.

briefs.evs:
The categories. “He created the two mates, the male and the female” (53:45). Classical fiqh devotes chapters to the khuntha, the person of ambiguous sex, with rulings on prayer rows, inheritance and marriage, and the jurists assign the person to a sex by physical signs wherever these exist, which presupposes the two categories.
The hadith. “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed men who imitate women and women who imitate men” (Bukhari 5885, from Ibn Abbas).
The mukhannathun. The Prophet ﷺ ordered the effeminate men (mukhannathun) who had been allowed into women's quarters to be kept out after one described a woman's body (Bukhari 5235); the report is also cited by jurists in discussing gender behaviour.
Medical rulings differ. Contemporary scholars generally allow surgery to correct a physical ambiguity in intersex people. Rulings on sex reassignment for people without a physical ambiguity differ: many bodies, including councils of fiqh scholars, forbid it, while a few authorities (for example, a 1980s ruling associated with Ayatollah Khomeini in Iran) permitted it in some cases.
Pastoral note. Islamic law protects the dignity of all people, forbids insults, and requires equal justice in courts, whatever a person’s status.

briefs.title: Secular liberalism is a worldview, not a neutral referee
briefs.thesis: Secular liberalism claims to be neutral between ways of life, but its tests for what counts as harm, consent and personhood depend on disputed views of the good. It is one worldview among others and has to argue its case like the rest.
briefs.sum: Liberalism’s tests for harm, consent and personhood rest on disputed moral views, and liberal states restrict consensual acts on moral grounds. It is a worldview to be argued for, not a neutral referee.

obj.q: “Liberalism at least lets everyone live as they choose.”
obj.a: It protects real goods, and Muslims benefit from freedom of conscience in liberal states. But it does not let everyone live as they choose: it forbids polygamy, drug sale, certain consensual acts and some speech. Every society draws lines, and liberalism draws its lines using its own contested values.

obj.q: “Religious claims need justification; liberal values do not.”
obj.a: Both do. Appealing to “harm” or “autonomy” without an account of why those are the right values is as much a faith commitment as appealing to revelation. The debate should compare grounds, not exempt one side from giving them.

prac.q: “Secular law is neutral. Religious law imposes one group’s morals on everyone.”
prac.a: All law imposes someone’s morals. France bans dwarf-tossing with the dwarf’s consent, and the European Court upheld a ban on consensual adult incest. Those are moral judgements about dignity. Rawls himself accepted that liberalism could claim only a limited, political neutrality. So the real question is which moral foundations are true, and I am glad to compare grounds.

briefs.evs:
Philosophers admit it. Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981; Whose Justice? Which Rationality?, 1988) argued that there is no tradition-independent standpoint of reason. Michael Sandel (Liberalism and the Limits of Justice, 1982) argued that liberalism presupposes a particular picture of the self. John Rawls himself retreated in Political Liberalism (1993) to claim only a limited, “political” neutrality.
Mill’s test needs a view of harm. John Stuart Mill’s harm principle (On Liberty, 1859) allows interference only to prevent harm to others. But what counts as harm (offence? damage to the social fabric? harm to the self?) is exactly what people dispute.
Consent is not enough even for liberal states. In 1995 France’s Conseil d’État upheld the ban on dwarf-tossing despite the consent of the dwarf, on grounds of human dignity (Commune de Morsang-sur-Orge). In Stübing v. Germany (2012) the European Court of Human Rights upheld a criminal ban on consensual incest between adult siblings. Both restrict consenting adults on moral grounds.
Quran 2:256. Islam does not claim to coerce belief (2:256; 10:99), and so argues its case in public. The Quran invites evidence: “Bring your proof, if you are truthful” (2:111).

briefs.title: Where do universal human rights come from?
briefs.thesis: Universal, equal human rights need a ground that makes every person’s worth equal and non-negotiable. Some leading secular thinkers acknowledge the religious roots of equal human dignity (Habermas), argue that Locke's equality rested on theology (Waldron), or deny that rights need any foundation (Rorty), while Islam supplies one in creation and honour from God.
briefs.sum: Equal, universal rights need a ground. Habermas concedes their religious lineage, Rorty finds no deeper foundation, and the Quran grounds dignity in God’s honouring of humanity (17:70, 49:13).

obj.q: “Atheists can be good without God.”
obj.a: Of course; the argument is about grounding and not about behaviour. The question is not whether atheists behave well but what makes human equality true, rather than a useful convention. A convention can be changed by a majority, while a right grounded in God cannot.

obj.q: “Religion has been used to deny rights.”
obj.a: That is true of every ideology that has held power, secular ones included. It shows that a ground can be misused. It does not remove the need for a ground, and it does not tell us whether the Islamic ground in 17:70 and 49:13 is true.

prac.q: “Human rights do not need God. They are common sense.”
prac.a: If they were common sense, there would be no need for the philosophy. Habermas, who is not religious, concedes that universal egalitarianism is the legacy of Jewish and Christian ethics, and Rorty admits rights rest on sentiment, not a foundation. In Islam the ground is that God honoured every child of Adam (17:70) and that only taqwa ranks people (49:13). I am asking what grounds rights for you.

briefs.evs:
Habermas. The German philosopher Jürgen Habermas, a non-believer, wrote that universalistic egalitarianism, “from which sprang the ideas of freedom and social solidarity”, is “the direct legacy of the Judaic ethic of justice and the Christian ethic of love” (Time of Transitions, 2006).
Waldron and Wolterstorff. Jeremy Waldron (God, Locke, and Equality, 2002) argues that Locke’s basic equality depends on theological premises. Nicholas Wolterstorff (Justice: Rights and Wrongs, 2008) argues that rights are grounded in being loved by God.
Rorty’s alternative. Richard Rorty (“Human Rights, Rationality, and Sentimentality”, 1993) argued that rights rest on no deep foundation, only on cultivated sentiment, a view Rorty held to be sufficient, and which critics say leaves rights without a ground.
The Islamic ground. “We have certainly honoured the children of Adam” (17:70). “We created you from a male and female… the most honoured is the most God-conscious” (49:13). “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely” (5:32). The Prophet ﷺ declared in the Farewell Sermon that “your blood, your wealth and your honour are sacred to each other” (Bukhari 1739, Muslim 1218), and that no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab except by taqwa (Ahmad 23489).

briefs.title: “Religion causes most wars” and the data
briefs.thesis: The claim that religion is the main cause of war is not supported by the historical record, and the category “religious violence” is itself contested. This is not a defence of every act done in religion’s name.
briefs.sum: About 7 percent of 1,763 wars are classified as religious (66 of 123 involving Islam), the category is contested, the largest modern atrocities were secular, and Islam’s own rules forbid killing civilians.

obj.q: “But what about ISIS and Muslim terrorism?”
obj.a: Acknowledge it and condemn it. Groups that kill civilians violate the Quran’s rules (5:32) and the Prophet’s instructions in war, and the great majority of Muslim scholars and the victims of such groups are themselves Muslims. Naming Islam as the cause requires showing the groups’ conduct follows the sources, and it does not.

obj.q: “The 7 percent figure is only for wars labelled religious.”
obj.a: That is the point of the coding dispute: if nationalism and ideology are also treated as secular belief systems, the picture shifts further away from religion as a special cause. The honest claim is that the evidence does not support the slogan, not that religion is harmless.

prac.q: “Religion is the biggest cause of war in history.”
prac.a: That is not what the data shows. In the Encyclopedia of Wars, 123 of 1,763 wars are classified as religious, about 7 percent, and I should add that 66 of those involve Islam, so I am not hiding anything. William Cavanaugh also argues that the line between religious and secular violence is arbitrary. The deadliest conflicts of the last century were fought by nations and ideologies that were openly secular. And Islam’s rules of war forbid harming civilians (5:32).

briefs.evs:
The Encyclopedia of Wars. Charles Phillips and Alan Axelrod’s Encyclopedia of Wars (2005) records 1,763 wars, of which 123 (about 7 percent) are classified as religious. Be honest about the rest of the figure: the 123 figure is taken from the encyclopedia's index, and secondary tallies put about 66 of them as involving Islam; the encyclopedia does not itself make that classification. The coding is also debated, so cite it as a rough measure.
The category itself. William Cavanaugh (The Myth of Religious Violence, 2009) argues that the line between “religious” and “secular” violence is an arbitrary modern construction, and that nationalism and liberal ideology function as quasi-religions that also command killing and sacrifice.
The twentieth century. Estimates put the deaths of the Second World War at around 70 to 85 million, and the Soviet and Chinese famines and purges at tens of millions more, under states that officially rejected religion or acted on nationalist and racial ideology.
Islam’s own rules. “Do not transgress; indeed Allah does not like transgressors” (2:190). “Whoever kills a soul unjustly… it is as if he had killed all mankind” (5:32). Abu Bakr’s instructions to his armies forbade killing women, children, the elderly and monks and cutting down fruit trees (Muwatta Malik, Book of Jihad, a mursal report widely cited by jurists).

briefs.title: Muslims as citizens of secular states
briefs.thesis: Classical and contemporary jurists broadly hold that Muslims living in a non-Muslim state are bound by their agreements and by the law of the land wherever it does not require disobeying God. The charge that sharia makes Muslims disloyal confuses personal religious practice with imposing penal law.
briefs.sum: Muslims in non-Muslim states are bound by their covenants (17:34), the Prophet ﷺ sent Muslims to live under a Christian king, and most contemporary jurists tell them to obey the law of the land.

obj.q: “Muslims want sharia to replace our laws.”
obj.a: Most Muslims in secular states want the freedom to pray, fast, eat halal and dress modestly, which is religious freedom, and they argue for their views by lawful means like any other group. Islamic penal law requires an Islamic court and state, and no jurist authorises individuals in a non-Muslim country to apply it. A person can hold that God’s law is best and also keep his covenant with his neighbours.

obj.q: “An oath of allegiance conflicts with allegiance to God.”
obj.a: Most scholars say a citizenship oath can be taken where it does not require disobeying God, in the same way that Muslims honour contracts and visas. Some stricter scholars object. The majority position is the one most Muslims in the West follow.

prac.q: “Muslims cannot be loyal citizens of a secular state because they answer to sharia.”
prac.a: Islamic law tells Muslims to keep their covenants (17:34, Abu Dawud 3594), and the Prophet ﷺ sent his followers to live under a Christian king. Contemporary scholars of Muslim minorities tell Muslims in the West to obey the law of the land where it does not demand disobeying God. Sharia covers prayer, fasting and ethics in a person’s own life, and the penal rulings need a court and a state, so no individual or community living in a secular country may apply them. Some stricter scholars differ and I would tell you that too.

briefs.evs:
Abyssinia. The Prophet ﷺ sent persecuted Muslims to the Christian king of Abyssinia, “a king in whose land no one is wronged” (the account of Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib, Ahmad 1740). They lived there for years under his protection without rebelling against it.
Covenants. “Fulfil the covenant; indeed the covenant will be questioned” (17:34). “Muslims are bound by their conditions” (Abu Dawud 3594, Tirmidhi 1352). “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise” (Bukhari 3166).
Hudhayfa at Badr. Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman and his father promised the Quraysh not to fight alongside the Prophet ﷺ in return for being let go. The Prophet ﷺ told them to keep the promise: “We will fulfil their covenant and seek Allah’s help against them” (Muslim 1787).
Jurists on minorities. Contemporary scholars of the “fiqh of minorities”, such as Taha Jabir al-Alwani and the European Council for Fatwa and Research (founded 1997), rule that Muslims in the West should obey the law of the land and honour the covenant of residence. The old division of the world into dar al-Islam and dar al-harb is a juristic construct from a period of constant war, not a Quranic category, and al-Shafi‘i is usually credited with recognising a third category of covenant (dar al-‘ahd / dar al-sulh).
Where scholars differ. A minority of scholars, especially in some Salafi circles, discourage naturalisati

briefs.title: Shura, sovereignty and the “Islam versus democracy” charge
briefs.thesis: Islam has no clergy or priestly rule, requires consultation in public affairs, and places ultimate sovereignty with God. Whether this is compatible with democracy depends on definitions, and Muslim thinkers differ.
briefs.sum: Islam commands consultation (42:38), has no priesthood and holds rulers accountable, and puts ultimate limits with God. Compatibility with democracy depends on the definition, and Muslim thinkers disagree.

obj.q: “A system with divine limits is not a democracy.”
obj.a: It is not a system of unlimited majority rule, and Islam says so. Many constitutional democracies also have limits that majorities cannot cross, such as entrenched rights. The question is which limits and who decides, and Islam places the limits in revelation, with consultation in everything else.

obj.q: “Muslim countries are not democratic.”
obj.a: Many are authoritarian, and Muslim societies need accountability. That is a fact about governments, and several Muslim-majority states hold elections. Judge the doctrine by its texts and the competing scholarly views, not only by the worst governments.

prac.q: “Islam and democracy cannot go together.”
prac.a: It depends on what you mean. If democracy is consultation, participation and accountable rulers, the Quran commands consultation (42:38) and the early caliphs were chosen by pledge and publicly corrected. If it means a majority can decide any question, including what God has forbidden, then Islam differs, and so do many constitutional democracies that limit what majorities can do. Muslim thinkers differ among themselves on this, and I would show you where.

briefs.evs:
Consultation. “And whose affair is consultation among themselves” (42:38) describes the believers. “And consult them in the matter” (3:159) was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself.
No priesthood. Islam has no sacramental clergy. Scholars (‘ulama) hold authority by knowledge and can be challenged; the caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar were publicly corrected by ordinary Muslims, and the rulers were accountable to the law.
Early practice. Abu Bakr was chosen at the gathering at Saqifa and then given the public pledge (bay‘a), and Umar appointed a consultative council for his succession. These show consultation in practice, though not a modern electoral system.
Where Muslim thinkers differ. Some (such as Abul A‘la Mawdudi) stressed God’s sovereignty (hakimiyya) as opposed to popular sovereignty; others (such as Rashid al-Ghannushi and many contemporary scholars) argue that democratic institutions are a way to implement consultation and accountability within Islamic limits.

briefs.title: What the classical law says on apostasy, stated honestly
briefs.thesis: The majority of classical jurists held that a Muslim who publicly abandons Islam is to be called to repent and then, if he refuses, faces the death penalty from a court. There are early and modern dissenting views. A debater should state this plainly before giving context.
briefs.sum: The majority classical ruling is death for apostasy after a call to repent, by a court. There is early and modern dissent, no private person may apply it, and a debater should say all three.

obj.q: “So you want to kill people who leave Islam?”
obj.a: No Muslim in a non-Muslim society is allowed to punish anyone, and no individual in any society may do so. The classical law assigns the decision to a court and has the conditions above. The question of whether and how it should be applied in modern states is debated among Muslim scholars, as the dissenting views show. I would rather give you the accurate position than deny it.

obj.q: “Your dissenters are a minority.”
obj.a: They are a minority on the question of punishment, and I said so. But they are classical as well as modern, and their argument is based on the sources, the Quran’s silence on any earthly penalty and the Prophet’s own practice (see the next two arguments).

prac.q: “Islam says apostates must be executed. Is that true or not?”
prac.a: The majority of classical jurists said yes, after a call to repent, and carried out by a court, based on Bukhari 6922 and the hadith of the three cases (Bukhari 6878). I won’t deny it. But there is a long tradition of dissent from al-Nakha‘i and al-Thawri to Shaltut and al-Alwani, Umar objected to a man’s execution without a chance to repent, and the Quran itself names no earthly penalty. So the honest answer is: that is the majority classical ruling, and it is debated.

briefs.evs:
The hadith. “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” (Bukhari 6922). And: “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except for one of three: a life for a life, a married adulterer, and the one who leaves his religion and separates from the community” (Bukhari 6878, Muslim 1676). The second wording ties the offence to leaving and “separating from the community”.
The schools. The majority hold that the apostate is called to repent first. The Hanafis hold that women are imprisoned and not killed, while the other schools include women. The Malikis give three days’ delay.
Umar’s reaction. When told that an apostate had been killed straight away, Umar said: “Why did you not imprison him for three days, give him a loaf every day, and call him to repent? Perhaps he would have repented and Allah would have accepted him” (Muwatta Malik).
Dissent. Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i and Sufyan al-Thawri held that the apostate should be invited to repent indefinitely. In modern times Mahmud Shaltut and Taha Jabir al-Alwani (La ikraha fi al-din) argued that the penalty is discretionary or limited to those who fight the community, and Abdullah Saeed and Hassan Saeed wrote Freedom of Religion, Apostasy and Islam (2004) in the same direction.
Who applies it. Fixed penalties are for a judge in a functioning Islamic court, never for individuals, and a Muslim minority living in a non-Muslim state is not authorised to

briefs.title: “No compulsion in religion” and the apostasy ruling
briefs.thesis: The Quran guarantees freedom to choose belief, never prescribes an earthly penalty for apostasy, and the classical ruling is linked to public defection from the community. The tension is real and the answers are scholarly, not rhetorical.
briefs.sum: The Quran guarantees no compulsion (2:256) and names no earthly penalty for apostasy. The classical ruling rests on hadith and public defection, and modern scholars dispute whether it still applies.

obj.q: “You cannot have both 2:256 and a death penalty.”
obj.a: The verse guarantees that nobody is forced in, and Islamic law has historically distinguished a private change of belief, which jurists said could not be investigated, from public renunciation. The ruling is a point of dispute inside the tradition, and I have not claimed that it fully resolves the tension; I have said where the debate lies.

obj.q: “Treason is about betraying the state, not changing your mind.”
obj.a: That is the strongest objection and the reason many modern scholars reject the penalty for private belief. The classical position is a claim about a particular historical polity, and modern jurists such as al-Alwani argue the reasoning does not carry over.

prac.q: “How can Islam say there is no compulsion in religion and then execute apostates?”
prac.a: The Quran does say there is no compulsion (2:256), and it names no earthly punishment for apostasy. The classical jurists attached the penalty to public defection from the community, comparing it to treason, and many modern scholars say that reasoning no longer applies. I admit there is a tension and that scholars dispute how to resolve it, but I would not say the rule is simply a command to force belief.

briefs.evs:
Freedom of belief. “There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clear from the wrong” (2:256). “Would you then compel the people until they become believers?” (10:99). “Say: the truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve” (18:29). “You are only a reminder; you are not a controller over them” (88:21-22).
The Quran’s verses on apostasy. 2:217, 3:90, 4:137 and 16:106 speak of loss in this world and the next and a severe punishment from God, but none prescribes an earthly penalty.
The treason analogy. Many classical jurists linked the death penalty to apostasy together with leaving the community (the second wording of the hadith in Muslim 1676). Most states treat betrayal in wartime harshly: treason can carry death under US federal law (18 U.S.C. § 2381), and wartime desertion was punished by execution (Private Eddie Slovik in 1945).
The limits of the analogy. A critic will say that belief is not treason. The classical argument is that in the early community religion was the political identity, so public renunciation was treated as defection. Whether that logic applies now is exactly what contemporary scholars dispute.

briefs.title: The Prophet’s own record with those who left
briefs.thesis: The Prophet’s ﷺ recorded handling of people who left Islam, or were suspected of insincere belief, was largely restraint, and the people executed were tied to murder, theft or armed rebellion.
briefs.sum: The Prophet ﷺ let the Bedouin go, spared Ibn Ubayy, pardoned Abdullah ibn Sa‘d and accepted the Hudaybiyyah clause; those executed had killed or rebelled. Majority jurists still read the hadith more broadly.

obj.q: “Bukhari 6922 says kill him. You are ignoring it.”
obj.a: I am not ignoring it; it is the main proof of the majority view and I have set it out. The question is how the Prophet ﷺ applied his own words, and the record shows restraint and punishment tied to violence or rebellion. The majority jurists read the hadith as general; the dissenters read it in light of this record.

obj.q: “Those pardoned were exceptions.”
obj.a: They are the recorded cases. If belief alone were a capital offence enforced without exception, the exceptions would be the rule. That the Prophet ﷺ gave reasons (such as avoiding the label ‘Muhammad kills his companions’) shows he considered the effect on the community.

prac.q: “The Prophet ordered people killed for leaving Islam.”
prac.a: The recorded cases show otherwise. A Bedouin withdrew his pledge and was let go (Bukhari 7211), Ibn Ubayy was left alone (Bukhari 4905), Abdullah ibn Sa‘d was pardoned (Abu Dawud 2683), and at Hudaybiyyah the Prophet accepted that people who went to Quraysh would not be pursued (Muslim 1784). The group executed in Bukhari 233 had killed and robbed. The majority jurists read Bukhari 6922 more broadly, and I would tell you that.

briefs.evs:
The Bedouin who left. A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ, pledged allegiance, fell ill, and asked to withdraw it. The Prophet declined three times, and the man left Medina; no action was taken (Bukhari 7211).
Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The leader of the hypocrites was not executed, though Umar asked, because the Prophet ﷺ said: “People would say that Muhammad kills his companions” (Bukhari 4905, Muslim 2584).
Abdullah ibn Sa‘d ibn Abi Sarh. A scribe who apostatised and fled to Mecca, then was pardoned at the conquest after Uthman’s intercession (Abu Dawud 2683).
Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh. He left Islam for Christianity in Abyssinia, and the sources report no action against him (Ibn Ishaq).
Hudaybiyyah. The treaty of Hudaybiyyah required Muslims to send back anyone from Quraysh who came over without his guardian’s permission, while Quraysh was not required to return anyone who went from the Muslims to them. The Prophet ﷺ accepted this and said: “Whoever goes from us to them, may Allah keep him far away” (Muslim 1784). He did not order such people pursued.
Those who were executed. The ‘Urayna group accepted Islam, killed a shepherd, mutilated him and stole the camels; some narrations add that they left Islam, and the punishment is usually argued to be for the murder and robbery (Bukhari 233, 3018, 6802). The Ridda wars involved both tribes that withheld zakat and tribes and claimants who abando

briefs.title: Blasphemy: classical rulings, patience, and the free-speech comparison
briefs.thesis: Classical law treats public insult of the Prophet ﷺ as a grave offence, schools differ on the penalty and on non-Muslims, and the Quran and Sunnah command patience under insult. Modern statutes are often broader than the classical law, and mob action has no basis in it.
briefs.sum: Classical schools treat insulting the Prophet ﷺ as grave but differ on penalties, the Quran and Prophet teach patience, vigilantism is forbidden, modern statutes overreach, and no society has unlimited speech.

obj.q: “So Muslims want to kill anyone who draws the Prophet.”
obj.a: No. The classical law gives the penalty to a court, the Quran commands leaving mocking gatherings (4:140), and the Prophet’s own example was patience (Bukhari 6024, 3231). Individuals who kill over insult act against Islamic law, and many scholars have said so after each such incident.

obj.q: “Free speech is an absolute value in the West.”
obj.a: It is not. Germany and France criminalise Holocaust denial, the UK criminalises incitement to hatred, and until 2008 England had a blasphemy offence, and Ireland abolished its own blasphemy offence by referendum in 2018 and statute in 2019. The real question is which speech a society chooses to restrict and why. Muslims say the sacred also deserves protection, and you may disagree, but then we are discussing where to draw a line, not whether to draw one.

prac.q: “Islam punishes blasphemy by death. That is the opposite of free speech.”
prac.a: The classical schools do treat insulting the Prophet ﷺ as grave, and they differ on the penalty and on non-Muslims. But the Quran tells believers to leave mocking gatherings (4:140) and repel evil with good (41:34), and the Prophet ﷺ answered abuse with patience (Bukhari 6024). Private violence is forbidden, and modern laws like Pakistan’s 295-C go beyond the classical rulings and are abused. And no society has absolute free speech: Germany and France criminalise Holocaust denial, and England had a blasphemy law until 2008.

briefs.evs:
The Quran’s tone. “Do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge” (6:108). “Repel evil by that which is better” (41:34). “When you hear the verses of Allah denied and mocked, do not sit with them” (4:140), which prescribes leaving the gathering, not violence.
The Prophet’s patience. When some Jews greeted him with “al-sam ‘alaykum” (death be upon you), Aisha answered in kind and he said: “Gently, Aisha” (Bukhari 6024). At Ta’if the angel of the mountains offered to crush the town, and he refused (Bukhari 3231).
Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf. The best-known case of a man killed for insulting the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari 4037) is one where he was also inciting Quraysh to war, breaking the Medina covenant, and composing verses against Muslim women. Classical jurists differ on whether the case shows a rule on insult alone.
The schools. The Malikis, Shafi‘is and Hanbalis (see Ibn Taymiyya’s al-Sarim al-maslul) hold that insulting the Prophet ﷺ merits death. The early Hanafi position is that a non-Muslim who insults is not put to death for it, and that a Muslim who does so is an apostate, though later Hanafi jurists allowed discretionary death for repeat offences. The details of repentance also differ.
Modern statutes. Pakistan’s section 295-C was introduced in 1986, and the Federal Shariat Court in 1990 held that death should be the only penalty. A

briefs.sec: Manuscripts and the history of the text
briefs.title: Seven ahruf, seven readings, ten readings: three different things
briefs.thesis: Critics often run together three different terms: the seven ahruf of the hadith, the seven or ten canonical readings (qira’at), and the Uthmanic text itself. Keeping them apart removes most of the force of the “seven versions of the Quran” charge.
briefs.sum: The ahruf, the qira’at and the Uthmanic text are three distinct things. The ten readings share one written outline and a listed set of authorised variants, so “seven Qurans” is a confusion of terms.

obj.q: “Uthman burned six of the seven ahruf and kept one.”
obj.a: That was the view of al-Tabari and some others. Many scholars, such as Ibn al-Jazari, hold instead that the Uthmanic outline preserves the readings confirmed in the Prophet’s ﷺ final recitation of the Quran to Gabriel (the ‘ardah al-akhira), which is why more than one reading fits it. Scholars differ on this point, so present it as a scholarly debate and not as a settled fact.

obj.q: “Different readings mean the text was not fixed.”
obj.a: They mean the recitation was transmitted with authorised variations. The text, in the sense of its consonantal skeleton and the content, is the same. The existence of an authorised variation is a feature of the revelation as the sources describe it, not a defect in preservation.

prac.q: “Muslims admit there are seven versions of the Quran, so it cannot be one preserved book.”
prac.a: Three different things are being run together. The seven ahruf are a Prophetic permission for variation in recitation. The readings are the later canonical systems, seven or ten depending on the list, each with an unbroken chain to the Prophet ﷺ and each fitting the same written outline. The written text is a single one. The differences are listed, small and transmitted by name, which is the opposite of a text drifting through copying errors.

briefs.evs:
The ahruf. “The Quran was revealed in seven ahruf, so recite whichever is easy for you” (Bukhari 2419, 4992; Muslim 818). The word harf means “mode” or “manner”. Scholars have proposed many meanings (dialects, synonyms, types of variation), and a classical view held that the permission narrowed after Uthman’s standardisation.
The readings. Ibn Mujahid (d. 324 AH/936 CE) selected seven leading readers of the early centuries, and later Ibn al-Jazari (d. 833 AH/1429 CE) set out ten, with three conditions: an authentic chain back to the Prophet ﷺ, conformity with Arabic, and agreement with one of the Uthmanic copies. A reading that fails any of the three is not canonical.
The text. All ten readings fit the Uthmanic consonantal outline, with a handful of well-known rasm differences between the regional codices (for example 2:132, 9:100, 57:24) and differ mainly in vowels, in whether a letter is pointed one way or another, and in a limited number of word forms.
Not seven books. The hadith of Bukhari 2419 shows the Prophet ﷺ affirming two recitations of one surah as both revealed. It does not describe seven different Qurans.
Comparison. The New Testament exists in more than five thousand Greek manuscripts whose variants are counted in the hundreds of thousands (estimates differ), with several passages disputed even by conservative editors. The variants of the Quran are a fixed, listed

briefs.sec: Manuscripts and the history of the text
briefs.title: The Sana’a palimpsest: what it shows and what it does not
briefs.thesis: The Sana’a palimpsest has a lower text with variants from the standard text, and it is often presented as proof that the Quran evolved. On the researchers’ own account, the lower text is overwhelmingly the same Quran, the parchment is dated by radiocarbon to between 578 and 669 CE, which is no later than the first decades of Islam, and a codex that differs from the standard text is exactly what the Islamic account of the Companion codices predicts.
briefs.sum: The Sana’a lower text is an early Companion-type codex, dated to the first generation, overwhelmingly the same Quran with variants in wording and order, which is what the Islamic account already says existed.

obj.q: “The variants show the Quran was changed after Muhammad.”
obj.a: The variants show that one early codex differed in some wording and surah order from the standard. The sources already say that such codices existed. What the palimpsest does not show is a different message, different laws, a different narrative or a text that was composed in the next century. Even its editors treat it as a Qur'an text, while arguing that it represents a different, pre-Uthmanic text-type.

obj.q: “The material has been kept secret.”
obj.a: Sadeghi and Goudarzi’s 2012 article transcribes the lower text of Sana’a 1 and reproduces images, and Asma Hilali’s The Sanaa Palimpsest (Oxford, 2017) studies the whole palimpsest. Early press claims about it were often exaggerated, so rely on the specialists’ published work.

prac.q: “The Sana’a palimpsest proves the Quran was edited after Muhammad.”
prac.a: It proves that one early codex had some different wording and surah order, which is exactly what the Islamic sources say about the Companions’ codices and about Uthman’s standardisation (Bukhari 4987). Radiocarbon puts the parchment in the first half-century after the Prophet’s death, and the scholars who edited it describe a text that is, apart from limited variants, the same Quran. It confirms the story rather than contradicting it.

briefs.evs:
What it is. A set of parchment leaves found in the Great Mosque of Sana’a in 1972, in which an earlier Quranic text was washed off and a later Quranic text was written over it (the upper text is close to the standard Uthmanic text). The scholars Behnam Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi published the lower text in 2012 (“Ṣanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān”, Der Islam).
Its date. Sadeghi and Uwe Bergmann’s radiocarbon dating of the parchment (Arabica, 2010) placed it, with about 95 percent probability, between 578 and 669 CE, a range that covers the Prophet's lifetime and the following decades (they argue for a date before about 671).
What the lower text shows. According to Sadeghi and Goudarzi, the lower text is a non-Uthmanic codex that contains the same Quran with differences in wording and a different order of some surahs. Their conclusion is that it is a non-Uthmanic text-type of the kind the sources attribute to Companion codices, though not identical to any reported codex; they draw conclusions about the text's early history that go beyond the traditional account, which a debater should acknowledge
The Islamic account. The sources report that Ibn Mas‘ud, Ubayy and others had private codices with variant wording and a different surah order, that this alarmed Hudhayfa, and that Uthman had a standard copy written and sent to the main cities (Bukhari 4987 for Hudhayfa and the co

briefs.sec: Manuscripts and the history of the text
briefs.title: Birmingham, Tübingen and the radiocarbon dates
briefs.thesis: Radiocarbon dating of early Quran manuscripts places them in the lifetime of the Prophet’s Companions. The dates are ranges for the animal skin, not for the writing, so they should be presented carefully, and critics who claim a date before Muhammad are reading the range wrongly.
briefs.sum: Birmingham (568-645), Tübingen (649-675) and Sana’a (about 578-669) put written Quranic text within the Companions’ lifetimes. The dates are for the skin, and claims of a pre-Muhammad text misread the range.

obj.q: “568 is before Muhammad was born, so the Quran predates him.”
obj.a: The range is for the death of the animal, which is the earliest the writing could be, and the probability is not spread evenly across it. A parchment is normally written on within years or decades of preparation. A range that reaches back to 568 and forward to 645 includes the whole lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ and the early caliphate, and Surahs 18-20 are traditionally classed as Meccan.

obj.q: “Scholars like Alba Fedeli say the Birmingham leaves are a palimpsest, so they were rewritten.”
obj.a: Fedeli’s proposal about a possible earlier layer is debated. In any case a palimpsest shows that parchment was reused, which would make the writing later than the skin, still within the early period and still the same Quranic text. The dating tells us the text in those surahs was in circulation very early.

prac.q: “Radiocarbon dates show the Quran existed before Muhammad was born.”
prac.a: They give a range for when the animal died, and the writing is the same age or later. The Birmingham range is 568-645 CE, and it starts two years before the Prophet’s birth and includes his entire life and the caliphate of Abu Bakr and Umar. The probability is not flat across the range, and the Hijazi script and the Meccan surahs on the leaves fit the first generation. Tübingen is 649-675, and Sana’a around 578-669. All point to a written Quran inside the lifetimes of the Companions.

briefs.evs:
Birmingham (Mingana 1572a with Paris BnF Arabe 328c). Two leaves with parts of Surahs 18-20 in Hijazi script. The Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit dated the parchment in 2015 to 568-645 CE with 95.4 percent probability. The Prophet ﷺ was born around 570 and died in 632.
Tübingen (Ma VI 165). A manuscript that covers 17:36 to 36:57, dated by radiocarbon (2014) to 649-675 CE with 95.4 percent probability.
Others. The Sana’a leaves (see the previous argument), and manuscripts such as Paris BnF Arabe 328a and British Library Or. 2165, belong to the same early Hijazi tradition; the Sana'a leaves are radiocarbon-dated, the others are dated palaeographically to roughly the first two centuries of Islam.
The comparison. The oldest New Testament fragment (P52, a few verses of John) is dated by palaeography to the second century CE, and the oldest complete New Testament manuscripts are from the fourth century. The Quran has substantial parts in manuscripts within a century at most of its revelation, and the oral chain was running from the beginning.
The caution. The date refers to the skin. The parchment can be older than the ink by years or decades, or reused. State the ranges as they are and avoid saying that “the manuscript is from the Prophet’s time”.

briefs.sec: Manuscripts and the history of the text
briefs.title: Uthman’s standardisation: what it did and did not do
briefs.thesis: The Islamic sources describe the Uthmanic recension as a public, consultative standardisation of a text that already existed in written and memorised form, accepted by the Companions. It neither created the Quran nor silenced all other readings.
briefs.sum: Uthman’s standardisation was a public, consultative step based on an existing text, accepted by the Companions, and the readings of those whose codices were retired survive in the canon.

obj.q: “Ibn Mas‘ud was angry about the burning of his codex.”
obj.a: The sources do report his objection, and a debater should say so. They also report that the Companions as a body supported the decision, that Ibn Mas‘ud’s readings were taught through Kufa and survive in the reading of ‘Asim, and that no early Muslim community produced a rival text of the Quran. A disagreement about method, voiced and recorded, is not evidence of a corrupted text.

obj.q: “Burning copies is destroying evidence.”
obj.a: The aim was to stop a dispute over recitation in the army. It was done in public with the main Companions present, and the content of the retired codices is known from the reports, which still circulate. Compare Part I on the “missing verses” reports.

prac.q: “Uthman burned every copy that disagreed with him, so the Quran is just his version.”
prac.a: The sources say that Uthman used a text collected under Abu Bakr from the Prophet’s scribes and from memorisers, that he did it in public with a committee headed by Zayd, and that the Companions agreed. The disputed readings were retired, but the reading of Ibn Mas‘ud and Ali survives through ‘Asim, so nothing the community counted as Qur'an was lost. And the oldest manuscripts we have match this text, with only the limited variants the sources themselves describe.

briefs.evs:
The first collection. After the Battle of Yamama, Abu Bakr asked Zayd ibn Thabit, a scribe of the Prophet ﷺ who had memorised the Quran, to collect the text, which he did from writings and from memories (Bukhari 4986-4987). The sheets passed to Umar and then to Hafsa.
The second step. Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman saw people differing in recitation on the campaign in Armenia and Azerbaijan and urged Uthman to act. Uthman asked Hafsa for the sheets and appointed Zayd, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa‘id ibn al-As and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith, telling them that where they differed they should write in the dialect of Quraysh, in which it was revealed (Bukhari 4987).
Distribution. Copies were sent to the Muslim regions (Bukhari 4987); later reports name centres such as Kufa, Basra and Damascus, with Medina keeping one, and accounts differ on the number of copies
Consent. Ali is reported to have said that Uthman acted on the Mushaf with the agreement of the Companions (Ibn Abi Dawud, al-Masahif).
The other readings survive. The reading of ‘Asim, which gives us the Hafs text most Muslims recite today, passes through readers who learned from Ali (Hafs, via al-Sulami) and Ibn Mas'ud (Shu'ba, via Zirr), so part of the Kufan tradition is in the canon, though Ibn Mas'ud's variants that depart from the Uthmanic outline are not.
Compare. The Church’s canon was shaped over centuries by councils and re

briefs.sec: “The Quran came from Syriac and Christian sources”
briefs.title: Luxenberg’s “Syro-Aramaic reading” and why specialists reject it
briefs.thesis: Christoph Luxenberg argued that many obscure Quranic words are Syriac words misread by later Muslims. Specialists in Arabic and Syriac have criticised the method, and the best-known examples fail on the text itself.
briefs.sum: Luxenberg’s Syro-Aramaic reading fails on the verses (one cannot marry raisins, 44:54), on the dots (attested from 643 CE), and on the methodological critiques of de Blois and Saleh.

obj.q: “Many Quranic words are admittedly obscure, so Luxenberg may be right.”
obj.a: Every ancient text has rare words, and the classical commentators discussed them from the start. A rare word is not a mistranscription. Rare words in Arabic poetry and the Quran are matched by cognates in other Semitic languages, and borrowing a word is not the same as borrowing a message.

obj.q: “The Quran contains many words that came from Syriac and other languages.”
obj.a: Some words are loanwords, as in every language, and Muslim scholars discussed this openly: al-Suyuti’s al-Itqan collects reports on words of non-Arabic origin. Arabic had long been in contact with Aramaic and Syriac through trade, so a shared word is expected. A loanword is not a mistranscription, and borrowing a word does not show that a message was borrowed.

prac.q: “The Quran is a mistranslated Syriac lectionary. Even paradise’s virgins are really white grapes.”
prac.a: Read 44:54: “We shall marry them to hur ‘in.” You cannot marry grapes. Luxenberg’s method picks a Syriac word whenever an Arabic one is rare, and specialists like François de Blois and Walid Saleh criticise it. Arabic with dots appears in papyri from 643 CE, so the premise of misreading undotted letters fails, and the Quran calls itself clear Arabic (16:103). The reading is not accepted in the field.

briefs.evs:
The book. Die syro-aramäische Lesart des Koran (2000; English 2007), written under a pseudonym. Its famous proposals are that qur’an means a Syriac “lectionary” and that the hur ‘in promised in paradise are “white grapes” or raisins.
Test it on the verse. “And We shall marry them to hur ‘in” (44:54; 52:20). One does not marry raisins. The same figures are “restrained of glance” (55:56) and “confined in tents” (55:72).
The dots. Luxenberg’s method assumes that early Arabic script lacked dots and was misread. Arabic writing with dots is already attested in papyri from the 640s (for example PERF 558, dated 22 AH/643 CE), and some early Quran manuscripts carry dots and strokes in places.
The critics. François de Blois reviewed the book in the Journal of Qur’anic Studies (2003) and found its methods unreliable, and Walid Saleh’s “The Etymological Fallacy and Quranic Studies” (2010) argues that tracing a word to a Syriac root does not show that the Quran uses it with the Syriac meaning.
The Quran’s own claim. “This is a clear Arabic tongue” (16:103, 26:195). The Quran was recited aloud to Arabic speakers who understood it, which a text of misread Syriac could not have been.

briefs.sec: “The Quran came from Syriac and Christian sources”
briefs.title: The “teacher” claims: Bahira, Waraqa and the foreign tongue
briefs.thesis: The Quran records the accusation that a human taught Muhammad ﷺ and answers it. The proposed teachers (the monk Bahira, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a foreign craftsman) either met him briefly, died too early, or could not have supplied the content.
briefs.sum: The Quran records the “teacher” charge (16:103, 25:5) and answers it. Bahira met him once, Waraqa died as revelation began, and the named craftsman was a non-Arabic speaker.

obj.q: “Muhammad could have learned from many travellers over the years.”
obj.a: That is a theory without a witness. It must explain how an unlettered man in a trading town gathered, from unnamed people, the content of Genesis, the Gospels and their commentaries in a way that disagrees with the Bible on the Trinity, the crucifixion and the nature of Jesus, and why his opponents, who were looking for a source, could name only a foreign craftsman.

obj.q: “16:103 shows that the Quran admits someone was teaching him.”
obj.a: It reports an accusation and refutes it. The refutation is that the supposed teacher’s tongue is foreign, while the Quran is in clear Arabic, which is an argument its Meccan audience could test.

prac.q: “Muhammad learned the stories from the monk Bahira and from Waraqa.”
prac.a: Bahira is a single meeting when Muhammad ﷺ was about twelve, with no teaching described, and the revelation came decades later. Waraqa died soon after the first revelation (Bukhari 3), and the Quran went on for twenty-three years. The Quran itself records that the Meccans said a human taught him, named a foreign craftsman, and was answered in 16:103: his tongue is foreign, the Quran is clear Arabic.

briefs.evs:
The charge in the Quran. “We know that they say: ‘It is only a human being who teaches him.’ The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, and this is a clear Arabic tongue” (16:103). Also: “They say: ‘Legends of the ancients, which he has had written down, and which are dictated to him morning and evening’” (25:5).
The Meccan candidate. The commentators (al-Tabari) report that the accusers pointed to a Christian non-Arab craftsman in Mecca, named variously as Bal‘am, Jabr or Yasar. The verse answers that a man who barely speaks Arabic cannot teach a text in eloquent Arabic.
Bahira. The story of the monk Bahira meeting the boy Muhammad ﷺ on a trading journey with his uncle (Ibn Ishaq; Tirmidhi 3620) describes one short encounter when he was about twelve. Scholars debate its details, but even as told there was no teaching, and the revelation came some thirty years later.
Waraqa. Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Khadija’s cousin, was a Christian who knew scripture. After the first revelation he said that the Prophet ﷺ had received the same angel who came to Moses. He died soon after, and the revelation paused for a while (Bukhari 3, paraphrased). The Quran continued to be revealed for some twenty-three years after his death, covering law, politics and polemics he never discussed.
Later informants. Salman al-Farisi and Abdullah ibn Salam came to Islam in Medina after the Hijra, so they cannot

briefs.sec: “The Quran came from Syriac and Christian sources”
briefs.title: A student who contradicts his teachers on every central doctrine
briefs.thesis: If the Quran were a Syriac Christian text reworked, it should reproduce Christian doctrine. Instead it rejects the Trinity, the divinity of Jesus and the crucifixion, while agreeing with the Jewish-Christian understanding of Jesus as a prophet. That is a pattern of independence, not dependence.
briefs.sum: The Quran shares figures and stories with Syriac Christian literature and rejects its central doctrines (5:72-73, 4:157), which fits correction of a common source, not dependence.

obj.q: “It borrowed the stories but changed the theology to suit Muhammad.”
obj.a: That claim assumes the conclusion. If the stories are from a common earlier revelation, as the Quran says, then the corrections are the point. If they were borrowed and changed deliberately, the borrower had to know the doctrines well enough to reverse each one, in a town whose Christian contacts were mainly through travel and trade, with no Arabic Bible (see Part V on the absence of an Arabic Bible).

obj.q: “Scholars like Reynolds do say the Quran depends on Syriac sources.”
obj.a: Reynolds argues for a conversation with a shared biblical and Syriac subtext, and he is explicit that the Quran’s purposes are its own. Shared themes and a shared language of scripture do not show that the content is derived. Say you accept the intertextuality and dispute the inference.

prac.q: “The Quran is just recycled Syriac Christianity.”
prac.a: Recycled Syriac Christianity would teach the Trinity, the divinity of Christ and the cross. The Quran rejects each of them (5:72-73, 4:157), calls Jesus a servant and prophet (19:30), and even calls him ‘Isa, a name no Christian used. Scholars like Reynolds see a conversation with Jewish and Christian traditions, which is just what the Quran says it is (5:48). A student does not contradict his teachers on every central doctrine.

briefs.evs:
Contradicted doctrines. “Those who say that Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary, have disbelieved” (5:72). “Those who say that Allah is the third of three have disbelieved” (5:73). “They did not kill him and they did not crucify him” (4:157). “He is Allah, One” (112:1-4). Syriac Christians held the Trinity, the divinity of Christ and the cross as central.
Shared material. The Quran discusses Mary, the birth of Jesus, the Apostles and the miracles of Jesus (3:35-59; 19:16-36), with details that differ from the Gospels (Mary’s mother’s vow; the speaking infant).
The name of Jesus. Arab and Syriac Christians called him Yasu‘ or Yeshu‘. The Quran calls him ‘Isa (see Part V, The names Yahya and ‘Isa), a form that differs from the usual Arabic Christian Yasuʿ and whose origin is debated (an Aramaic Ishoʿ or a Jewish form).
Scholarly view. Gabriel Said Reynolds (The Qur’an and Its Biblical Subtext, 2010) and Sidney Griffith argue that the Quran engages in dialogue with Jewish and Christian traditions of its time. This is what the Quran claims, since it describes itself as confirming and correcting (5:48; 2:213; 27:76).
Jewish-Christian parallels. The Quran’s Jesus (a human prophet and messiah, born of a virgin, who says “I am the servant of God”, 19:30) agrees with the Jewish-Christian view that Jesus was a human prophet and messiah, though on the virgin birth the Quran agrees with the

briefs.sec: Revisionist claims about Mecca and the early history
briefs.title: The Petra qibla theory
briefs.thesis: Dan Gibson argues that the earliest mosques faced Petra and that Mecca was a later construction. Specialists reject the theory, because early qibla orientations were approximate, the Quran’s description of Mecca does not fit Petra, and the argument has no textual support.
briefs.sum: The Petra theory conflicts with the Quran’s description of Mecca (14:37), ignores that early qibla finding was approximate (Tirmidhi 342), and is rejected by specialists.

obj.q: “The orientation of early mosques shows they did not face Mecca.”
obj.a: It shows that early builders did not have accurate methods. Early mosques are off by many degrees in many directions, and a spread of orientations is the expected result of estimating from local custom.

obj.q: “Hagarism argued something similar in the 1970s.”
obj.a: Patricia Crone and Michael Cook’s Hagarism (1977) proposed that the early Muslims’ sanctuary lay in north-west Arabia. Crone’s own later book on Meccan trade treated Mecca and its tribe Quraysh as historical, and the manuscripts and inscriptions found since then do not support the northern-sanctuary idea. It is a historical hypothesis that did not survive the evidence.

prac.q: “The first Muslims prayed towards Petra, and Mecca was invented later.”
prac.a: The Quran describes a valley without cultivation beside the sacred house (14:37), and Petra was famous for its water engineering. The Prophet ﷺ told Medinans that what lies between east and west is a qibla (Tirmidhi 342), and historians of science show that early orientations were approximate, so scatter is expected. Gibson is not a specialist and historians of early Islam, including non-Muslim ones, do not accept the theory.

briefs.evs:
The claim. Dan Gibson (Qur’anic Geography, 2011; Early Islamic Qiblas, 2017) argues that the first Muslims prayed towards Petra, that a Nabataean sanctuary there was the original sacred site, and that Mecca replaced it later. He is a Canadian researcher and filmmaker, not a specialist in Arabic or early Islamic history.
The Quran’s geography. “Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in a valley without cultivation near Your sacred House” (14:37). Petra, by contrast, had one of the most sophisticated water systems of the ancient world. The Quran names Bakka (3:96), mentions Mecca (48:24), Safa and Marwa (2:158) and the Hajj sites (2:196-203).
Qibla was approximate. The Prophet ﷺ said: “What is between the east and the west is a qibla” (Tirmidhi 342; Ibn Majah 1011), which scholars apply to those living north of Mecca, such as Medina. The history of science on this topic (David King, World-Maps for Finding the Direction and Distance to Mecca) shows that Muslims used rough methods, such as winds and the rising of stars, and that orientations varied between regions for centuries.
Petra’s history. The Nabataean city declined after the earthquake of 363 CE and by the seventh century was greatly reduced. A pilgrimage centre there would have left evidence in the Byzantine and Muslim records, and none exists.
The sources. The conquest accounts, the Hudaybiyyah treaty and the ear

briefs.sec: Revisionist claims about Mecca and the early history
briefs.title: From the Meccan trade debate to “Mecca did not exist”
briefs.thesis: The serious scholarly debate was whether Mecca was a major long-distance trading hub, not whether it existed. The popular claim that Mecca did not exist turns a narrow academic argument into a different one that few specialists make (it is argued by popular writers and revisionists such as Gibson).
briefs.sum: Crone argued Mecca was not a major spice-trade hub, not that it did not exist; the Quran’s picture of a modest sanctuary town (6:92, 14:37, 106) fits even her reconstruction.

obj.q: “Crone proved the Meccan trade story was a myth.”
obj.a: She argued that the stories of vast spice trade were overstated, and her work forced a better-grounded picture. That does not make the Quran’s account of a trading and pilgrimage town false, and her thesis was challenged by Serjeant and others on the evidence of the Quran and the early sources.

obj.q: “No Greek or Syriac source names Mecca before Islam.”
obj.a: Absence from the surviving sources of a small Arabian town is expected, as Arabia was outside the empires’ records, and Part I gives the candidate references. It is an argument from silence about a region that has hardly been excavated.

prac.q: “Scholars have shown Mecca was a nothing town on no trade route, so the Islamic story is invented.”
prac.a: What Crone argued in 1987 is that Mecca was not a major spice-trade hub. She did not argue it did not exist, and Serjeant and others replied with the Quran’s own evidence of local trade and the pilgrimage season (106:1-2, 2:198). The Quran calls Mecca ‘the mother of towns’ and a barren valley (14:37), which is a modest place. A modest town can be a sanctuary and a birthplace of a prophet, so that debate does not touch the Islamic account.

briefs.evs:
The thesis. Patricia Crone’s Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987) argued that Mecca was not a major node in the spice trade and that earlier historians had overstated it. Her target was the theory that Islam arose from a trade crisis, not the existence of Mecca.
The responses. R.B. Serjeant (Journal of the American Oriental Society, 1990, “Meccan trade and the rise of Islam: misconceptions and flawed polemics”) and others argued that Mecca’s trade in local goods and its role in the pilgrimage season is well supported by the Quran and early sources.
The Quran. It refers to the trading journeys of Quraysh in winter and summer (106:1-2) and to trade during the Hajj season (2:198). It also calls Mecca “the mother of towns” (6:92; 42:7), a local centre, and describes its valley as barren (14:37).
Evidence of antiquity. Diodorus Siculus’s account of a revered Arabian temple and Ptolemy’s “Macoraba” (identifications with Mecca are disputed and Crone rejected them) are discussed in Part I. Treat these as suggestive, since Arabia is the least excavated region of the Near East.
The inference. “Not a global trade hub” does not entail “did not exist”. Even on Crone’s own picture the town had a sanctuary and a tribe.

briefs.sec: Revisionist claims about Mecca and the early history
briefs.title: The Quran in stone: the Dome of the Rock inscriptions (691 CE)
briefs.thesis: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 72 AH/691-2 CE, carries long inscriptions that quote Quranic verses closely. This is monumental evidence of the Quran’s text within about sixty years of the Prophet’s death, and it also contradicts the idea that the Quran was composed in the eighth or ninth century.
briefs.sum: The Dome of the Rock (72 AH/691-2) quotes the Quran closely on its walls, so the text was authoritative within about sixty years of the Prophet’s death, long before any “late composition” could have happened.

obj.q: “The inscription differs from the standard text in places.”
obj.a: Some scholars note small differences in wording or selection, which is expected when verses are chosen and combined for a building and when the text was still in an oral and early written phase. The point stands: the passages, themes and wording are those of our Quran, and a building of 691 relies on them as already authoritative.

obj.q: “Abd al-Malik’s Dome is political propaganda.”
obj.a: It may well be, since it asserts Islam in a city full of Christian monuments. But propaganda quotes an existing text, and it needs its audience to recognise the verses as authoritative. That is the evidence that the Quran existed and was known.

prac.q: “The Quran was put together in the 8th or 9th century.”
prac.a: The Dome of the Rock was completed in 72 AH/691-2 CE, and its inscriptions quote Surat al-Ikhlas, 4:171, 19:33-36 and 3:18-19 closely and name Muhammad ﷺ as God’s messenger. So by 691 the text was known and authoritative enough to be inscribed in the most prominent monument of the empire. The Birmingham, Tübingen and Sana’a manuscripts also date within the first century. A text composed in the 700s cannot appear in a building of 691.

briefs.evs:
The Dome of the Rock was built by the Umayyad caliph ‘Abd al-Malik; the foundation inscription gives the date 72 AH (691-2 CE) but now carries the name of the Abbasid al-Ma'mun, who substituted it It is one of the oldest surviving Islamic monuments and carries a long inscription.
The text. The mosaic inscriptions around the inner arcade quote Surat al-Ikhlas (112), 4:171-172, 19:33-36, 3:18-19 and other verses, together with the formula that Muhammad is the messenger of God. The quotations broadly follow the text we have, with some small variants and additions, and scholars such as Oleg Grabar (The Shape of the Holy, 1996) have studied them.
The message. The inscription’s central statements are the Quran’s: that God is One, that Jesus is the messenger of God and not His son (4:171), and that “the religion with God is Islam” (3:19).
Other early evidence. Coins and the Hisma inscription also name the Prophet ﷺ (see Part I), and the Birmingham, Tübingen and Sana’a manuscripts date from the same period (see Section A).
The inference. If the Quran had been composed gradually in the eighth and ninth centuries, as the late-composition theory (Wansbrough) proposed, a monument of 691 could not quote it.

briefs.title: “Grammatical errors” (20:63, 4:162, 5:69) and the reports of scribal mistakes
briefs.thesis: The verses cited as grammatical errors have established explanations from the earliest grammarians and readers, and the reports that Aisha or Uthman acknowledged scribal mistakes are weak or were read by the scholars as describing dialect and permitted variation.
briefs.sum: The cited “errors” have established explanations in dialect, rhetorical constructions and alternative readings, and the reports of scribal mistakes are weak or describe permitted variation.

obj.q: “Even the reports admit the scribes made mistakes.”
obj.a: The Uthman report is weak by chain, and the Aisha report is answered on grounds of meaning; the most natural reading of lahn in early usage is dialect or style. They are also at odds with the claim attributed to the same figures that the text was recited by many Companions, who would have corrected an error. Nothing in the manuscripts shows these words differently.

obj.q: “If the Quran is perfect Arabic, why do its words break the rules?”
obj.a: It does not break rules, it breaks the later simplified rule the critic is applying. Arabic had dialects and rhetorical constructions, and the grammarians who built the rules treated the Quran as a primary authority on correct usage.

prac.q: “The Quran says ‘inna hadhani lasahirani’, which is bad grammar. Even Aisha said the scribes made a mistake.”
prac.a: Hafs reads it as ‘in hadhani’ with a light ‘in’, which is regular, and Abu ‘Amr reads ‘inna hadhayni’; the majority reading follows the dialect of Kinana. Sibawayh, who wrote the first grammar of Arabic, explained the other cases in 4:162 and 5:69 as well-known constructions. The report about Aisha has a disputed chain, and al-Suyuti and Ibn Hajar read ‘lahn’ as dialect, not error. Grammar was written after the Quran and took the Quran as evidence.

briefs.evs:
20:63. “Inna hadhani lasahirani” has the dual noun in the nominative where standard grammar would expect the accusative. Hafs and Ibn Kathir read it as in hadhani with a light in (“these two are sorcerers”), which is regular. Abu ‘Amr reads inna hadhayni, also regular. For the majority reading, the grammarians cite the dialect of Kinana and the Harith ibn Ka‘b tribe, which keeps the dual in -ani in all cases.
4:162. “wa al-muqimina al-salata” has the accusative where the nominative is expected. Sibawayh explained it as an accusative of praise, in which the speaker breaks the construction to emphasise a group (“I single out the establishers of prayer”). This construction is well attested in Arabic.
5:69. “wa al-sabi’un” in the nominative. Sibawayh and later grammarians explained this as a postponed subject (ta’khir) whose predicate is understood earlier in the sentence.
The order of discovery. The early grammarians (Abu al-Aswad al-Du’ali, then Sibawayh in the later eighth century) collected their rules from the Quran, poetry and the Bedouin, so where the Quran departed from a later rule, the rule was adjusted to the Quran and not the reverse.
The reports. Reports attributed to Aisha (naming 4:162, 5:69 and 20:63) and to Uthman (generic) say the scribes made a lahn; Ibn Abbas is reported for other verses (13:31, 24:27); all are collected in Ibn Abi Dawud’s al-Masahif. The Uthman

briefs.title: Abrogation (naskh) is not God changing His mind
briefs.thesis: The Quran says that God replaces some rulings with better or equal ones (2:106). Abrogation is a feature of progressive revelation, it covers a small and carefully studied set of cases, and it appears in the Bible too. It does not imply that God learned something new.
briefs.sum: Abrogation is graded revelation announced in 2:106, limited to a studied set of cases (twenty by al-Suyuti, five by Shah Waliullah), and mirrored in the Gospels and Hebrews. It is not a change of divine knowledge.

obj.q: “A perfect God would not need to revise.”
obj.a: Revising a rule does not mean the lawgiver did not know. Any wise teacher who gives a student a graded course knows from the start that the early steps will be replaced. 2:106 itself says God knows and has power over all things. The Gospels make the same move when they replace Mosaic rulings, and the objection would apply to them as well.

obj.q: “Naskh was invented by jurists to cover contradictions.”
obj.a: The principle is announced in the Quran (2:106; 16:101) and the cases of wine, the qibla and the waiting period are clear in the text and the early sources. The jurists’ own long disputes over how many cases exist show a discipline that was restricted, not invented to hide contradictions.

prac.q: “Allah changes His mind in the Quran, so He cannot be all-knowing.”
prac.a: A change in ruling is not a change in knowledge. The Quran announces the principle (2:106) and the clear cases are gradual: wine in three stages, the qibla, the widow’s waiting period. Scholars disagree on how many verses are abrogated, from about twenty to five, so it is a limited, studied discipline. The Gospels do the same: ‘You have heard it said… but I say to you’ (Matthew 5), all foods clean (Mark 7:19), the first covenant made obsolete (Hebrews 8:13). If that shows ignorance in God, it would show it in the Bible too.

briefs.evs:
The text. “We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except that We bring one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?” (2:106). Also 16:101 and 13:39.
Clear examples. Wine was restricted in stages (2:219; 4:43; 5:90-91). The qibla changed from Jerusalem to the Ka‘ba (2:142-150). The widow’s waiting period of a year (2:240) was replaced by four months and ten days (2:234). The requirement to give charity before consulting the Prophet ﷺ (58:12) was lifted in the next verse (58:13).
The scope. The scholars differ on how many verses are abrogated. Al-Suyuti accepted about twenty, and Shah Waliullah al-Dihlawi reduced the number to five. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani went further and denied abrogation of Quranic verses by other verses. The disagreement shows that this is a controlled technical discipline, not an open licence.
It is also biblical. Jesus says “You have heard it said… but I say to you” on retaliation and oaths (Matthew 5:33-34, 38-39), Mark 7:19 declares all foods clean, Acts 10 ends the food laws, and Hebrews 8:13 says that by calling a covenant new, God “has made the first one obsolete”.
The analogy. A physician who changes the prescription as the patient improves does not show he was wrong at first, since the treatment suited the stage.
